1181.title: How it's built

1182.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [Desk Clock] ──> [Cues Clock]
[Desk Section] ──> [Cues Follow] (Cues follows Desk's sections)
[Desk Lane 6] ──> [Mixer Body Level 2] (the pad, both sides) ──> [Mixer Body Level 3]
[Cues Lane 3] ──> [Mixer Sky Level 4] (the riser's level)
[Cues Gate 3] ──> [Riser ADSR Gate] (and its envelope) All three Arrangers count the Clock's sixteenths, sixteen to a bar, through the same 22 sections: First Sound, Echo, Sparkles, Arp, Pulse, Bass, Bells, Riser, Groove, Fill, Lift, Fill, Memory, Answer, Build, Everything, Fill, Second Wave, Lead Returns, Fill, Return, One Sine and Broaden. They change section on the same clock edge as the sequencers step on, so the score and the music can't drift apart, even when the Clock slows . Loop to is 1, so the song goes round again. Desk , the Arranger on the left, has a lane for each fader: the sine, arpeggio, bells, sparkles, bass, pad, wind and lead. On the Echoes, Body and Sky mixers each channel's Level knob is at zero, and its Level input adds the lane on top. The faders swell and fade more than they jump. The wind breathes in over the first twelve bars on a Log curve. Echo brings the pad in at 28% and ramps it in a line to 42% over twelve bars, through Sparkles and Arp, which hold. The sparkles rise over eight bars and thin away over the next twelve as the band arrives. The arpeggio swells in under the sine, then lifts into the Pulse as the sine rests. The bass and the bells come in on swells of their own. Where the music turns on a downbeat (a crash, the breakdown, the drop) the faders still jump: everything that leaves at Memory, or comes back at Everything, goes or comes at once. One Sine and Broaden, the last twelve bars, are the score's longest fade. The fades are cued in One Sine, and the ones longer than its eight bars carry on through Broaden, which holds them. Each part falls on its own curve over its own length, so they leave one after another in the reverse of the order they came: bells, bass, arpeggio, sparkles, pad and wind. Meanwhile the sine climbs a little, to stand alone at the end, as it began. The pad and wind, the bed under everything, fade last, on the gentler S-curve. The mixer adds a control voltage without smoothing it, so each lane has a Glide for its jumps: a second for the pad, wind and sparkles, 0.8 s for the sine, 0.3 s for the lead, and 40 ms for the arp, bass and bells, which still land on the downbeat but never cut a tail short. Cues , on the right, has the rest. It follows Desk: Desk's Section is patched into its Follow , so its sections are always Desk's, and an edit to them on Desk is made on Cues too. Drums picks the drum pattern (see Drums and fills ). Crash hits on the downbeat of each big section, and its level is the cymbal's accent. Riser jumps to 30% for the Riser section and 32% for the Build. Its CV is the riser's level, and its gate holds the riser's envelope open for exactly those four bars. Heat ramps up through the opening, 8% to 48% over seven sections, and keeps climbing through the groove. The Build drops it to 50% and sweeps it up an Exp curve to its peak, 86%, on the drop. The ending darkens it back down to 10% as the parts fade. Through two Attenuverters it opens the pad's Ladder and drives the bass harder. Memory is the Looper's level. It swells in over the breakdown's first four bars and recedes under the Build's riser. Rec and Clear hit the Looper's pedals. Line picks the melody's pattern (see The motif and the line ). Tape , on the far right, follows Desk too. It has one lane, Wow , which bends the master tape through the breakdown (see A warped memory ).
1182.title: The score

1183.body:
[Clock Divider ÷16 Trig] ──> [Chord Sequencer Clock]
[Chord Sequencer Root] ──> [Pad Root Oscillator V/Oct] ──> [Arp Oscillator Exp FM] ──> [Bass Oscillator Exp FM]
[Chord Sequencer Pitch] ──> [Pad Chord Oscillator V/Oct] (three voices)
[Pad Root Oscillator Out] ──> [Mix In 1]
[Pad Chord Oscillator Out] ──> [Mix In 2] (Sum Voices on) Sixteen bars of chords: Dm(add9), Bbmaj7, Fmaj7 and Cadd9 twice, then Gm7, Bbadd9, Dm, C, Gm7, Bbmaj7, Csus4 and C. A Chord Sequencer takes a step a bar, so changing a chord is one edit. The Chord Sequencer in the Harmony frame, playing Everything The harmony in Everything, on Gm7: the strip shows the pad's three voices, F, Bb and D. The steps name the chords, and the notches on the first Dm(add9) and the second Gm7 mark the two steps that name their top note. Its Root output plays each chord's root on a saw of its own, an octave down. Rootless is on, so the three voices on its Pitch cable leave the root to that saw and play the 3rds, 7ths and 9ths above it. Voice Leading gives each chord the inversion nearest the one before, so the voices move by step instead of jumping in parallel. Two steps also set a Top , the chord tone they want on top. The opening Dm(add9) keeps its 9th, E, at the top of the pad, so every pass round starts from the same voicing. The second Gm7 puts D on top, so the line climbs back up after the C, where voice leading alone would sink to Bb. The voices all come out of one Oscillator, three saws on one cable. A Ladder Filter on that cable would filter each voice on its own, and drive each one less hard than the whole chord. So the root saw and the chord meet in a Mix with Sum Voices on, which adds the three voices into one channel. Then one Ladder Filter drives the chord as a whole, the Compressor ducks it under the kick, and the Chorus spreads it into stereo. The arpeggio and the bass are written over C, and the Root moves them to each chord through Exp FM at 1 octave per volt, as in Afterglow . That only stays in key if the shapes have no third, so the arpeggio is made of roots, ninths and fifths, and the bass of roots, fifths and octaves. Over these roots, every note they play is in D minor.
1183.breadcrumbs: From One Sine » Harmony, a chord a bar
1183.title: Harmony, a chord a bar

1184.body:
[Clock Divider ÷4 Trig] ──> [Motif Clock]
[Cues Lane 8] ──> [Motif Pattern] (the Line: a pattern a pass)
[Motif Pitch] ──> [Sine V/Oct], [Supersaw V/Oct]
[Sine VCA Out] ──> [Mixer Echoes Ch 1] ──> [Looper In L]
[Cues Gate 6] ──> [Looper Rec]
[Clock Divider ÷16 Trig] ──> [Looper Clock]
[Looper Loop L/R] ──> [Mixer Sky Ch 2/3] The motif is four bars of quarter notes, A, D E | F, D | C, A C | G, with ties for the long notes. It leans on notes that both halves of the progression share. A over Dm is the fifth and over Gm the ninth. C over F is the fifth and over Dm the seventh. So it fits whichever chords it lands on. It's pattern A of the motif's Step Sequencer , and three more patterns make it a sixteen-bar line, one for each four bars of the progression. The second half of the progression gets patterns of its own, written to its chords, so the line follows the harmony instead of sitting over it: Pattern Over Notes Its part in the line A Dm(add9), Bbmaj7, Fmaj7, Cadd9 A, D E / F, D / C, A C / G The motif. It ends open, on the fifth of C B the same A, F E / D, F / E, C A / C The answer. It starts on the motif's note, leaps where the motif stepped, and comes to rest on C C Gm7, Bbadd9, Dm, C D, G A / F, D / F, D F / E The motif a fourth higher, and the top of the line D Gm7, Bbmaj7, Csus4, C G, F E / D, Bb / C, A C / G Down the scale, and home on the motif's own last two bars, which lead back to A The motif's Step Sequencer at the Lift, playing pattern C The motif's sequencer at the Lift, two bars into pattern C. C wears the green dot and D, ringed, comes next. The Chain is dimmed, because the orange cable into Pattern picks the patterns instead. The Line lane on Cues picks which pattern plays. The sequencer reads its Pattern input once a pass, on the clock that starts it, and each quarter of the range is a pattern, so 12.5% is the middle of A and 87.5% the middle of D. Where the song wants the motif alone, the lane jumps to A and stays there. Where it wants the whole line, the lane ramps in a straight line, Linear , from A to D over twelve bars. On the first beat of each pass it stands in the middle of the next pattern's quarter, so the four passes play A, B, C and D, and then it holds D. On the Cues timeline you can see where the line grows: a flat lane, then a slope. First Sound: the sine plays the motif alone, four times. That's what the Looper keeps. Lift: the lead plays the whole line for the first time. Answer and Build: over its reversed ghost, the sine plays the motif forward. The Build plays D, and D's descent leads into the drop. Everything: the whole line on the lead. Second Wave: the sine sings the line, and the lead returns for C and D. Return and One Sine: back to the motif alone, so the song ends as it began. The Looper listens to the sine. At bar 5, the Echo section hits Rec . With bar pulses on its Clock and Bars at 4, the take starts on the downbeat and closes itself after four bars. The Looper is set to ½× and Rev from the start. Neither changes what it records, only how it plays it back, so the loop plays reversed, an octave down, at half speed: eight bars, landing on the progression's own eight-bar grid. Its level stays at zero until the breakdown. First Sound hits Clear at bar 1, so each time the song comes round the Looper records the opening afresh.
1184.breadcrumbs: From One Sine » The motif and the line
1184.title: The motif and the line

1185.body:
[Cues Lane 1] ──> [Drum Trigger Sequencer Pattern]
[Cues Gate 2] ──> [Cymbal Trig]
[Cues Lane 2] ──> [Cymbal Accent] The drum sequencer's Pattern input picks a pattern for each new bar in quarters: 0 to 0.25 is A, then B, C and D. A is silence, B is a pulse of kick, rim and offbeat hats, C is the groove, and D is a build: four-on-the-floor kicks, toms, and a snare roll whose ratchets climb to four hits a step. The Drums lane jumps to 0.10 for A, 0.35 for B, 0.52 for C and 0.85 for D. Each phrase of the groove ends on a one-bar Fill section, which jumps it to D for that bar, and the section after jumps it back. The sequencer reads its Pattern on the same sample the lane jumps, so the lane has no Glide. The closed hat's gate chokes the open hat. The kick is tuned to A1, the fifth of D, and the tom to A2, so the drums sit in the key.
1185.breadcrumbs: From One Sine » Drums and fills
1185.title: Drums and fills

1186.body:
[Mixer Kit 2 Chain Out] ──> [Mixer Kit Chain In]
[Mixer Kit Chain Out] ──> [Mixer Body Chain In]
[Mixer Body Chain Out] ──> [Mixer Sky Chain In]
[Mixer Sky Out L/R] ──> [Tape In L/R] ──> [Audio Output Left/Right]
[Mixer Sky Send L/R] ──> [Plate Reverb In L/R] ──> [Mixer Sky Return L/R]
[Mixer Echoes Send L/R] ──> [Stereo Delay] ──> [Mixer Echoes Return L/R]
[Mixer Echoes Out L/R] ──> [Hall Reverb] ──> [Mixer Body Return L/R] The sine, arpeggio, bells and sparkles share the Echoes mixer, whose send feeds a ping-pong tape delay on dotted eighths. Its output passes through a big hall and comes back on Body's Return . Body carries the bass, the pad in stereo and the wind. Sky carries the lead, the Looper's two sides and the riser. The two kit mixers chain into Body, and Body into Sky. Each chain cable carries a mixer's mix and its sends together, so the sends of all four ride along to Sky, where one plate reverb serves them. Echoes keeps its send for the delay. Sky's mix goes onto tape on its way to the Audio Output.
1186.title: The desk

1187.body:
[Desk Section] ──> [Tape Arranger Follow]
[Tape Arranger Lane 1] ──> [Tape Wow] (the Wow lane)
[Mixer Sky Out L/R] ──> [Tape In L/R] ──> [Audio Output Left/Right] The whole mix goes onto a Tape last. For most of the song it's a well-kept machine at 15 ips. Wow and Flutter are at 10%, which sways the pitch by less than a cent. Saturation at 25% rounds the loud sections a little, and there's a touch of Age and Hiss . The record head squashes the loudest sections by up to a decibel. Sky's Master at −2.9 dB sets how hard the mix meets the head, with the Output's Volume at its usual 80%, and leaves the song at −16 LUFS, where every example sits. The tape earns its place in the breakdown. The Looper plays the opening back reversed, the rack remembering how it began, and memories don't hold their pitch. A third Arranger, Tape , follows Desk as Cues does. Its first lane is patched into the Tape's Wow , where it adds to the knob: Section Wow lane What you hear Memory Log ramp to 45% over 4 bars The warp arrives with the ghost, which swells in over the same four bars. The whole mix sways by about 12 cents Answer Hold The sine answers its ghost on the same wavering tape Build Exp ramp to 75% The sway deepens under the riser, to nearly 30 cents by the last bar: a held breath Everything Jump to 0 On the drop's downbeat the tape snaps back to speed Wow's swing grows with the square of the setting, so the knob's 10% alone is under half a cent, the knob and lane together at 55% are 12 cents, and at 85% they're 29. The drop lands harder for coming out of a lurch. The Tape glides the depth of its wobble over 300 ms, so the jump back to 0 is a snap and not a click. First Sound jumps the lane to 0 as well, so the song comes round on steady tape. The warp needs an Arranger of its own because Cues has no lane to spare. Its Rec and Clear lanes are only used for their gates, but a lane that rose through the breakdown would raise its gate too, and press the Looper's pedal.
1187.breadcrumbs: From One Sine » A warped memory
1187.title: A warped memory

1188.body:
A player slows into the end of a piece, and the score does too. Broaden, the last four bars, is a section only so that a ramp can start there. The Tape Arranger's second lane, Tempo , is patched through an Attenuverter at −0.23 into the Clock 's Tempo jack, which bends the BPM by octaves: [Tape Lane 2] ──> [Attenuverter In] (Amount −0.23)
[Attenuverter Out] ──> [Clock Tempo] Section Tempo lane What you hear First Sound Jump to 0 112 BPM, each time the song comes round Broaden Exp ramp to 100% The first bar barely gives. The next three stretch by 2%, 5% and 12%, and the song ends near 95 BPM, 15% slower than it ran Exp holds nearly steady and then gives way, which is how players slow: a ritardando that starts evenly sounds like a machine running down. The cable closes a loop, since the Clock drives the Arranger that bends it, and the Clock hears it a block late, a few milliseconds no tempo shows. Everything that keeps time by the Clock broadens with it. The sequencers' notes lengthen, and the delay's dotted eighths, synced to the patch tempo, stretch with them, so the sine's last echoes trail further apart. The delay is a tape echo, and its motor glides to each new time, so as they stretch the echoes sag a little flat, about 30 cents by the last bar: a tape machine winding down under the last notes. The bars still count, so the score keeps its sections in bars and the sequencers stay on them. Only the seconds change: the last four bars take 8.99 seconds where they took 8.57.
1188.title: Broadening

1189.body: Rearrange it. Drag a lane on the Desk up or down in any section to move that fader, or right-click it to ramp instead of jump. Delete a Fill section on the Desk for a phrase of groove without a fill: Cues follows, and its cues for the Fill go with it. A shorter song. Set the Desk's Loop to to 9, the Groove, and Cues follows. The opening plays once, and then the song goes round from the groove to the end. The line all through. Pull the Line cable out of the motif sequencer's Pattern . Its Chain is A B C D, so the sine plays the whole line from the very first bar, and the breakdown remembers the answer, B, instead of the motif. Other chords. Right-click a step of the Chord Sequencer and pick another type: one edit, and the pad, the arpeggio and the bass all follow. Keep the roots, which the arpeggio and bass are tuned to. Dm9 on the first step adds a C to the opening, and Bbmaj9 on the second puts a C over the Bb. Each voice through its own filter. Switch off the pad Mix's Sum Voices . The Ladder then filters each voice on its own, and the pad comes out cleaner and about a decibel louder. The root saw now joins all three voices, so turn the Mix's Level 1 down to a third (18%) to keep the bass where it was. Remember something else. Patch the Arp's VCA into the Looper's In L instead of the sine. The breakdown then hears the arpeggio, slowed and backwards. Brighter all through. Raise the Offset on the pad's brightness Attenuverter: each 0.1 opens the Ladder a tenth of an octave further, all song long. More or less warp. The Build's cue on the Tape Arranger sets how far the tape bends before the drop. At 90% it lurches by 40 cents; at 40% it only wavers. Pull the cable out of the Tape's Wow and the breakdown plays on steady tape. Straighter. Set the Clock's Swing to 50%. Arp, bass and drums all straighten together, because they share its sixteenths.
1189.title: Variations

119.body: The Note In module is where polyphony starts when you play. Its Voices knob (1 to 8) sets how many channels its Pitch , Gate and Velocity cables carry, and each note you play is given a channel of its own. It plays from your computer keyboard as well as from MIDI. In a patch that plays itself, the Chord Sequencer starts it instead. It sends a progression's chords down the same Pitch , Gate and Velocity cables, one channel per note, so a voice built for Note In plays it unchanged.
119.title: Where voices come from

1190.body: Arranger : sections, lanes, and the cues that move them Tape : the master tape, and its Wow input Afterglow : transposing an arpeggio with a second sequencer Roll Call : one Trigger Sequencer, eight drums Live Looper : the Looper with your own instrument Interlock : Logic deciding whose turn it is Tempo and Sync : one Clock for the whole patch
1190.title: Related

1191.body: A song in the manner of the French duo Air: four minutes of A minor at 88 BPM, with a Rhodes, a string machine, a round bass, soft drums, tape echo, and a vocoder that sings on the chords. It opens on a satellite beeping over tape hiss and ends the same way. In between, a robot voice sings Satellite… passing over you… , and near the end it asks can you hear me… The band falls away for one bar, and a plain human voice answers: still? The patch plays the whole song itself. Three Arrangers are the score, in 19 sections. Each part of the band is a group with jacks of its own, so the top level reads like a score: harmony, band, voice and desk. Open any group to see its insides. Load it: choose 📚 Examples → Clair de Satellite in the toolbar and press ▶ Play . It needs no keyboard. The patch file is patches/clair-de-satellite.json . Or play it here: press ▶ Play in the corner. The full app is a click away under Open in Soba . The score's three Arrangers run along the top, with the mixing desk at the right. Below them are the harmony (two Chord Sequencers, the Rhodes and the String Machine), the band (each part a group) and the voice.
1191.breadcrumbs: Clair de Satellite » Clair de Satellite
1191.title: Clair de Satellite

1192.body: Bars Section What happens 1–8 Signal A satellite beeps over tape hiss, each beep falling a little in pitch as it passes. The Rhodes fades in on the verse chords. 9–16 Drift The strings swell, the bass enters on whole notes and the drums on brushes, as the chorus chords lift into F major. The satellite fades. 17–24 Verse The groove, and the voice: Satellite · passing over you · Satellite · every night, every night . 25–32 Chorus A reedy whistle plays the hook while the strings open up. 33–48 Verse II, Chorus II Again, with FM bells, and the verse ends can you hear me? 49–56 Bridge The drums drop out. The voice alternates Clair de satellite and can you hear me? over held chords, and the satellite returns. 57–64 Build, Encore, Breath A riser climbs under I'm sending you signals · from so far away · Satellite . The robot asks can you hear me… . Then the band falls away, and the plain voice answers: still? 65–72 Solo A crash, and a Minimoog-style lead takes the verse melody. 73–80 Last Chorus Everything at once, the Rhodes comping harder. 81–88 Outro The first verse returns as the drums and bass thin out and the satellite comes back. 89–93 Last Light, Ring One last Am9. The sequencers stop, the chord rings out, and the tape sags as the signal dies. Left running, the song starts again on the satellite.
1192.title: The song

1193.body: Chords on one cable. Two Chord Sequencers play the same sixteen-bar progression: close and voice-led for the Rhodes, spread and tied for the strings. The slash basses (Am/G#, Am7/G, D9/F#) make the walking line on the Bass output. A rhythm from one module, chords from another. The Rhodes takes its notes from a Chord Sequencer and its rhythm from a Step Sequencer 's gate. A mono gate into a polyphonic voice strikes every note of the chord. A vocoder that can be understood. A vocoder reads words best from a carrier that is low, dense and held. Here that's the strings' spread chord, with its lows filtered off. The voice is brightened and compressed on its way in, and the vocoder's attack and release are kept short. A carrier up in a melody's register, an octave or two higher, loses most of the words. Many lines in one sample. The voice's eight lines are eight slices of one file. A Step Sequencer that steps every two bars picks a line by note: C4 sings the first, C#4 the second, and so on. Groups as instruments. Each part is a group with named jacks: Bass takes Clock , Reset , Pattern and Bass note , and gives Out . A few knobs are pinned to each group's face. Slides. The Solo's lead glides into chosen notes, the way a Minimoog player slurs a phrase. The song on tape. The whole mix runs through Tape , and an Arranger lane on its Wow input warps it in the Ring.
1193.breadcrumbs: Clair de Satellite » What it teaches
1193.title: What it teaches

1194.body: Module Role Clock BPM 88, Div 1/16, Swing 56% Arranger ×3 The score: 19 sections, 93 bars. Faders rides eight mixer channels, Cues picks patterns and strikes and warps, Voices brings in the vocoder and the plain voice Chord Sequencer ×2 The progression, a chord a bar, for the Rhodes and the strings Step Sequencer ×6 The Rhodes' comping and the bass riff (sixteenths), the lead and hook (eighths, four chained patterns), the bells (quarters) and the lyrics (a step every two bars) Trigger Sequencer The drums and the satellite's beeps: four patterns, picked by the Kit cue Clock Divider ×3 Eighths, quarters, and every two bars Electric Piano, String Machine, FM Bell From the Library . The String Machine has a second output for stereo, and the bell a Root jack so it follows the chords Oscillator ×12 Bass, lead, hook, satellite and the vocoder's carrier, plus the Library voices' own Drum ×8 Kick (A1), snare, rim, tom, closed and open hats, a shaker and the crash Compressor ×4 The kit's glue, the metals' level, the voice into the vocoder and the plain voice Sampler ×2 The sung lines, and still? Vocoder Bands 24, attack 2 ms, release 35 ms, Sibilance 60%, Unvoiced 50% Slope The satellite's Doppler fall 3-Band EQ The voice's lows cut and highs lifted, before the vocoder Mixer ×4 Top (with the tape echo), Drums, Band and Room (with the hall), on one chain. Room's Master −3.7 dB sets the level onto the tape Stereo Delay Sync 1/8D, P-P and Tape on Reverb The hall everyone shares Tape 15 ips, a little saturation, wow and age Audio Output Vol 80%, Limiter and Character on The rest are the voices' own envelopes, VCAs, filters, LFOs and Mixes.
1194.title: Modules

1195.breadcrumbs: Clair de Satellite » How it's built
1195.title: How it's built

1196.body: Three Arrangers count the Clock's sixteenths through the same nineteen sections, from Signal to Ring. Faders has a lane per mixer channel: EP, Strings, Bass, Drums, Lead, Hook, Bells and Space. Each channel's Level knob is at zero, so the lane is the fader. Cues picks the patterns for the drums, the Rhodes' comping and the bass (A to D in quarters of the lane), hits the crash, raises the riser, holds the chords in the Ring, and warps the tape. Voices rides the vocoder and, on the Breath alone, the plain voice. A one-bar Fill closes most phrases. The Build is split into Build, Encore and Breath, so the reveal lands on its own bar: the robot's last line plays in Encore, and Breath drops the drums, bass and hook and dips the Rhodes and strings, so the one plain word is heard clearly.
1196.title: The score

1197.body: The verse is a line cliché: Am9, Am/G#, Am7/G, D9/F#, then Fmaj9, Em7, Dm9 and E7. The chorus lifts to Fmaj7, G11, Em7, Am7, Dm9, G13, Cmaj9 and E7. The roots are written in octave 2, so the Bass output is a bass line and the bass voice only adds a riff over it: the note, its octave, and slides between them. The strings' Chord Sequencer ties every step, so the String Machine's swell never restarts and the chords change under one long breath. The Rhodes' is untied, and its gate comes from the comping sequencer.
1197.title: Harmony

1198.body:
[Lyrics Pitch] ──> [Sampler V/Oct] (8 slices: note 60 + k sings line k + 1)
[Lyrics Gate] ──> [Sampler Gate] (Gated: one line, then stop)
[Sampler L] ──> [EQ] ──> [Compressor] ──> [Vocoder Modulator]
[Strings' Chord Sequencer Pitch] ──> [Saw] ──> [Chorus] ──> [SVF high-pass] ──> [Vocoder Carrier]
[Voices Gate 2] ──> [Still Sampler Gate] (the Breath) The voice is the author's, cloned with ElevenLabs and saying each line once. The vocoder sings it on the strings' chord, voiced low and wide, where the harmonics sit close enough together to trace every vowel. The words and the chord move independently, as on Air's own vocoder songs.
1198.title: The voice

1199.body: Sing it yourself. Patch an Audio Input 's L into the Voice group's modulator path, in place of the Sampler, and sing over the chords. Wear headphones. A smaller throat. Raise the vocoder's Formant , pinned to the Voice group's face, by a quarter octave. All robot. The still? Sampler feeds the vocoder too. Mute the Room mixer's fourth strip, and give the Voices Arranger's Vocoder lane a Hold in Encore instead of its ramp to zero: the robot answers itself.
1199.title: Variations

12.body: Once a day, Soba asks GitHub whether a newer release is out. When one is, the dot after the version number in the bottom-right corner lights up blue, and a note says what's new. Click the version number to see the note again. What's New shows the release notes for every version since yours. Install downloads the new version, checks it against the release's published checksums (SHA256SUMS), puts it in place and restarts. Your patch, including changes you haven't saved, your audio and MIDI devices, and your view of the canvas come back as they were. If the patch has unsaved changes, Soba offers to save them first. Install waits while a recording is running. Later puts the note away; the dot stays lit. Skip this version stops offering that version; a newer one is still offered. Help → Check for Updates… checks now, and says so if you're up to date. What the check sends: one request to GitHub's public list of releases, saying it comes from soba and which version. Nothing about you or your computer, and no usage data. A check that doesn't work, when you're offline say, does nothing visible and tries again next time. To stop checking altogether, turn off Help → Check for Updates Automatically ; Soba then makes no requests at all. Rolling back: the version you updated from stays beside the new one, and Help → Roll Back to … swaps back to it and restarts. The version you left is skipped, so it isn't offered again straight away. Where Soba can't replace itself, Install becomes Download , which opens the release page: A copy built from source (cargo run), which only says that an update exists. A copy in a folder it can't write to, such as Program Files. macOS, until the app is signed: macOS doesn't let a downloaded app replace itself. Linux, when a package manager installed it. Each copy updates to the same kind of download it came from: the low-latency Windows build to the next low-latency build, the standard one to the standard one.
12.title: Updates

120.body: These modules run one voice per channel of their widest input: Module Each voice has its own Oscillator Phase, sync and unison stack Noise Random stream, so no two voices hiss alike Drum Hit, so fast notes ring over each other instead of cutting each other off SVF Filter Filter state and resonance Ladder Filter Filter state and resonance ADSR Envelope Stage and level Slope Level, so a chord glides voice by voice VCA Gain Attenuverter Scaling Mix Sum Sample & Hold Held value Quantizer Note, and its Trig, so a chord comes out as a chord in the scale Their outputs carry as many channels as their widest input. The knobs are shared: turning Cutoff moves every voice's cutoff.
120.title: Polyphonic modules

1200.body: A song in the manner of Bonobo: four and a quarter minutes of F minor at 116 BPM, on a swung sixteenth. Two little pentatonic loops, a kalimba and a set of bells, run at lengths that don't fit the bar, so the figure they make together is never quite the same twice. Under them come a strummed harp, a Rhodes, a string machine that breathes with the kick, a round sub bass and a broken beat with a real break chopped beneath it. Over them, pitched vocal chops carry the hook and a breathy flute the melody. It starts at dawn with birds and wind, and ends at night the same way. The patch plays the whole song itself. Three Arrangers are the score, in sixteen sections. Each part is a group with jacks of its own, so the top level reads as a score: harmony, loops, band, forest and desk. Open any group to see its insides. Load it: choose 📚 Examples → Canopy in the toolbar and press ▶ Play . It needs no keyboard. The patch file is patches/canopy.json , and its singer is patches/samples/canopy-chops.wav . Or play it here: press ▶ Play in the corner. The full app is a click away under Open in Soba . The score's three Arrangers and the mixing desk run along the top, with a Dancer at the end of the desk. Below them, left to right: the harmony (three Chord Sequencers and the Rhodes, Strings and Harp they play), the two loops, the band, and the forest.
1200.title: Canopy

1201.body: Bars Time Section What happens 1–8 0:00 Dawn Wind, and birds calling. The kalimba fades in on its twelve-step loop. 9–16 0:17 Canopy The bells join on their ten-step loop, the strings swell, a shaker starts, and two faint vocal chops answer from far off. 17–32 0:33 Groove A crash, and the beat: kick, rim and swung hats, the sub bass and the Rhodes. The room closes in round them. The vocal chops come in a bar at a time, with rests between, and fill in to the whole hook. A drum fill closes the phrase. 33–48 1:06 Groove II The snare comes in with its ghost notes, the hats go to sixteenths, the harp strums a chord each bar, and the chopped break slips in under the kit. 49–56 1:39 Clearing The drums fall away and the hall opens. Over held chords, whole-note bass and the strings, the flute plays its melody for the first time, and the birds come back. The tape sways. 57–64 1:56 Rise The beat builds back over seven bars, under a rising wash of noise, into a fill. 65–80 2:12 Peak Everything at once: the full kit and break, the busier bass and comping, the chops and the flute. 81–96 2:46 Peak II The flute goes up an octave and the break comes forward. The chops sing only the calls, and the high flute fills the bars between. 97–112 3:19 Dusk The kit thins back to the groove and fades, the bass fades out over sixteen bars, and the wind rises. The chops thin out as they fade. The room opens with the evening. 113–124 3:52 Night, Ring The kalimba, wind and birds, as at dawn. Then the sequencers stop and the last notes ring out into the whole hall. Left running, the song starts again at dawn.
1201.title: The song

1202.body: Loops that don't fit the bar. The kalimba's Step Sequencer has 12 steps of sixteenths, three beats against the bar's four. The bells' has 10 steps of eighths, five beats. Neither is reset by the bar, so they drift against it and against each other, and the three line up again only every fifteen bars. Bonobo builds tracks such as Cirrus from loops layered this way. One scale over every chord. Every loop note is from F minor pentatonic (F, A♭, B♭, C, E♭), and every chord in the song contains or colours those notes. So the loops can land anywhere against the harmony and never clash. Three voicings of one progression. Three Chord Sequencers play the same sixteen bars: close for the Rhodes, spread and tied for the strings, and open and strummed for the harp, 70 ms between strings, with Strum dir on Alt so it strokes up one bar and down the next. Pitched vocal chops from one file. Twelve sung syllables ( ah , oh , ya , hey , mah …) sit in twelve slots of one sample. Two Step Sequencers step together: one plays the note through the Sampler 's V/Oct , and the other picks the syllable through Start , where note 60 + k starts at k /12 of the file. Played a few semitones either side of the sung C5, the voice moves up and down the way a chopped vocal does. A break under a drum machine. The Chopper plays Soba's own two-bar break in time, 20 BPM faster than it was played, with dice on three of its sixteen steps. A high-pass at 380 Hz takes out its kick, so it adds air and ghost notes without fighting the kit. Strings that breathe with the kick. The string machine's two sides each run through a Pump from the Library , struck by the kick's gate, so the pad dips on each kick and swells back. Birds from a sine. Each chirp is a sine flicked up nearly an octave by a Slope , plus a random offset that a Sample & Hold takes from noise on every chirp, so no two calls match. The drum sequencer's eighth lane plays them, with ratchets for the trills.
1202.title: What it teaches

1203.body: Module Role Clock BPM 116, Div 1/16, Swing 56% Arranger ×3 The score: 16 sections, 124 bars. Faders rides eight mixer channels. Cues picks the drum, bass and comping patterns, hits the crash, raises the riser, lifts the flute, stops the sequencers in the Ring and warps the tape. Voices rides the chops, flute, wind and birds, and the room, and picks the chops' phrase Chord Sequencer ×3 The progression, a chord a bar, for the Rhodes, the strings and the harp Step Sequencer ×8 The kalimba (12 steps), bells (10 eighths), Rhodes comping, bass, flute (eighths, four chained patterns), the chops' notes and syllables (four one-bar patterns), and the chops' Phrase , a step a bar, which picks those patterns Logic AND of the chops' gate and the Phrase's, so a rest in the Phrase rests a bar of chops Trigger Sequencer The drums and the birds: four patterns, picked by the Kit cue Chopper samples/soba-break.wav, Beats 8, Slices 16, chance on steps 6, 11 and 15 Sampler samples/canopy-chops.wav, Mode Gated, Root C5 Electric Piano, String Machine, FM Bell, Mallet, Pump ×2, Wind From the Library . The Mallet is the harp Oscillator ×13 Kalimba, bass, flute and birds, plus the Library voices' own Drum ×8 Kick (F1), snare, rim, a high tom for a conga, closed and open hats, a shaker and the crash Compressor ×4 The kit's glue, the metals' level, the break and the harp Stereo Delay Sync 1/8D, P-P and Tape on: the echo on the loops, chops and flute Reverb The room everyone shares, ridden by the score Mixer ×4 Top (with the echo), Drums, Band and Room (with the reverb), on one chain. An LFO pans the bells slowly across, and the score rides the Room's Return Tape 15 ips, a little saturation, wow and age Audio Output Vol 75%, Limiter and Character on Dancer Style Disco, at Size 2.4. It hears the finished mix from the Tape, so it barely moves at dawn and goes all out at the Peak, and the Faders' Section Trig gives it a big move at every change of section The rest are the voices' own envelopes, VCAs, filters, LFOs and Mixes.
1203.title: Modules

1205.body: Three Arrangers count the Clock's sixteenths through the same sixteen sections, from Dawn to Ring. Every mixer channel's Level knob is at zero, so an Arranger lane is the fader. Faders rides the Kalimba, Bells, Harp, Rhodes, Strings, Bass, Drums and Break. Cues picks the patterns: A to D for the drums, two bass lines and three kinds of comping. Voices rides the vocal chops, the flute, the wind and the birds, and the room, and its Phrase lane picks which way the chops sing the hook. A one-bar Fill closes each long section, playing the drums' D pattern: a snare roll that ratchets up to fours, over a run of congas.
1205.title: The score

1206.body: The four Mixers are one chain, and every channel's send runs down it into the Room Mixer's reverb. So that Mixer's Return is the whole room's fader. Its knob is at 0, and the Voices Arranger's Room lane plays it, a cue a section, on two-bar S-curves: Section Room Dawn 80% rising over four bars, out of nothing the first time and down from the Ring's full hall on a loop Groove, Groove II 25%, 30% close and dry, so the beat is tight Clearing 100% the drums go and the hall opens for the flute Rise 30% closing again in a straight line, under the riser Peak, Peak II 35%, 50% dry for the drop, then a little air for the high flute Dusk 90% opening over the whole sixteen bars Ring 100% the last notes ring into all of it Listen at 1:39 : the beat stops, and the chords and the flute's first phrase bloom into a room that was barely there a bar before. Then at 2:12 the Peak lands close and dry again. On the canvas the Room Mixer's Return knob shows it, its orange arc opening and closing as the lane moves it.
1206.title: The room

1207.body: Fm9, D♭maj9, B♭m9 and E♭(add9), two bars each. On the second pass the last four bars become G♭maj7 and Cm7, to turn the progression round. The roots are written low, so the Rhodes' Chord Sequencer's Root output moves the bass from F down to B♭ and back. G♭maj7 under the pentatonic loops makes their C a raised eleventh: one bar of brightness in sixteen.
1207.title: Harmony

1208.body:
[Chops Pitch] ──> [Sampler V/Oct] (the note: C5 plays the syllable as sung)
[Syllables Pitch] ──> [Sampler Start] (note 60 + k starts at k/12: syllable k)
[Chops Gate] ──> [Logic A]
[Phrase Gate] ──> [Logic B]
[Logic AND] ──> [Sampler Gate] (Gated, so each chop is as long as its notes)
[Phrase Pitch] ──> [Chops Pattern], [Syllables Pattern] The singer is nobody's recording. Like Held Vowels ' singer, it comes from the small formant synthesizer in tools/voice/, this time chops.py , with the formants raised for a lighter voice. The hook is four bars: oh · ah · ya · ah · oh , then mah · hey · ah-oh , then the first bar again, rising to hey · lah , and an ooh to end. Every note is pentatonic, so it sits over all six chords. The chops go to the echo more than anything else, and their repeats fill the gaps between them.
1208.title: The voice

1209.body: The hook's four bars are the chop sequencers' patterns A to D. A third Step Sequencer in the group, the Phrase , steps once a bar on the Faders Arranger's Bar output and picks which of them plays. Its Pitch goes to both chop sequencers' Pattern input, where 0 to 1 is split into four zones, A to D, so a note picks a pattern: C♯4 (1/12 V) is A, E4 is B, G4 is C and A♯4 is D. A Phrase step with its gate off rests that bar: a Logic module lets the chops' gate through only while the Phrase's is high. Its steps are tied, so its gate holds across the barline and each bar's first chop lands on the beat. The Phrase has four patterns of its own, sixteen bars each, and the Voices Arranger's Phrase lane picks one a section through the Phrase's own Pattern input. The Phrase's sixteen bars line up with the sections, so each pattern covers a section (Canopy is the second half of the line Dawn starts): Phrase Bars Sections A, Far A B C D · A – – D · – – – B · – – – D Canopy, Dusk Canopy hears its last eight bars, two answers far apart. Dusk hears its first eight as the chops fade: the hook once, then thinning B, Gathering A – – B · A – C D · A B C D · A B C D Groove the hook comes in a bar at a time, and is whole by the ninth bar C, Hook A B C D four times Groove II, Peak the whole hook, as it always was D, Call A – C – · A – C – · A – C – · A B C D Peak II only the calls, the first and third bars, with the high flute in the bars between. The last four bars give the whole hook back before the fill Change the Phrase lane's cue in a section, or a Phrase pattern's steps, to rearrange the chops without touching the hook itself.
1209.title: The phrase

121.body: A polyphonic cable is drawn as a bundle of strands , one per channel, in a dark sheath that narrows where it plugs into a jack. The bundle widens as the channel count grows, so you can tell mono from poly at a glance at any zoom. Each strand lights with its own voice. Hold a chord and light runs along the strands of the notes you're playing while the rest stay dark. When you let go, each note's release fades down its own strand. The glow around the bundle grows with the number of voices playing, so a chord glows brighter than a single note. See Reading the signal in a cable . Output labels show the channel count too: Out ×8 means that output carries eight channels. The count comes from the running patch, so press Play to see it. Once shown, it stays while the transport is stopped.
121.title: Seeing polyphony

1210.body: Line them up. Open the Bells group and set its sequencer to 8 steps: a bar of eighths. The bells now repeat every bar, and they and the kalimba meet every three bars instead of fifteen. Put it back to 10 to hear the drift return. Your own chops. Open the Vocal Chops group and load any short vocal phrase into the Sampler. Set Root to the note it was sung on and leave Slices off, and the Syllables sequencer picks twelve places in it. One part in the room. Patch a free Voices lane into the Top Mixer's Send 4 , turn that knob to 0, and cue the lane up for the Clearing only. With a Glide of 1 s on the lane, the flute steps into the echo and the hall alone while the rest stays where it was. Swing harder. Turn the Clock's Swing to 62%. The kit, the loops and the chops all lean back with it. The break keeps its own swing, because it's sliced in eighths, which swing doesn't move.
1210.title: Variations

1211.body: A song with no score: five minutes of E minor at 112 BPM, from a gong at dawn to a gong at nightfall. Nothing tells the patch when to play what. There's no Arranger , only slow orbits. A Day rises for 200 seconds and sets in 100, and each voice waits for the Day to reach its height before it comes in, then leaves as the Day goes down. A Tide takes the rhythm away once and brings it back. Two clock gears, five bars and seven, meet every 35 bars, and each meeting is an eclipse. This is how a modular player builds a piece that plays itself: patterns that move against each other, and slow voltages that decide who is up. The top level is the orrery itself. The clockwork and the orbits are in plain view, and each voice is a group you can open. Load it: choose 📚 Examples → Orrery in the toolbar and press ▶ Play . It needs no keyboard. The patch file is patches/orrery.json . Or play it here: press ▶ Play in the corner. The full app is a click away under Open in Soba . The clockwork's dividers are at the top left, with the orbits beside them. Below them is "Who is up", one Logic module for each voice, waiting for its height. The voices and the mixing desk come last.
1211.title: Orrery

1212.body: There are no sections, only the Day. The names below describe where it is. Bars Time The Day What happens 1–4 0:00 Dawn An eclipse: a gong, and its ring. As it fades, the Moon begins to sway between two notes. 5–8 0:09 A low E and B drone, and the steady Twin, which sets the bar. 9–12 0:17 A heartbeat: a soft kick on beats 1 and 3. 13–16 0:26 The Sun: a string pad, one chord every four bars. It dips with each kick. 17–20 0:34 The drifting Twin, one eighth shorter, starts to slip against the steady one. 21–28 0:43 Morning The bass: a Berlin-school ostinato under the chords. 29–35 1:00 The full kit: four on the floor, offbeat hats and a shaker. 36 1:15 An eclipse: the gong and a crash. The Twins snap back into step. 49–68 1:43 Noon The Day passes halfway. The drums step up to their groove, with clap, ride and open hats, and a fill closes every eighth bar. The Moon now sings in wide arcs. 69–84 2:26 The Tide The Tide is at its lowest, so the bass and drums rest. An eclipse rings out in the space (2:30), and the Comet arrives over the drone (2:34): a gliding lead that only flies near noon. 85–105 3:00 Afternoon The rhythm comes back in, with the Comet over it. 106 3:45 An eclipse. Soon after (3:51), the Comet leaves. 117–128 4:09 Dusk The Day falls below halfway, and the drums step back down. 129–140 4:34 The kit goes, then the bass, then the pad and the drifting Twin. The heartbeat is the last pulse, and the Moon narrows back to its two-note sway. 141 5:00 Night The last eclipse, a gong, rings out. Left running, the Day rises again and a second day begins. The Tide is 80 bars round, not 140, so the second day's rest falls somewhere else.
1212.title: The song

1213.body: Form from a slow LFO and a few thresholds. The Day is a triangle LFO , unipolar, so it runs 0 to 1. Each voice has a Logic module whose Above is high while the Day is over its Threshold : 0.02 for the drone, 0.06 for the heartbeat, 0.2 for the bass, 0.74 for the Comet. That gate rides the voice's fader through a Slope , so each one fades in and out. The order voices come in is the order they leave. Read the orbits once a phrase. A Sample & Hold reads the Day every four bars, from a Clock Divider at ÷64. So every entrance lands on a phrase, not wherever the LFO crosses the line. Gears. Two dividers count bars, one at ÷5 and one at ÷7, and a Logic AND fires only where they meet: every 35 bars. Each meeting strikes a gong and resets both Twins. A smaller pair at ÷5 and ÷7 sixteenths ticks a woodblock where they meet. A melody from two drifting orbits. Moon A and Moon B are LFOs 7.1 and 4.95 dotted eighths long. Mixed, and sampled every dotted eighth, they never repeat the same way twice. A Quantizer snaps them to E minor pentatonic, and the bell is struck only on its Trig , when the note changes. The Day sets how wide they swing: two notes at dawn, more than an octave at noon. Phasing. The Twins play one two-bar figure of sixteen eighths on two Step Sequencers . One plays all sixteen steps and the other only fifteen, so it slips an eighth on every pass, the way Steve Reich's Piano Phase drifts. Panned apart, the two parts slide against each other and lock back together at each eclipse. Set the meter before the cross-rhythms. The Moon strikes in dotted eighths, three sixteenths apart, which on its own suggests a different bar. So the steady Twin and the heartbeat come in first, leaning on the beats. By the time the Moon and the drifting Twin have something to cross, you already know where the bar is.
1213.title: What it teaches

1214.body: There are 177 modules of 27 kinds. The ones that do the work: Module Role Clock BPM 112, Div 1/16 Clock Divider ×10 Eighths, dotted eighths, bars and phrases; the Comet's five-eighth clock; the last bar of every eight, for fills; and two pairs of gears (bars at ÷5 and ÷7, sixteenths at ÷5 and ÷7) LFO ×7 The orbits: the Day (triangle), the Sundial (saw) that sets the Day's dusk, the Tide (80 bars), the Breath (13 bars, which moves the bass), Moon A and B; and the Comet's vibrato Logic ×20 Who is up: one for each voice's height, two for the drums' steps, and the eclipses; two more let only the drums you hear through to Seoul Sample & Hold ×5 The orbits read once a phrase, and the Moon's and Comet's notes Quantizer ×4 The Moon's and Comet's scale, and two used as steady voltages to set the slowest LFO rates Chord Sequencer Em9, Cmaj9, G6, Dadd9, Em9, Am9, Cmaj7, Bsus4: a chord every four bars, for the pad and the bass's root Step Sequencer ×4 The Twins (16 and 15 steps), and the bass: notes in four patterns, chosen by the Breath, and accents Trigger Sequencer The drums: a heartbeat (A), a beat (B), the groove (C) and the fill (D), stepped up by the Day Drum ×9 Kick, clap, closed and open hats, shaker, tom and ride; the eclipse's crash; the tick's woodblock String Machine, FM Bell ×2, Pump ×2 From the Library : the Sun's pad, the Moon and the gong, and the kick's pump on the pad Ladder Filter ×3 The bass, the Comet and the drone Noise Pink surf that swells with the Tide Stereo Delay Sync 1/8D, P-P and Tape on: the echo, with a hall of its own Reverb ×2 The hall everyone shares, and the echo's Mixer ×4 Sky, Earth, Pulse and Air, on one chain Tape A little wow, saturation and age over the whole mix Audio Output Vol 60%, Limiter and Character on Link Out The orbits and the drums, sent to the Seoul visualizer The rest are the voices' own oscillators, envelopes, VCAs and filters, and the Attenuverters and Mixes that scale the orbits.
1214.title: Modules

1216.body: A day that rises for 200 seconds and falls in 100 isn't a plain triangle, so the Day's rate changes at dusk. Its Rate knob is at 0.01 Hz, and a steady −2 V on its rate input takes it two octaves down, to 0.0025 Hz: a 200-second climb. At dusk, a gate adds +1 V, and the Day falls twice as fast as it rose. That gate comes from the Sundial , a saw LFO once round the whole song, through a Logic at 2/3. The Day can't time its own dusk: a cable from its Phase back to its own rate would make a loop, and Soba leaves loops out. The −2 V comes from a Quantizer . A Mix rounds off anything past about ±1, so it can't sum to −2. The Quantizer's Transpose adds its semitones as volts (12 semitones is 1 V) to an Attenuverter's −1 V, and the dusk gate adds its +1 V through the Transpose input.
1216.breadcrumbs: Orrery » The Day, and its dusk
1216.title: The Day, and its dusk

1217.body:
[Day] ──> [S&H, every phrase] ──> [Logic CV] Threshold: the voice's height [Logic Above] ──> [Slope] ──> the voice's fader
[Tide] ─> [S&H] ─> [Logic] ──AND──┘ (for the bass, the heartbeat and the drums) The bass, heartbeat and drums need the Day and the Tide, so each of their Logics also takes the Tide's gate on B and passes AND . The bass and the kit swell with the Day too: they come in quieter in the morning and play out in full at noon.
1217.title: Who is up

1218.body: The Trigger Sequencer's Pattern input picks A, B, C or D from four quarters of its range. Three gates add up into it: past the kit's height, the drums step to B (+0.3); past halfway, to C (+0.25); and in the last bar of every eight, while the Day is past halfway, the fill (+0.3) takes them to D.
1218.title: The drums climb

1219.body: At the top right, a Link Out sends the orrery to Seoul , a music visualizer, so the picture follows the song's own orbits rather than guessing at them from the sound. It follows Seoul's lane convention, so any of Seoul's link-aware presets plays along: Lane From In Seoul CV 1 The Day Energy: the picture brightens toward noon and dims at dusk CV 2 The Breath Color, turning every 13 bars CV 3 The Tide Motion, which slows while the rhythm rests CV 4 , CV 5 Moon A and Moon B The melody's two orbits, for presets that read them (Obangsaek's white and black) Gate 1 The heartbeat and kick, while the heartbeat is up The kick Gate 2 The clap, while the kit is up The snare Gate 3 The closed hats, while the kit is up The hats Gate 4 Each eclipse A bloom, in Obangsaek The Drums group runs its sequencer the whole song and leaves the faders to decide when it's heard, so its gates fire in the silence too. That's why gates 1 to 3 come through Logic AND s with the same "who is up" gates the faders follow: Seoul sees only the drums you hear. The Drums group has Clap and Hats outputs for them, beside its Kick . Link Out makes no sound, so the mix is exactly as it was. Try Seoul's Han River (fountains on the kick, fireworks on the clap) or Hongsalmun (a stride on every kick), and watch the city go dark through the Tide.
1219.title: To Seoul

122.body: A mono cable into a polyphonic module is shared by every voice. One LFO into a polyphonic filter's Cutoff sweeps all the voices together. To move each voice on its own, use a polyphonic source such as the envelope or Note In's Velocity . A polyphonic cable into a mono module is folded down to one channel: Audio inputs hear every channel summed. That's why a polyphonic voice can go straight into an effect or the Audio Output. The Mixer is the exception. It hears each voice of a polyphonic cable apart, and its per-channel Width knobs fan them out across the stereo field, so a chord opens up instead of sitting in the middle. With Width at 0% it sums them like any mono module. Control and gate inputs take the first channel only, since adding CVs together rarely means anything useful. Voices add up, so a four-note chord is roughly four times as loud as one note. Leave headroom with the VCA's Level or the Mixer.
122.title: Mixing mono and poly

1220.body: Line up the Twins. Open Twins → Fifteen and set its sequencer's Steps to 16. The two parts now play the figure in unison, and the drift is gone. Set it back to 15 to hear them slide apart again. A different noon. In "Who is up", the Logic at Threshold 0.74 is the Comet's. Raise it to 0.9 and the Comet flies only for the top of the Day, or lower it to 0.5 for a longer afternoon. More eclipses. In "The clockwork", find the two gears clocked by the bar divider, at ÷5 and ÷7, and set the ÷7 one to ÷3. The gears now meet every 15 bars, and the gong and the Twins' reset come round more than twice as often.
1220.title: Variations

123.body:
[Note In Pitch] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct]
[Note In Gate] ──> [ADSR Gate]
[Note In Velocity] ──> [ADSR Velocity]
[Oscillator Out] ──> [SVF Filter In]
[ADSR Out] ──> [SVF Filter Cutoff]
[SVF Filter LowPass] ──> [VCA In]
[ADSR Out] ──> [VCA CV]
[VCA Out] ──> [Reverb In L]
[Reverb Out L / R] ──> [Audio Output Left / Right] Every module up to the VCA runs one copy per voice. The Reverb hears the voices summed, as a single stereo instrument.
123.title: A polyphonic voice

124.body: Each voice is a full copy of the module, so eight voices use about eight times the CPU of one. If a patch strains your computer, turn down Voices on the Note In module. With mono cables, a polyphonic module runs a single voice and costs no more than before.
124.title: Cost

125.body: A patch has one tempo and one beat, and modules that care about time share them. Turn the Clock 's BPM and the echoes of a synced Delay move, a synced LFO speeds up, and every sequencer the Clock steps keeps pace. None of them needs a cable from the Clock to know.
125.breadcrumbs: Tempo and Sync » Tempo and Sync
125.title: Tempo and Sync

126.body: The patch's first Clock is its transport . Before each block of audio, Soba reads three things from it and hands them to every module: the tempo , in beats per minute; the beat : how many beats have passed since the Clock started, counted from its downbeat; whether it's playing : the beat moves while the Clock runs, and holds while it's stopped. A patch without a Clock has no transport. Synced modules then assume 120 BPM, and a synced LFO keeps its own beat. If a patch has more than one Clock, the transport is the first one in processing order, which is usually the one nothing else feeds. Other Clocks still pulse at their own settings; they just don't set the patch's tempo. The tempo doesn't have to stay put. A CV in the Clock's Tempo jack bends it, and everything synced bends with it: an Arranger lane there slows the song into its last chord. See Tempo CV . For a pulse slower than the beat, such as once every four bars, divide the one Clock with a Clock Divider rather than adding a second, slower Clock. A divider counts the Clock's pulses, so it stays on the beat at any tempo, and it can't become the transport by accident.
126.title: The transport

127.body: Following the tempo. The Delay's Sync turns a note length into a time: a 1/8 at 120 BPM is 250 ms. It needs only the tempo. Following the beat. A synced LFO reads where the beat is and works out its phase from that. A 1 bar LFO is at the start of its cycle on every downbeat, a quarter of the way through on beat 2, and so on. Because it reads the beat rather than counting its own cycles, it can't drift, however long it plays, and every synced LFO in the patch moves in step. When the Clock starts from the top, they all start from the top with it. That's the difference from patching a Clock's Gate into an LFO's Sync input. A gate only restarts the cycle at each pulse, and between pulses the LFO runs at its own Rate, which you have to set to match.
127.breadcrumbs: Tempo and Sync » Two kinds of sync
127.title: Two kinds of sync

128.body: Set the Clock's Source to MIDI and it follows a MIDI clock master: a DAW, a drum machine, a hardware sequencer. The master sends 24 clock ticks per beat, plus Start, Stop and Continue messages for its transport. The Clock: counts the ticks , so its beat is exactly the master's, tick by tick; measures the tempo from their spacing, averaged over the last two beats, so the knob reads the master's BPM and synced modules follow it; starts, stops and continues when the master does. Start fires the Clock's Reset output, so patched sequencers start from step 1 on the downbeat. The whole patch then plays in the master's time: sequencers step on its grid, LFOs sweep with its bars, and the Delay echoes on its eighth notes. See Following MIDI clock for setting it up. Set Source to Auto and the Clock leads and follows by turns: its own time until a device plays, the device's while it does, and its own again when the device stops, carrying on at the device's tempo from the beat it had reached. See Leading or following . Set Source to Link instead, and the Clock joins an Ableton Link session on the network. There's no master: Live, Bitwig, phone apps and other copies of Soba all share one tempo and one bar line, and any of them can change the tempo or start and stop the others. The Clock: plays at the session's tempo , and its BPM knob turns to match when another app changes it. Turning the knob changes the tempo for everyone; lines up its bars with the session's, so beat 1 is everyone's beat 1; starts and stops with the session . Ticking its Run starts every app in it, on the next bar if others are already there. Where MIDI clock carries the master's time down a cable, Link has every app keep the same time from the network's shared clock. Each app allows for its own audio delay, so they agree on when a beat reaches the speakers, not just when it's computed. See Playing in a Link session .
128.breadcrumbs: Tempo and Sync » Playing in time with other gear
128.title: Playing in time with other gear

129.body: It works the other way round too. Turn on a port's Clock in the Rig and the patch's Clock becomes the master: a DAW, a drum machine or an arpeggiator on that port, set to follow MIDI clock, plays in Soba's time. The port, with Clock + Transport : sends Start when the Clock starts from the top, or on the first downbeat after a count-in; sends 24 ticks per beat , each placed on the beat to the sample, and sent as the audio beside it reaches your speakers, so the other gear and Soba's own sounds line up; sends Stop when the Clock stops, and Continue , after a Song Position saying where, when it plays on from there. With Clock only it sends the ticks alone, for gear that should follow the tempo but start and stop by itself. Each port also has an Offset , to line up gear that's slow to sound (see MIDI Out ). A follower measures the tempo from the ticks' spacing, so change the Clock's BPM and it follows. Soba doesn't send clock back to the gear the Clock follows, since two clocks can't lead one another: while a device leads, the ports that play it are sent none. A Clock playing in a Link session can lead MIDI gear, though. A MIDI Out on the same port can also play the device's notes.
129.breadcrumbs: Tempo and Sync » Leading other gear
129.title: Leading other gear

130.body: The Clock counts its beat precisely enough that every pulse lands within a sample of where it belongs, even after ten minutes, so a slow phrase clock and a fast sixteenth clock started together stay together. Modules read the transport once per block of audio (a few milliseconds). Within the block, a synced LFO moves on at the tempo it read. When the beat jumps, as when the Clock restarts or a MIDI master suddenly changes tempo, a synced LFO can be up to one block late in following it. On a steady tempo, and from the next beat on, it's exact.
130.title: Precision

131.body: A good voice (an oscillator, a filter, a VCA and an envelope) is the same few modules in patch after patch, and three voices side by side turn into a wall of cables. A group collapses modules into one node of your own. It has jacks where cables crossed into and out of the selection, plus any you add, and the controls you choose to keep on its face. Open it to work on what's inside. Save it to My Modules , and it's in the add menu of every patch. A group called Voice, playing, with a Wave dropdown and four knobs on its face Voice holds an oscillator, an envelope and a VCA. Its face shows them in miniature, with the oscillator's Wave and four knobs pinned.
131.title: Groups

132.body: Select some modules and press Ctrl + G, or right-click one of them and choose Group . They collapse into one rose-colored node where the top-left corner of the selection was. Type a name and press Enter. Every cable that crossed the edge of the selection becomes a jack: An input jack for each output outside the group that fed something inside it. If one output fed several modules inside, as a keyboard's Gate might feed two envelopes, that's one jack. An output jack for each output inside the group that fed something outside it. Jacks are named after the port inside, numbered if two names would be the same ( In , In 2 ). They're colored by the signal they carry, like every jack, and ordered top to bottom by where their modules sit. Grouping doesn't change the sound: every module hears exactly what it heard before. To take a group apart, select it and press Ctrl + Alt + G, or right-click it and choose Ungroup . Its modules come back out where the group was, laid out as they were, and every cable through its jacks becomes a plain cable again.
132.title: Making a group

133.body: Double-click a group, select it and press Tab, or click the miniature on its face, to go inside. A trail at the top of the canvas shows where you are, such as First Sound › Voice . Click any name in the trail to go back out to it, or press Escape to go up one level. Going in, the view zooms into the group's miniature, and the inside grows out of it, each module coming from where the miniature showed it. Going back out with Escape, the inside shrinks back into the miniature on the group's face. Hold Shift as you go in or out to skip the zoom. Clicking the trail always takes you straight there. Inside the Voice group Inside Voice. Inputs carries what's plugged into the group's jacks outside; Outputs sends its signals back out. Inside, two nodes stand for the group's jacks: Inputs has an output for each input jack. Whatever is plugged into that jack outside comes out here. Outputs has an input for each output jack. Whatever you plug in here comes out of that jack outside. Everything else works as it does at the top of the patch. Modules you add, paste or drop from the palette land inside the group, and you can group modules inside a group too. The cables from Inputs show the signal arriving from outside. Frames and notes belong to the top level of the patch, so they're hidden while you're inside a group.
133.title: Inside a group

134.body: A group starts with the jacks its cables gave it, and you can change them whenever you like. Inside the group, right-click a port's name: Show on group , on an output or an unplugged input, gives the group a new jack named after the port, wired to it through Inputs or Outputs. A filter's Cutoff shown this way can be modulated from outside, and a second output can be brought out beside the first. An input that's already plugged in inside the group can't take a jack too, so the item is greyed. Hide from group , on a port wired to one of the group's jacks, unplugs it. If that leaves the jack carrying nothing inside, the jack goes, and so does any cable into it outside. If the jack still feeds another module, as a shared Gate might, it stays. Right-click a jack itself, on the group's node or on Inputs or Outputs inside, for its own menu: Name opens with the jack's name selected, so you can type a new one and press Enter. A Gate jack might become Trig , or Out might become Wet . The group's node and its Inputs or Outputs change together, and every cable stays plugged in. If another jack on that side already has the name, the new one is numbered. Move up and Move down move the jack one place along the group's jacks, with its cables. Remove jack takes the jack away, with its cables inside and out. New jacks go at the bottom of the group's jacks. Inside a group within a group, an inner group's jacks are ports like any other, so you can show them on the group around it. Undo covers adding, renaming, moving and removing jacks, and a saved patch keeps them.
134.title: Changing a group's jacks

135.body: The group's face shows a miniature of what's inside: each module as a small card in its header color, wired as it is. Hover it to see Open ▸ , and click to go inside. Below the miniature are any controls you've pinned to the group. Inside the group, right-click a knob, a dropdown or a toggle and choose Show on group . It appears on the group's face, in its module's color: dropdowns and toggles in a row of their own, with the knobs under them. It's the module's own control, not a copy: Turning or changing either one changes both, and undo takes back either. A MIDI Learn mapping on a knob works from either place. Dropdowns and toggles can't learn a CC, inside or on the face. If a cable inside the group moves a knob, the face shows it moving. A toggle with a jack, such as the Slope's Cycle , is greyed on the face while a cable sets it. Controls from modules nearer the face come first, then top to bottom by where the modules sit, then in each module's own order. Right-click a control on the face and choose Hide from group to take it off. If the group is inside another group, Show on outer group too puts it on that group's face as well.
135.title: The face

136.body: A pinned control wears its module's short name, such as FM , CV Amt or 2 . That says what the knob is, not what it does for this group. To name it, right-click it on the face. The menu opens on Name with the current name selected: type a new one and press Enter. An electric piano's FM might become Tine , and a mixer's 2 might become 4' . The name shows only on the face. Inside the group, the module keeps its own names, so you can still see which knob is which when you open it. Hover a named control to see what it drives, such as Tine: Oscillator FM Depth . Clear the field and press Enter, or type the module's own name, to go back to it. The name goes with the control to an outer group's face, and into a saved patch or My Modules. Undo takes it back.
136.title: Naming a face control

137.body: Right-click a group and choose Save to My Modules . The group is saved as a file named after it, in Documents/Soba/My Modules . Saved groups come first in the quick-add palette (Space), under My Modules , and in the add menu's My Modules submenu. Each one is described by its jacks and size, such as In, Gate, Velocity → Out · 2 modules . Choosing one adds a copy of the whole group at the cursor, with its modules, cables, jacks and pinned controls. Saving a group under a name that's already there updates it. The folder holds ordinary patch files, so you can copy them to another computer or share them. To find the folder, choose Open folder at the bottom of the add menu's My Modules submenu.
137.title: My Modules

138.body: The Library is a shelf of ready-made groups that ships with Soba. Each one is an ordinary group: add it, play it from the controls on its face, then open it to see how it's made and change anything inside. Find them under Library at the bottom of the add menu, sorted into sections, or type a name or lib into the quick-add palette . Group What it is Jacks Subtractive Voice A saw through a ladder filter, one envelope opening the filter and one shaping the level Pitch, Gate, Velocity → Out FM Voice Two-operator FM at 1:1, an electric-piano bark that mellows as it rings. Oct and Semi set the ratio Pitch, Gate, Velocity → Out FM Bell Two-operator FM at 1:3.5: clangorous partials that fade to a pure tone Pitch, Gate, Velocity → Out Electric Piano A Rhodes-style tine: FM at 1:1 that barks the harder you play and mellows as it rings, with a 14:1 ping on the strike and a slow tremolo. Its face: Tine , Bark , Decay , Tremolo and Rate Pitch, Gate, Velocity → Out Supersaw Pad Seven detuned saws, a slow swell and a filter that breathes Pitch, Gate, Velocity → Out String Machine A Solina-style ensemble: detuned saws at 8' and 4', thinned and swelling, through a three-voice chorus. Its face: Swell , Release , Ensemble , Bright and 4' Pitch, Gate, Velocity → Out Mallet A short strike rings a resonant filter tuned to the note, like a marimba bar Pitch, Gate, Velocity → Out Acid Bass A resonant, driven ladder snapped open on every note; velocity accents. Step Sequencer slides glide it like a 303 Pitch, Gate, Velocity → Out Reese Bass Three detuned saws beating against each other, with a slow LFO in the filter Pitch, Gate, Velocity → Out Drum Kit Kick, snare and hats on a stereo mixer, the closed hat choking the open one Kick, Snare, Hat, Open Hat, Accent → Out L, Out R Random Melody Plays itself: a wandering voltage sampled on the beat and kept in a scale, A minor pentatonic until you change Root and Scale . Range sets how far it wanders, Rests how many beats it sits out → Pitch, Gate Wind Plays itself: pink noise through a wandering band-pass, whistling higher as each gust rises → Out L, Out R Stereo Space Chorus, ping-pong tape echo and a room, in pedalboard order In L, In R → Out L, Out R Pump Each trigger ducks the sound and lets it swell back, like a compressor keyed from the kick In, Trig → Out Auto-Pan An LFO sweeps a mono sound from side to side. Tempo locks the sweep to the Clock In → Out L, Out R Slicer The Slicer rebuilt from stock modules, to open and see how a slicer pedal works: a synced LFO clocks a Step Sequencer whose steps open a VCA and a step filter. Its face: Rate , Steps , Duty , Atk , Rel , Filter , Depth and Close In, Reset → Out, Gate, Env The voices share a shape: plug a Note In into Pitch , Gate and Velocity , and Out into a mixer or the output. They're built from polyphonic modules, so Note In, or a Chord Sequencer , plays chords through any of them. The String Machine's chorus is the one exception: like a real string machine's ensemble, it hears the whole chord at once. They're also levelled to match, so swapping one voice for another doesn't jump in volume. A Library group you've changed can be saved to My Modules under its own name, like any other group.
138.title: The Library

139.body: Copy, paste, duplicate and delete treat a group as a whole: deleting one deletes everything inside it. Undo covers grouping, ungrouping, renaming, pinning, naming face controls, changing jacks and every edit you make inside a group. Undoing an edit that was made inside a group shows you that group as it happens.
139.title: Editing and undo

Install the Rust toolchain with rustup : # Windows
winget install Rustlang.Rustup # macOS and Linux

140.body: The audio engine never sees a group. It only hears the modules and the cables between them, followed through any number of jacks. Groups use no CPU, and grouping or ungrouping never interrupts the sound. A grouped patch plays sample for sample what the ungrouped patch plays, and the test suite checks this for every example. Groups are saved in the patch file, each holding its own modules, cables and groups. A patch with groups needs this version of Soba or later to open. A patch without groups is saved just as before, so older versions still open it.
140.title: How the sound works

141.body: Soba has 44 modules in six categories. Each category has its own header color, so you can tell what a module is for at a glance across a crowded patch. The categories match the right-click menu and the quick-add palette, and the modules are listed here in the order the menu shows them. The ID is the name a patch file uses to refer to the module.
141.title: Module Overview

143.body: Blue header. Modules that start a sound or a note: the oscillator, the noise source, the drum voice, the resonator, the sampler, the chopper and the cloud, the audio input, and the modules that turn your playing into pitch and gate signals. Module ID What it does Oscillator osc.sine Band-limited VCO with a tune section, hard sync, through-zero FM, a sub-oscillator and unison Noise source.noise White, pink and brown noise, and a smooth random voltage Drum source.drum An analog-style drum voice: kick, snare, tom, clap, hats, cymbal, rim, cowbell or shaker, with accent and choke Resonator source.resonator A physical model: a plucked string, or a struck bell, bar, glass or block of wood, played by a gate or by any sound Sampler source.sampler Plays a WAV, MP3, FLAC or Ogg file: one-shots from a gate, an instrument across the keyboard, or its slices by note Chopper source.chopper Plays a sliced break in time with the Clock, at any tempo, rearranged step by step Cloud source.cloud Granular: clouds of small grains from a file or live audio, with Freeze, and a cloud per voice of a chord Audio Input source.audio_input A microphone, guitar or line input, with an envelope follower and a gate Note In input.poly_midi Play notes from the computer keyboard, its piano or a MIDI controller: one voice, or up to eight for chords Controls input.controls A MIDI controller's faders, knobs, mod wheel, pitch bend and pressure as cables, learned from the hardware Pads input.pads A pad controller's pads as eight gates, with velocity and pressure: finger drums, triggers and latches
143.title: Source

144.body: Teal header. Modules that shape a sound's tone by removing or emphasizing frequencies. Both can be bypassed . Module ID What it does SVF Filter filter.svf 12 dB/octave multimode filter with lowpass, highpass, bandpass and notch outputs Ladder Filter filter.ladder Moog-style 24 dB/octave lowpass, saturating and oversampled
144.title: Filter

145.body: Orange header. Sources of movement: control signals that change other modules' parameters over time. Module ID What it does ADSR Envelope mod.adsr Attack, decay, sustain and release, with exact stage times, curve shaping, velocity and CV on every stage LFO mod.lfo Low-frequency oscillator for cyclic modulation, free or locked to the beat Slope mod.slope Rises and falls at set rates: slew and glide, a trigger envelope, or a cycling LFO with skew
145.title: Modulation

146.body: Cyan header. Processors for finished sound. Every effect can be bypassed . Module ID What it does Stereo Delay fx.delay Echoes with feedback filtering, ping-pong, tempo sync and tape mode Reverb fx.reverb Stereo feedback-delay-network reverb with a modulated tail 3-Band EQ fx.eq Low shelf, parametric mid and high shelf Distortion fx.distortion Oversampled soft clip, hard clip, wavefolder, tube and bit crush Chorus fx.chorus Stereo chorus and flanger Tape fx.tape A tape machine for a bus: wow, flutter, saturation, age and hiss Slicer fx.slicer Chops a held sound into a rhythm in time with the Clock: sixteen steps, a step filter and ping-pong Compressor fx.compressor Dynamics compressor with sidechain and a gain-reduction output Vocoder fx.vocoder Puts a voice's spectrum on a synth: 8 to 24 bands, formant shift, sibilance and unvoiced noise, Freeze and carrier Flatten
