147.body: Gray header. The plumbing of a patch: levels, timing, sequencing, looping, and tools for seeing what a signal is doing. Module ID What it does Clock util.clock Steady gate pulses at a tempo; sets the patch tempo, and can follow MIDI clock VCA util.vca Voltage-controlled amplifier: sets a signal's level from a CV Attenuverter util.attenuverter Scale, invert and offset a control signal Mix util.mix Add up to four signals, audio or CV, into one mono sum Mixer util.mixer Four-channel stereo console with pan, width, sends, mute and solo Sample & Hold util.sample_hold Capture a signal's value on each trigger and hold it Quantizer util.quantizer Snap a pitch to the nearest note of a scale Clock Divider util.divider Fire once every so many clocks, and hold a gate open for a phrase Logic util.logic Combine gates with AND, OR, XOR and NOT, and turn a control voltage into a gate Looper util.looper Record, overdub and undo live layers, like a looper pedal, in time with the Clock Oscilloscope util.oscilloscope Draw up to two signals as waveforms Dancer util.dancer A stick figure who dances to the patch, on the beat and as hard as the music is loud Step Sequencer seq.step 16 steps of pitch, gate and velocity, in four chained patterns Chord Sequencer seq.chord 16 chords, each a root, a type and a slash bass, voice-led and played on polyphonic cables, in four patterns played in a chain Trigger Sequencer seq.trigger Eight lanes of drum hits in four chained patterns, with accents, probability and ratchets Arranger seq.arranger A song's timeline: named sections of bars, moving eight lanes of automation by jumps, ramps and hits Scenes util.scenes Keeps the knobs as scenes A to H, and glides every knob between two of them with one Morph knob MIDI Monitor util.midi_monitor Show incoming MIDI messages
147.title: Utility

148.body: Purple header. Where the patch leaves Soba: for your speakers, for other instruments, or for Seoul's visuals. Module ID What it does Audio Output output.audio Stereo master output with volume, DC blocking and a peak limiter Link Out output.link Send eight CV lanes, four gates and the Clock to the Seoul visualizer, to play its pictures from the patch MIDI Out output.midi Play hardware and other apps: gates and pitch as notes (poly cables as chords), bend and aftertouch, four CCs (7-bit, 14-bit or NRPN), programs and banks, and the Clock as MIDI clock Instrument source.instrument A piece of hardware as a node: a synth's or drum machine's own knobs, by name, to turn and patch, and its notes over MIDI Kit source.kit A hardware drum machine, sampler or groovebox as a node: its tracks, pads or parts as eight lanes to strike from a Trigger Sequencer, and its knobs by name, over MIDI Setlist output.setlist Each Arranger section changes the room: a device's pattern, scene, patch or memory, sent as Bank Select and Program Change ahead of the bar FM Voice output.fm_voice A DX7 voice for a volca fm, sent by SysEx as it changes: mutate it, cross two, and keep a garden of the voices bred by ear Header colors describe what a module is . The colors of its jacks and cables describe the signals it handles, which is a separate palette: see Signal Types .
148.title: Output

149.body: The Oscillator, Noise, Drum, Resonator, both filters, the ADSR Envelope, Slope, the VCA, the Attenuverter, Mix, Sample & Hold and the Quantizer run one voice per channel when a polyphonic cable reaches them. Everything else treats a polyphonic cable as one signal. Note In and the Chord Sequencer are where polyphonic cables start. See Polyphony .
149.title: Polyphonic modules

15.body: Windows and macOS need nothing more: Soba uses WASAPI and CoreAudio, which come with the system. (ASIO on Windows is optional: see Build with ASIO .) On Linux, install the development packages for ALSA (audio), X11 and keyboard handling. On Debian and Ubuntu: sudo apt install libasound2-dev libxcb-render0-dev libxcb-shape0-dev \ libxcb-xfixes0-dev libxkbcommon-dev libssl-dev On other distributions, install the equivalent ALSA, xcb and xkbcommon development packages (for example alsa-lib-devel on Fedora, alsa-lib on Arch).

152.body: Module ID osc.sine · Category Source Oscillator Module Three detuned voices of a square wave, an LFO sweeping its pulse width through PWM : the trace is Out as it plays, and PW follows the CV. Under it, the tune, timbre and ensemble rows. The Oscillator is the main sound source in Soba. It is a VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator): a tuned waveform whose pitch follows a keyboard, an LFO or another oscillator. Beyond the four classic waveforms, it has the features that make an oscillator an instrument: a tune section in octaves, semitones and cents; hard sync to another oscillator; through-zero linear FM and exponential FM ; a sub-oscillator one octave down; unison of up to seven voices, with stereo spread. Seven detuned saws is the classic supersaw . The display draws a cycle of the wave at the Pulse Width, and reads the pitch the tune section sets. With more than one unison voice, the others are drawn faintly over it, sliding along the cycle at the rate each beats against the pitch: a gentle Detune drifts, a wide one shimmers. With Sub patched, two cycles show, with the sub's square under them. While the patch plays, what Out really carries is drawn over that shape, lit, and the shape steps back to a faint guide. Each trace starts where the cycle does and keeps the time scale of the cycle the knobs set, so a note V/Oct takes an octave up fits two cycles in, and one an octave down shows half a cycle: a melody squeezes and stretches the wave. PWM sweeps the edge, FM wrinkles the wave, Sync cuts each cycle short, and unison voices beat in it as they sound. Older traces fade behind the newest, like a scope's phosphor, so a moving wave leaves a soft trail. With V/Oct or Exp FM patched, the top reads the note being played. When the sound stops, the shape comes back. Every waveform is band-limited. Each voice runs at twice the sample rate with polyBLEP corrections on its edges and polyBLAMP corrections on its corners, then a halfband filter brings it back down. A 5 kHz saw's aliasing sits around -80 dB, so high notes and sync sweeps stay clean.
152.title: Oscillator

153.body: Port Signal Type Description V/Oct Control (Orange) Pitch, 1 per octave. Each +1.0 raises the pitch one octave, on top of the tune section FM Control (Orange) Through-zero linear FM, scaled by the FM knob Exp FM Control (Orange) Exponential FM, Exp FM knob octaves per unit PWM Control (Orange) Pulse-width modulation around the PW knob (±1 moves it ±0.4) Sync Control (Orange) Hard sync. Each rising zero crossing restarts the cycle. Accepts audio, control or gates
153.title: Inputs

154.body: Port Signal Type Description Out Audio (Blue) All unison voices, mixed to mono Sub Audio (Blue) Square wave one octave below the tuned pitch Out L Audio (Blue) Unison voices spread to the left Out R Audio (Blue) Unison voices spread to the right
154.title: Outputs

155.body: The knobs sit in three rows: tune , timbre and ensemble . Control Range Default Description Oct -4 to +4 0 Octaves above or below C4. Clicks in whole octaves Semi -12 to +12 0 Semitones. Clicks in whole semitones Fine ±100 cents 0 Fine tuning FM 0 – 5 0 Linear FM index (see below) Exp FM 0 – 4 oct 1 Octaves of pitch change per unit at the Exp FM input PW 0.1 – 0.9 0.5 Pulse width of the square (0.5 is a 50% duty cycle) Voices 1 – 7 1 Unison voices Detune 0 – 100% 40% How far apart the unison voices are tuned Spread 0 – 100% 50% How wide the unison voices sit across Out L and Out R Wave Sine / Saw / Square / Tri Sine Dropdown on the node With every tune knob at 0, the oscillator plays C4 (261.63 Hz) . Note In sends 0.0 for C4, so it plays in tune with nothing else to set. MIDI note 69 plays 440 Hz to within a tenth of a cent. Pitch is smoothed in octaves, not Hz, so a jump of an octave up takes as long as an octave down.
155.title: Parameters

156.body: The preview at the top of the node draws one cycle of the selected waveform, and follows the PW knob on the square. Sine is a pure tone with no harmonics: sub-bass, FM carriers and modulators, flute-like tones. Saw has every harmonic, falling as 1/n: classic leads and basses, strings, brass. It is the richest source for filtering, and the one to use for a supersaw. Square has odd harmonics only, for hollow, woody, clarinet-like tones. Pulse width reshapes it, from the square at 0.5 to thin and nasal near 0.1 or 0.9. Tri (triangle) has odd harmonics that fall away fast: softer than the square, brighter than the sine.
156.title: Waveforms

157.body: Oct and Semi set the note; Fine trims it in cents. To tune a second oscillator a fifth up, set Semi to +7. To make it beat slowly against the first, add a few cents of Fine .
157.title: Tune section

158.body: Patch another oscillator's Out into Sync : [Osc 2 Out] ──> [Osc 1 Sync] Every time Osc 2's waveform rises through zero, Osc 1 starts its cycle again. The result repeats at Osc 2's pitch, but its tone comes from Osc 1's pitch. Tune Osc 1 above Osc 2 and sweep its pitch (a slow LFO or envelope on V/Oct or Exp FM ) for the classic tearing sync sweep. The reset itself is band-limited, so sync sweeps don't fizz with aliasing.
158.title: Hard sync

159.body:
The FM input multiplies the pitch by 1 + FM × input, where FM is the knob: At an FM of 1, an input of -1 just reaches 0 Hz. Past 1, the frequency swings through zero and the waveform runs backward for a moment, instead of stalling at 0 Hz. That keeps the average pitch where it was, so deep FM stays in tune and keeps the bright, glassy character of DX-style FM. Because the depth is relative to the pitch, the timbre stays the same as you play up the keyboard. [Osc 2 Out] ──> [Osc 1 FM]
[Osc 1 Out] ──> [VCA In] ──> [Audio Output] Sine into sine gives the cleanest FM tones. Whole-number pitch ratios (Semi +12, or +19 for 3:1) sound harmonic. Other ratios sound bell-like and metallic. Shape the modulator's level with an envelope (through a VCA) to make the brightness decay like a struck bell. The FM Synthesis recipe builds a complete patch around this.
159.title: Through-zero FM

16.body:
git clone https://github.com/chrischaps/Soba.git
cd Soba
cargo run --release The first build takes a few minutes. Always use --release to play: the debug build is much slower and can't keep up with a busy patch, so you'll hear dropouts. The finished binary is target/release/soba. The app opens on the First Sound example. Press ▶ Play , then play the Z to M keys on your computer keyboard. If you hear a note, everything is working.
16.title: Build and run

160.body: Exp FM works like a second V/Oct input with its own depth knob. An LFO into it gives a vibrato that's even in pitch: the same width in cents on every note. Keep the depth small (Shift-drag the knob for fine steps): 0.02 octaves is about ±24 cents. At audio rates it gives a rougher, less pitch-stable kind of FM than the linear input.
160.title: Exponential FM

161.body:
Sub is a square wave one octave below the tuned pitch. It divides the main oscillator's own cycle, so it follows V/Oct, FM and sync. Mix it in under a saw for weight: [Oscillator Out] ──> [Mix In 1]
[Oscillator Sub] ──> [Mix In 2]
[Mix Out] ──> [Ladder Filter In]
161.title: Sub-oscillator

162.body: Voices stacks copies of the oscillator, each slightly detuned: Detune sets how far apart they are. Its curve is gentle at the bottom: 20% puts the outer voices about ±4 cents apart, 40% about ±16 cents, and 100% a full ±100 cents. The voices bunch toward the middle, close to Roland's JP-8000 supersaw. The spacing is deliberately uneven, so the voices never beat in lockstep. Each voice starts at a different point in its cycle, so the stack doesn't open with one loud spike. Out sums all the voices at about the loudness of one voice. Out L and Out R pan the voices across the stereo field, outer voices widest. Spread sets the width. For a supersaw: Wave on Saw, Voices at 7, Detune about 40%, and Out L and Out R into the output's Left and Right .
162.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Oscillator » Unison and supersaw
162.title: Unison and supersaw

163.body: With the square wave selected, modulate the pulse width with an LFO: [LFO Out] ──> [Oscillator PWM] Slow rates give a chorus-like shimmer; fast rates, a more dramatic wobble in the tone. The PW knob stays where you set it, as the centre of the sweep. An orange arc on its rim runs out to a bead at the width the oscillator is playing, and the number under it reads that width in orange.
163.title: Pulse-width modulation

165.body:
[Note In Pitch] ──> [Osc 2 V/Oct] ──> [Osc 1 V/Oct] (Osc 1 Oct +1)
[Osc 2 Out] ──> [Osc 1 Sync]
[ADSR Out] ──> [Osc 1 Exp FM]
[Osc 1 Out] ──> [SVF Filter In] Each note sweeps Osc 1's pitch up with the envelope, while sync holds it to Osc 2's pitch.
165.title: Sync lead

166.body:
[Note In Pitch] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct] (Saw, 7 voices)
[Oscillator Out L] ──> [Reverb In L]
[Oscillator Out R] ──> [Reverb In R]
[Reverb Out L] ──> [Audio Output Left]
[Reverb Out R] ──> [Audio Output Right]
166.title: Supersaw pad

167.body: The Oscillator is polyphonic. Patch a polyphonic Pitch cable from Note In into V/Oct and each note gets its own oscillator, with its own phase, sync and unison stack. The knobs are shared by every voice. Unison multiplies the cost: eight notes of a seven-voice supersaw is 56 oscillators. See Polyphony .
167.title: Polyphony

168.body: Older patches load at the same pitch. Their Frequency setting is split into Oct, Semi and Fine. FM Depth, which used to be in Hz, becomes the matching index at that pitch. A MIDI controller mapped to Frequency moves to Oct over the same range. The old Frequency input jack is gone; a cable into it is skipped with a load warning. Band-limited edges overshoot a little. Saw and square peak at about 1.3 for a few samples after each edge. This is ringing near 24 kHz, which is inaudible, and any filter or the output stage takes it away. The tune section reaches from about 7.7 Hz to 8.9 kHz. Use V/Oct or Exp FM to go further.
168.title: Notes

169.body: LFO for vibrato and PWM SVF Filter to shape the oscillator's harmonics Ladder Filter , the fat, saturating 24 dB alternative VCA and ADSR Envelope to turn a tone into notes

17.body: For playing a guitar or singing through Soba, Windows Audio's round trip of 60 ms or so is too slow to play against. An audio interface's ASIO driver talks to the hardware directly and gets it down to 11–20 ms on a Scarlett 2i2. ASIO is a registered trademark of Steinberg Media Technologies GmbH The low-latency Windows download (soba-windows-asio.zip, see Download a release ) has ASIO built in: install your interface's driver (step 1) and choose ASIO in the Output menu. To build it yourself, it's a build option, off by default: Install your interface's ASIO driver from its maker. For a Focusrite Scarlett, that's the Focusrite USB driver from focusrite.com . Restart, or unplug the interface and plug it back in, once it's installed: until then the driver may not find the interface. Install LLVM , which the build uses to read the ASIO headers: winget install LLVM.LLVM Then point the build at it. In a new terminal: setx LIBCLANG_PATH "C:\Program Files\LLVM\bin" Build with the asio feature: cargo run --release --features asio The first build downloads Steinberg's ASIO SDK into your temp folder. To use a copy you already have, set CPAL_ASIO_DIR to its folder. If the build stops at "Failed to extract ASIO SDK", Windows PowerShell couldn't load its unzip command, which happens when the build runs from PowerShell 7. Build from Git Bash with env -u PSModulePath cargo run --release --features asio, or unzip %TEMP%\asio_sdk.zip yourself and set CPAL_ASIO_DIR to the folder inside. Then choose ASIO at the top of the Output menu. See Audio Input for choosing a buffer size. Steinberg licenses the ASIO SDK under the GPLv3 (or its own proprietary terms). Soba's source is MIT, but a binary built with ASIO includes the SDK, so if you share one, the GPLv3 applies to it. The low-latency download is such a binary: it's distributed under the GPLv3, with the GPL, Steinberg's licence for the SDK and a notice in its zip and installer. The exact SDK it was built from (ASIO SDK 2.3.4, pinned by its checksum in release.yml) is attached to the same release as asio-sdk-source.zip. The other downloads leave ASIO out and stay MIT.
17.title: Build with ASIO (Windows, optional)

170.body: Module ID source.noise · Category Source Noise Module White and Pink are patched, so their lines are lit; Brown, unpatched, is dimmed. Noise is a sound with no pitch: every frequency at once, at random. Through a filter and an envelope it becomes a snare, a hi-hat, a breath, wind or surf. Sampled by a clock, it becomes a melody that never repeats. The module makes three colours of noise, an output that wanders smoothly at modulation speed, and one that scatters triggers at random: White : equal energy at every frequency. Bright, hissing, like steam or an untuned radio. Pink : falls 3 dB per octave, so every octave holds the same energy. To the ear it is the most balanced noise: rain, surf, a waterfall. Brown : falls 6 dB per octave. A deep, soft rumble, like wind or thunder far away. The name is for Robert Brown, whose random walk of pollen grains it imitates, not the colour. Random : a smooth random voltage that glides to a new value Rate times a second. Dust : single triggers at random moments, Rate of them a second on average. Crackle, raindrops, a ghost note now and then. Noise is polyphonic. Patch a polyphonic cable into Level or Rate and each voice plays noise of its own, so a four-note chord of filtered noise is four different hisses, not one copied four times.
170.title: Noise

171.body: Port Signal Type Description Level Control (Orange) Added to the Level knob, and followed instantly. An envelope here, with the knob at 0, shapes the noise into a hit Rate Control (Orange) Speeds up or slows down Random and Dust . Each +1 doubles the rate; -1 halves it
171.title: Inputs

172.body: Port Signal Type Description White Audio (Blue) White noise, spread evenly over ±1 at full Level Pink Audio (Blue) Pink noise, about -12 dBFS RMS at full Level Brown Audio (Blue) Brown noise, about -12 dBFS RMS at full Level Random Control (Orange) A smooth random voltage between -1 and 1. Level doesn't affect it Dust Gate (Green) One-sample triggers at random moments, Rate a second on average. Level doesn't affect it
172.title: Outputs

173.body: Knob Range Default Description Level 0 – 100% 50% Level of White, Pink and Brown Rate 0.01 – 20 Hz 1 Hz How many new values Random glides to each second, and how many triggers Dust scatters
173.title: Parameters

174.body: The display draws the three noises the way a spectrum analyzer would read them, on a frequency axis from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. All three start from one point at the low end and fan out: W stays flat, P falls gently and B falls twice as steeply. The lines shimmer as a real reading of noise does, most at the low end, where an analyzer has fewer frequencies to average in each octave. Patched outputs light up and unpatched ones dim, so you can see at a glance which noise a patch is using. The lines sink as Level comes down.
174.title: The display

175.body: White uses the whole ±1 range, so it makes a full-range random source for Sample & Hold . Pink and Brown are set about 7 dB lower, so their rare peaks stay inside ±1. A gentle ceiling holds those peaks in without touching anything below 0.8. Brown is a leaky random walk: it rises 6 dB per octave as frequency falls, down to about 10 Hz, then levels off. That keeps it from drifting away from zero and pushing your speakers with a slow offset.
175.title: Levels

176.body: Random picks a new value between -1 and 1 Rate times a second, and glides to it along a cosine curve. It arrives at each value at rest and leaves it smoothly, so it has no corners. It sounds less like a stepped sample-and-hold and more like something drifting: a filter that breathes, or a pitch that wavers like an old tape. At 0.05 Hz it takes twenty seconds to move, which is slow enough to change the character of a whole pad over time. At 10–20 Hz it becomes a fast flutter.
176.title: Random

177.body: Dust fires a trigger one sample long at moments nobody can predict. Every sample has the same small chance of one, Rate over the sample rate, so the triggers fall the way raindrops do: on average Rate a second, sometimes two close together, sometimes a long gap. (It's a Poisson process, and the name comes from the Dust generators of SuperCollider.) At 0.5 Hz it's an occasional tick, a record's dust. At 20 Hz it's a steady drizzle, and Rate CV takes it up to a thousand a second, a hiss of grains. Random and Dust share Rate , so a Noise used for both moves them together; use a second Noise to set them apart. A trigger, not a level: patch Dust into anything that listens for a rising edge, like a Drum 's Trig , an ADSR 's Gate (with a short decay) or a Sample & Hold 's Trig . To let only some of a regular rhythm through instead, use Logic 's Maybe .
177.title: Dust

179.body:
The classic: noise, sampled on every clock pulse, played as pitch. [Clock Gate] ──> [Sample & Hold Trig]
[Noise White] ──> [Sample & Hold In]
[Sample & Hold Out] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct]
[Clock Gate] ──> [ADSR Gate] Each pulse catches a new value of the noise and holds it as a note. Level sets the range: at 50%, the notes wander up to half an octave either side of the oscillator's pitch. The pitches are unquantized, so they fall between the keys of a piano; put a Quantizer after the Sample & Hold to keep them in a key. A little Slew on the Sample & Hold turns the jumps into glides.
179.title: Random melody

Ableton Link lets the Clock play in time with other apps on the network: see Playing in a Link session . It's a build option, off by default, because Ableton licenses the Link SDK under the GPLv2 (or its own commercial terms). Install CMake , which builds the Link SDK, and LLVM , which reads its headers (see step 2 above for pointing the build at LLVM). On Windows: winget install Kitware.CMake
winget install LLVM.LLVM On macOS, brew install cmake llvm. On Linux, your distribution's cmake, clang and libclang-dev packages. Build with the ableton-link feature: cargo run --release --features ableton-link It goes with ASIO too: --features asio,ableton-link. 180.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [ADSR Gate] (Atk 1 ms, Dec 45 ms, Sus 0, Rel 40 ms)
[ADSR Out] ──> [Noise Level] (Level knob at 0)
[Noise Pink] ──> [SVF Filter In] (Cutoff 4.5 kHz, take HighPass) The envelope opens Level for each hit, so no VCA is needed. Only the knob is smoothed; CV at Level is followed sample by sample, so a 1 ms attack stays a 1 ms attack. A short decay gives a closed hat; lengthen Dec to 250 ms for an open one. The Rhythmic Sequence example plays exactly this under its bassline.
180.title: Hi-hat

181.body: Mix a short burst of noise with a pitched body. Patch Pink through a bandpass around 2 kHz, open it with a 120 ms decay, and add a sine at 180 Hz with a shorter envelope. The noise is the snare wires; the sine is the drum.
181.title: Snare

182.body:
[Noise Pink] ──> [SVF Filter In] (Res 60%, take BandPass)
[Noise Random] ──> [SVF Filter Cutoff] (Noise Rate 0.1 Hz) Random sweeps a resonant band slowly through the noise, so it rises and falls like gusts. Use Brown for a deeper, more distant wind. Put a slow LFO on a VCA after it, at about 0.1 Hz, and the swell of waves comes and goes. The Shoreline example builds a whole beach this way, using every output of one Noise module: Pink and Brown for the surf, Random to vary the waves, and White, through a Sample & Hold, to play a wind chime.
182.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Noise » Wind and surf
182.title: Wind and surf

183.body:
[Noise Dust] ──> [Drum Trig] (Noise Rate 6 Hz; Drum: Rim, Tune +24, Decay short)
[Drum Out] ──> [SVF Filter In] (Cutoff 3 kHz, take HighPass) Each trigger plays a tiny pitched-up click, at random, about six a second. Turn the Drum down until it sits under the music rather than on it. Patch Dust into a Sample & Hold's Trig with White in its In , and the S&H's Out into the Drum's Tune , and no two clicks are the same pitch.
183.title: Vinyl crackle

184.body: Sample & Hold : turns noise into stepped random values Quantizer : snaps random pitches to a scale SVF Filter : shapes noise into drums, wind and breath Drum : a finished drum voice, with its noise and filters built in ADSR Envelope : gives noise a shape in time LFO : regular movement, where Random is irregular Logic : Maybe passes a regular rhythm only sometimes, where Dust has none
184.title: Related modules

185.body: Module ID source.drum · Category Source Drum Module A kick just after a hit. The orange line is its pitch, falling two and a half octaves to 48 Hz in the first few milliseconds. The blue curve is its level, lit up to the playhead. Drum is one analog drum voice. Its Type turns it into a kick, snare, tom, clap, closed hat, open hat, cymbal, rim, cowbell or shaker, each built the way an 808 or 909 builds that sound: a few oscillators, a noise source, filters and decays. Send it a trigger and it plays one hit. The same five knobs serve every type, and each means what it would on that drum's own panel. Tune sets the pitch of a kick and the metal of a hat. Snap sets a kick's beater and a snare's wires. The names never change, so a MIDI mapping keeps working when you change the Type. Drum is polyphonic. A polyphonic gate, from Note In say, plays a new voice for each note, so fast hits ring on over each other instead of cutting each other off.
185.title: Drum

186.body: Each type has its own pitch, its own range of decay, and its own meaning for Tone and Snap. The times are how long a hit takes to fall 60 dB, from Decay at 0 to Decay at 100%. Type Built from Tune 0 Decay Tone Snap Kick A sine that falls in pitch, and a beater click 48 Hz 0.12 – 2.5 s Drive, from a pure sine to a rounded, 909-like thump How far the pitch falls (half an octave to four) and how hard the beater clicks Snare Two drumhead tones, and noise for the wires 185 Hz 0.08 – 0.8 s The wires, from dull to bright Wires against the drum: more rattle, less tone Tom A sine that falls half an octave, and a stick click 110 Hz 0.12 – 1.8 s Drive The stick on the head Clap Four bursts of noise a few milliseconds apart, then a tail 1150 Hz band Tail 0.08 – 1.0 s Narrow and dark to wide and bright The bursts against the tail Closed Hat Six square waves at the 808's inharmonic ratios, ringing in a band around 6 kHz, with hiss above it 205 – 800 Hz squares 25 – 300 ms Where the band sits, and how much air is over it Hiss against metal Open Hat The same The same 0.15 – 1.8 s The same The same Cymbal The same squares through a low and a high band, a bright splash over a long wash The same 0.6 – 5 s From the low band to the high Sizzle against metal Rim Two tones, 1667 and 455 Hz, and a crack of noise 1667 Hz 15 – 200 ms Drive The crack Cowbell Two squares a sixth apart, through a bandpass 540 and 800 Hz 0.1 – 1.2 s The bandpass, dark to bright The clank of the strike over the ring Shaker A band of noise that swells in over 3 ms, as the beads arrive, rather than striking 6.7 kHz band 40 – 200 ms Where the band sits, from 5 to 9 kHz The rattle: the beads landing unevenly inside each grain The hats' six squares run all the time, as the 808's do. They are never caught at the same place twice, so no two hits sound exactly alike. Every other type starts at full level the instant it's struck. The Shaker's grain swells in, because the beads in a shaker don't all hit the wall at once. Accent shapes that as a wrist does: a full shake swells in over 3 ms, and a soft one over as much as 8 ms, as well as being quieter and darker.
186.title: The types

187.body: Port Signal Type Description Trig Gate (Green) A rising edge strikes the drum. Patch a sequencer's Gate , a clock, or a MIDI gate Accent Control (Orange) How hard each hit is, from 0 to 1, read as the hit lands. Patch a sequencer's Velocity . Unpatched, every hit is full Choke Gate (Green) A rising edge damps the drum within 5 ms. A choke that arrives before a hit does nothing to that hit Tune Control (Orange) V/Oct, added to the Tune knob at each hit: 1 V is an octave Decay Control (Orange) Added to the Decay knob at each hit
187.title: Inputs

188.body: Port Signal Type Description Out Audio (Blue) The drum. At default settings a full-accent kick peaks around -4 dBFS, and the hats and the rim sit a few dB lower
188.title: Outputs

189.body: Control Range Default Description Type Kick … Shaker Kick Which drum. The knobs keep their settings when it changes Tune ±24 st 0 st Pitch in semitones from the drum's own Decay 0 – 100% 50% How long it rings, over the type's own range Tone 0 – 100% 50% Dark to bright, as the table describes Snap 0 – 100% 50% The noise or click in the hit, as the table describes Level 0 – 100% 80% Output level Tune , Decay , Tone and Snap are read when a hit lands, as on a drum machine. A hit keeps its sound however the knobs move while it rings, and the next hit takes the new settings. Level follows the knob at once.

19.body:
Soba also runs inside a DAW, as an instrument on a track. It's a CLAP plugin, for Bitwig Studio, REAPER, FL Studio and Studio One, and it can be built as a VST3 for DAWs without CLAP, such as Ardour and Cubase. The plugin is the whole app: the node graph is its window, and the patch plays whatever the track sends it. Notes and CCs from the track reach Note In modules, the MIDI Monitor and MIDI Learn, as a MIDI device's do in the app. Tempo and transport. Set a Clock's Source to Host and it plays at the DAW's tempo, on its beat, starting and stopping with it (see Playing in a DAW ). Macros. The plugin offers the DAW eight parameters, Macro 1 to Macro 8 , to automate. Right-click a knob, then Map to Macro , and the knob follows that macro. The patch is saved with the project. Samples are kept by path, as in a patch file, so keep them where they are. The DAW plays the patch, so the plugin has no Play button and no device menus. Open and Save As still read and write patch files, so a patch moves between the plugin and the app. There's no download of the plugin yet. To build one from source (see Build from source above for Rust): python tools/plugin_bundle.py # builds dist/Soba.clap
python tools/plugin_bundle.py --install # ...and copies it where DAWs look --install puts it in your own CLAP folder: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Common\CLAP on Windows, ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/CLAP on macOS, ~/.clap on Linux. Then rescan plugins in the DAW and add Soba to an instrument track.
19.title: The plugin (CLAP and VST3)

190.body: Accent scales the hit's level, so at 0.4 it plays 8 to 10 dB quieter, and at 0 not at all. A softer hit is also darker and less snappy, as on a real drum: Tone drops by up to a quarter and Snap by up to half, and a soft kick falls a little less far in pitch. A ghost note on a snare is a different sound from a backbeat, not just a quieter one. While Accent is patched, the Tone and Snap knobs show this. An orange arc on each runs out to a bead at what the Accent makes of it, and the number under the knob reads that value in orange.
190.title: Accent

191.body:
A hi-hat is two drums that can't ring at once: closing the pedal stops the open hat. To do this, patch the closed hat's trigger into the open hat's Choke as well as its Trig : [Closed lane Gate] ──> [Drum (Closed Hat) Trig] └──> [Drum (Open Hat) Choke]
[Open lane Gate] ──> [Drum (Open Hat) Trig] The open hat rings until the next closed hat lands, then dies in a few milliseconds, the way a drummer's foot shuts it. Any gate can choke any drum: a kick that chokes a long cymbal makes a cut-off crash. A voice struck again while it's still ringing starts the new hit at once. It lets go of the old one over a millisecond or two, so a fast roll on a long kick doesn't click.
191.title: Choke

192.body: The display draws the hit the knobs will play next. The blue curve is its level. Time runs on a warped axis that is wide at the start, so a kick's 10 ms drop and a cymbal's five-second wash both fit, with faint marks at 10 ms, 100 ms and each second. The ring time is at the top right. The orange line is pitch. For a kick, snare, tom or rim it is the fall from the strike to the drum's resting pitch, which is printed at the top left. For the hats, cymbal and cowbell it is one line per square wave, each fading as the ring dies. For a clap or a shaker it marks the band the noise rings in, and the shaker's level curve rises from nothing as its grain swells in. When the drum is hit, the fill flashes, and a playhead travels along the curve, lighting it as it goes. The lit curve is as tall as the hit's Accent, so ghost notes and backbeats read at a glance. A choked hit drops to nothing where the choke caught it. Hover the display for the numbers.
192.title: The display

194.body: The Drum Machine example is a whole kit in 14 modules: a Clock, five sequencer lanes, five Drums, a Mixer, a Reverb and the Output. Each sequencer's Gate goes to its Drum's Trig and its Velocity to Accent .

[Sequencer Pitch] ──> [Drum (Tom) Tune]
[Sequencer Gate] ──> [Drum (Tom) Trig]
[Sequencer Velocity] ──> [Drum (Tom) Accent] Each step's note sets the tom's pitch, with middle C at the Tune knob's pitch. Set the Type to Cowbell for the classic 808 cowbell line, or to Kick with a long Decay for an 808 bass.

199.body: Module ID source.resonator · Category Source Resonator Module, a bell A bell 0.4 seconds after it was struck. Each mode is a ring on a log-frequency axis. The hum on the left is still ringing wide, and the high partials on the right have already shrunk back to their dots. Resonator is a physical model. It doesn't make a waveform and then shape it. It works out how a real string or a real bell would move when something plays it, sample by sample. That's why it sounds alive straight away, with no envelope to set. A pluck rings and fades by itself, its top dies before its note does, and no two plucks are quite alike. Two models share one set of knobs: String is a plucked string, built the way Karplus and Strong built theirs in 1983: a burst of noise runs round a loop exactly one period long, and a gentle lowpass in the loop takes a little of the top off on every pass. Body is a struck bell, bar, glass or block of wood: twelve tuned modes, each ringing at its own frequency and dying at its own rate. A Gate plays it, as a finger or a mallet would. So does any sound patched into In . A drum, a voice or a burst of noise makes it ring at its own pitch, the way a shout makes a piano's open strings hum. A Drum into a tuned Resonator is a new instrument in itself. Resonator is polyphonic. A chord on its V/Oct , from a Chord Sequencer or Note In , is a string or a bell for each note, so a chord rings as a chord. One mono drum into In rings them all at once.
199.title: Resonator

2.body: Each cable carries one of three kinds of signal, and takes its color from it: Color Signal What it carries Blue Audio Sound, from −1 to 1 Orange Control Modulation (CV): envelopes, LFOs, pitch Green Gate On or off: a key held down, a clock tick A cable can also carry up to eight voices at once, which is how Soba plays chords. MIDI doesn't travel on cables: Note In listens to the controller you choose in the toolbar and turns what you play into pitch, gate and velocity. Signal Types and Polyphony cover both in depth.
2.title: Signals

20.body: python tools/plugin_bundle.py --vst3 --install # dist/Soba.vst3 as well, installed beside the .clap The VST3 goes in your own VST3 folder: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Common\VST3 on Windows, ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 on macOS, ~/.vst3 on Linux. A DAW that only looks in the shared folder won't find it there. In Ardour, add the folder under Edit ▸ Preferences ▸ Plugins ▸ VST , in the VST3 paths, then rescan. Or copy Soba.vst3 into C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3 (that needs an administrator). The VST3 is the same plugin: the same editor, Host clock, macros and saved patch. Its licence differs. Soba's plugin wraps VST3 with nih-plug, whose VST3 support is built on vst3-sys, a GPLv3 library. So a VST3 build of Soba falls under the GPLv3, as the ASIO download does. The .clap is built without it and stays MIT. Steinberg's own VST3 SDK went MIT in 2025, but Soba doesn't use it directly.

201.body: Resonator Module, a string A string 80 ms after its pluck, still ragged with the top it's losing. The orange mark on the floor is where Position plucks it. A gate plucks the string with one period of noise under a smooth swell, as a finger pulls a string aside and lets go. Brightness is the pick: a soft thumb at 0, a plectrum at 100%. Strike is how hard: softer is quieter, and smoother too, with less of the pick's grain in it. Damping is what the string is made of. At 0 every partial rings as long as the note, like a bright steel wire. Turn it up and the top dies faster than the note, towards nylon or a string under a felt. Damping never changes the pitch: the loop is shortened by exactly the delay its lowpass adds at the note. Position is where along the string it's played. Near the end (0) the sound is thin and bright with every partial. In the middle (100%) it's hollow and round, because a string plucked in the middle has no even partials: they all have a node there.
201.title: String

202.body: A gate strikes the body with a mallet. Brightness is the mallet: felt is wide and dark, steel is narrow and rings every mode. Position is where it lands, from the edge to the middle. A mode with a node where the mallet lands barely sounds. Material sets where the modes sit and how long they ring: Material Modes (times the note) Rings Sounds like Bell 1, 2, 2.38, 3.01, 4, 5.03 … Long A church bell: the hum, the prime an octave up, and the minor third above it that makes a bell sound like a bell Bar 1, 2.76, 5.40, 8.93, 13.3 … Medium An untuned glockenspiel or a struck metal rod Glass 1, 2.32, 4.25, 6.63, 9.38 … Longest A wine glass: pure, with little damping Wood 1, 2.57, 4.47, 6.60, 7.92 … Short A wood block or a thick wooden bar The lowest mode is always the note you play, so every material is in tune with the keyboard. Inharm moves the modes. At 0 they sit on the harmonic series (1, 2, 3, 4 …), which turns any material into something string- or pipe-like. In the middle (the default) they're the material's own. At 100% they're stretched further apart, more clangorous and metallic. Damping makes the high modes die faster than the low ones, on top of the material's own.
202.title: Body

203.body: Port Signal Type Description Gate Gate (Green) A rising edge plucks the string or strikes the body. A poly cable plays a string or a body per note Strike Control (Orange) How hard each gate plays, from 0 to 1, read as it lands. Patch a sequencer's Velocity . Unpatched, every one is full In Audio (Blue) Any sound to excite it with. It rings at its own pitch with whatever you feed it. You hear only the ringing, not the sound you fed in, so mix that in yourself if you want both Decay Control (Orange) Added to the Decay knob Damping Control (Orange) Added to the Damping knob Brightness Control (Orange) Added to the Brightness knob, read at each pluck or strike

206.body: A string excited from In builds up for as long as the sound goes on, and at the longest Decay each pass round the loop keeps 99.99% of what went in. On an ideal string that would climb without end. This one can only swing so far, as a real one can: a soft ceiling sits inside the loop, so even full-scale noise held into the longest Decay rings loudly but stays inside ±1, with no blow-ups.

207.body: For a String , the display is the string itself, between its bridge and its nut. The shape is one period of the loop, read from the voice as it plays, so it moves the way the sound does: ragged just after a pluck, then smoothing to a single arc as the top dies away. The blue haze either side is how far it's swinging. The orange mark on the floor is where Position plucks it. For a Body , it's the modes: a dot for each across a log-frequency axis, as large as a strike will ring it. Struck, each dot blooms into a ring as wide as the mode is loud, and shrinks as that mode dies. A bell's high partials vanish first and its hum lingers. The note and its pitch are at the top left. What's ringing, and for how long, is at the top right. Hover the display for the modes' ratios.
207.title: The display

21.body:
Pass a patch file to open it instead of First Sound: cargo run --release -- patches/lush-pad.json The render tool plays a patch into a WAV file without opening the app or using an audio device, then prints each channel's peak, true peak and RMS level, the mix's loudness, and how hard the patch drives the output limiter: cargo run --release --bin render -- patches/fm-synthesis.json out.wav --seconds 5 Option Default Effect --seconds N 5 Length of the render --sample-rate HZ 48000 Sample rate of the file --block-size N 256 Samples processed per block --audition off Plays a short phrase into the patch's Note In modules --input FILE.wav none What Audio Input modules hear, in place of an input device. It must be at the render's sample rate --cue FILE.txt none Parameter changes to play into the patch as it renders, one per line: <seconds> param <module>[#n|@id] <parameter> <value>, as in a capture script: #n is the nth of its kind, @id the module with that id in the patch file. Press a Looper 's footswitches this way --compare FILE.wav none An earlier render to measure against: prints how far peak, true peak, RMS, loudness and range have moved since --bench off Times the render: how long processing took, how many times faster than real time that is, and the five modules that took longest --runs N 3 with --bench Renders this many times and reports the fastest --trace OUTPUTS FILE.csv none Follows module outputs as the patch plays and writes them to a CSV (see Following a song ) --trace-every S one block How often --trace writes a row, in seconds --stems FOLDER none Writes each Mixer channel with something patched into it, and each Mixer's return, to a WAV of its own A patch that waits for a player renders silence unless something inside it plays notes (a Clock or Step Sequencer, say) or you add --audition. Audio Input modules render silence unless you give them a file with --input. Samplers find their files relative to the patch, as the app does. Here Lush Pad's filter has been closed from 2500 Hz to 833 Hz since before.wav: rendered 'Lush Pad' (8.00 s @ 48000 Hz) -> after.wav L: peak -4.8 dBFS true -4.7 dBTP rms -22.2 dBFS R: peak -4.3 dBFS true -4.3 dBTP rms -21.4 dBFS loudness -17.4 LUFS range 12.3 LU limiter in -4.3 dBFS took 0.0 dB at most, 0% of the time over 1 dB
against before.wav: L: peak -1.5 dB true -1.5 dB rms -1.0 dB R: peak -1.2 dB true -1.2 dB rms -0.9 dB loudness -1.3 LU range -0.1 LU True is the true peak, in dBTP, also after BS.1770-4: how high the waveform goes between the samples, which can be higher than at them. A converter playing the file, or an encoder squeezing it into an MP3 or a video, rebuilds that waveform and clips whatever goes over full scale, so a render whose samples all sit under 0 dBFS can still clip when it's played. A smooth pad reads its sample peak or a tenth above it. Sharp transients go higher: Backbeat's drums read 0.8 dB above their samples. Keep it under −1 dBTP to be safe. Loudness is integrated loudness after ITU-R BS.1770-4, the measure streaming services normalize to. It weights the mix the way the ear does, so it's the number to compare when you want to know whether a change made a patch sound louder. RMS overweights the bass: above, it says the darker pad lost 1 dB, but the ear hears the treble it lost and puts it at 1.3. Range is the EBU loudness range, the spread between the quiet and loud passages. It reads -- on renders shorter than three seconds. Limiter is how hard the patch drives the Audio Output 's limiter: the highest peak going into it, which can be over 0 dBFS, the most it turned the output down, and for how much of the render it took off more than 1 dB. The limiter is there to catch accidents. A patch whose peaks stay under −1 dBFS leaves it idle, as every example does. The examples also sit within a decibel or so of −16 LUFS, so switching between them doesn't jump in volume; aim there to match them.

214.body: Module ID source.sampler · Category Source Sampler Module A five-note chord on a looped bell, and the file heard from ▶ . The orange flags mark the loop and the blue ones what plays. Each white line with a dot is a voice, circling inside the loop at its own speed. The line capped at both ends is ▶ 's, out in the bell's tail. Sampler plays a WAV file. Patch a gate in and it plays one-shots: a kick under a sequencer, a vocal chop, a door slam. Patch in V/Oct as well and a polyphonic gate, and it becomes an instrument: one recorded note spread across the keyboard, each key playing it at its own pitch. Set Slices and it becomes a chopped break: the recording is cut into equal slices, or at each hit it finds, and each key plays one of them. Every other sound in Soba is synthesized. The Sampler brings in sound you've recorded, or one Soba rendered itself, and keeps it with the patch. It can make the recording itself, too: patch something into In and press Rec (see Recording into it ).
214.title: Sampler

215.body: Click Open… under the waveform, or click an empty Sampler's display, and choose a WAV, MP3, FLAC or Ogg (Vorbis or Opus) file. Drag a sound file from your file manager onto a Sampler to replace its file. Drop one on empty canvas and a new Sampler appears there, already playing it. The node lights up under the file while you drag, to show where it will land, and plays the file from Start to End with its waveform on the panel. Over empty canvas, a faint Sampler follows the pointer where the new one would appear, and the whole file plays in its waveform. That way you can audition files from the file manager before you choose one, with or without a Sampler to try them on. It stops when the file leaves the node or you give up the drag, and a file dropped while it plays carries on. (In the browser a file can only be heard once it's dropped.) In the browser, drag a file onto the page the same way. Loading a file is a step you can undo. A file is read and converted once. Samplers that play the same file share it. An MP3 plays without the silence its encoder leaves at the start, so a loop saved as an MP3 still loops cleanly. So does an Ogg file, whether it holds Vorbis or Opus audio (an .ogg, .oga or .opus file). A FLAC file plays exactly as it was recorded. Opening or dropping a file plays it once, from Start to End , so you hear what you chose. Undoing back to an earlier file doesn't.
215.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Loading a file
215.title: Loading a file

216.body: You don't have to patch anything to hear what a Sampler holds. ▶ , beside the file's name, plays it from Start to End and stops there. It plays at the Sampler's Tune and Fine , at a Speed of 1. Press it again (it shows ■ while playing) to stop. Alt-click the waveform to play from that point to End . Past End , it plays on to the end of the file. With Alt held, a dashed line follows the pointer to show where it will start. Dragging the markers works as before. Sliced , Alt-click a slice to play just that slice, from its start to its end. With Alt held, the slice under the pointer is outlined. Let go of a marker with Alt held to hear what it now marks. A slice marker plays the slice it begins, Start the first slice and End the last. Unsliced, Start and End play Start to End . While you drag with Alt held, the slice you'll hear is outlined. You can nudge a marker and hear the result each time you let go, as in ReCycle or Simpler. This works whether the transport is running or not. What you hear is the file itself, not the patch: it plays dry, beside the patch rather than through it, after the Audio Output's limiter, 6 dB below the file's own level. It isn't in a recording made with Record . It's how a sampler's or a DAW's file preview works. One file plays at a time. Starting another, from this Sampler or any other, fades the first out over 5 ms. Deleting the Sampler or giving it another file stops it. While it plays, a white playhead capped at both ends shows where it is, with the part it has played washed faintly behind it. The voices' playheads are lines with a blue dot, so the two never look alike.
216.title: Hearing it

217.body: Patch something into In L (and In R , for stereo) and press the red Rec button beside Open… . Press it again to stop. There's no file dialog: the take plays at once, and becomes the Sampler's file. Anything can be recorded. Patch an Audio Input to record yourself. Patch the patch's own sound, a Vocoder 's output or a Mixer 's send, to resample it into a new instrument. One side patched records the same on both. From a right-click. Right-click an Audio Input and choose Record into a new Sampler . A Sampler appears beside it, already patched, with Thresh at −40 dB and Rec already pressed, so the next thing you say is the take. Any other audio output offers Resample into a new Sampler : on its module's menu (with a submenu where there's more than one, like a Mixer's Out and Send ), or on the output's own name. If the patch is stopped, it starts playing. With a Clock in the patch, each of these offers Free , 1 bar , 2 bars or 4 bars : a take in bars sets Take to match and Thresh to −∞, starts on the next bar line instead of the next sound, stops itself, and lands with Loop on Forward, ready to play. Start on a sound. Turn Thresh up from −∞ dB and Rec waits until In is that loud before it starts, keeping the 30 ms before. The take starts on your first word, not on reaching for the mouse. While it waits, the panel dims and shows how loud In is against the threshold. Takes in bars. Set Take to a number of bars with a Clock running. Rec then starts on the next bar line and stops after exactly that many bars, so the take is already a loop. As it records, the panel counts it in bars and beats, REC 2.3 / 4, not seconds. A press up to 50 ms after a bar line counts as on it. Stopping. Rec again, the Rec gate falling, the bars running out, or the room: a take lasts at most a minute. Stopping the transport ends a take there. The Rec jack takes over from the button, as Freeze does on the Vocoder: the Sampler records while the gate is high. A sequencer's gate resamples a phrase on cue. Tidied as they're kept. Right-click Rec and tick Tidy takes , and each take is trimmed to its sound and set to −16 dBFS RMS as it's kept (see Tidy takes ). On a footswitch or a pad. Right-click Rec and choose Learn MIDI , then press a MIDI footswitch or hit a pad. Live input reaches the patch a round trip after it was played, so the take is written that much earlier, as the Looper 's overdubs are. A take in bars begins with what you played on the bar line, within a few milliseconds at the latency your device reports. The patch's own sound has no round trip, and is taken as it comes. While a take comes in, the panel draws it in red, across a span that doubles whenever the take outgrows it, with the time so far in the corner and Rec showing ■. The Sampler goes on playing its old file until the take is done. Recording needs the patch playing.
217.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Recording into it
217.title: Recording into it

218.body: When a take ends it's written as a WAV beside the patch, as <patch name> samples/Take 1.wav, Take 2.wav and so on, and the Sampler's file names it. That's a step you can undo: undo gives the Sampler back the file it had before. Saving the patch saves the take with it, and opening the patch plays it again. A patch that hasn't been saved yet, a new one or an example, keeps its takes in a temporary folder until you save it. Save As then copies them beside the patch with its other samples. In the browser there's no folder beside the patch, so a take lives only in the tab, as a dropped file does. To keep one, save the patch: 💾 Save then downloads a zip of the patch with its takes and dropped files, as WAVs in a <patch> samples folder beside it, the way Save As gathers them on the desktop. Unzipped, it opens whole in Soba on the desktop. To keep just one file, click its name under the waveform and choose Download , which saves it as a WAV. The browser also keeps each one for the page itself, so it's still there after a reload, when an autosave is recovered, or when you open the downloaded patch in the browser again. Once nothing names a file any more, the next visit lets it go. Takes nobody keeps don't pile up. Saving removes the takes this session wrote that the patch no longer plays and undo can't bring back. Closing the patch (New, Open or Quit) removes those no saved patch names, the temporary folder among them. That covers the files Trim and Normalize write too. A file Soba didn't write is never touched. After a crash, the temporary folder it left behind is tidied too: recovering the patch makes its takes this session's, and choosing Discard removes them. Room for a take is set aside, a minute of stereo (about 23 MB at 48 kHz), when something is patched into In , so recording never has to find memory mid-take. Unpatch In and it's given back.
218.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Where takes go
218.title: Where takes go

219.body: A take comes in raw: silence at each end, whatever level the mic gave it, perhaps a bump before the first word. Click the file's name, under the waveform, for two fixes. They work on any file the Sampler plays, not only takes. Trim to the sound cuts the recording from where its sound begins to 300 ms after it ends. Normalize peak to −1 dBFS turns the whole recording up (or down) until its loudest sample is at −1 dBFS. Its shape is unchanged. Normalize RMS to −16 dBFS sets the level of the sound itself, so recordings sit at one level: a quiet take and a loud one come out alike. Up to 6 dB of peaks over −1 dBFS are taken down by a gentle look-ahead limiter. A peak louder than that, such as a popped "p", lowers the whole recording instead, and the status bar says by how much it fell short. Trim, previewed on the Sampler's face A spoken line with room at both ends, and Trim to the sound under the pointer. The hatched parts would go: 1.12 s from the start, up to the breath before the first word, and 1.42 s from the end. The crop marks frame what stays. Each item says what it would do before you choose it: how much each end loses, or how many dB the level moves. While the pointer is on an item, the waveform shows it too. A trim veils the parts it would cut and sets crop marks round what it keeps. A level writes its change across the panel, since the waveform is always drawn to fill it. Neither touches the original. Each writes a new WAV beside the patch, in <patch name> samples, named for what was done (Take 1 trimmed.wav, then Take 1 trimmed normalized.wav), and the Sampler plays it once, as it does a file just opened. It's a step you can undo: undo brings back the untouched file. A trim moves Start , End and the loop's markers with the sound, so they mark the same moments in it. A marker in a part that was cut goes to that end. Sliced, the slices are cut from what's left.
219.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Trim and Normalize
219.title: Trim and Normalize

22.body: --bench measures how heavy a patch is to run. It times only the processing, not loading the patch or measuring the result, and renders three times, keeping the fastest. A busy machine can only slow a run down, never speed it up, so the fastest is the closest to the patch's own cost: bench: 1.3546 s for 20.00 s of audio, 14.8x realtime (best of 3) osc.sine (node 2) 576.9 ns/sample 41% filter.svf (node 3) 347.7 ns/sample 25% fx.reverb (node 6) 291.1 ns/sample 21% fx.chorus (node 5) 66.4 ns/sample 5% util.vca (node 4) 32.4 ns/sample 2% That is Lush Pad, auditioned. Realtime is how much faster than playback it rendered: below 1x it couldn't keep up live. Below it are the modules that took longest, by their module and their id in the patch file, in nanoseconds per sample and as a share of the whole. Lush Pad's oscillator plays every held voice, so it takes the most. Timing each module costs a little in itself, so the whole runs a few percent slower than it would without --bench.
22.title: Timing a render

220.body: To have every take come in tidy, right-click Rec and tick Tidy takes . Each take is then trimmed to its sound and normalized to −16 dBFS RMS the moment it's kept, both in one go, into one file: Take 1 tidied.wav. The panel frames the waveform in crop marks for a moment and says what was done, such as Tidied −0.42 s, +5.2 dB , and so does the status bar. While it's on, Rec wears small crop marks of its own. The choice is saved with the patch, Sampler by Sampler. The take as it came in is still written first, as Take 1.wav, and tidying is its own step after it. One undo brings back the raw take, and a second gives the Sampler back the file it had before. A take in bars ( Take set to a number of bars) is never trimmed, since its length is the loop. It's only normalized. With Thresh turned up, the trim still finds where the sound begins: the 30 ms Thresh keeps before it is there for the trim to walk back into, and it keeps what it finds. A take that's already tidy, its sound filling it and its level on −16 dBFS, is left as it is.
220.title: Tidy takes

221.body: The rule is the one the Soba Speaks example's voice was made with (tools/voice/record.py). The recording is measured in 10 ms steps, with any rumble under 70 Hz left out of the measurement. The room's level is that of its quietest tenth. The sound begins at the first sustained sound: one that lasts at least 80 ms, within 30 dB of the loudest and at least 10 dB over the room. A lone thump or lip smack is too short to count. From there the start walks back while the level keeps falling, to keep the breath before a word or a note's attack. It stops in the dip before anything earlier, such as a bumped stand, or where the level reaches the room, and never walks back more than 300 ms. The sound ends 300 ms after the last sustained sound, so a word can breathe out and a note ring. A cut start fades in over 5 ms, and a cut end fades out over 80 ms. A recording with no quiet room to cut, a drone or a pad, has nothing to trim. Neither does one that's already been trimmed.
221.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Where the sound begins
221.title: Where the sound begins

226.body: Patch a sequencer's Gate into Gate , and its Velocity into Velocity . Leave V/Oct unpatched and every hit plays at the recording's own pitch. One-Shot mode plays each hit to the end, however short the gate.
