227.body: Patch Note In 's Pitch , Gate and Velocity into V/Oct , Gate and Velocity , and set Root to the note the file was recorded at. Each key plays the recording faster or slower: an octave up is twice as fast and half as long, as on tape. Set Mode to Gated so that letting go of a key lets its note go, over Rel .
227.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Across the keyboard
227.title: Across the keyboard

228.body: Pitch and speed are one thing here, as on a tape machine. Tune , Fine , Root , V/Oct and Speed all set how fast the recording is read, and so how high it sounds and how long it lasts. A recording made at a different sample rate from your audio device still plays at its own pitch. At negative Speed a note plays backwards, starting at End and finishing at Start . A Speed that changes sign mid-note turns the note around where it is: an LFO into Speed scratches, and an envelope that falls to zero is a tape stop.
228.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Pitch and speed
228.title: Pitch and speed

229.body: Start and End set the part of the recording a note plays. The rest of the waveform sinks into the background. A note fades out over its last 3 ms, so a recording cut mid-sound doesn't click at the end. With Loop on, a note plays from Start to Lp End , then goes round. Forward jumps back to Lp St . Ping-Pong turns around and plays backwards to Lp St , then forwards again. Forward crossfades the jump over 8 ms, blending the end of the loop into the sound just before Lp St , so wherever the points sit the loop goes round without a click. A loop that starts at the very beginning of the recording has nothing before it to blend, so it borrows those 8 ms from its own start and comes round that much sooner. Ping-Pong never jumps. In Gated mode a looping note keeps looping through its release, then fades. In One-Shot mode a looping note never ends. It plays until a new note takes its voice or the transport stops. That's a drone: a field recording slowed down an octave, looping forever.
229.title: What plays

23.body:
A level for the whole mix says little about a song that changes as it goes. Two options take it apart, from the same render, without changing what it sounds like. --trace follows outputs of the patch's modules, named as --cue names them, a colon, then the output (quote the list: output names have spaces). It writes a CSV with a row every --trace-every seconds: the time at the end of the row, then a column for each output. An audio output gives its RMS over the row, its voices summed. A gate gives its highest, so a trigger anywhere in the row reads 1. A CV gives where it ended. Here are Canopy's sections as they go by, and how loud its second Mixer plays: cargo run --release --bin render -- patches/canopy.json out.wav --seconds 120 \ --trace "seq.arranger:Section,seq.arranger:Bar,util.mixer#2:Out L" trace.csv --trace-every 10 seconds,"seq.arranger:Section","seq.arranger:Bar","util.mixer#2:Out L"
10.0000,0.000000,1.000000,0.025193
20.0000,0.031250,1.000000,0.070801
...
70.0000,0.125000,1.000000,0.124964 The Arranger 's Section is the index of the section playing ÷ 32, so 0.125 is the fifth. --stems FOLDER writes each Mixer channel that has something patched into it to a stereo WAV of its own, and each Mixer's return, named by the Mixer's id in the patch file and the channel (util.mixer@126-ch2.wav). A stem is the channel after its Level, Pan, Mute and Solo and the Mixer's Master, before the soft clip that keeps a hot mix from clipping hard, so a Mixer's stems add up to its mix. A chained Mixer's mix arrives on its own stems, not on the Mixer it joins. Each stem is listed with what feeds it and its levels: stems -> stems: util.mixer@126 Ch 1 <- util.vca@70 Out peak -16.0 dBFS rms -24.0 dBFS util.mixer@126-ch1.wav util.mixer@126 Ch 2 <- util.vca@46 Out peak -9.4 dBFS rms -25.3 dBFS util.mixer@126-ch2.wav util.mixer@127 Return <- fx.reverb@128 Out L peak -5.6 dBFS rms -26.0 dBFS util.mixer@127-return.wav
23.title: Following a song

230.body: Set Slices to cut the recording into equal parts, and each key plays one part: Root (C4 unless you move it) plays slice 1, C#4 slice 2, D4 slice 3, and so on up the keys. This is how samplers lay a chopped drum break or a set of vocal phrases across the keyboard. Each slice plays only itself. A note starts at its slice's start and stops at its end, with the same 3 ms fade as at End . In One-Shot mode a short gate still plays the whole slice. In Gated mode the note stops at the slice's end or when the gate falls, whichever comes first. The key picks the slice, not the pitch. V/Oct no longer transposes. Tune , Fine and Speed still do, and a slice played faster goes by sooner. Notes below Root , or past the last slice, play nothing. Slices divide Start–End. Move Start past a silence at the head of the file and the slices are cut from there. A loop goes round the slice. With Loop on, a held note in Gated mode repeats its slice until it's let go. That's a stutter. The Lp St and Lp End markers step aside while sliced. Backwards , at negative Speed , a slice plays from its end to its start. Start CV moves where a note starts inside its slice. 0.5 V starts halfway in. Patch an Arranger lane, a Sample & Hold or an LFO into Slice to pick slices without a keyboard. Its value spreads evenly across them, 0 for the first and 1 for the last, and adds to whatever the note picked. With V/Oct unpatched, Slice alone chooses. On the display, rules divide the waveform into its slices, numbered while they're wide enough to read. The slice a voice is playing glows. Hover a slice to see which key plays it, and Alt-click it to hear it. Sliced by Onsets , the rules are markers you can drag (see Slicing at the hits ).
230.title: Slices

231.body: Equal slices suit a file laid out in slots, a line or a note to each. A drum break or a spoken phrase isn't equal. Its hits and words land where they land, and a hit pushed a little early or dragged a little late is the feel that makes a break worth sampling. Equal sixteenths would cut through those hits. Turn Slices past 64 to Onsets and the Sampler puts a marker where each hit begins: each drum, each syllable, each plucked note. Slice 1 runs from Start to the first marker, and each marker after that starts a slice of its own, up to End . As before, Root plays slice 1 and each key up plays the next. Onset markers on a swung break Two bars of a swung break, sliced by Onsets at 50%: a marker at every kick, snare and hat, wherever the swing put it. The pointer is on the marker that starts slice 9. Sens sets how many hits count. Turned down, only the loudest hits get a marker: the kick and the snare. Turned up, ghost notes, hi-hats and quieter syllables get one too. The markers move as you turn it. The markers are where the sound rises. The recording is split into four bands, from the bass up. A hit is a moment when several of them suddenly get louder together: a quiet hi-hat over a ringing kick still counts, in the top band. A marker goes a millisecond before its hit, so the slice keeps the whole attack. Drag a marker (the white tabs along the top) to move it. Drag it off the panel , up or down, to take it away, and double-click between markers to add one. Each change is a step you can undo. Let go with Alt held to hear the slice the marker now begins. Markers you've moved are kept with the patch. Turning Sens finds them afresh, letting go of what you moved. Undo brings them back. A new file finds them afresh too, as does a new take. Trim to the sound moves them with the sound. Up to 64 slices. Markers outside Start – End cut nothing and are drawn faint. So are markers past the 63rd, and the last slice runs on to End . The hits are found once, when the file loads. Turning Sens only chooses among them, so the markers move as soon as it turns. They're found on the file as it was recorded, so they're the same whatever your device's rate, and the render tool hears the same slices.
231.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Slicing at the hits
231.title: Slicing at the hits

232.body: Sampler is polyphonic. Each channel of the Gate cable is a voice of its own, with its own pitch, velocity and place in the recording. Note In hands each new note the next voice. When all its voices are busy, it takes the oldest note's voice, which lets go of the old note over 5 ms as the new one starts. Retriggering a note that's still sounding does the same, so fast repeated notes never click. Loading a new file while notes play fades them out over 5 ms. The next notes play the new file.
232.title: Voices

233.body: The waveform shows the whole recording, scaled to fill the panel. What plays is lit blue, and the loop is washed orange. Start and End have blue flags at the foot, and the loop points orange flags at the head. Drag any of them like a knob. Hover a marker to see what it is, or the waveform to see the file's path, length and format. Every voice draws a white playhead where it is in the recording, as bright as it is loud. A chord is several lines moving at their own speeds, and a released note fades where it stands. Under the waveform are ▶ (see Hearing it ), the file's name and length, which open Trim and Normalize , and Rec (see Recording into it ), dim until something is patched into In and the patch is playing. A file that can't be found shows its name in orange. An empty Sampler asks for a file.
233.title: The display

234.body:
The Sampler plays WAV files: 8-, 16-, 24- or 32-bit integer, or 32-bit float. Mono files play on both sides. Files with more than two channels play their first two. Each file is resampled to your audio device's rate when it loads, and again if the device's rate changes. A Sampler keeps up to five minutes of audio, about 115 MB of stereo at 48 kHz. A longer file is cut to its first five minutes, and the status bar says so. A patch saves each Sampler's file as a path: Beside or below the patch , the path is relative: samples/kick.wav. Move or zip the patch's folder and it still finds its samples. Elsewhere , the path is absolute: C:/Music/choir.wav. Save As copies samples from outside the patch's folder into a folder beside it named <patch name> samples, and points the patch at the copies. The patch's folder then holds everything it needs to be shared. If the samples come to more than 50 MB, it asks first. Saving an example works the same way, so its samples come with the copy. Save does the same for a sample you've brought in since, from your Downloads say. If those come to more than 50 MB, it leaves them where they are and says so, rather than asking at every save; Save As offers to copy them. A patch whose sample is missing still opens. The Sampler keeps the path but plays nothing, and the status bar lists the missing file with the other load warnings. Open the file again to fix it. In the patch file, the path is the module's file field. Slice markers you've moved are its slice_markers, with the Sens they were placed at, as fractions of the recording. Modules without either leave them out, so patches from before the Sampler read and save as they always did: { "id": 2, "module_id": "source.sampler", "position": [300.0, 74.0], "parameters": [{ "name": "Mode", "type": "Select", "value": 1 }], "file": "samples/fm-bell-c4.wav"
} The render tool finds a patch's samples the same way, relative to the patch file.
234.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Files and patches
234.title: Files and patches

235.body: Voices read between samples on a cubic (Hermite) curve. That's clean at ordinary speeds and pitches. Played more than an octave or so above its root, a bright recording begins to alias: its highest harmonics fold back as a faint metallic edge. Record the sample nearer the range you'll play it in, or filter it after the Sampler.
235.title: Sound quality

237.body: The Sampled Keys example plays a bell across the keyboard: one strike of the FM Synthesis example, rendered by Soba and loaded into a Sampler.
237.title: Sampled keys

238.body:
[Trigger Sequencer Gate 1] ──> [Sampler (kick.wav) Gate]
[Trigger Sequencer Vel 1] ──> [Sampler (kick.wav) Velocity]
[Trigger Sequencer Gate 2] ──> [Sampler (snare.wav) Gate]
... One Sampler per sound, each in One-Shot mode, into a Mixer to place them. Mix them with Drum voices for a kit that's part recorded and part synthesized.
238.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » A drum kit from recordings
238.title: A drum kit from recordings

239.body: Load a long recording (rain, a room, a held note) and set Speed to 0.5, Loop to Ping-Pong with the loop over a steady stretch, Atk to 2 s and Mode to One-Shot . One gate starts a drone an octave down that never ends. Two Samplers on the same file, one at Speed 0.5 and one at 0.749 (a fifth above it), make a chord.
239.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » A drone from anything
239.title: A drone from anything

24.body: Soba opens a microphone or other input only when you choose one in the toolbar's Input menu. macOS asks for permission the first time. If you run Soba from a terminal (cargo run), macOS asks on behalf of the terminal app, and the permission belongs to it. If you said no, or the input stays silent, turn it on under System Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone , then quit and reopen the terminal or the app. Windows lets desktop apps use the microphone unless it's turned off under Settings → Privacy & security → Microphone ( Let desktop apps access your microphone ). Linux has no permission prompt; the input appears if ALSA (or PipeWire's ALSA support) lists it. To run the test suite, use cargo test.
24.title: Microphone access

240.body: Load a one-bar drum loop and set Slices to 8 or 16, so each slice is an eighth or a sixteenth note. Or set it to Onsets , so each hit is a slice however it was played, and move any marker that landed somewhere you don't want it. Patch a Step Sequencer 's Pitch into V/Oct and its Gate into Gate , clocked at the same division. Steps on C4, C#4, D4… play the break as recorded. Change a step's note and that step plays another hit. Patch a Sample & Hold of noise into Slice instead of V/Oct and the break rearranges itself on every hit.
240.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » A chopped break
240.title: A chopped break

241.body: The Clair de Satellite example keeps all eight of its sung lines in one file, a line to a slice. A Step Sequencer that steps every two bars sings line k on note C4 + k .
241.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Sampler » Many lines in one file
241.title: Many lines in one file

242.body: Patch a slow LFO into Start , and a Clock into Gate . Each note starts a little further into the recording, so a spoken phrase or a melody comes out in stutters that wander through it.
242.title: Scrubbing

243.body: Note In : plays the Sampler as an instrument, a voice per key Trigger Sequencer and Step Sequencer : one-shots in time Audio Input : outside sound live, as it happens. Patched into In , the Sampler records it Looper : records and layers live loops, where the Sampler records a take to play from a key or a gate Drum : synthesized drums to sit beside recorded ones Vocoder : a recorded voice that makes a chord speak, as in the Soba Speaks example
243.title: Related modules

244.body: Module ID source.chopper · Category Source Chopper Module Two bars of a break in sixteen slices, each in a hue of its own, and the row of steps under them, each tinted like the slice it plays. Step 6 plays slice 2 backwards, step 12 plays its slice a fourth down, step 14 rests and step 16 stutters ×4. The dots in the corners are dice. The tick under the row is where the loop is in time; the white playhead is where it's reading. Chopper plays a drum break in time with the Clock , and lets you rearrange it step by step. A Sampler sliced into a break plays a slice for each note: the right tool for playing a break from a keyboard. A break played in a groove asks for more. It has to stay in time, follow the patch's tempo without changing pitch, and be re-sequenced: a snare moved, a kick doubled, a fill stuttered, a hit played backwards. Doing that with a Sampler and a Step Sequencer means a note for every slice of every step, set by hand, and retuning the break whenever the tempo moves. The Chopper does it all in one module.
244.title: Chopper

245.body: The break is cut into slices: equal ones, or one at each hit. Each slice starts on the beat it started on in the break, and plays at its own speed. A file that plays a REX loop works this way, and so did the samplers the breaks of jungle and hip-hop were chopped on. Faster than the break was played, each slice starts sooner and cuts the one before it short. Slower , each slice ends before the next begins, and a short fade closes the gap. At its own tempo , every slice runs on into the next, which fades in over the same 3 ms. The two read the same sound at that moment, so the crossfade is invisible and the break plays back exactly as recorded, round and round. Either way the pitch never moves, and nor does the groove: a hit pushed late in the break is still late, by the same share of a beat, at any tempo. Patch the Clock's Gate into Clock , and set Pulse to the Clock's own Div : 1/16 for sixteenths. Then set Beats to how long the break is: 4 for one bar of 4/4, 8 for two. The name under the waveform shows the tempo the break plays at unchanged, as long as Beats says. Patch the Clock's Reset into Reset too, so the loop starts from its top whenever the Clock does.
245.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chopper » How it keeps time
245.title: How it keeps time

246.body: Under the waveform is a row of steps, one for each slice. Each step's turn comes where its slice began in the break, and left alone it plays its slice. Unedited, the row runs through the slices' hues in order, a spectrum from end to end, and the break plays as recorded. Each step can be told to play it differently: Another slice. Drag the step up or down, or right-click it and choose one. The step takes on that slice's hue, so a rearranged pattern can be read at a glance: which slices come back, which never play. Backwards (Alt+click). It plays its slice from the end, and carries an arrow pointing back. Repeat ×2, ×3 or ×4 (Shift+click). It plays its slice from the top that many times, evenly across its turn: a stutter, or a roll at the end of a phrase. The step splits into its hits. Pitch , from 12 semitones down to 12 up (right-click). Tape-style: higher plays faster and leaves a gap before the next step, lower plays slower and is cut short by it. The step shows the semitones. Rest (click). Nothing plays, and the Gate stays low. The step is an empty outline. Chance (Ctrl+click steps through 0, 25, 50 and 100%). How often the step swaps its slice for one at random, so the break varies itself. A dot in the step's corner grows with the chance. A pattern plays its dice the same way each time the transport starts from the top. A rest remembers what it was, so clicking it again plays it as before. Right-click a step for all of these, Back to slice n, as it was , Shuffle the slices (every step a slice at random, each slice once) and Reset every step . Every edit is a step you can undo.
246.title: The steps

247.body: A chopped break often runs under a longer pattern: two bars of break, four bars of pattern, the second half a variation on the first. Steps sets how long the row is: 1 per slice (the row as above), or 2 , 3 or 4 per slice . Past the first pass the row wraps over the break again, and each extra step starts out playing its slice in the next pass, so left alone it still plays the break as recorded, round and round. The face shows a line of steps for each pass, each line under the same slices, so a step reads straight down to the same slice's turn in the other passes. Edit any of them on its own. A step past the first pass has two more things on its right-click menu: Same as pass n copies the pass above into its own, to vary from there, and Shuffle the slices in pass n shuffles only its own line. Reset every step resets the whole row. The row has at most 64 steps, so more slices allow fewer passes: up to 16 slices take all four, up to 21 three, up to 32 two, and more than that one.
247.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chopper » A pattern longer than the break
247.title: A pattern longer than the break

248.body: Load a file as on the Sampler: click Open… , or the empty panel, or drag a WAV, MP3, FLAC or Ogg file onto the node. While a dragged file is over the node you hear it, so you can audition files before you drop one. It plays once when it loads, so you hear what you chose, and ▶ plays it again at any time, dry, beside the patch. Alt-click a slice to hear just that slice. The file should be the loop itself, start to end: a break cut on its downbeats, as you'd cut one to loop it in a sampler. The Cut-Up example's break is made by Soba's own Drums (tools/breaks/make_break.py), so it's free to use however you like.
248.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chopper » Loading a break
248.title: Loading a break

249.body: The Chopper can record its own break. Patch something into In L (and In R , for stereo) and press the red Rec button beside Open… . It's the Sampler's recorder : the same button, the same take drawn in red as it comes in, and the same file beside the patch when it's done. Play a phrase into the patch, from a Note In , an Audio Input or the patch's own drums, and chop it up straight away. Take starts at 1 bar . With a Clock running, Rec then waits for the next bar line, which the panel says, and records exactly that many bars, so the take is already a loop. As it comes in, the panel ticks its beats, each bar more strongly, and counts bar and beat of the bars, REC 2.3 / 4, so you can see how much of the phrase is left to play. When it ends, it's the break: it plays at once, from its top on the bar it ended, and Beats is set to its length, 8 for two bars of 4/4, so it loops in time. Undo brings back the break you had, with its Beats . Free records until Rec is pressed again. A free take made while a Clock runs is set to as many beats as it nearly is; without a Clock, Beats is left as it was. Patch a gate into the Rec jack and it takes over from the button: a take starts as it rises (or on the next bar) and ends as it falls. Right-click Rec to learn a MIDI footswitch for it.
249.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chopper » Recording a break
249.title: Recording a break

25.body: No sound. Check that ▶ Play is pressed: the app opens stopped. Then check the Output device menu in the toolbar. It lists every output device, with the system default marked (Default) ; pick the one you're listening on. 🔄 Refresh at the bottom of the menu picks up a device you plugged in after starting. Until you pick one, Soba plays to whatever Windows has as its default, and follows it: plug in headphones and the sound moves to them, with Output moved to … in the status bar. If the default goes away with nothing to take its place, the sound comes back on its own once a device does. "Audio unavailable" in the toolbar. Soba couldn't open an output device. Make sure one is connected and that no other application holds it exclusively, then restart. Crackles and dropouts. Make sure you're running the release build. The toolbar's CPU meter, shown while the patch plays, tells you how close the engine is to its limit. If it's near the top, remove modules or lower Voices on Note In and the Oscillator's unison. My MIDI controller does nothing. Choose it in the toolbar's MIDI In menu: Soba doesn't connect to a controller until you do. In the browser, click 🎹 Connect MIDI there first. A filled dot (●) before the name means it's connected. Connection errors appear in the status bar at the bottom of the window. See MIDI .
25.title: Troubleshooting

250.body: Slices cuts the loop into 2 to 64 equal slices. Eighth notes suit a swung break, since swing moves the sixteenths in between, not the eighths. Turn it past 64 to Onsets and the loop is cut at its hits instead, exactly as on the Sampler : Sens chooses how many hits count, and the markers drag, come off the panel and are added by double-click. Let go of a marker with Alt held to hear the slice it now begins. Cut at the hits, the steps stay evenly spaced under the waveform but the slices don't, so the fan of rules between them leans. Each hit then starts on its own place in the beat, swing and all, and the step row still gives every hit a step.
250.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chopper » Slicing at the hits
250.title: Slicing at the hits

251.body: Port Signal Type Description Clock Gate (Green) Each rising edge is a pulse, worth what Pulse says. The loop plays from the first pulse after a reset. With nothing patched, nothing plays Reset Gate (Green) A rising edge starts over: the next pulse plays the loop from its top Slice Control (Orange) Picks the slice each step plays as its turn comes, in place of its own: 0 to 1 across the slices. An Arranger lane or a Sample & Hold here rearranges the break from outside. Repeats, pitch and rests still come from the step In L , In R Audio (Blue) What Rec records (see Recording a break ). One side patched records on both Rec Gate (Green) Records while high. Patched, it takes over from the button
251.title: Inputs

252.body: Port Signal Type Description L Audio (Blue) The left channel. A mono file plays the same on both outputs R Audio (Blue) The right channel Gate Gate (Green) High for half of each slice played, repeats included, and low through a rest. An envelope, a Drum or a sequencer's Clock here follows the chop
252.title: Outputs

253.body: Control Range Default Description Pulse 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 1/16 What each pulse at Clock is worth. Set it to the Clock's Div Beats 1 – 64 4 How long the loop is, in beats Slices 2 – 64, Onsets 16 Equal slices, or one at each hit. Each slice gets a step Sens (Sensitivity) 0 – 100% 50% Sliced by Onsets , how strong a hit must be to get a marker Level 0 – 100% 80% Output level Steps 1 – 4 per slice 1 per slice How long the row is: a pass over the break for each (see A pattern longer than the break ) Take Free, 1 – 16 bars 1 bar In bars, with a Clock running, a take starts on the next bar and lasts that long, and sets Beats to match
253.title: Parameters

254.body: Find the break's tempo. A loop of 2.000 seconds at Beats 4 is 120 BPM, and the name under the waveform says so. If the number looks odd (91.3 BPM), Beats is likely wrong, or the file isn't cut on its downbeats. Slow it right down and the gaps between slices become part of the sound: a break at half speed is a sparse, clipped pattern of hits, each followed by silence. One break, two Choppers. Patch the same file into a second Chopper with another pattern and pan the two apart, or let one take over from the other by riding the Mixer. Resample a groove. Patch the mix of a few drums into In , record four bars, then rearrange what you just played: the drums can keep going beside it, or be muted for the chopped version to take over. Follow the chop. The Gate output rises on every slice, so a bass line clocked by it moves with the drums, and an envelope from it pumps a pad in time with each hit.
254.title: Tips

255.body: Module ID source.cloud · Category Source Cloud module Canopy's twelve sung syllables, played as a cloud of a Dmaj9 chord. The wash is where grains may start: Position, as wide as Spray scatters them. Each spark is a grain, at its place in the file and as high or low as it sits in the stereo field, bright as it swells and fading as it ends Cloud is a granular source. It plays clouds of small grains read from a recording, each a few milliseconds to two seconds long, faded in and out under a smooth window. Every other sample tool in Soba ( Sampler , Chopper , Looper ) plays time in order. Granular takes it apart: a sung syllable stretched into a held chord, a drum loop turned into a hiss of sparks, a moment of a voice frozen and played for as long as you like. It plays a WAV, MP3, FLAC or Ogg file, opened or dragged onto it as for the Sampler, or live audio patched into In : the last six seconds of it, which Freeze holds.
255.title: Cloud

256.body: A grain is a short read of the source: Where. It starts at Position , across the source from its start (left) to its end (right). Spray scatters it either side. How long. It lasts Size , under a Hann window that rises from nothing and falls back to nothing, so no grain clicks, however short. How high. It reads the source faster or slower by Pitch , tape-style, so its pitch and its formants move together. A grain read faster than the recording runs through a steep lowpass of its own first, so nothing folds back down as aliasing, even three octaves up. Where in the field. It sits at a random place across the stereo field, as wide as Spread . Density says how many grains start each second. With Spray at nothing they start on a regular beat and read the same place, which buzzes at the Density's rate: turn Density into the audio range and Size down and you hear it as a pitch. Spray scatters them in place and in time until they blur into a cloud. Up to 64 grains play at once. Past that, a new one waits for a free place: a dense, long-grained cloud thins out rather than clicking or overloading. However many overlap, the cloud keeps about the same loudness.
256.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Cloud » How it works
256.title: How it works

257.body: Patch something into In L (and In R , or leave it and In L plays on both sides) and the Cloud plays the last six seconds of it in place of the file. Position 1 is just now, and 0 six seconds ago. Grains always read audio already recorded, and never the moment being written. Freeze stops recording, so the six seconds it holds stay to be played. Turn the switch on, or patch a gate: while the gate is high, it's frozen. A Clock Divider 's Gate on Freeze catches a new moment every few bars; a footswitch catches whatever you just played. While it fills, the face shows the part not yet recorded in the dark, and a grain needs a whole Size of audio behind it before it can start.
257.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Cloud » Live audio and Freeze
257.title: Live audio and Freeze

258.body: A polyphonic cable into Pitch grows a cloud for each of its channels, each at its own pitch, out of the one pool of grains. A Chord Sequencer 's Pitch into it plays a cloud of each chord: see Choir of One . A chord's clouds add up as a chord's notes do, so a four-note chord is louder than one note. Patch a polyphonic Gate as well and each channel's cloud grows only while its gate is high. The grains still sounding play out.
258.title: Polyphony

266.body: Module ID source.audio_input · Category Source Audio Input Module A drum loop coming in on input 1, with Channel on 1 so both meters carry it. Follow scrolls past the Threshold line, turning green wherever the gate opened: the kicks get through, the snares stay under. Audio Input brings sound from outside into the patch: a microphone, a guitar, a synth on a line input. 269.body: An audio interface hands its inputs over as a pair: input 1 on the left, input 2 on the right. That's right for a stereo source, like a synth's two outputs, but a guitar or a microphone plugged into input 1 alone would play only in your left ear, and a stereo delay or reverb after it would get a lopsided signal. Channel picks what the module hears: Channel L hears R hears For 1+2 input 1 input 2 A stereo source across both inputs, or a device with a single input (see below) 1 input 1 input 1 A guitar or microphone in input 1, heard in the centre 2 input 2 input 2 The same, in input 2 3+4 , 5+6 … input 3 input 4 A stereo source on a later pair: a synth's two outputs on a mixer's channels 3 and 4 3 , 4 … that input that input A mono source on any input Follow and Gate hear what the module puts out. On one input they follow that input alone. On a pair they follow whichever side is louder. Each Audio Input module chooses for itself, so several of them can split an interface: one on 1 for a guitar through a filter and an echo, one on 2 for a voice through a reverb, each in its own chain.

270.body: Some interfaces and mixers hand the computer every input they have, each its own channel. A Tascam Model 12 or a Zoom L6 sends each mixer channel, so a drum machine, a sampler and a synth plugged into it can each come back on their own, with their own effects, rather than as one stereo mix. Give each its own Audio Input: say 1+2 for the drum machine's stereo pair, 3 for a mono synth and 5+6 for the sampler. An interface like a Scarlett 18i20 works the same way. While a device is open, the menu offers only the inputs it has: 1+2 , 1 and 2 on a stereo interface, up to 11+12 and 12 on a twelve-input one. Soba hears up to 16 inputs of a device. They're listed by number: the names an interface gives its inputs don't reach Soba through its audio library yet. A patch made on a bigger interface keeps its choice: an Audio Input set to an input this device hasn't is silent, and hovering its menu says so. A device that has only one input, like a laptop's built-in microphone or a USB mic, already plays on both sides of 1+2 , 1 or 2 . Patches saved before Soba heard every input open on the same choice they had: Stereo is now 1+2 .

271.body: On the left, two slim meters show the input's peaks after Gain , on the same scale as the Audio Output meter. Hover them for the levels in dBFS. Set Gain so your loudest playing stays out of the red. On the right, the last three seconds of Follow scroll past, newest at the right edge. The Threshold lies across them as a dashed green line, and the trace turns green wherever the gate was open, so you can see which hits got through. Drag the line up or down to move the Threshold; the lamp at its end lights while the gate is open. The name of the device it's listening to sits faintly in the corner.

272.body: Follow is an envelope follower: it rises with the input's peaks at the Attack speed and falls back at the Release speed. Its scale is in decibels, not raw level. A whisper and a shout are 40 dB apart, which is a hundredth to one in raw level but 0.3 to 1 in Follow, so quiet and loud playing both move what it's patched to. Short Attack times catch the front of a drum hit. Longer ones, 20–50 ms, smooth out the fast wiggles of a voice. Release sets how long Follow hangs on after a sound stops: around 100 ms for a tight pumping effect, a second or more for a slow swell. Gate opens when Follow rises above the Threshold , and closes again only once Follow falls 6 dB below it. That gap stops the gate chattering open and shut when the level hovers right at the threshold. Because the gate follows Follow, a longer Release also holds the gate open longer.
272.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Audio Input » Follow and Gate
272.title: Follow and Gate

273.body: Right-click the module and choose Record into a new Sampler . A Sampler appears beside it, patched from L and R , listening at −40 dB with Rec already pressed. The take starts on your first word. Press the Sampler's Rec to stop it, and play the take from a key or a gate.

273.title: Recording yourself

274.body: Live input passes through two devices, each with its own clock and buffer: the input and the output. To keep the sound smooth, Soba holds a little audio between them, about one buffer of each. While an input is open, the status bar shows In and the round trip: how long a sound takes from the input jack to the speakers, often around 60 ms on Windows. Hover it for the parts that add up to it, then the device and any dropouts so far. It turns amber for a few seconds after a dropout, or after a glitch the device itself reports (a lone one when the input first opens is common, and harmless). Part Typical (Windows) What it is Input device ~10 ms The input device's own buffer: audio waits there until a packet is full Buffer ~13 ms What Soba holds between the two devices to ride out their uneven timing, once settled Output device ~30 ms The output device's own buffer and the Windows audio engine behind it, before the speakers play it Limiter 1 ms The Audio Output limiter's look-ahead Each device's figure comes from the timestamps it puts on its audio. Windows doesn't time captured audio usefully, so there the input is counted as one packet, the least it can be, and the hover marks it with ~ . If a device reports nothing at all, the label gets a + ( In 22+ ms ): the real round trip is longer than the parts Soba can count. Neither figure includes the converters inside the interface, usually another millisecond or two each way. The Buffer settles on its own. It opens holding enough for the worst timing the two devices could have, then over the first few seconds it watches how much of that they really need, and trims the rest, a frame at a time so you don't hear it. If the two devices' clocks drift apart, as separate devices' do, it eases a block a fraction faster or slower to keep in step rather than letting the audio drop out. After a dropout it holds a little more, then tries the leaner amount again after a quiet half minute. The hover shows how much it has trimmed and stretched. Different sample rates are fine. Windows often runs a microphone at 48 kHz and speakers at 44.1 kHz, even on one interface. Soba converts the input to the output's rate on the way in. For the cleanest sound, set both to the same rate in your system's sound settings; the status bar tooltip says when it's converting. Changing the Output device reopens the input at the new device's rate. If the input device is unplugged, the status bar shows ⚠ Input lost . Choose it again under Input . A mono device is heard on both sides. With an interface of two inputs or more, set Channel to the input you're using; see Choosing a channel .
274.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Audio Input » Latency and devices
274.title: Latency and devices

275.body: ASIO is a registered trademark of Steinberg Media Technologies GmbH Windows Audio is shared by every app, and each direction passes through the Windows audio engine: fine for a pad or a sampled loop, but a guitarist hears 60 ms as a slap-back echo of their own playing. An audio interface's ASIO driver skips all of that. Input and output come from one driver, on one clock, in buffers a few milliseconds long, and Soba holds nothing between them: each output buffer is computed from the input that arrived moments before. To use it, download the low-latency Windows build, or build Soba with ASIO yourself (both in Build with ASIO ), then open the Output menu and choose ASIO under Audio system . The menu then lists ASIO drivers, and Input offers that driver's inputs. Choose it there to hear your interface. Buffer sets how many frames the driver hands over at a time, and the closed Output menu shows it beside the driver's name: Buffer At 48 kHz Round trip, measured 32 0.7 ms 11 ms The quickest; needs a computer with headroom 64 1.3 ms 14 ms Tight enough to play guitar against 128 2.7 ms 20 ms A good start: feels immediate for most playing 256 5.3 ms 32 ms Busy patches with long reverbs 512 10.7 ms 52 ms Room to spare; too slow to play against Measured on a first-generation Scarlett 2i2 with Focusrite's driver. The round trip is more than one buffer in and one out: each driver keeps a safety margin of its own, Focusrite's about another buffer and a few milliseconds each way, and Soba's limiter adds 1 ms. The status bar's In shows yours. If you hear crackles, or the CPU meter runs high, go up a size. Smaller buffers make Soba answer more often, with less time for each answer. ASIO drivers serve one app at a time. If another app (a DAW, say) has the interface, choosing ASIO says so and stays on Windows Audio. Changing the buffer from the driver's own control panel restarts audio at the driver's new size, with a note in the status bar. Soba remembers the audio system and buffer between sessions.
275.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Audio Input » Low latency with ASIO (Windows)
275.title: Low latency with ASIO (Windows)

277.body: The render tool has no input device, so Audio Input renders silence. Give it a WAV file to hear instead with --input: cargo run --release --bin render -- my-patch.json out.wav --input voice.wav The file plays from the start of the render, converted to the render's sample rate (48 kHz unless you pass --sample-rate) if it was recorded at another. 284.body: Module ID input.poly_midi · Category Source Note In module A chord from a MIDI keyboard and a note on the computer keys, lit on its piano. Note In is how you play a patch. It takes notes from your computer keyboard, from the piano on its face (held with the mouse or a finger), and from a MIDI device: a keyboard, a pad controller, or a DAW or sequencer sending MIDI. It turns them into a V/Oct Pitch , a Gate , a Velocity and an Aftertouch signal that any module can use. It needs no setup and no hardware, which makes it the quickest way to hear a patch: the First Sound example that opens with the app is played from one. With Voices at 1 it plays one note at a time, as a classic monosynth does: Priority decides which held key sounds. With more voices it plays chords. Every note you play gets a voice of its own, and the Pitch , Gate and Velocity cables carry all the voices at once, one channel per voice. Patch them into the polyphonic modules (Oscillator, SVF and Ladder filters, ADSR, VCA) and each held note plays through its own oscillator, filter and envelope. See Polyphony for how polyphonic cables work. Every note, from the keys or from MIDI, starts on its exact sample, however short it is.
284.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » Note In
284.title: Note In

288.body:
The bottom two letter rows form a piano keyboard starting at C4. The bottom row plays the white keys and the row above it plays the black keys, sitting between them as they would on a piano. The top letter row and the numbers above it are a second piano laid out the same way, an octave higher, as in a tracker: Black keys: 2 3 5 6 7 9 0
White keys: Q W E R T Y U I O P
Note: C5 D E F G A B C6 D E Black keys: S D G H J L ;
White keys: Z X C V B N M , . /
Note: C4 D E F G A B C5 D E That's C4 to E6, a little over two octaves. The pianos overlap by a few notes: , . / play the same C, D and E as Q W E , so a run up the bottom row can carry on along the top. Turn Oct to move the whole range. The piano on the face plays too. Hold a key with the mouse, or a finger on a touch screen, and it plays like a computer key; slide across the keys and the pitch follows. It's how Note In is played on a phone. Keys don't play notes while you hold Ctrl or Alt (those are shortcuts), while you're typing in a text field, or while the quick-add palette is open. Space and Tab open the palette, so they're never notes. The app has to have keyboard focus: if nothing happens, click the canvas. Switching to another window lets go of every key held. The keys play every Note In whose Source isn't MIDI, in the browser and inside a DAW as well as in the app, with or without a MIDI device. The MIDI Monitor shows them as Keys .

289.body: MIDI comes in from the devices ticked in MIDI In on the toolbar. The menu lists every MIDI input the system can see. Tick one and the dot fills in (●) once it's open. Tick as many as you play at once, up to eight: a keyboard, a pad controller and a drum machine sending clock can all be open together. Untick one to close it. None (Disconnect) closes them all. Plugged in a device after starting Soba? Open the menu and click 🔄 Refresh . In the browser, the menu is a 🎹 Connect MIDI button until you allow MIDI, and a device plugged in later appears by itself. See MIDI . Connection failed? The reason appears in the status bar at the bottom of the window, and the device stays unticked. On Windows, a device another app already has open (a DAW, a browser, a controller's editor) can't be opened a second time, so close the other app and tick the device again. Closing or unplugging a device releases the notes still held on it, so nothing sticks. Notes held on the other devices play on. Inside a DAW, Soba plays the notes on its track, and there's no MIDI In menu. Soba remembers the devices ticked and opens them again next launch, or as soon as each is plugged in.

290.body: Every Note In hears every device open, until you give it a Device . Right-click the module, open Device and choose one of the devices open. Its name appears faintly after the module's title, and from then on the module hears that device alone. Two keyboards can then play two synths, each through its own Note In, on the same MIDI channel. Any hears them all again. The Device is saved with the patch, by the device's name, so the patch finds it on another computer with the same gear. While no device of that name is open, the name dims and the module hears no MIDI. It still hears the computer keys and the piano, which aren't a device. Pads , Controls , the Clock and the MIDI Monitor have a Device too.
290.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » Listening to one device
290.title: Listening to one device

291.body: A Pads module claims the notes its pads listen to, on their channel: by default notes 36 to 43 on channel 10, which most pad controllers send. A Note In on Omni skips those notes, so hitting a pad plays its drum and not the synth as well. The piano doesn't light for them either. A Pads set to one Device claims that device's notes alone. With the Pads on the pad controller, a keyboard's note 36 on channel 10 still plays the synth. A Note In set to a channel hears all of that channel's notes, claimed or not. Set Ch to the pads' channel to play notes from the pads too. The computer keys and the piano are never claimed.
291.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » Claimed notes
291.title: Claimed notes

292.body: Note On raises the voice's gate and moves its Pitch to the note. Note Off drops the gate. Pitch stays on the note, so a release tail stays in tune. Pitch bend moves Pitch by up to ± Bend semitones. It glides over about 5 ms between the wheel's steps, so bends never zipper. Channel pressure appears on Aftertouch . The sustain pedal (CC 64) holds notes after their keys come up. Lifting it releases them all. All Notes Off (CC 123) and All Sound Off (CC 120) release every note the device that sent them is playing, pedal or not, and lift its pedal. Soba sends one when a device is closed or unplugged, so a Note In on Any lets go of that device's notes and plays on with the others'. From a DAW, they release everything. Each semitone is 1/12 on Pitch , so MIDI note 72 (C5) is +1.0 and note 48 (C3) is −1.0. With every tune knob at 0, the Oscillator plays C4 at 0.0, so Note In plays it in tune with nothing to set.
292.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » How notes become CV
292.title: How notes become CV

293.body: Notes are handled on the audio thread. Each one is stamped the moment it arrives, from a device or from the keys, and placed at the matching sample of the next audio buffer. Every note is delayed by the same amount, one audio buffer (a few milliseconds), so a steady sequence from a DAW plays back steady, with no jitter. Even the shortest note produces a gate.
293.title: Timing

294.body: With Voices at 1, Note In plays legato. The first key raises the gate, and while any key is held the gate stays up: pressing another key moves Pitch to it without retriggering the envelope, so overlapping your key presses slurs one note into the next. When several keys are held, Priority picks the one that sounds: Priority The key that sounds Good for Last The most recently pressed Most playing Low The lowest Basslines: a held bass note wins over anything played above it High The highest Leads over a held drone Release the sounding key and another held key takes over, so you can trill against a held note. With Retrig off, playing legato changes the pitch but keeps the gate high, so the envelope carries on, for smooth, connected lines. With Retrig on, each legato note drops the gate for a single sample, so the envelope starts again on every note. The cables carry one channel, so a monophonic patch hears one note.
294.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » One voice
294.title: One voice

295.body: With several voices, Rotate gives each new note the next free voice in turn. A released note keeps ringing through its release while the next note sounds on a different voice, so release tails overlap naturally. Reuse sends a note played again back to the voice that last played it, the way a piano string is struck again. Any other note takes the voice that has been free the longest, which gives release tails the most time to finish. In either mode, a note played again while it's still sounding (held by the sustain pedal, say) restarts on its own voice rather than taking a second one.
295.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » Voice allocation
295.title: Voice allocation

296.body: When every voice is busy, a new note takes one over. It chooses: a voice the sustain pedal is holding (its key already up), oldest first; otherwise, the oldest note still held. The taken voice's gate drops for one sample, so its envelope starts again for the new note.
296.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » Voice stealing
296.title: Voice stealing

297.body: Glide makes the pitch slide from one note to the next instead of jumping, like the portamento on a classic monosynth. The knob sets how long the slide takes, from Off up to 2 seconds. Most of its travel covers the short times, where glide is most useful: 200 ms is a little past halfway. Even across the keyboard. The slide moves evenly in pitch, so it sounds the same low or high. The same time for any distance. An octave leap arrives as quickly as a step to the next semitone. Eases in. The pitch covers most of the distance early and settles gently onto the note: about two thirds of the way in the first fifth of the time, and within 1% of the note by the end of it. The Glide dropdown picks which notes slide: Glide Mode Which notes slide Feels like Legato Only a note played while another key is still held. A note after a gap starts on its own pitch A Minimoog or a 303: you choose each slide with your fingers Always Every note, from wherever the last one left off Portamento that's always on Pitch bend rides on top of the glide: the wheel moves the pitch at once while the note underneath slides. With one voice, Glide and Retrig work together, so with both on, each legato note restarts the envelope and slides into pitch. With several voices, each voice slides from its own previous note. Change chords with Glide up and every voice takes its own path, crossing and converging, the way the voices of a vintage polysynth do. A stolen voice slides from wherever it was. Mode decides where each slide starts: with Reuse , a note played again returns to the voice that last played it, so it doesn't slide at all; with Rotate , the voices take turns, so each slide starts from a different note of the last chord or two. In Legato mode a chord struck from nothing starts on its own pitches: notes arriving within 30 ms of the first count as part of that chord, since no hand strikes every key at once. To hear it, open First Sound and turn Glide to about 200 ms. Hold Z (C) and tap B (G): the pitch slides up to G and, when you let go of B, back down to C.
297.title: Glide

298.body: Any knob in the patch can follow a MIDI controller (a mod wheel, a fader, a knob on your keyboard), and so can toggles, dropdowns and footswitches, from pads as well as knobs. This works with or without a Note In in the patch. Right-click the knob and choose Learn MIDI . A purple M badge blinks above it, and the status bar asks you to move a control. Move the knob or fader on your controller. The badge stops blinking: the knob is mapped. Changed your mind, or no controller to hand? Press Escape, or right-click the blinking knob and choose Cancel MIDI Learn , and nothing is mapped. Starting learn on another knob moves it there instead. The controller sweeps the knob's whole range, on the channel it was learned on. A fader picks the knob up where it stands rather than jumping it, and an endless encoder steps it. Right-click a mapped knob to see its CC number and channel, to Re-learn MIDI , or to Clear MIDI . Mappings are saved with the patch. Moves made by a controller aren't added to the undo history. MIDI Learn in the interface overview says what pads do to each kind of control.
298.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » MIDI Learn
298.title: MIDI Learn

299.body:
The smallest playable voice, as in the First Sound example, with Voices at 1: [Note In Pitch] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct]
[Note In Gate] ──> [ADSR Gate]
[Oscillator Out] ──> [VCA In]
[ADSR Out] ──> [VCA CV]
[VCA Out] ──> [Audio Output Mono] Chords, with Voices at 8: [Note In Pitch] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct]
[Note In Gate] ──> [ADSR Gate]
[Note In Velocity] ──> [ADSR Velocity]
[Oscillator Out] ──> [Ladder Filter In]
[Ladder Filter LP24] ──> [VCA In]
[ADSR Out] ──> [VCA CV]
[VCA Out] ──> [Audio Output Mono] Hold a chord and each note has its own oscillator, filter and envelope. The Audio Output is a mono module, so it hears the voices summed. Voices add up, so a four-note chord is about four times as loud as one note: leave headroom with the VCA's Level . The Lush Pad example is built this way. Velocity on the ADSR Envelope makes harder notes louder. Patch Aftertouch into the filter's Cutoff to brighten a note as you press into the key. Two voices on two channels, for a bass and a lead from one DAW: [Note In (Ch 1, Voices 1, Priority Low)] ──> [Bass voice]
[Note In (Ch 2, Voices 1, Priority High)] ──> [Lead voice]
299.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » Patch examples
299.title: Patch examples

3.body: There are 44 modules in six categories. A module's header takes its category's color: Category Header Modules Source Blue Oscillator, Noise, Drum, Resonator, Sampler, Chopper, Cloud, Audio Input, Note In Filter Teal SVF Filter, Ladder Filter Modulation Orange ADSR Envelope, LFO, Slope Effect Cyan Stereo Delay, Reverb, 3-Band EQ, Distortion, Chorus, Tape, Slicer, Compressor, Vocoder Utility Gray Clock, VCA, Attenuverter, Mix, Mixer, Sample & Hold, Quantizer, Clock Divider, Logic, Looper, Oscilloscope, Dancer, Step Sequencer, Chord Sequencer, Trigger Sequencer, Arranger, MIDI Monitor Output Purple Audio Output, Link Out The Module Overview introduces each one.
3.title: Modules

300.body: Note In takes the place of three modules: Keyboard (the computer keys, one voice), MIDI Note (MIDI, one voice) and Poly MIDI (chords). A patch saved with any of them opens with Note In in their places, and plays as it did: a Keyboard becomes a Note In with one voice on Keys , at the Keyboard's velocity; a MIDI Note becomes one with one voice on MIDI ; and a Poly MIDI is a Note In already.
300.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » Older patches
300.title: Older patches

301.body: No sound. Press Play : notes only sound while the patch is playing. Check Source . For MIDI, check that the device is selected in MIDI In and that its dot is filled, and set Ch to Omni in case the device sends on another channel. A MIDI Monitor shows whether anything is arriving at all. Only one note of a chord sounds. Voices is at 1, or the cables run into a module that isn't polyphonic, which hears one channel. Some notes don't play. A Pads module in the patch claims its pads' notes from a Note In on Omni (see Claimed notes ). Learn the pads onto other notes, or set Ch to the channel you play on. Wrong pitch. Check Oct , and that the pitch bend wheel is centered. Stuck note. Send All Notes Off from your controller, or select the device again in MIDI In . Either releases every note held from that device.
301.title: Troubleshooting

302.body: MIDI Monitor – see the notes that are arriving Pads – a pad controller's pads as gates, for finger drums Oscillator – where Pitch usually goes ADSR Envelope – where Gate and Velocity usually go Chord Sequencer – plays chords for you
302.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Note In » Related modules
302.title: Related modules

303.body: Module ID input.controls · Category Source Controls turns the faders, knobs, wheels and strips of a MIDI controller into cables. Each of its four slots, A to D , hears one control and puts it out as a Control signal, so you can patch it wherever a cable goes: one fader into a filter's Cutoff , another into a VCA, a third through an Attenuverter into an LFO's Rate . MIDI Learn can also turn a knob from your controller, but only a knob that's already on a module. Controls is for when the controller is the source: one move feeding several places, a fader scaled and flipped before it arrives, or a control mixed with an LFO. It listens to the devices ticked in MIDI In on the toolbar, or to the one chosen under Device in its right-click menu (see Listening to one device ), and reads each move on its own sample, as Note In reads notes.
303.title: Controls

304.body: Port Signal Type Description A , B , C , D Control (Orange) Each slot's control: 0 to 1, or −1 to 1 when its range is bipolar
304.title: Outputs

305.body: Each slot is a slim fader that moves with the hardware, showing what its cable carries. The fill rises from the bottom, or from the middle for a bipolar slot. The cap warms to orange while the control moves, and cools again once it rests. A slot's letter lights up once a cable leaves it. Under each fader is what the slot hears (CC 74, Bend, Mod, Press) and its channel. Hover a fader to read it in full, with the value it's sending now. When you add a Controls module, its slots already hear a keyboard's own controls, so they work before you learn anything: Slot Hears A The mod wheel (CC 1) B The pitch bend, from −1 to 1 C Channel pressure D CC 74, which many controllers send from their first knob
305.title: The face

306.body: Right-click a slot's fader and choose Learn MIDI . Its label blinks purple, and the status bar asks you to move something. Move a fader or a knob, bend the pitch wheel or strip, or press a key down on your controller. The slot now hears that control, on the channel it came on. Learning a slot again replaces what it heard, and Undo takes a learn back. To give up before moving anything, press Escape, or right-click the blinking slot and choose Cancel MIDI Learn . What the slots hear is saved with the patch. Learning a slot only teaches the slot. Nothing is mapped, and a note you play while it waits still plays.
306.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Controls » Learning a control
306.title: Learning a control

307.body: Right-click a fader to choose what its slot hears by hand: Item Choices Description Source CC / Pitch Bend / Mod Wheel / Pressure What the slot hears. For a CC, set its number here too Channel Omni / 1 – 16 Only hear this MIDI channel. Omni hears all of them. A learned slot hears the channel it was learned on Range Auto / 0 to 1 / −1 to 1 0 to 1 runs from the bottom of the control's travel to the top. −1 to 1 puts 0 at the middle, for a bend or for a fader that should push both ways. Auto is −1 to 1 for the pitch bend, which rests in the middle, and 0 to 1 for everything else Hardware Absolute / Encoder (64 ±) / Encoder (1 / 127) For a CC: a knob or fader with ends, or an endless encoder that sends steps. Learning tells them apart from the first few values the control sends An endless encoder has no ends, so the slot counts its steps instead: each step moves the slot 1% of the way, up or down, from wherever it is, and it stops at the ends. A hundred steps take it from the bottom to the top.
307.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Controls » A slot's menu
307.title: A slot's menu

308.body: Control Range Default Description Slew Off – 2 s 20 ms How long each output takes to follow its control. A MIDI CC has only 128 steps, and a filter's cutoff swept by one jumps from step to step with a faint zipper. 20 ms smooths the steps away without making the control feel late. Turn it up for slow, gliding moves, or down to Off for a control that should land at once
308.title: Parameters

309.body: A fader on a filter. Learn slot A from a fader and patch A into an SVF Filter's Cutoff . The filter follows the fader with no zipper noise at the default Slew . The touch strips. Slot B hears the pitch strip and slot A the mod strip as soon as the module is added. Patch them into anything: the bend into a filter for a wah, the mod strip into a vibrato's depth. One fader, several places. Patch one output into as many inputs as you like, and put an Attenuverter in front of any that should move the other way or less. Pressure as expression. Slot C hears how hard you press a held key: patch it into a VCA or a filter to swell a note as you lean in.
309.title: Uses

31.body: Right-click empty canvas to open the add menu. It lists the six categories in their header colors; hover or click one to see its modules, then click a module to place it where you right-clicked. Hover a module's name to read what it does. Groups you've saved are under My Modules , in rose (see Groups ). Below the categories, Frame and Note add a frame or a note . On a touch screen, hold a finger still on empty canvas for half a second instead. The menu opens with finger-sized rows. Tap a category to see its modules, then tap a module. To read what a module does, rest a finger on it and the footer under the list tells you. If you then lift the finger after a moment, nothing is added. On a phone, a category's modules often have no room beside the menu, so they open in its place, with ‹ Back at the top. The add menu, showing the Effect category Right-click empty canvas, pick a category, then a module.
31.title: The add menu

310.body: Module ID input.pads · Category Source Pads turns the pads of a MIDI pad controller into gates: finger drums, triggers and latches. Each of its eight pads has a Gate output, so a pad can strike a Drum , open an ADSR or reset a sequencer. It also puts out how hard each pad was hit and how hard the held pads are pressed. Pads send notes. Played into a Note In they would be pitches: pad 1 a low C, pad 2 a C♯. Pads hears those notes as pads instead, and claims them, so a Note In listening on Omni lets them be. Hitting a pad plays its drum and never also plays the synth (see Claimed notes ). It listens to the devices ticked in MIDI In on the toolbar, or to the one chosen under Device in its right-click menu (see Listening to one device ), and reads each hit on its own sample, as Note In reads notes. The Pad Kit example plays five Drums from it.
310.title: Pads

311.body: Port Signal Type Description Gate 1 – Gate 8 Gate (Green) Each pad, as Mode says: high while held, flipped by each hit, or a short trigger Velocity Control (Orange) How hard each pad was last hit, 0 to 1: a polyphonic cable with one channel per pad Hit Control (Orange) How hard the latest hit was, 0 to 1, held until the next Pressure Control (Orange) How hard the held pads are pressed (aftertouch), 0 to 1: the hardest of them. It falls to 0 when you let go Hit is the cable for velocity on a kit. Patch it into every Drum's Accent : a Drum reads its Accent at the moment its trigger rises, and Hit changes on that same sample, so each Drum hears how hard its own pad was struck. Two pads hit together, as a two-finger hit sends them, are struck a sample apart (about 20 µs), so each still gets its own. Pressure hears polyphonic aftertouch, pad by pad, and channel pressure on the pads' channel. A pad controller sends whichever it is set to.
311.title: Outputs

312.body: Control Choices Default Description Mode Momentary / Latch / Trigger Momentary Momentary : a pad's gate is high while the pad is held. Latch : each hit flips it, open then shut, however long the pad is held. Trigger : a 5 ms gate per hit, however long the pad is held A pad hit again while its gate is high (held in Momentary, or inside its 5 ms in Trigger) drops its gate for one sample and raises it again, so a drum hears a new hit.
312.title: Parameters

313.body: Eight pads in two rows of four, pad 1 at the top left. A hit flashes its pad in the gate's green, brighter and wider the harder it was struck, and the flash fades over about a third of a second. A pad whose gate is open, held or latched, stays softly lit, and glows a little more the harder you press it. Each pad shows its note in the corner, and its channel too if it has one of its own. Along the top are the channel the pads hear and, unless the Mode is Momentary, the mode. Click a pad to play it. Toward the top of a pad is a hard hit, toward the bottom a soft one. In Momentary mode the gate stays high for as long as you hold the mouse button.
313.title: The face

314.body: When you add Pads, it hears notes 36 to 43 on channel 10. Those are the General MIDI drum notes, which most pad controllers send out of the box, so the pads often work before you learn anything. If yours send something else: Click learn at the top right of the face. Pad 1 blinks purple, and the status bar asks you to hit a pad. Hit the first pad on your controller. Pad 1 takes that note and the channel it came on, and pads 2 to 8 follow on the next seven notes. Undo takes a learn back. To give up before hitting anything, press Escape or click cancel . One pad on its own. If your controller's pads aren't seven notes in a row, right-click a pad and choose Learn MIDI for this pad , then hit the pad it should be. That pad keeps its own note and channel even when the row is learned again. Follow pad 1 in the same menu gives it back to the row. A pad's menu also sets its Note and Channel by hand. Pad 1's are the row's: changing them moves every pad that follows it. What the pads hear is saved with the patch.
314.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Pads » Learning the pads
314.title: Learning the pads

315.body: The notes a Pads module listens to are its own. A Note In whose Ch is Omni skips them, so a pad never also plays the synth, and the pianos and the sequencers' ears don't light for them either. The MIDI Monitor still shows them. A Pads set to one Device claims only that device's notes. Set it to the pad controller, and another keyboard's note 36 on channel 10 still plays the synth. A Note In set to a channel hears that channel's notes, claimed or not. To play a melody on the pads as well as drums, set a Note In to the pads' channel. The computer keys and the on-screen pianos are never claimed: they always play Note In.
315.title: Claimed notes

316.body: Finger drums. Each Gate into a Drum 's Trig , and Hit into every Drum's Accent . That's Pad Kit . A choke. Patch the closed hat's pad into the open hat's Choke as well as the closed hat's Trig , as a drummer's foot does. Swells and stabs. In Momentary , a pad's gate into an ADSR holds a chord as long as you hold the pad. Pressure into a filter's Cutoff opens it as you lean in. Switches. In Latch , a pad holds its gate open until you hit it again: a drone through a VCA you start and stop by hand, or a Logic module's B , letting a sequencer's gates through only while the pad is lit. Triggers. In Trigger , a pad's short gate into a Step Sequencer 's Reset starts the pattern over, however long the pad is held.
316.title: Uses

317.body: Module ID source.instrument · Category Output An Instrument is a piece of hardware as a node. Choose MicroFreak on its face and its twelve knobs become the MicroFreak's own: Cutoff , Resonance , Osc Type , Osc Wave . Each knob has a jack beside it with the same name. Patch an LFO into Cutoff and the real filter sweeps. A Scene can morph the knobs, and the patch remembers where every one of them is. That last part matters most for gear that can't store a sound. A volca forgets its sound when you switch it off. With an Instrument, the patch becomes its preset memory : open the patch and Soba sends every knob back to the device. The Instrument also plays notes, as MIDI Out does, from a Gate and a Pitch cable. It makes no sound of its own: the hardware does.
317.title: Instrument

318.body: Click Choose an instrument on the face (or the name that's there) for the list of profiles : the ones that ship with Soba, then your own. Choosing one: gives each knob one of the profile's parameters, its first twelve in order; sets each knob to the parameter's default, if the maker's chart gives one, or else to the middle; sets Ch to the device's factory channel; sets Port to the port whose device looks like it (a port playing "MicroFreak MIDI" for the MicroFreak), if the Rig has one; and sends every knob to the device. It's one step to undo. None , at the bottom of the list, empties the knobs. Or skip the face: in Quick add , type a device's name or its maker (freak, korg) and choose Instrument · MicroFreak . The node arrives already playing it, chosen just as above, and one undo takes it away again.
318.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Instrument » Choosing what it plays
318.title: Choosing what it plays

319.body: Port Signal Type Description Pitch Control (Orange), poly V/Oct, 0 = C4 (note 60). Read as each gate rises Gate Gate (Green), poly A note starts as a channel's gate rises and ends as it falls. A poly cable plays chords Velocity Control (Orange), poly How hard each note is struck, 0 to 1. 0.8 with no cable Bend Control (Orange) -1 to 1, sent as Pitch Bend wherever it moves. Unplugged, it springs back to the middle Pressure Control (Orange), poly 0 to 1, sent as aftertouch: Channel Pressure from a one-channel cable, each note's own from a poly cable Cutoff , Resonance … (one per knob) Control (Orange) 0 to 1 across the knob's travel. Patched, the cable turns the knob, and the knob follows it Each knob's jack is named for the parameter the knob holds. An empty knob's jack is called Slot 1 to Slot 12 , as it is in the patch file. Every input is optional. The module has no outputs.
319.title: Inputs

32.body: Press Space or Tab with the mouse over the canvas. A search box opens at the cursor, listing every module by category, with your saved groups first under My Modules and the ready-made groups of the Library last. Type a few letters to narrow the list, then press Enter, and the module appears where the box opened. (With a group selected, Tab opens the group instead.) In the browser, the + button on the toolbar opens it too, in the middle of the view: the way in on a phone, which has neither key. The quick-add palette Type a few letters of a module's name or category, then press Enter. The search is forgiving. Letters only need to appear in order, so lfo, svf, dly and s&h all find what you'd expect. Typing a category name (effect, mod) lists that category. Typing a device's name or maker (freak, volca, elektron) offers an Instrument already playing it, Instrument · MicroFreak , or a Kit for a drum machine, with the profiles you've saved among them. Move through the list with the arrow keys or Tab, add the highlighted module with Enter, or close the box with Escape.
32.title: Quick add

320.body: Control Range Default Description Port A – H A Which device plays, as MIDI Out's ports do: each port's device is a setting of this computer Ch 1 – 16 1 The MIDI channel the notes go out on, and every knob without a channel of its own Slot 1 … Slot 12 0 – 1 0.5 Each knob's travel. The knob shows what it sends, as the device names it
320.title: Parameters

321.body: The lamp and device , top left. Green while messages are going out, and it flashes with each one. Amber while the port has no device, or its device is unplugged. Red when the device won't open. Click the device's name to choose another. The channel is at the right. The profile's name , beneath, with its maker. Click it to choose another. A name with a ? is a profile this computer doesn't have (see below). Send all , at the right, sends every knob to the device again. Twelve knobs , four to a row. Each is named for its parameter and coloured by its group: an oscillator's blue, a filter's teal, an envelope's orange, an effect's cyan. Each reads out what it sends, as the device names it: Saw , +12 , 74 . Right-click a knob to change what it holds. Holds lists the profile's parameters by group. Nothing empties the knob. The menu's heading says where the knob sends: Cutoff · CC 23 , or Delay Time · CC 85 ch 9 for a parameter on a channel of its own. The menu's Value field is in the device's numbers too, so you can send an exact value: type 100 into Cutoff and CC 23 goes out at 100. For a parameter with named values, type the name ( Fall 2 , in any case, or just enough of its start to pick one out) or choose it from Steps . For one that nudges, type an offset: +12 or −5 . Reset to names the chart's default, and double-clicking the knob goes there too.
321.title: The display

322.body: The device comes back to the patch whenever every knob is sent: when you open the patch; when you choose a profile; when you click Send all . Do this after you've switched the device on after the patch, or turned it by hand while Soba wasn't listening to it (see below). Each knob sends its value as a CC (or a 14-bit pair, or an NRPN, as its profile says). The port's budget paces them on a DIN port, so twelve knobs at once don't swamp it. Knobs that nudge rather than set are left out. The FANTOM-06's Cutoff is one of these: its middle means no change, and every value sent moves the sound a little further. Turn one of these knobs and it sends as you turn it. Send all leaves it alone.
322.title: Send all

323.body: Most synths send their knobs as CCs as you turn them. The MicroFreak and the Digitakt both do. Open the device's MIDI input ( MIDI In in the toolbar), and the Instrument listens to it. Turn the MicroFreak's real Cutoff , and the node's Cutoff turns with it. Save the patch, and the patch keeps the sound you made by hand. It hears its own device, and nothing else. The Instrument listens to the MIDI input whose name matches its port's device, as the Rig matches them, on the channels its knobs send on. A keyboard sending the same CC on the same channel doesn't move it. Nothing goes back. The device already has the value you turned it to, so the knob doesn't send it again. An echo doesn't fight you. Some devices send back every value they're sent. A value Soba sent that knob in the last 0.15 seconds is taken as an echo and ignored, so the knob doesn't jump back while you drag it. A patched knob stays the cable's. A faint purple tick on its rim shows where the hardware's knob was turned to. The tick fades after a moment, because the cable soon moves the device on from there. Undo takes back a turn of the hand. The moves of one turn are one step, the same as a mouse drag. The step ends after a second of stillness. Undoing it sends the knob's old value to the device. A stepped knob goes to the step nearest the value it hears. Knobs that nudge (the FANTOM-06's) send no value of their own back, so they don't listen.
323.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Instrument » The hardware turns it too
323.title: The hardware turns it too

324.body: Mutate works on hardware too. Select the Instrument and press Ctrl + M: its knobs move a small random step, and the device follows. Press it again to wander further, or hold it to go a long way. Each press is one undo step, so Ctrl + Z walks back to the sound you liked, sending the old values as it goes. Think of the MicroFreak as a partner suggesting the sound next door, not a menu to dig through. What stays put: a knob a cable drives, an empty knob, any parameter the profile marks "mutate": false (a volume, a tuning, a MIDI setting) or whose name says it's loud (a level, drive or feedback), and knobs that nudge, since undo couldn't take a nudge back. Named values (an arpeggio type, a clock division) move only with Ctrl + Alt + M, and then by whole steps, so the device always lands on one of its own values. Keeping one: Ctrl + Shift + M keeps the knobs in a Scenes module. Scenes morph an Instrument's knobs as they do any other knobs. A knob of named values holds until halfway, then switches once, rather than stepping through every value in between. Knobs that nudge aren't kept.
324.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Instrument » Exploring its sounds
324.title: Exploring its sounds

325.body: Knobs. A knob sends when you turn it. A patched knob sends wherever its cable moves within a block, up to a thousand times a second, so an LFO sweeps a filter as smoothly as the device can follow. A stepped knob (an oscillator type, an arpeggio mode) shares its travel evenly among its steps, and sends each step's own value from the maker's chart, so it lands on the right step whatever numbers the device uses. Notes. Notes, bend and pressure play as MIDI Out plays them: in time with the sound, chords from poly cables, and no stuck notes. When the Clock stops, a channel changes or the port changes, every note is let go. A new port hears every knob afresh: move the Instrument to port B, and port B's device gets the whole sound. The profile is read, not copied. Each knob plays its profile's parameter of that name. Correct a CC in your profile and every patch that uses it sends the corrected one. The patch also writes each knob's parameter down, so it still plays on a computer that doesn't have the profile. Its name shows with a ? , and its knobs send what the patch wrote. Add the profile to that computer's Documents/Soba/Instruments folder and it reads the profile again.
325.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Instrument » How it works
325.title: How it works

326.body: A filter sweep on real hardware. An LFO , slow, into Cutoff . Turn the LFO's Rate up for a wobble. A sequencer playing the device. A Clock into a Step Sequencer , its Gate and Pitch into the Instrument's. A second sequencer lane into Osc Type changes the oscillator step by step. Saved sounds for a volca. Choose volca fm , set the knobs, and save the patch. Next time, open the patch and the volca plays that sound again.
326.title: Playing it

327.body: Instrument Profiles : what a profile is, the ones that ship, and how to make your own by listening to a device Kit : a drum machine's tracks or pads as eight lanes, for a Trigger Sequencer MIDI Out : for gear without a profile, or for CCs by number The Rig : which device each port plays
