328.body: Module ID source.kit · Category Output A Kit is a drum machine, sampler or groovebox as a node. An Instrument plays one voice, but a drum machine doesn't. A Digitakt has a track on each channel, the SP-404MKII's pads are notes, and a volca drum has a channel for each part. Choose one on the Kit's face, and its eight lanes take the device's own parts by name: Track 1 to Track 8 , Pad 1 to Pad 8 , Part 1 to Part 6 . Each lane has a Gate and a Vel jack, in the same order as a Trigger Sequencer 's outputs. Patch the sequencer's eight lanes straight across, and it plays the device's eight tracks. The Kit has twelve knobs, as an Instrument does: the device's own controls, by name, each with a jack. It makes no sound of its own. The hardware does.
328.title: Kit

329.body: Click Choose a kit on the face for the list of kit profiles : the Digitakt, the SP-404MKII, the volca drum, and any kits of your own. (Or type digitakt in Quick add and choose Kit · Digitakt .) Choosing one: gives each lane one of the device's parts, its first eight in order; gives each knob one of its parameters, as an Instrument's does; sets Ch to the device's channel, and Port to the port whose device looks like it; and sends every knob to the device. It's one step to undo. None , at the bottom of the list, empties the lanes and the knobs.
329.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Kit » Choosing what it plays
329.title: Choosing what it plays

33.body: Every module has the same layout: Header. The module's name and category icon, on a bar in the category's color. Hover the header to read what the module does. The × at the right end deletes the module. Filters and effects also have a power switch at the left end: see Bypass . Inputs , down the left edge. Each jack is labeled and colored by the signal it expects. Outputs , down the right edge, colored by the signal they send. An output lights up while signal is coming out of it. Displays. Many modules draw what they're doing: the oscillator its waveform, the envelope its shape, filters their frequency response, the LFO its wave with a dot riding its phase. Knobs , along the bottom, with the current value under each. Hover any jack's name or knob for a tooltip: what it does, its signal type in the cable's color, and for knobs, its range.
33.breadcrumbs: Interface Overview » Anatomy of a module
33.title: Anatomy of a module

330.body: Port Signal Type Description Track 1 , Pad 13 … (one per lane) Gate (Green) Strikes the lane's part as it rises, and lets the note go as it falls Track 1 Vel … (one per lane) Control (Orange) How hard the lane strikes, 0 to 1, read at the moment its gate rises. Unpatched, the Velocity knob says Filter Freq , Decay … (one per knob) Control (Orange) As an Instrument's : 0 to 1 across the knob's travel Each lane's jacks are named for its part. An empty lane's are called Gate 1 and Vel 1 to Gate 8 and Vel 8 , as they are in the patch file. Every input is optional. The module has no outputs.

331.body: Control Range Default Description Port A – H A Which device plays, as MIDI Out's ports do Ch 1 – 16 1 The channel for parts without one of their own, and for the knobs, unless they turn a track Velocity 0 – 1 0.8 How hard a lane strikes while its Vel jack is unpatched Slot 1 … Slot 12 0 – 1 0.5 Each knob's travel, as an Instrument's Track , the lane whose track the knobs turn, is chosen from the pads (see below).
331.title: Parameters

332.body: The top is an Instrument's: the lamp, the device and the channel, then the profile's name and Send all . The knobs are at the bottom. Between them: Eight pads , two rows of four, each named for the part its lane plays. A pad flashes green as its lane strikes, brighter the harder it was struck, and stays softly lit while its gate is open. Each pad has its lane's number in a corner. The Velocity knob , at the right. Click a pad to choose the part its lane plays. The menu lists every part the profile has, so a lane can play any of the SP-404MKII's sixteen pads, not only the first eight. Nothing empties the lane. Hover over a pad to see exactly what it sends: Pad 13 · note 36 (C2) on channel 1 .
332.title: The display

333.body: Some devices take the same CCs on every track, each on its track's own channel. The Digitakt's Filter Frequency on channel 3 turns track 3's filter. On a device like that, the knobs turn one track at a time. That pad wears an orange bar . To turn another track, click its pad and choose Knobs turn this track . Turning the knobs to another track sends nothing. The track keeps its sound until you move a knob, and then only that knob is sent. Send all sends every knob to the track the knobs turn. The SP-404MKII is different: its pads are notes, and its knobs are its effects. Its knobs stay on their own channels whichever pad you click. The Kit listens to its device as an Instrument does. Turn the Digitakt's filter on the track the knobs turn, and the Kit's knob follows. Turning another track's filter doesn't move it, because that track's CCs come on another channel.
333.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Kit » Tracks and the knobs
333.title: Tracks and the knobs

334.body: A strike. A lane's gate rising sends a Note On: its part's note, on its part's channel, or on Ch if the part has none. A part with only a channel (a volca drum's, which any note plays) is struck with middle C (note 60). The gate falling sends the Note Off. Notes go out in time with the sound, stamped with their sample, as MIDI Out's do. A busy port's budget never holds back a note. No stuck notes. A note is let go when its gate falls, when its jack is unplugged, when its lane is given another part, and when the Clock stops. Two lanes playing the same part share its note: the second strikes it again, and it's let go when the last of them falls. The profile is read, not copied. As an Instrument's knobs do, each lane plays its profile's part of that name, so a note corrected in the profile reaches every patch. The patch writes each lane's part down too, so it still plays on a computer without the profile.
334.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Kit » How it works
334.title: How it works

335.body: The Digitakt's eight tracks from Soba. A Clock into a Trigger Sequencer , its eight lanes and their velocities into a Kit playing the Digitakt . Program a beat on the sequencer's grid. A Soba hi-hat from the same sequencer plays in time with the hardware. Pads for the SP-404MKII. The same sequencer into a Kit playing the SP-404MKII . Click a pad to move its lane to any of the sixteen, the bottom row's (13 to 16) say. A filter on one track. Click a Digitakt pad, choose Knobs turn this track , and patch an LFO into Filter Freq . Only that track sweeps.

337.body: Module ID output.setlist · Category Output The Arranger knows when the verse ends. A Setlist passes that on to the room. At the chorus, the Digitakt moves to pattern A05, the FANTOM recalls Scene 12, the ZOIA loads patch 4 and the RC-505 recalls memory 7. Each section of the song has up to eight rows . A row is one device's program, sent as Bank Select and Program Change. A row with a lead goes that long before the bar line, so a device that needs warning still lands on the downbeat. The Setlist makes no sound. The hardware changes.
337.title: Setlist

338.body: Patch three of the Arranger's outputs into the Setlist's inputs of the same names: Section : which section is playing. Next : where the song goes at the next bar line. The Arranger knows this from the downbeat of a section's last bar, when its Next dice are thrown, or as soon as a Jump is asked for. Bar : measures how long a bar is, so a row knows when its lead starts. With all three patched, every row goes at its lead before the bar line. Without Bar , a row with a lead goes as soon as Next names its section, which can be up to a bar early. Without Next , every row goes on the downbeat its section starts on, lead or not.
338.title: Patching it

339.body: Port Signal Type Description Section Control (Orange) The Arranger's Section . On the downbeat a section starts, any of its rows that haven't gone ahead go now Next Control (Orange) The Arranger's Next . The rows of the section it names go their lead ahead of the bar line Bar Gate (Green) The Arranger's Bar , which measures the bar Send Gate (Green) Sends the playing section's rows again as it rises, whether the transport is playing or stopped The module has no outputs and no knobs: its rows are all on its face.
339.title: Inputs

34.body: To Do this Change a value Drag up or down Make fine adjustments Hold Shift while dragging Nudge it Hold Alt and scroll over it, or click it and press the arrow keys Set an exact value Right-click, type into Value and press Enter: 440, 1.2 kHz, 250 ms, -6 dB, C#3 Return to the default Double-click, press Home once you've clicked it, or right-click and Reset Map to a MIDI controller Right-click, then Learn MIDI Let the DAW automate it (in the plugin ) Right-click, then Map to Macro A knob's ring lights up in its module's header color. Knobs with a range either side of zero, like Semi and Fine , light outward from the top, so you can see at a glance which way they're set. A small mark stands where zero is, so a knob at zero shows a dark ring with its pointer on the mark. Some knobs move in whole steps, like the Oscillator's Oct and Semi : they click from one value to the next as you drag.
34.title: Knobs

340.body: Each section's rows are listed under its name, as its Arranger names it. Click + beside a section to add a row. The new row copies the row in the same place in the section before it, moved on one program. If you start with the verse's Digitakt on A01, the chorus gets the Digitakt on A02. Click a row to change it: Setting What it is Device One of the instrument profiles with programs, or Plain numbers . Choosing a device sets the row's channel to the one the device takes programs on, and sets its port to the port whose device looks like it Port A to H : which device it goes to, as MIDI Out's ports do. Hover over a port to see its device Channel 1 – 16. For a device banked by channel (the SP-404MKII), this is the first bank's channel Bank The device's banks (the FANTOM's Scene A and Scene B), or for plain numbers, Bank Select MSB and LSB, each 0 – 127 or off Program Named the way the device names it: Pattern A05 , Scene 12 , Memory 7 . You can type a name ("B16") or drag. A plain row shows the Program Change number as it's sent, 0 – 127 Lead 0 – 4000 ms: how long before the bar line it goes Remove row at the bottom takes the row away. Every change is one undo step.
340.title: Rows

341.body: Most devices switch as soon as they hear a program change, so give them a lead of 0 and they change on the downbeat. A Digitakt doesn't. It queues its next pattern and switches when the one playing ends. Give its row a lead inside the last bar, 500 ms or so: the pattern is queued during the last bar and starts on the downbeat. A row's lead shows in orange at its right.
341.title: Leads

342.body: Along the top : a lamp that flashes purple as rows go, and the Arranger it follows. While a section's rows are on their way, the time to the bar line shows at the right: bar in 0.4 s . Each section has a tab beside its name. The tab is green when the room is playing that section, meaning all its rows have gone. It's amber , pulsing, while that section's rows are going ahead of its bar line. A section with no rows says no change : the room stays as it is. Each row shows a lamp that glows as the row goes, then its port, then the device and its program, then its lead. The port is lit the way its port is in the Rig : green when sending, amber when the port has no device or it's unplugged, and red when the device won't open. Hover over a row to see exactly what it sends: Pattern A05: Program Change 4 on channel 1, port A, 500 ms before the bar line .
342.title: The display

343.body: Only while playing. Rows go only while the Clock runs. When the Clock starts, the section that's coming first goes at once, before its downbeat. That's section 1 from the top, or wherever a Jump starts the song. Stopping and starting again sends the section again. A change of plan. Say the chorus's rows have gone ahead, and then a Jump sends the song back to the verse before the bar line. The verse's rows go next, at their leads, so the room follows the song back. The profile is read, not copied. As an Instrument's knobs do, a row naming a device goes as its profile says: the channel a bank is on, and the bank's Bank Select. If a number is corrected in a profile, every patch that uses it gets the correction. The patch also writes each row down, so it still plays on a computer without the profile. There, a row sends its program as the Program Change, on its channel, after the bank it wrote down. On time. Each program change is stamped with its sample and goes out as that sample is heard, the way MIDI Out's messages do. A busy port's budget never holds one back. A port no row uses is left alone, so the Rig doesn't show it as in use.
343.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Setlist » How it works
343.title: How it works

344.body: Three patterns on the bar. An Arranger with Intro, Verse and Chorus, each with a row for the Digitakt on its own pattern with a 500 ms lead. The Digitakt moves through the three patterns, each exactly on its bar line. A scene for the chorus. A row for the FANTOM-06 in the Chorus, Bank Scene A , Scene 12. The FANTOM changes scene on the chorus's downbeat. Put the room back. Patch a Pads gate into Send . After you've been turning things on the hardware, one hit brings every device back to the section playing.
344.title: Playing it

345.body: Arranger : the song the Setlist follows, and its Next output Instrument Profiles : how each device's programs are named and numbered MIDI Out : a single program and bank, sent on a trigger

346.body: Module ID output.fm_voice · Category Output The volca fm speaks DX7. A DX7 voice has six operators, 32 ways to wire them and 155 numbers, and it's famously hard to program by hand. It's easy to wander through by ear, though. An FM Voice holds one voice and sends it to the volca every time it changes. Mutate makes a child of it, and Cross makes a child of it and another voice. You hear each child as soon as it's made. The voices bred so far grow in the node's garden . Each one is a click away from playing again, and the patch keeps them all. The FM Voice makes no sound of its own. The volca plays the voice.
346.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » FM Voice » FM Voice
346.title: FM Voice

347.body: Plug the volca fm's MIDI In into one of the Rig's ports (Ctrl+Shift+H), and choose that port as the FM Voice's Port . Clicking the device's name at the top of the face also chooses a port's device. Play the volca: from its own keys, a MIDI Out , or an Instrument with the volca fm's profile. The voice goes to the volca's edit buffer, the program it's playing. Press Mutate . The volca takes a voice on any channel, so Channel matters only for a DX7. A voice sent to the volca plays from its edit buffer, and the volca doesn't save it on its own. To keep one on the volca, write it to a program there, or send the whole garden to its memories (see Files and banks ). The patch keeps the voices either way, and opening the patch sends the playing voice again.
347.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » FM Voice » Setting it up
347.title: Setting it up

348.body: Control Range Description Port A – H Which device the voice goes to, as MIDI Out's ports do Ch 1 – 16 The channel the voice is addressed to. A volca fm takes it on any; a DX7 only on its own Format volca fm, DX7 What it's sent to: see volca fm or DX7 Amount 0 – 1 How far Mutate moves a child from its parent. A little is a neighbour; all the way is a wander The module has no inputs or outputs.
348.title: Knobs

349.body: Mutate makes a child of the playing voice and plays it. At a low Amount , a few numbers move a little. At a high one, most of them move far. Cross makes a child of the playing voice and the picked one. Shift+click a voice in the garden to pick it, or right-click it and choose Pick it to cross with . Each operator comes whole from one parent or the other. The algorithm and feedback come from one parent, and the pitch envelope and the LFO each from one. The picked voice stays picked, so you can cross the same pair again and get a different child. Both keep the voice about as loud as its parents and in the same key, as Mutate keeps a patch's loudness: A carrier is an operator you hear. Its output level, the peak of its envelope and its ratio stay the same. Only a hair of its detune moves. The algorithm changes only to one whose carriers are the same operators. In a cross, each carrier takes its loudness and pitch from the parent whose algorithm the child takes. So a modulator at 14 times the note never turns up as an operator you hear. What moves is timbre: the modulators' levels and ratios, every envelope's rates, the keyboard scaling, the feedback and the LFO. A fixed-frequency operator stays fixed, and the transpose stays. Every child is named after its family. A mutant takes its parent's name with its generation at the end ( SOFT KEY 3 ). A cross takes half of each parent's name ( SOFT BELL ). Each breed is one undo step, so Ctrl+Z walks back to the parent, and the parent is sent again.
349.title: Breeding

35.body: Many parameters have both a knob and an input jack of the same name. Patch a cable into the jack and the knob sets the center while the incoming signal moves the value around it. Each module page gives the scale. The knob stays live while the cable is patched, so you can keep moving the center as the signal plays. Its pointer stays where you set it. Once signal arrives, an orange bead on the knob's rim shows where the signal has carried the value, joined to the pointer by a thin orange arc. A faint band behind the bead shows the range the signal has covered over the last second or so, so you can see how deep an LFO swings even when it's too fast to follow. The number under the knob turns orange and reads that carried value. Hover over the knob or drag it and the number goes back to white and shows the center you're setting. Unplug the cable and the knob alone sets the value again. In a busy patch, hover over a patched knob to find the cable carrying its signal: that cable glows and the rest dim, and its route shows through any module it runs under. It works the other way too. Hover over a cable and the bead on the knob it feeds swells and glows. Until signal arrives, a small green dot above the knob shows that a cable is patched in.
35.breadcrumbs: Interface Overview » Knobs with a jack
35.title: Knobs with a jack

350.body: The garden holds up to 32 voices, one DX7 bank's worth, in the order a bank saves them. A new FM Voice starts with four seeds: Seed What it is SOFT KEYS An electric piano: three pairs of operators (algorithm 5), a round body, a struck tine at 14 times the note and a detuned shimmer, brighter played harder GLASS BELL A bell: each carrier struck by a modulator at an inharmonic ratio, 3.5 and 5, ringing long over a low hum WOOD BASS A plucked bass (algorithm 1): a half-ratio body bitten by its modulator's quick decay, with a woody knock above INIT VOICE The DX7's blank page: operator 1 alone, a plain sine Each voice is a chip. A brighter chip is a brighter voice: its modulators drive harder. The playing voice is ringed in white. Lines run from it to the voices it came from. Hover over another chip to see its parents too. The picked voice is ringed in green. A kept voice has an amber dot. Click a chip to play it, and Shift+click to pick it. Right-click a chip to play, pick, keep or weed it out. Once the garden holds 32 voices, a new one takes the place of the oldest voice that isn't playing, picked or kept. A faint stroke through a chip marks the next to go. Keep (or Kept , to let it go) saves the playing voice from weeding. If every voice but the playing one is kept, the garden can't grow until you let one go.
350.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » FM Voice » The garden
350.title: The garden

351.body: The ⋯ menu at the right of the buttons: Item What it does Open .syx… Plants a DX7 single voice, a bank of 32, or a file of several, after the voices growing. To make room the oldest go, except kept and picked ones. A bank of 32 opened whole is a garden of its own Save voice as .syx… Saves the playing voice as a DX7 single voice, which Dexed and a DX7 read too Save garden as a bank… Saves every voice as one DX7 bank of 32, in the garden's order, with INIT VOICE filling any places left over Send garden to port's memories… Sends the garden as a bank. A volca fm writes a bank over all 32 of its programs , so it asks first. Save the volca's own programs first if you want them back Start over with the seeds The four seeds again, and the voices kept Opening a file says in the status bar how many voices it planted.
351.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » FM Voice » Files and banks
351.title: Files and banks

352.body: A DX7 single voice ends with a checksum. The volca fm reads that byte as which operators are on, and a checksum switches some of them off. So with Format on volca fm , a voice ends with all six operators on. With DX7 , it ends with the checksum, for a DX7, Dexed or a volca fm2. A saved .syx file is always a DX7 file. Banks carry a checksum for both. This comes from Volcako, an editor written for the volca fm. Korg's chart says only that the volca takes DX7 bulk data, and Volcako finds it takes it on any channel.
352.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » FM Voice » volca fm or DX7
352.title: volca fm or DX7

353.body: A voice is 163 bytes, about 55 ms down a DIN cable. The FM Voice sends one no more often than every 120 ms, and never while its port still has SysEx to send. Breed faster than that and only the newest voice goes. A bank is 4,104 bytes, about a second and a half. The Rig's Last sent column shows a dump on its way. In the browser, SysEx waits until the page is allowed to send it. Send a .syx file from the Rig once to ask.
353.title: Pacing

354.body: Along the top : a lamp that flashes purple as a voice goes, then the port and its device. Send sends the voice again. The voice's name , its algorithm ( ALG 5 ) and feedback ( FB 5 ), and where it came from: A seed , From a file , Mutant of SOFT KEYS (1) or Cross of SOFT KEYS (1) and GLASS BELL (2) , with its generation and its place in the garden. The algorithm , drawn the way the DX7 draws it. The carriers sit along the bottom in the blue of audio, joined to the output line. The modulators stack above them in the orange of modulation. Each operator glows brighter the louder it is. The feedback loop brightens as the feedback rises. Each operator beside it, 1 to 6: its ratio ( ×3.50 , or a fixed frequency in amber), its envelope's shape and its output level. Hover over one for its numbers.
354.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » FM Voice » The display
354.title: The display

355.body: A walk : start from a seed, Mutate at a low Amount, and keep going while you like what you hear. Ctrl+Z when you don't. Two families : grow a bell and a bass apart, then cross across them. A set of sounds for a song : keep the voices you love, let the garden weed the rest, and send the garden to the volca's memories at the end of the session.
355.title: Ideas

356.body: Module ID filter.svf · Category Filter SVF Filter Module The response curve on the node is computed from the filter itself, so it matches what you hear. The SVF (state variable filter) is the all-purpose filter: one input, four outputs, all running at once. LowPass darkens, HighPass thins, BandPass keeps a band around the cutoff and Notch takes one out. Patch whichever you need, or several at once, without switching modes. It is a 12 dB/octave filter with an analog-style resonance. Turn the resonance up and the peak grows and saturates rather than getting louder without limit; turn it all the way and the filter sings on its own as a clean sine at the cutoff. Cutoff moves in octaves, so a sweep sounds even from bass to treble, and it stays stable right up to 20 kHz. The display draws each output's response, the patched ones lit and the rest faint (with nothing patched, LowPass is lit). With CV in Cutoff or Resonance , the curves follow where the CV has taken the filter, a faint copy stays where the knobs put it, and the cutoff's tick on the floor turns orange: an envelope into Cutoff opens and closes the curve with each note. When the resonance is high enough to ring on its own, the peak glows and the display says sings . Beneath the curves lies the sound itself. What comes into In is a faint blue landscape, and what the lit output lets through is green over it, so the gap between them is what the filter is taking away, and a resonant peak shows where the green rises above the blue. It's scaled to the loudest part of what comes in, so a quiet sound fills the display as well as a loud one, and a polyphonic cable shows all its voices together. When the sound stops, the landscape sinks away and the curve's own glow fills in beneath it. With CV in Cutoff or Resonance , a thin strip along the floor keeps the last two seconds of what comes out, newest at the top and falling away beneath, brighter where it's louder. As an LFO sweeps the cutoff up and back, each harmonic's column lights as the cutoff passes over it and dims as it moves on, so the sweep leaves its trail through the sound. For a thicker, steeper lowpass, see the Ladder Filter .
356.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » SVF Filter » SVF Filter
356.title: SVF Filter

357.body: Port Signal Type Description In Audio (Blue) Audio to filter Cutoff Control (Orange) Cutoff CV, in octaves: each unit moves the cutoff by CV Amt octaves. At the default of 1, +1 doubles the cutoff and -1 halves it: the V/Oct scale, so a keyboard's pitch tracks directly Resonance Control (Orange) Adds to the Res knob: +1 adds 50% Cutoff and Resonance modulate around their knobs. The knob sets the center, and stays live while a cable is patched in.
357.title: Inputs

358.body: Port Signal Type Description LowPass Audio (Blue) Passes frequencies below the cutoff HighPass Audio (Blue) Passes frequencies above the cutoff BandPass Audio (Blue) Passes a band around the cutoff Notch Audio (Blue) Removes a band around the cutoff and passes the rest
358.title: Outputs

359.body: Knob Range Default Description Cutoff 20 Hz – 20 kHz 1000 Hz Where the filter starts cutting Res (Resonance) 0 – 100% 50% Peak at the cutoff. Self-oscillates above about 97% CV Amt (Cutoff CV) -4 – +4 oct 1 oct Octaves the cutoff moves per unit at the Cutoff input. Negative turns the CV upside down Drive 1x – 10x 1x Input gain into a soft saturator, for warmth and grit
359.title: Parameters

36.body: Drag from an output to an input to patch a cable; a jack turns white when the cable is close enough to land on it. You can also drag from an input to an output. Cables only connect where the signals make sense: audio and control mix freely, and a gate can drive a control input, but a cable between jacks that can't work won't attach. Bring one near a jack that can't take it and the ring round the jack breaks in two, half in the cable's colour and half in the jack's. Let go there, and the halves spring apart as a small tag beside the jack says why, for example Control cannot connect to Gate ; the status bar says it too. Signal Types has the full rules. One output can feed many inputs. Each gets the full signal. Each input takes one cable. Dropping a new cable onto an occupied input replaces the old one. No loops. A cable that would feed a module's output back into its own input, directly or through other modules, is refused, and the tag at the jack and the status bar name the modules round the loop. To remove a cable, drag its end off the input jack and let go over empty canvas. Cables run behind the modules, and behind frame titles and notes, showing faintly through them so a route can still be followed without covering the controls or the words. 〰 Cables ▸ Under modules and labels sets how faintly. While the patch plays, cables show what their signal has been doing over the last few seconds. Reading the signal in a cable explains what you're seeing.
36.title: Cables

360.body: LowPass is the classic subtractive synth filter. It rolls off everything above the cutoff at 12 dB per octave, taking the edge off a bright oscillator. Most patches start here. HighPass is the mirror image: it removes everything below the cutoff. Use it to thin a sound out, clear rumble, or leave room for a bass part. BandPass keeps a band around the cutoff and rolls off both sides. The band narrows as resonance rises. It gives vocal, nasal and telephone-like tones, and swept by an envelope or LFO it becomes a wah. Notch removes a band around the cutoff and leaves the rest. The notch is deepest exactly at the cutoff and narrows as resonance rises. It equals LowPass and HighPass added together. Swept slowly, it gives a phaser-like movement that hollows a sound without darkening it.
360.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » SVF Filter » The four outputs
360.title: The four outputs

361.body: Resonance feeds part of the filter's output back into itself, which adds a peak at the cutoff. A little (20 to 40%) adds character; a lot (70 to 90%) gives the squelchy, whistling peak of an acid bassline. The feedback runs through a saturator, so a loud input at high resonance pushes back instead of running away. Above about 97% the filter self-oscillates: It produces a sine at the cutoff frequency, with nothing patched into In . The oscillation grows out of a tiny noise floor, like circuit noise in an analog filter. The pitch lands within a few cents of the Cutoff knob, so the knob reads as a pitch. The saturator holds the level at about -12 dBFS. Patch a keyboard's Pitch into Cutoff and it plays in tune. Feed audio in while it oscillates and the two interact, with the resonance pushing back against loud input.
361.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » SVF Filter » Resonance and self-oscillation
361.title: Resonance and self-oscillation

362.body: CV Amt sets how far the Cutoff input reaches: how many octaves one unit of CV moves the cutoff. It runs from -4 to +4 octaves per unit, and starts at 1, the V/Oct scale. An envelope runs from 0 to 1, so CV Amt is the size of its sweep, the knob a hardware synth calls Env Amount or Contour : 1 opens the filter one octave at the envelope's peak. Gentle: a sound that brightens a little at each note. 2 to 3 suits a pluck or a brassy swell. 3 to 4 is acid: a resonant peak that shoots up from the bass to the treble and falls back. Negative values turn the CV upside down. An envelope then closes the filter as the note starts and opens it again as it releases, so set the Cutoff knob high. With pitch on Cutoff , CV Amt is the keyboard tracking: 1 keeps the filter's brightness the same on every note, 0.5 tracks at half the rate, and 0 ignores the keys. CV Amt scales whatever is patched into Cutoff before it's added to the Cutoff knob, so the knob still sets where the sweep starts. With a polyphonic envelope, each voice's sweep is scaled the same way.
362.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » SVF Filter » CV Amt
362.title: CV Amt

363.body: Drive raises the level into a soft saturator before the filter. At 1x it is nearly clean. Turning it up thickens the sound and then adds grit, and the louder signal also pushes harder against the resonance.
363.title: Drive

37.body: To hear what a cable carries on its own, hold Alt over it while the patch plays. You'll hear the LFO before it reaches the filter, or the dry voice before the reverb. A small scope beside the pointer shows the signal's waveform and names the output it comes from. The probe plays on top of the patch at the same fixed level as a Sampler's ▶. It never comes out louder than that. While you probe, the rest of the patch is turned down beneath it: by 20 dB under an audio cable, which all but solos it, and by 6 dB under a control or gate cable, so you can still hear the music the signal moves. 〰 Cables ▸ Patch under a probe sets each amount, from Off to Solo , and Soba remembers them. Neither the probe nor the ducking goes into a recording. The probe fades in, and when you let go of Alt or move off the cable it fades out and the patch comes back up. Audio cables play as they are. On a polyphonic cable, all the voices are summed. Control cables play as a quiet sine whose pitch follows the value: A3 at 0, two octaves higher at 1, and two octaves lower at -1. You hear an LFO as a siren and a stepped sequence as a tune. Gate cables play a soft click each time the gate opens, with a faint tone while it's held, so you can hear how long each gate lasts as well as when it starts. Probing works on cables inside groups and on cables into a group's jacks, where you hear the module output the cable carries. MIDI cables have no sound to probe.

373.body: Module ID filter.ladder · Category Filter Ladder Filter Module The ladder's response curve, drawn from the filter's own transfer function. The Ladder Filter models the transistor ladder Robert Moog patented in 1969: the filter behind the Minimoog, and still the sound most people mean by "analog". It is a 4-pole lowpass, built from four one-pole stages in a row, with the last stage's output fed back to the first to make the resonance. What gives it its character: A steep 24 dB/octave slope that darkens a sound decisively, plus a gentler 12 dB/octave tap from the middle of the ladder. Saturation at every stage. Push it with Drive and it rounds off and thickens rather than clipping. The output never goes past full scale, however hard you drive it. Bass compensation. The original ladder loses low end as resonance rises. This one adds the lost bass back, so turning up the resonance adds a peak without thinning the sound. Self-oscillation over the top fifth of the resonance knob: a sine at the cutoff frequency, in tune to within a cent or two. 2x oversampling. The saturators run at twice the sample rate, so a high note driven hard stays clean instead of picking up inharmonic aliasing. The display draws LP24 and LP12, the patched ones lit, at the cutoff and resonance CV has taken them to, as on the SVF Filter . Past the top fifth of Resonance , where the ladder rings on its own, the peak glows and the display says sings . Beneath the curves lies the sound itself, as on the SVF: what comes in as a faint blue landscape, and what the lit output lets through in green over it. The green is measured rather than worked out from the curve, so the harmonics Drive adds show up too, as green rising where the blue was low. With CV in Cutoff or Resonance , the strip along the floor keeps the last two seconds of what comes out, as on the SVF, so an envelope or LFO on the cutoff leaves its trail through the sound.

388.body: Each stage is a one-pole lowpass with a tanh at its input. The first stage's input is the signal minus the fed-back output, so the same tanh saturates the resonance. The loop is solved with zero delay (TPT), with the saturators linearized around a one-pass estimate of the current sample. That keeps the resonance in tune at high cutoffs. The oversampler uses polyphase IIR halfband filters: flat to within 0.01 dB up to 20 kHz, with about 100 dB of stopband. In tests, a 5 kHz tone driven into the filter has 30 to 55 dB less audible aliasing than the same filter run at the base rate. At extreme Drive combined with high resonance the gain is smaller (about 10 dB), because the harmonics reach beyond even twice the sample rate.

390.body: Module ID mod.adsr · Category Modulation ADSR Envelope Module The display draws the same curve the audio follows. An LFO is patched into Release , so the R is lit and Rel reads the time it has stretched to. The ADSR Envelope gives each note a shape in time. When a gate goes high (a key goes down), it rises, falls to a held level, and when the gate goes low (the key comes up), it fades away: Attack , Decay , Sustain , Release . Patch it into a VCA to shape a note's loudness, or into a filter's Cutoff to shape its brightness. Every stage takes exactly the time on its knob: a 100 ms release is silent 100 ms after you let go. Each stage's curve knob sets its shape, from a straight line to a deep analog curve. While a note plays, the display follows it: the stage it's in lights its letter, a dot rides the curve at the envelope's level, and the glow under the curve swells with it. A soft note's dot rides lower, at the peak its velocity gave it.
390.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » ADSR Envelope » ADSR Envelope
390.title: ADSR Envelope

Scales the peak; see Vel Attack , Decay , Release Control (Orange) Stretch the stage's time around its knob, in octaves: +1 doubles it, −1 halves it. Knob Range Default Description Atk (Attack) 1 ms – 10 s 10 ms Time to rise from the current level to the peak Dec (Decay) 1 ms – 10 s 100 ms Time to fall from the peak to the sustain level Sus (Sustain) 0 – 100% 70% Level held while the gate is high, as a fraction of the peak Rel (Release) 1 ms – 10 s 300 ms Time to fall from the current level to 0 after the gate goes low A Crv (Attack Curve) 0 – 100% 20% Attack shape: 0% is a straight ramp, higher bows it outward D Crv (Decay Curve) 0 – 100% 50% Decay shape: 0% is a straight ramp, higher drops fast then eases in Vel (Velocity Amount) 0 – 100% 50% How much the Velocity input scales the peak R Crv (Release Curve) 0 – 100% 50% Release shape: 0% is a straight ramp, higher drops fast then trails off
393.title: Parameters

394.body: Attack begins when the gate goes high. The envelope rises from where it is (0, or wherever a release had got to) to its peak in exactly the attack time. A few milliseconds gives a percussive start; tens of milliseconds, the soft start of strings or a bowed pad; hundreds, a slow swell. Decay begins the moment the attack reaches the peak. The envelope falls to the sustain level in exactly the decay time. Short decays are plucky; long ones ease gradually into the held note. Sustain is a level, not a time: what the envelope holds for as long as the gate stays high. At 0% the note dies away even with the key held, like a plucked string. At 100% it holds at full level, like an organ. Turning it while a note is held glides to the new level over a few milliseconds, so it never clicks. Release begins when the gate goes low. The envelope falls from wherever it is to 0 in exactly the release time, even if the key was let go mid-attack. Short releases stop abruptly; long ones leave a tail that lingers after the key comes up.
394.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » ADSR Envelope » The four stages
394.title: The four stages

395.body: Each stage is an analog-style RC curve aimed past its target, so that it lands on time instead of creeping toward the target forever. The curve knob sets how far past: 0% : aimed far past, so the stage is a straight line. 20% (the attack default): aimed about 15% past the peak. The rise is nearly straight, which is what makes an analog attack sound punchy. 50% (the decay and release default): a classic RC fall. It drops quickly, then eases into its target, which suits how the ear hears loudness. 100% : a deep curve. Most of the change happens in the first fifth of the stage, followed by a long tail. Curves change only the shape of a stage. Its time stays exactly the knob's.
395.title: Curves

396.body: Patch a velocity source (the Velocity output of Note In ) into Velocity , and the Vel knob sets how much it matters: Vel 0% : every note peaks at 1.0. Vel 50% : the softest note peaks at 0.5 and the hardest at 1.0. Vel 100% : the peak equals the velocity. Sustain is a fraction of the peak, so a soft note sustains lower too. With velocity patched, the node's display draws a faint second envelope for the softest note. The gap between the two lines is your dynamic range. With nothing patched into Velocity , every note peaks at 1.0, whatever the knob says.
396.title: Velocity

397.body: Each stage has a jack beside its knob. CV there moves the stage around where the knob puts it, so the knob stays the starting point and the cable bends it: Attack , Decay and Release count in octaves of time. +1 doubles the knob's time, +2 quadruples it, and −1 halves it. A 500 ms release with +3 patched in rings for 4 s. The time stays within the knob's 1 ms – 10 s. Sustain adds to the knob's level, so +0.3 lifts a 40% sustain to 70%. Most CV swings between −1 and +1, so an LFO patched straight into Attack only halves and doubles the attack. A 10 ms attack moves between 5 and 20 ms, which is hard to hear. To sweep it further, scale the LFO up first through an Attenuverter set to Range ×4. At ±4 octaves a 50 ms attack moves from about 3 ms to 0.8 s, from a snap to a swell. The envelope reads CV on every sample, not just at each note. A cue that lands while a release is already falling stretches what's left of it, and the curve bends there without a step. While a stage's jack is patched, its knob shows where the CV has taken it: an orange arc out to a bead on its rim, and the number under the knob in orange. The display draws that stage the way the envelope is running it, with its letter tinted. When a lane ramps the release out, you can watch the tail widen.

4.body: If you're new to modular synthesis, read the Getting Started pages in order: Installation gets the app running. Interface Overview shows you around the window. Your First Patch builds a playable synthesizer from an empty canvas, one cable at a time. Lessons teach the same ideas inside the app: five short tutorials that show you each move, then wait while you make it. If you already know your way around a modular, open the 📚 Examples menu, load a patch, and keep the module reference to hand. The recipes explain how each example works, one idea at a time, and the songs are whole pieces that play themselves from the first note to the last.

Paste (Ctrl + V) drops them at the mouse cursor, keeping their layout, settings and the cables between them. Pasting again without moving the mouse fans the copies out. The clipboard holds modules as patch text, so you can paste between two Soba windows, or paste the contents of a whole patch file to add its modules to the current patch. 407.body: The ADSR Envelope is polyphonic. Patch a polyphonic gate (from Note In ) into Gate and every voice gets its own envelope, with its own stage and level, so each note of a chord attacks and releases on its own. Polyphonic velocity into Decay gives each note its own decay; a mono cable, like an Arranger lane, moves every voice together. The display shows the first voice. See Polyphony .
407.title: Polyphony

409.body: Module ID mod.lfo · Category Modulation LFO Module Synced to 1/4: the Rate knob reads the division, and the dot rides the waveform in step with the beat. The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) makes slow, repeating shapes for moving other modules: a filter that breathes, a vibrato, a tremolo, a pulse width that drifts. It runs from one cycle every 100 seconds up to 100 Hz, so it can also be pushed into the audio range for rough, buzzy modulation. The display on the node draws one cycle of the selected waveform, with a dot that travels along it at the LFO's actual phase, trailing a brighter stretch of the curve behind it. What you see is where the modulation is right now. Bipolar swings about a centre line; with Bipolar off, the wave stands on the floor, since it never goes below 0. A tick on the floor marks where the Phase knob starts the cycle. Across the top it reads the rate, after any Rate CV, or the division and the rate it comes to.
409.title: LFO

41.body: Filters and effects can be bypassed: their audio inputs pass straight to their outputs, as if the module weren't there. Click the power switch at the left of the header, choose Bypass from the module menu, or select modules and press Ctrl + B. A bypassed module's header fades to gray and its controls dim. Switching takes a 20 ms crossfade, so it never clicks, and a bypassed module uses no CPU.
41.title: Bypass

413.body: Sine moves smoothly with no corners. The natural choice for vibrato, tremolo and slow sweeps. Triangle rises and falls in straight lines. It sounds steadier than a sine at the turnarounds. Square jumps between its two extremes, half the cycle at each. Use it for trills, choppy tremolo and two-step filter jumps. Saw ramps steadily up, then drops back. A rising sweep that resets each cycle. At the start of a cycle the sine and triangle sit at the midpoint, heading up, the square is high, and the saw is at its lowest.
413.title: Waveforms

414.body: With Bipolar on (the default), Out swings evenly around zero. Into a filter's Cutoff or an oscillator's V/Oct , that sweeps both above and below the knob's setting, which is what you want for vibrato. With Bipolar off, Out stays between 0 and 1: the same shape, lifted and halved. Use it where modulation should only add, as with a VCA's CV , where a bipolar LFO would spend half its cycle silent.
414.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » LFO » Bipolar and unipolar
414.title: Bipolar and unipolar

415.body: Set Tempo to a division and the LFO locks to the patch's beat: one cycle per division, in step with the Clock . A 1 bar LFO sweeps once a bar; a 1/8 tremolo pulses on every eighth note. Change the Clock's tempo and the LFO follows, and if the Clock follows a MIDI clock, so does the LFO. Tempo One cycle every At 120 BPM 4 bars , 2 bars , 1 bar 16, 8 or 4 beats 8 s, 4 s, 2 s 1/2 , 1/4 , 1/8 , 1/16 , 1/32 2, 1, ½, ¼ or ⅛ of a beat 1 s to 62.5 ms D (dotted) One and a half times the plain length 1/4D = 750 ms T (triplet) Two thirds of the plain length, three in the time of two 1/4T = 333 ms A synced LFO doesn't count its own cycles. It reads where the Clock's beat is, so it can't drift, however long it runs, and every synced LFO in the patch moves in step with the others. The cycles start on the Clock's downbeat: when the Clock starts from the top, so does the LFO. While synced: The Rate knob dims and reads the division. Its pointer shows the rate that comes to at the current tempo. Rate CV has no effect. Sync still restarts the cycle, and the cycles then run from that moment, at the division's length, until the Clock starts from the top again. Phase still shifts the waveform, so a 1 bar LFO at 90° peaks on the downbeat. When the Clock stops, the LFO holds where it is, and carries on when the Clock does. Without a Clock in the patch, the LFO keeps its own time at 120 BPM. Set Tempo back to Off and the LFO runs free at Rate , from the point it had reached.
415.title: Tempo sync

416.body: The Rate input works in octaves, like V/Oct. +1 doubles the rate, +2 quadruples it, -1 halves it. The knob stays live while it's patched and sets the base rate the CV works from, so you can keep turning it. [LFO 2 (slow)] ──Out──> [LFO 1 Rate] A slow LFO into another's Rate makes modulation that speeds up and slows down on its own.
416.title: Rate CV

417.body: Each rising edge at Sync restarts the cycle from the Phase setting. Patch a Clock into it and the LFO starts over on every pulse. To keep an LFO in time with the beat, though, Tempo is simpler and never drifts between pulses. Phase shifts the starting point. Two LFOs at the same rate, one at 0° and one at 180°, move in opposite directions; at 90° they chase each other. The Phase output is the LFO's position in its cycle, a 0-to-1 ramp whatever waveform is selected. Use it as an extra rising sawtooth, unipolar, alongside Out .
417.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » LFO » Sync and phase
417.title: Sync and phase

419.body: [LFO Out] ──> [Oscillator Exp FM] Rate around 5 to 6 Hz, Sine, Bipolar on. Turn the oscillator's Exp FM knob down to about 0.02 octaves (Shift-drag for fine steps) for a gentle ±24 cents.
419.title: Vibrato

42.body: Select a module or a group and press Ctrl + M. Each of its knobs moves a small random step, and pressing it again wanders further. Hold it, and the knobs glide out further the longer you hold, from a nudge to a big jump; let go when you like what you hear. It's a way to explore by listening: mutate a Library group until it's yours. What moves: every knob of the selected modules, and of every module inside a selected group. Ctrl + Alt + M moves their whole-number knobs, switches and dropdowns too. What doesn't: a knob a cable drives, the Audio Output, and any knob that sets how loud something is (a level, gain, makeup, drive, feedback or velocity), so a variation is never louder than the patch was. Nor does a port or a channel, which say where a module plays, not how it sounds. Hardware: an Instrument 's or a Kit 's knobs move the device, but not the ones its profile keeps from Mutate. A knob of named values moves by whole steps. Keeping one: a strip of chips under the selection holds the knobs as they were and the last eight variations, each drawn as a tick per knob, as high as the knob is turned. Click one to go back to it. Undo: each variation, and each click on the strip, is one step. Keeping it for good: Ctrl + Shift + M keeps the knobs as they stand in the next free scene of a Scenes module: the one in the selection's group, or the patch's.
42.title: Mutate

[Oscillator Out] ──> [VCA In]
[LFO Out] ──> [VCA CV] Rate 4 to 8 Hz, Sine or Triangle, Bipolar off , so the level dips and returns rather than cutting out for half of each cycle.

A slow Triangle gives a smooth wah; a Square jumps between two brightnesses. Turn CV Amt down to sweep less, or up to sweep more.

422.body: [LFO Out] ──> [SVF Filter Cutoff] Tempo 1 bar, Sine. The filter opens and closes once a bar, wherever the Clock's tempo goes. Try 2 bars for a slower swell, or a Square at 1/8 for a gated rhythm.

423.body: [LFO Out] ──> [Oscillator PWM] With the oscillator on Square, a slow LFO (0.3 to 2 Hz) makes the tone shimmer and thicken like a chorus.

[LFO Out (fast Triangle)] ──> [Sample & Hold In]
[Clock Gate] ──> [Sample & Hold Trig] Each Clock pulse freezes wherever the LFO happens to be, and Sample & Hold holds that value until the next one. Set the LFO's rate so it isn't a simple multiple of the Clock's and the steps take a long time to repeat. (The trigger has to be a gate: an LFO can't patch into Trig .)
424.title: Stepped random

425.body: The LFO is monophonic. One LFO patched into a polyphonic module moves every voice together. See Polyphony . The Rate and Phase knobs are smoothed, so turning them while the LFO runs doesn't click or jump. Run up into the audio range with Rate CV (it goes to 1 kHz), the LFO still sounds clean: the Square's and Saw's jumps, the Triangle's corners and each Sync restart are smoothed over a few samples, so they don't alias or click. At ordinary rates that touches only the samples right at each edge. Pressing Play starts every LFO from the beginning of its cycle. See Tempo and Sync for how the patch's tempo and beat reach the LFO.
425.title: Notes

426.body: ADSR Envelope for modulation that follows each note instead of repeating Clock , which sets the beat a synced LFO follows Attenuverter to scale, invert or offset the LFO Sample & Hold for stepped patterns Slope for a cycle with its rise and fall set apart, from a ramp through a triangle to a saw

427.body: Module ID mod.slope · Category Modulation · Polyphonic Slope Module Cycling, with a 1.2 s rise and a 400 ms fall, Shape 0.5. The dot is on its way down the fall, which is lit, and EOR glows until the fall ends. A Slope rises and falls at rates you set. That one idea does four everyday jobs. Patch a signal into In and Out follows it, slowly or quickly: slew, glide, portamento, lag. A gate into In makes that an attack-release envelope. A trigger into Trig plays one whole rise and fall, however short the trigger: a function generator. Turn on Cycle and each fall starts the next rise: an LFO whose rising and falling halves you set apart. It is the slope generator from a Make Noise Maths, where all four are one circuit. The node draws the rise and the fall side by side, each as wide as its share of the time, both bent by Shape . A dot rides the curve where the slope is, the stage it's in lights up, and the glow under the curve swells with Out, so a cycling Slope breathes. Above, the two times, and the rate when it cycles.
427.title: Slope

A trigger mid-fall turns round and rises from where it is Rise Control (Orange) CV around the Rise knob, exponential: +1 halves the time, -1 doubles it Fall Control (Orange) CV around the Fall knob, the same way Cycle Gate (Green) While high, every fall starts a new rise. 43.body: A patch can explain itself. A frame is a titled, tinted backdrop behind a group of modules, like a section printed on a synth's front panel: Voice , Modulation , Echoes . A note is a card of text on the canvas. Neither makes a sound. Every example patch uses them, so you can read how it works while you play it. The First Sound example, with its Shape frame's menu open Two frames and two notes. Right-click a frame's title to rename or recolor it.

The knob is logarithmic Fall 1 ms – 20 s 300 ms The time to fall from 1 to 0 Shape -1 – 1 0 The curve of both stages: -1 log, 0 linear, 1 exponential Cycle On / Off Off Checkbox on the node. On starts a new rise at the end of every fall

431.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Slope » How it works
431.title: How it works

432.body: Rise and Fall are rates : the time to move a whole unit, from 0 to 1. A trigger always runs a whole unit, so its rise takes exactly Rise and its fall exactly Fall . Following In, a smaller move takes less time: half a unit takes half the time. Pitch is in octaves, so with Rise at 60 ms an octave leap glides in 60 ms and a semitone in 5 ms. That's the analog way, and it's different from the Glide on Note In , which takes the same time for any interval. With the linear Shape, Out moves at a constant rate. When it reaches In it stops on it exactly, to the last bit, and stays there for as long as In holds still.
432.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Slope » Rates, not times
432.title: Rates, not times

433.body:
Trig sends the slope up to 1 and back down to In. It doesn't matter how long the trigger lasts: a single sample plays the whole shape, so a sequencer's gate length no longer shapes the sound. A trigger that arrives mid-fall starts a new rise from where Out is, with no jump. A gate into In behaves differently. Out rises toward 1 while the gate is high, holds there, and falls when the gate goes low: an attack-release envelope that sustains for as long as you hold the note. Trig: _|‾|____________________ In: __|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|_________
Out: _/‾‾‾\__________________ Out: __/‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾\_______
EOR: ____|‾|_________________ EOR: ____|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|______
EOC: _______|‾|______________ EOC: _________________|‾|___
433.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Slope » A trigger, a gate, and In
433.title: A trigger, a gate, and In

434.body: Shape bends both stages the same way, without changing how long they take. -1, log: the rise shoots up and eases in at the top; the fall eases off the top and drops to the bottom. 0, linear: straight lines, at a constant rate. 1, exponential: the rise starts slowly and accelerates; the fall drops fast and tails off, the way a struck sound decays. This is the shape for drums and plucks. Turning Shape while the slope moves never makes Out jump: only the road ahead bends. Outside 0 to 1, where a pitch or a bipolar signal can take Out, the slope is always a straight line.
434.title: Shape

435.body: With Cycle on, the end of each fall starts the next rise, so the Slope runs as an LFO at 1 / (Rise + Fall): 2 Hz at the defaults' 100 ms and 300 ms. Each stage ends between samples, and the next starts from exactly there, so the period is exact and doesn't drift, after ten minutes as after ten seconds. Turn Cycle off and the run in progress finishes its fall and stops.
435.title: Cycle

437.body:
[Step Sequencer Pitch] ──> [Slope In] (Rise 60 ms, Fall 60 ms, Shape 0)
[Slope Out] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct] Every note slides into the next: an octave in 60 ms, a fifth in 35 ms. Set Rise and Fall apart for a line that swoops up and drops down, or the other way round. Rhythmic Sequence has this as a variation. Because it's polyphonic, a chord from Note In glides voice by voice, each at its own pace.

[Step Sequencer Gate] ──> [Slope Trig] (Rise 1 ms, Fall 450 ms, Shape 1)
[Slope Out] ──> [VCA CV] A snap up and an exponential decay, from any length of gate. With an ADSR , a gate that falls during the attack sends it straight to release, so a short trigger can't play a long envelope; a Slope can.

44.body: To frame some modules, select them and press Ctrl + Shift + F, or right-click empty canvas and choose Frame . The frame is drawn around the selection and takes the color most of its modules share. Type its name and press Enter. To add an empty frame, right-click empty canvas with nothing selected and choose Frame . To move a frame, drag its title. Every module and note inside it moves with it, along with any smaller frame inside it. Its body lets clicks through to the canvas, so you can still add modules inside it or drag a selection box across it. To resize it, drag any edge or corner. To rename it, double-click its title. To change its color, right-click its title and pick a swatch. The same menu can Select modules inside it, or Delete frame . Deleting a frame leaves its modules where they are.

440.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [Slope "Energy" Trig] (Energy: Rise 1 ms, Fall 2.5 s; Clock 20 BPM, Div 1)
[Energy Out] ──> [Attenuverter In] (Amount -1, Offset 1)
[Attenuverter Out] ──> [Mix In 1] [Mix In 2]
[Mix Out] ──> [Slope "Bounce" Rise] [Bounce Fall] (Bounce: Rise 150 ms, Fall 150 ms)
[Energy EOR] ──> [Bounce Cycle]
[Bounce EOC] ──> [Drum Trig] (Rim, Tune 7 st)
[Energy Out] ──> [Drum Accent] One Slope is the ball's energy, draining away over 2.5 s. While it drains, its EOR keeps the second Slope cycling, and the second's EOC taps the drum once a bounce. As the energy falls, the Attenuverter turns it upside down and the Mix doubles it, so the CV into the bounce's times climbs and the bounces close up, from a gap of 240 ms to about 110 ms, while the Accent lets each one land softer. A patch can't feed a module back into itself, so the ball's energy lives in a Slope of its own.
440.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Slope » A bouncing ball
440.title: A bouncing ball

441.body:
[Drum Out] ──> [Slope In] (Rise 5 ms, Fall 1 s)
[Slope Out] ──> [VCA CV] Out climbs to each peak of the sound and sinks slowly between them, so a second sound swells and fades with the drum. Fall is the time for a whole unit, so from a peak of 0.3, Out is back to zero in 300 ms. Lengthen Fall for a slower release. For a microphone or guitar, the Audio Input 's Follow output does this already.

442.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [Slope Trig] (Rise 300 ms, Fall 10 ms, Shape 0)
[Slope Out] ──> [Logic CV] (Threshold 0.9)
[Logic Above] ──> [Drum Trig] Each clock pulse starts a rise, and Logic 's Above goes high when it crosses the Threshold, 270 ms later: each hit delayed by Rise × Threshold. Patch the gate into In instead of Trig , and Out holds at the top for as long as the gate is high. Then Above is the same gate, opening 270 ms late and closing 1 ms after the gate does (the Fall, from the top down to the Threshold). Turn Rise to set the delay.

444.body: Module ID fx.delay · Category Effect Stereo Delay module A clap into the left side only, ping-ponged on worn tape: the first echo lights on the left, the second comes back on the right The Stereo Delay plays back a copy of its input a moment later, then feeds that copy back in to make repeats. Filters in the feedback path darken or thin each repeat, P-P bounces the repeats between left and right, and Sync locks the time to the patch tempo. Switch on Tape and it becomes a worn tape echo: the repeats waver in pitch, saturate as they build, and get darker each time around. Push the feedback far enough and they run away into the classic dub swell. The Tape module puts the same machine on a whole bus.
444.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Stereo Delay » Stereo Delay
444.title: Stereo Delay

445.body: Each channel is written into its own delay line. A read head plays the line back Time later. Reads usually fall between two samples, and a cubic (Catmull-Rom) interpolator fills the gap, so time changes and modulation glide smoothly instead of clicking or dulling the highs. The playback runs through HiCut and LoCut , is scaled by FB , and goes back into the line with the input. Each repeat passes through the filters once more than the one before it. Mix blends the dry input with the playback.
445.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Stereo Delay » How it works
445.title: How it works

446.body: The display draws the train of echoes. Time runs to the right from the moment a sound goes in. The first bar is the dry sound, and after it come the echoes, one delay time apart. Each echo is as loud as the feedback leaves it, on a decibel scale so a long tail stays readable. The left channel stands above the centre line and the right hangs below it. Filters. Every repeat passes HiCut and LoCut once more, so each bar is a little warmer than the one before and a little thinner. Tape mode adds the tape's own darkening. The sound going through. Each echo lights as the sound coming in reaches it, so a hit visibly walks down the train and fades. An echo lit to the top of its bar is as loud as the loudest thing that came in. Ping-Pong. With P-P on, the echoes take turns: each side's second echo is the other side's first, come back across. It shows best with something only on one side, or a stereo source. Tape. The bars blur and sway with the wow. Past unity, the feedback runs away and the header says so in orange. Words. The top left gives the time, with the note length when Sync sets it, in orange while Time CV moves it. The top right gives the feedback and the switches that are on.
446.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Stereo Delay » The display
446.title: The display

450.body: In normal mode, feedback stops at 95%, and a soft clipper in the loop keeps the echoes from growing out of control. Around 30% gives a few echoes that fade naturally; 60% gives long trails; the top of the knob repeats almost forever. In Tape mode the knob reaches further. See Runaway .
450.title: Feedback

451.body: Set Sync to a note length and the delay time follows the patch tempo. A Clock anywhere in the patch sets that tempo, so turning the Clock's BPM knob moves the echoes with it; they glide to the new time with a brief bend in pitch. With no Clock in the patch, the delay assumes 120 BPM. If a patch has more than one Clock, only one of them sets the tempo, so keep one Clock as the master. Division Beats At 120 BPM 1/4D 1½ 750 ms 1/4 1 500 ms 1/8D ¾ 375 ms 1/8 ½ 250 ms 1/8T ⅓ 167 ms 1/16 ¼ 125 ms 1/16T ⅙ 83 ms 1/32 ⅛ 62.5 ms Synced times can run past the Time knob's 2 seconds, up to 4.5 seconds: long enough for 1/4D at the Clock's slowest 20 BPM, so every division stays on the beat. Time CV still works while synced, swinging the synced time.
451.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Stereo Delay » Tempo sync
451.title: Tempo sync

452.body: Tape models a tape echo: a loop of tape passing a record head and a play head. Switching it crossfades in about 15 ms, so you can flip it while echoes are still sounding. Wow and flutter. The play head wanders. A slow wow (about 0.5 Hz, plus a slower drift of the reel) and a fast flutter (6 to 10 Hz) bend the pitch of the repeats by a few cents. The four motions run at unrelated rates, so the pattern doesn't loop. Record-head saturation. The input and the feedback are recorded together through a soft, slightly lopsided curve. Quiet signals pass unchanged; loud ones round off and pick up the even harmonics of magnetized tape. Because the saturation sits inside the loop, a busy echo squashes and thickens as it builds. Tape loss. Tape loses top end every time it records, so each repeat is darker than the last. Longer delays mean slower tape and darker repeats: the loss starts around 7 kHz at 250 ms and falls to about 3.5 kHz at one second. HiCut still works on top of it. Motor glide. Time changes glide over about a quarter of a second, like a motor finding its new speed, and the repeats swoop in pitch as they go.
452.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Stereo Delay » Tape mode
452.title: Tape mode

453.body: In Tape mode, FB above about 90% pushes the loop past unity gain. The echoes grow until the record head's saturation holds them: the dub runaway. The output stays bounded at any setting, so you can ride it. Pull FB back below 90% and the echoes die away again.
453.title: Runaway

454.body: Click the power switch in the node header, press Ctrl+B with the module selected, or choose Bypass from its right-click menu. In L passes straight to Out L and In R to Out R (In R still copies In L when unpatched). The switch crossfades over 20 ms. A bypassed delay stops running, and it starts from silence when you switch it back in, so old echoes don't come back with it.
454.title: Bypass

455.body:
Slapback. Time 80–120 ms, FB 0%, Mix 30%, Tape on. A single, slightly smeared echo, like a 1950s vocal. Dotted-eighth rhythm. Sync 1/8D, FB 40%, Mix 40%. 457.body: Module ID fx.reverb · Category Effect Reverb Module A snare into a 3-second room, a second after the hit: the dot has run a third of the way down the slope The Reverb puts a sound in a space: a dense wash of reflections that builds, blooms and dies away. It reaches from a small, splashy room to a tail that rings for half a minute. Its knobs sit in two rows. The top row shapes the room and its tail ( Size , Decay , Damp , Mod ); the bottom row places it in the mix ( PreD , Width , Mix ).
457.title: Reverb

458.body: The Reverb is an eight-line feedback delay network (FDN). Pre-delay holds the input back before anything else happens. A four-step diffuser spreads the sound across eight channels. Each step delays the channels by different amounts, flips the polarity of some, and mixes them all together, so one click becomes 8 echoes, then 64, then 512, then 4,096. These are the early reflections. Eight delay lines circulate the sound. On every pass the lines are mixed into each other, so each echo spawns eight more and the tail thickens into a smooth, noise-like decay. Each line has its own gain and damping filter , both calculated from that line's length, so the whole tail decays at the rate Decay sets and every line loses its highs at the same rate. The lines drift slowly in length (the Mod knob). This keeps resonances from settling in and adds a gentle chorus to the tail. Simpler reverbs built from a few fixed comb filters tend to ring at the comb lengths, and sound metallic on snares and claps. The FDN's tail has no repeating period, so sharp transients spread into an even wash.
458.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Reverb » How it works
458.title: How it works

459.body: The display draws the room's decay. Time runs to the right from the moment a sound goes in, stretched so the first few milliseconds have room beside a long tail. Level falls from 0 dB at the top to −60 dB at the bottom. Pre-delay. Nothing happens for the PreD time, marked by a faint line. Early reflections. The spray of hairlines at the start is every path through the diffuser at this Size , brighter where more of them arrive together. A small room packs them tight; a large one spreads them out before they merge into the tail. The tail. Two slopes fall from the top. The darker one is the lows, reaching −60 dB at the Decay time. The brighter one is the highs, dying sooner the more Damp takes them. The room ringing. While the tail sounds, a dot rides down the slope at the level it has fallen to, and the tail still to come glows. Each new hit sends the dot back to the top. Mod. With Mod up, eight faint motes drift along the top, one per delay line, as their lengths sway. Words. The top left gives the pre-delay, or the size when there is none. The top right gives the decay time. Width and Mix aren't drawn: they place the reverb in the mix rather than shape the room.
459.title: The display

464.body: Size sets the dimensions of the room. The shortest delay line runs from 12 ms at 0% to 100 ms at 100%, and the early reflections scale with it. Small settings build up quickly, like a booth or a small room; large settings build slowly, like a hall. Size and Decay are independent, so a small room can still ring for a long time. Turn Size while a tail is sounding and the lines glide to their new lengths, bending the tail's pitch for a moment instead of clicking.
464.title: Size

465.body: Decay is the reverb time (RT60): how long the tail takes to fall by 60 dB. Measured on rendered impulse responses, it lands within about 5% of the knob across the whole Size range. Decay Space 0.1 – 0.5 s Small room, booth 0.5 – 1.5 s Studio, medium room 1.5 – 3 s Hall, church 3 – 10 s Cathedral, warehouse 10 s and up Endless ambient wash
465.title: Decay

466.body: Damping models soft surfaces absorbing high frequencies. It sets how fast 4 kHz dies relative to the lows: at 0% it lasts the full Decay time, and at 100% it dies ten times faster. Low frequencies always keep the full Decay. Low settings sound like tile and glass; high settings like carpet and curtains, and a darker reverb is easier to sit in a mix.
466.title: Damp

467.body: Mod lets each of the eight lines drift slowly in length, each at its own rate between about 0.3 and 1.1 Hz. The early reflections stay still. At 0% the tail is static, the most literal setting, though long tails can show faint resonances. Around 15–35% (the default is 25%) the movement smooths long tails without drawing attention to itself. From 60% up it becomes an audible chorus in the tail: lush on pads, seasick on piano.
467.title: Mod

468.body: Pre-delay is the gap between the dry sound and the start of the reverb. Up to about 10 ms the reverb starts at once and the source feels close. At 20–40 ms the attack of each note comes through clearly before the room answers, which keeps vocals and plucks distinct. Toward 100 ms the gap becomes an audible sense of depth.
468.title: PreD

469.body: Width sets how far apart the two sides of the reverb are. At 0% the reverb is mono, centered; at 100% the two sides come from different delay lines and are almost completely uncorrelated, so the tail fills the stereo field. Width affects only the reverb, not the dry signal.
469.title: Width

47.body: A group collapses modules into one node of your own, with jacks where cables crossed into it and the controls you choose on its face. Groups has the whole story; in short: Group: select modules and press Ctrl + G, then type a name and press Enter. Go inside: double-click the group, select it and press Tab, or click the miniature on its face. A trail at the top of the canvas shows where you are; click it, or press Escape, to go back out. Pin a control: inside the group, right-click a knob, dropdown or toggle and choose Show on group . Add a jack: inside the group, right-click a port's name and choose Show on group . Right-click a jack to rename it, move it up or down, or remove it. Rename: select the group and press F2, or right-click it and choose Rename . Ungroup: select the group and press Ctrl + Alt + G. Keep it: right-click the group and choose Save to My Modules . It's then in the add menu and quick-add palette of every patch. A group's right-click menu also has Open , Duplicate , Copy and Delete .
47.title: Groups

470.body: Mix sets how far away the sound seems. Around 10–20% it sounds close and present, 20–40% places it at a natural distance in the room, and above 50% it recedes into the space. At 100% you hear only the reverb.

471.body: Click the power switch in the node header, press Ctrl+B with the module selected, or choose Bypass from its right-click menu. In L passes straight to Out L and In R to Out R (In R still copies In L when unpatched). The switch crossfades over 20 ms. A bypassed reverb stops running, and it starts from silence when you switch it back in, so no old tail comes back with it.

475.body: Module ID fx.eq · Category Effect 3-Band EQ module Pink noise through a warm low shelf, a cut in the middle and an airy top, with the pointer on the mid band The 3-Band EQ boosts or cuts three regions of the spectrum: a low shelf for the bass, a fully parametric mid band , and a high shelf for the treble. Use it to fit a sound into a patch, take the mud out of a pad, put an edge on a lead, or darken a reverb tail. Where a filter removes whole parts of the spectrum, an EQ leans on them, up to 15 dB either way. Every knob glides, so you can sweep the mid band while a note plays without zipper noise.
475.title: 3-Band EQ

476.body: The display draws the curve the three bands add up to, from 20 Hz on the left to 20 kHz on the right, and ±18 dB around the 0 dB line. Each band's own share is a faint tinted fill: the low shelf amber, the mid band violet and the high shelf blue. The bright line is their sum, with Out added. Every curve comes from the band's own filter, so it bends exactly as the sound does. You can shape the EQ on the curve itself: Drag a dot to move its band: across for frequency, up and down for gain. The knobs follow. Drag a wing of the mid band (the short ticks either side of its dot, where its width ends) to set MdQ : out to widen it, in to narrow it. Double-click a dot to flatten its band back to 0 dB. Pointing at a dot shows its band's settings at the top left. Out shows at the top right when it isn't 0 dB. Beneath the curves is the sound itself: what comes into In is a faint blue landscape, and what leaves through Out is a pale line over it. A boost lifts the line above the landscape, and a cut carves a dip into it.
476.title: The display

481.body: A shelf raises or lowers everything beyond its frequency by the same amount, like a bass or treble knob on a stereo. The LoFrq and HiFrq knobs set the shelf's midpoint: the frequency where it has reached half its gain. The shelves are as steep as they can be without overshooting, so a boost rises cleanly to its level with no bump at the corner. The shelves have no Q of their own. To affect a narrower region at the bottom or top, use the mid band.
481.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » 3-Band EQ » Low and high shelves

482.body: The mid band is a bell-shaped peak or dip centered on MdFrq . MdQ sets its width: 0.1 to 1 : broad and gentle, spanning several octaves. Good for tonal shaping. 1 to 4 : focused but still musical. 4 to 10 : narrow and surgical, for picking out a single resonance. A good rule is to cut narrow and boost wide: narrow boosts sound unnatural, while narrow cuts can remove a problem without anyone hearing that it's gone.
482.title: Mid band

487.body:
After distortion. Distortion's harshness usually sits in the upper mids. A broad mid cut around 3 kHz after it smooths the edge without dulling the sound the way a lowpass would: [Distortion Out] ──> [EQ In] ──> [Audio Output Mono] Darker reverb. [EQ Out] ──> [Compressor In]

489.body: Module ID fx.distortion · Category Effect Distortion Module A low sine into the folder: the whole curve lit, and the wave on the right folding back at its peaks The Distortion adds harmonics by pushing a signal into a curve: rounding it off, clipping it, folding it back on itself, or crushing it into steps. Five types cover everything from a touch of warmth on a bass to a sine folded into a buzzing, vocal tone. Every curve runs at four times the sample rate with antiderivative anti-aliasing (ADAA). Even full drive on a high note adds only harmonics of that note, not the inharmonic "digital fizz" a naive distortion folds back into the audible range. The dry signal is mixed in at the same oversampled rate and aligned to the sample, so Mix blends cleanly without comb filtering.
489.title: Distortion

490.body: The display shows the bend and how far into it the sound goes. The curve. On the left, what goes in runs across from −1 to 1, and what comes out runs up. It is the module's own curve for the chosen Type , after Drive (and for Fold, Sym ), blended by Mix and scaled by Out . Soft is a gentle S, Hard flattens at the top, Fold zigzags back down, Tube leans, and Bit is a staircase with fewer steps the harder it's driven. The lit stretch. The part of the curve the input reaches right now is lit, with a dot at each end, and it glows hotter as Drive rises. Turn up a quiet input and you can watch it walk into the bend. The wave. On the right is one cycle of a sine at the input's level, faint, and over it what the curve makes of that sine. That is the shape the new harmonics come from: rounded shoulders for Soft, flat tops for Hard, extra wiggles for Fold. Words. The top right gives the drive, in orange while Drive CV moves it. For Bit it gives the bits kept and the crushed rate instead. Tone isn't drawn: it shapes the sound after the curve.
490.title: The display

The top of the range is off Tone 0 – 100% 50% Lowpass after the curve, from 200 Hz to 20 kHz Mix 0 – 100% 100% Dry (0%) to distorted (100%) Out (Output) −12 dB – +12 dB 0 dB Level after distortion Drive keeps working while Drive CV is patched: the knob sets the center and the CV moves around it.
