495.body: Smooth tanh saturation that rounds off peaks. Drive raises the input gain from 1x to 11x. It produces odd harmonics that fall away smoothly, and compresses as it goes: warmth at low drive, fuzz at high drive.
495.title: Soft

496.body: Clipping that flattens the peaks. Drive lowers the clipping point from full scale to a tenth of it. Bright, buzzy odd harmonics, with a transistor-fuzz edge.
496.title: Hard

497.body: A wavefolder in the West Coast tradition of the Serge and Buchla folders. Past the clipping point, the wave reflects back toward zero instead of flattening, then reflects again. Drive raises the gain from 1x to 6x, and each step adds another fold and another pair of peaks, up to about three folds per half-wave at full scale. The corners of each fold are rounded, as a real diode folder's are. A plain sine comes out bright, vocal or metallic, and sweeping Drive with CV gives the classic wavefolder sweep. Sym shifts the wave off center before it folds. The two halves then fold differently and even harmonics appear. Near ±100%, a quiet sine sits on a fold's peak and comes out an octave up.
497.title: Fold

498.body: Bit-depth and sample-rate reduction, for lo-fi character. Drive lowers the bit depth from 16 bits at 0% to 2 bits at 100%. Rate holds each sample for longer, like an old sampler. Below a few kHz, the crushed rate's mirror images ring out as metallic, inharmonic tones; that aliasing is the sound. It depends only on Rate: the engine's own sample rate adds none.
498.title: Bit

499.body: Asymmetric saturation, like a triode biased off center. Drive raises the input gain from 1x to 11x. The two halves of the wave saturate at different levels, so even harmonics appear from the first touch of drive: warm, thick, slightly hollow. The DC offset this creates is removed automatically.
499.title: Tube

5.body: Soba is written in Rust, with egui for the interface and cpal for audio. The audio engine runs on its own thread and never waits on the interface: edits travel to it over lock-free queues, every buffer is allocated before playback starts, and a test in the build fails if the audio thread ever allocates memory. That is what keeps the sound from glitching while you patch. The source is on GitHub .
5.title: Under the hood

50.body: Nothing sounds until you press ▶ Play (or Shift + Space, which also stops it). ⏹ Stop silences the patch, lets the last of the signal drain out of the cables, and clears echoes and reverb tails, so they don't resume when you play again.

500.body: Tone is a gentle lowpass on the distorted signal, spaced evenly in octaves from 200 Hz at 0% to 20 kHz at 100%. 50% is about 2 kHz, 65% about 4 kHz, 75% about 6 kHz. Distortion creates a lot of high harmonics, and Tone is the quickest way to take the harshness off them. It affects only the distorted signal, not the dry.

503.body:
Wavefolded sine. A sine has nothing for a filter to remove; folding gives it harmonics first: [Oscillator Out] ──> [Distortion In] Type Fold, Drive 50%
[Distortion Out] ──> [SVF Filter In] Octave fold. With Type Fold, Drive 0% and Sym 100%, a sine comes out an octave up. Envelope-driven drive. More distortion on the attack, cleaner as the note sustains: [ADSR Out] ──> [Distortion Drive CV] Before or after the filter. Distortion before the filter gives the filter more harmonics to work on, and the filter tames them. Distortion after the filter adds grit to whatever the filter left, so it changes character as the cutoff moves. Before the VCA, the amount of distortion stays constant; after it, quiet notes stay clean and loud ones break up.

505.body: Module ID fx.chorus · Category Effect Chorus Module Toms on every beat through three voices: the braid weaves slowly and lights where each hit passed The Chorus thickens a sound by layering copies of it, each delayed by a few milliseconds that keep changing. The moving delays bend each copy's pitch slightly up and down, and the copies beat against each other and against the original, the way several players on the same part never quite line up. It is true stereo, and it makes a mono source wide on its own. Short delays and a little feedback take it into flanging.
505.title: Chorus

506.body: Each channel has its own delay line: left stays left, right stays right. Each voice reads both lines through a pair of taps, and an LFO sweeps each tap's delay around Delay . At full Depth the delay swings all the way from zero to twice the Delay time. The voices are spaced evenly around the LFO cycle, so they never move in step. The voices are summed and blended with the dry signal by Mix .
506.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chorus » How it works
506.title: How it works

507.body: A stereo source keeps its image: nothing patched into In L ever reaches Out R . With In R unpatched, In L feeds both sides and the chorus creates the width itself. Each right tap's LFO sits halfway between two left taps (180° away with one voice, 90° with two), so the two sides always bend in pitch in opposite directions. Changing Voices fades voices in or out and slides the rest to their new places on the cycle, so it never clicks.
507.title: True stereo

508.body: The display draws the voices sweeping over the last two seconds, newest at the right edge. Up and down is how far each tap reads behind Delay : the centre line is the Delay itself, and the faint lines either side are as far as Depth lets the taps swing. Strands. Each voice is a strand in its own colour. The solid strand is its left tap, and the fainter one beside it is its right tap, half a voice-spacing behind. One voice draws a single wave, and four weave a braid. Rate sets how many cycles cross the panel, and Shape bends them from sine to triangle. A dot at the right edge marks where each voice is now. Light. The strands light up where sound came in, so the braid glows with whatever passes through it. Feedback. Positive FB thickens the strands. Negative FB, the hollow flanger sound, turns them hollow and violet. Words. The top left gives the rate and delay, with the rate in orange while Rate CV moves it. The top right gives the number of voices and the feedback.
508.title: The display

512.body: Rate and Depth. Slow rates sway gently; fast rates turn into vibrato. Light depth thickens without drawing attention; heavy depth wobbles until it sounds out of tune. The two work together, since the pitch bend depends on how fast the delay is changing: a fast rate needs less depth. Delay. Below about 5 ms the copies comb-filter against the dry sound, and with some feedback it becomes a flanger. From 5 to 15 ms is classic chorus. From 15 to 30 ms the copies separate into a wide, doubled sound. Voices. One voice is the simplest, almost flanger-like, with the two sides sweeping in opposite directions. Two is the classic stereo chorus. Three and four build toward a thick ensemble, at some cost in clarity. The output stays at about the same loudness whatever the voice count. Shape. Shape Character Sine Smooth and vocal: the pitch eases in and out of each bend Tri The delay sweeps at a constant speed, so each half-cycle holds one steady detune. Glassier, closer to the classic bucket-brigade choruses Switching shape morphs between the two over 20 ms. Feedback. Feedback deepens the comb-filter peaks and makes the sweep ring. The loop uses the voices' average, so its gain never exceeds the knob however many voices are running.

512.title: Shaping the sound

517.body: Module ID fx.tape · Category Effect Tape module The reels turn at the tape speed and lurch with the wow, dragging as the pitch sags and hurrying as it rises; the head glows as Saturation drives it. When the Stop gate brakes the tape, the reels slow to a halt and the speed between them counts down The Tape module is a tape machine for a bus. Much of what makes vintage-flavoured music sound warm happens on tape, after the instruments: the record head's soft squash, the head bump in the low end, the slow sway and fast shiver of the transport, the top end the tape can't hold, and, on an old reel, dropouts and hiss. Put it on a mix bus or in front of the Audio Output to give the whole patch that sound. It shares its transport and record head with the Stereo Delay 's Tape mode, which puts the same machine on the echoes only.
517.title: Tape

518.body: Each channel is recorded onto tape, then played back: Record. Pre-emphasis lifts the treble, the drive pushes the signal into the record head, and de-emphasis takes the treble back down, so the highs squash first, as they do on tape. The head bump and the speed's top end follow. Saturation sets the drive. Transport. The play head reads the tape a moment behind the record head, and that moment keeps changing with the wow and flutter, which bends the pitch. The right track sways a little differently from the left, by Width . Playback. Hiss is added, then the tape's Age : gap loss rolls off the top, and dropouts dip the sound where the oxide has worn away. A Stop gate brakes the whole machine to a halt, and winds it back up when it's let go: see Tape stop . With every knob at zero, Tape passes its input through bit for bit. It adds no latency: at rest the play head reads exactly what was just recorded, and the wobble only ever pulls it back in time, never ahead.
518.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Tape » How it works
518.title: How it works

52.body: Tick your controller in the toolbar's MIDI In menu; Soba doesn't connect to one until you do. Tick more to play several at once, up to eight. If the controller isn't listed, plug it in and click 🔄 Refresh at the bottom of the menu. Untick a device to close it, or choose None (Disconnect) to close them all. Soba remembers what's ticked: next launch it opens the same controllers, and if you plug one in after Soba starts it connects within a couple of seconds (unticking one, or choosing None , makes it forget). Closing a device releases the notes held on it. If a controller can't be opened, the reason appears in the status bar. In the browser , MIDI In starts as a 🎹 Connect MIDI button. A web page may use MIDI only once you allow it, so click it and your browser asks; Firefox first offers a small add-on for the site that allows it. Then the menu lists your controllers, and a controller you plug in later appears by itself, with no Refresh needed. Allowing it lets MIDI Out play your devices too. If you said no, allow MIDI in the site settings (the icon to the left of the address) and click Connect MIDI again. Chrome, Edge and Firefox have MIDI; Safari doesn't, and the button says so. Two modules listen to the controller: Note In , for one voice or chords, and MIDI Monitor to see what's arriving. With several devices open, each of them hears them all, until you give it a Device in its right-click menu: see Listening to one device . A mapping learned while several devices are open answers only the device it was learned from.

522.title: Speed

523.body: Saturation. Turning Saturation up puts the signal on tape: the head bump and the speed's top end come in over the first tenth of the knob, and the drive rises from there. Tape is calibrated to the studio convention, where a sine at −18 dBFS RMS sits at 0 VU and keeps its level at any drive. Quieter material comes up a little, louder material is squashed, and the louder it is the more it's squashed, with the treble first. On a full mix that sounds like glue at 20–40%, and like a cassette deck pushed into the red past 70%. Wow and Flutter. Both knobs work on a square law, so the bottom of each is fine and the top is extreme. The pitch swings by: Knob Wow at 15 ips Flutter at 15 ips 25% ±2.5 cents ±0.75 cents 50% ±10 cents ±3 cents 75% ±22.5 cents ±6.75 cents 100% ±40 cents ±12 cents Multiply by 1.6 at 7½ ips and by 0.6 at 30. A couple of cents of wow is felt more than heard; ten is a gentle seasickness; forty is a warped record. Wow is two slow sways at unrelated rates, so it never quite repeats. Turning Wow up quickly pulls the play head back and sags the pitch for a moment, as a dragging reel would. The depth glides over about a third of a second to keep that brief. Width. A mono source comes out mono at Width 0, and sways apart into stereo as Width rises. Hiss is always independent between the two sides. Age. Age rolls off the top, from nothing at 0 to the speed's worn cutoff at 100%. Dropouts start to appear around 30%. At 100% there are about two every three seconds, each 15–150 ms long, dipping the highs more than the lows. Age also adds a little hiss of its own, up to −48 dBFS. Hiss. Mostly treble, as tape hiss is, and it runs through the Age stage: an old tape hisses darker, and the hiss drops out with the music. Mix. Below 100%, the wobbling tape copy is blended with the dry signal, which beats against it like a chorus. With Saturation and Age at 0 that's all you hear: a slow, natural tape chorus. A 50% blend sounds about 3 dB quieter than either side alone, because the two copies drift apart.
523.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Tape » Shaping the sound
523.title: Shaping the sound

524.body: Press stop on a tape machine, or a turntable, in the middle of a song and everything on it slows down together, so the whole mix falls in pitch to nothing. Patch a gate into Stop and the Tape does the same to its bus. Braking. While the gate is high, the tape slows at a steady rate and comes to a halt after the Stop Time . The pitch falls in a straight line: a 1 kHz tone with a 1 s Stop Time is at 750 Hz a quarter of a second in, 500 Hz at half a second, and nothing at one second. Below about an eighth of full speed the sound has sunk below hearing, and it fades out there, so a stopped tape is silent rather than holding a frozen sample. Hiss stops with it. Winding up. Let go of the gate and the tape winds back up in half the Stop Time. Rather than picking up the old tape from where it stopped, which would leave the whole mix late, it picks up what's playing now and runs a little fast to catch up: the pitch climbs from nothing, overshoots by up to a major third, and settles exactly in time. Once it has, the output is the same as if the tape had never stopped, sample for sample, so a song on a clock comes back on the beat. Let go before the tape has stopped and it winds up from the speed it had reached, with the sound it was making fading out over 30 ms beneath it. Free when idle. With the gate low the stop adds nothing to the sound and no latency. Stop works on the tape side of Mix : at 100% the whole bus stops, and below that the dry signal plays on through it. For a stop on the master, put Tape last and keep Mix at 100%, even if Saturation, Wow and the rest are at zero. Stop Time Sounds like 50–150 ms A hiccup: the beat catches for a moment 0.3–0.8 s A DJ hitting stop on the deck 1–2 s A tape machine's motor winding down 3–4 s A slow, heavy spin-down, for the very end
524.title: Tape stop

525.body: An Arranger lane's Gate is high while the lane is above zero, so a lane can press Stop for exactly the bars you choose. Label one lane Stop and patch its gate in: [Arranger Gate 3] ──> [Tape Stop] At the end of the song. Give the last section a Jump to 100% on the Stop lane (cue 1001000), and set the Stop Time to a bar or so. On the last section's downbeat the whole song winds down to silence. A song that stops (Loop to off) keeps the lane high, so the tape stays stopped. A song that loops needs the first section to Jump the lane back to 0 (cue 1000000), and the next pass winds up on its downbeat. A brake fill. Jump the Stop lane to 100% on a one-bar Fill section, and back to 0 on the section after it. The tape brakes through the fill, sits stopped, and winds up on the next section's downbeat, back on the beat. With the Stop Time shorter than the bar there's a moment of silence before the drop; at about the bar's length the tape is still sinking when it's let go. A hiccup on a Hit. A Hit holds the lane's gate high for half a step, so with a Stop Time of 50–150 ms a Hit on a section's cue makes the bus catch on that downbeat and stumble back in time, a hiccup into the new section.
525.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Tape » With an Arranger

53.body: Any knob, toggle or dropdown can follow a control on your MIDI controller: a knob, a fader, a pad or a key. So can the Looper 's footswitches, the Sampler 's Rec and the pads of Scenes . Right-click it and choose Learn MIDI . A purple badge blinks on it, and the status bar asks you to move something. Turn a knob, move a fader, or hit a pad on your controller. The badge stops blinking and stays. Right-click again to see what it's mapped to (CC 74 · ch 1, or C2 · ch 10 for a pad), to Re-learn MIDI , or to Clear MIDI . Mappings are saved with the patch, and playing them isn't added to the undo history. What a control does depends on what it's mapped to: Mapped to A knob or fader (a CC) A pad or key (a note) A knob turns it across its range holds it at the top while held A toggle switches it on from halfway up flips it on each hit A dropdown sweeps through the choices steps to the next choice, and round A footswitch or Rec presses it from halfway up presses it while held A Scenes pad recalls the scene from halfway up recalls the scene Faders that don't jump. A fader or knob with ends doesn't yank the knob it's mapped to. Until you move the hardware past where the knob stands, a purple tick on the knob's rim shows where the hardware is, with a faint arc back to the knob, so you can see which way to go. Once the hardware reaches the knob it picks it up, the tick fades, and the knob follows. Turn the knob with the mouse, recall a scene or undo, and it waits to be picked up again. To have it jump instead, untick Pick up in its right-click menu. Endless encoders. Many controllers have knobs that turn forever and send steps rather than a position. Soba listens to the first few values after you learn one and tells it apart from a fader, so the knob steps from wherever it stands, a hundred steps end to end, and one number at a time on a whole-number knob. If it guesses wrong, choose under Hardware in the knob's right-click menu. Invert turns any mapping upside down. A controller turns a knob the way the mouse does: a fader sweeps a frequency by octaves, so the middle of its throw is in the middle of what you hear. To patch a fader or a wheel into a cable, rather than turn one knob with it, use a Controls module: its slots learn the same way. To play drums or fire triggers from a controller's pads, use a Pads module, whose notes a Note In on Omni then leaves alone. A mapping listens on the MIDI channel it was learned on, so the keys and the pads of one controller can send the same note numbers without mixing up. (Mappings made before Soba learned channels still listen on all of them.) To back out before moving anything, press Escape, or right-click the blinking control and choose Cancel MIDI Learn . Choosing Learn MIDI on a different control moves learn mode there instead. Map Mode To map a whole controller, turn on Map Mode : press Ctrl + L, or choose Map Mode at the foot of the MIDI In menu. A thin purple line runs round the canvas, and every control that can be learned wears a soft purple outline: knobs, toggles, dropdowns, footswitches, Rec and the Scenes pads. The ones already mapped keep their badges. Now a click on a control doesn't turn, flip or press it. It starts MIDI Learn on it instead, and its outline breathes while it waits. Move a knob or fader or hit a pad on your controller, and the control is mapped. Map Mode stays on, so click the next control and move the next thing, and so on down the controller: eight encoders, four faders and eight pads are twenty clicks and twenty moves, and no menus. Clicking another control before you move anything moves the learn there. The status bar says what Map Mode is waiting for, and what was mapped last. Right-click still opens a control's menu in Map Mode, to clear a mapping or change its hardware. Press Escape or Ctrl + L again to leave. The Controller Map Choose Controller Map… at the foot of the MIDI In menu to see every mapping in the patch on one panel, in the order you made them. Each row is one mapping: Column What it shows Source What turns it: CC 74 · ch 1, C2 · ch 10 for a pad, or Macro 3 in a DAW Module and Control The module, and the knob, switch or Scenes pad it turns Range The two ends a knob or fader sweeps the knob between, typed in the knob's own units (200 Hz, 8 kHz, 40%). Press Enter to set one. They stay inside the knob's own range Hardware Knob or fader , or one of the two kinds of Encoder , as under Hardware in the knob's menu Pick up A knob or fader waits to pick the knob up rather than jumping it Invert The hardware's top is the control's bottom The cross at the end of a row clears that mapping. Hover a row and its control lights up on the canvas, so you can find which knob it is. Changes here are changes to the patch: they're saved with it, and the patch shows it has unsaved changes until you save. A DAW macro's range and style are the DAW's, so its row only lists it. Map Mode has a button at the foot of the panel too, so you can keep mapping with the map open.
53.title: MIDI Learn

530.body: Module ID fx.slicer · Category Effect Slicer module Each step draws the slice it cuts: as tall as it's loud, as wide as Duty holds it open, its edges as soft as Shape. Ties join slices into one slab, the swung steps sit late, the filter's line falls through each slice, and with Ping-Pong the slices bound for the right are violet. A dot rides the slice playing The Slicer chops whatever passes through it into a rhythm, in time with the patch, the way a slicer pedal does. Hold a chord into it and out comes a gated sixteenth-note figure. A pad becomes a pulse and a drone becomes a groove. A live voice or guitar from Audio Input gets chopped as it's played. A row of sixteen steps says which slices open and how hard. It runs on the patch's Clock , so step 1 falls on the bar and the slices land with everything else.
530.title: Slicer

531.body: Each step is one of five things: Step Drawn as What it does Accent A full-height slice Opens at full level, and brightest through the Filter Hit A slice most of the way up Opens at 80% Ghost A low slice Opens at 45%, for the quiet notes between Tie The slice before, carried on Holds the slice before it open through its step too, without striking again Rest An empty floor Closed: the sound is cut, as deep as Depth says A slice opens at the start of its step and stays open for Duty of it, then closes. A tie after it holds it open to the end of its step, so X=== is one slice a beat long. Shape sets how each slice opens and closes. At 0 the edges are crisp, about a millisecond in and a few out: short enough to sound cut, long enough not to click. Turned up, the slices swell in over up to half their step and fade out over more, so a fast pattern turns to a soft tremolo. Depth sets how far the gaps cut: to silence at 100%, halfway at 50%, not at all at 0. Mix blends the input back in, untouched.
531.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Slicer » How it works
531.title: How it works

532.body: Filter gives each slice a resonant lowpass that opens as it strikes and closes through its step. A harder step strikes brighter: an accent opens it all the way, a ghost only partly. Turned all the way up, a soft step closes the filter as far as 6 octaves down. With Depth at 0 nothing is cut, and only the filter steps. That's the "wah step" of a slicer pedal's filter patterns: the sound stays whole, and its brightness jumps from step to step.
532.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Slicer » The step filter
532.title: The step filter

533.body: With Ping-Pong on, the slices alternate from side to side: the first in the row on the left, the next on the right, and so on. A tie stays on the side of the slice it holds. Each pass of the row starts on the left again, so a row with an odd number of slices plays the same way every time round.
533.title: Ping-Pong

534.body: The row follows the transport's beat: while a Clock plays, step 1 is the first downbeat, and the Slicer keeps its place however the tempo moves. Without a playing Clock it keeps a beat of its own, at the Clock's tempo or 120 BPM. A live input is still chopped while the transport is stopped. A rising edge at Reset starts the row over from step 1, on that beat: patch an Arranger 's section trigger there to line the row up with a section. Steps shortens the row. 12 steps against a bar of 16 drift across the bar and come back round every three bars. Swing pushes every second step late, as a drum machine's swing does: 50% is straight, 66% a triplet shuffle.
534.title: Timing

54.body: The Hands On example puts all of this to work on an Arturia MiniLab 3. Mapping is for a patch you've finished. While you're building one, you want the encoders under your hand to be the knobs of whatever you're working on: click an oscillator and they turn its knobs, click a filter and they turn the filter's. That's Hands Follow Selection . Teach Soba your controller first. You do this once per controller. Choose Teach Your Controller… in the MIDI In menu, and the status bar walks you through it. With several devices open, it teaches the one whose encoder you turn first, and keeps what it learns under that device's name. The hands then stay on the controller you taught last, for as long as it's open: "Turn encoder 1 a few clicks". Turn the first encoder a few clicks in one direction, at any speed. The status bar says what it heard (Encoder 1 is CC 74 · ch 1, endless) and asks for the next one, through encoder 8. "Move fader 1". Move each fader in turn, through fader 4. If your controller has fewer encoders or faders, press Tab (or Skip ) to pass one, and Enter (or Done ) to finish early. Escape gives up and keeps what Soba knew before. Turning slowly lets Soba tell an endless encoder, which sends steps, from a knob with ends, which sends where it is. Soba keeps what it learned under the controller's name, not in the patch, so it's there for every patch, and each controller you teach is remembered separately. Then turn on Hands Follow Selection in the MIDI In menu, or press Ctrl + Shift + L. Teaching turns it on for you. While it's on: The encoders turn the selected module's first eight knobs, in the order its face shows them, and the faders turn the next four. Select a group and they turn the knobs pinned to its face instead. With several modules selected, they turn the first one's. The knobs they turn wear small numbered purple badges, 1 to 8 for the encoders and F1 to F4 for the faders. The badges fade in each time you select something else. Endless encoders step the knob from wherever it stands. Faders, and knobs with ends, pick the knob up as mapped ones do: a tick on the rim shows where the fader is until it reaches the knob. The patch's own mappings on the taught encoders and faders pause, and their badges dim. Turn Hands Follow Selection off and they come back. Mappings on the controller's other controls, its pads and keys, carry on as before. As with mappings, turning a knob this way isn't added to the undo history. Map Mode and MIDI Learn come first. While either is on, the encoders don't follow the selection, so you can map them in the usual way. Seeing what each control does On stage it's hard to remember which fader does what in this patch. Choose Show the Controller in the MIDI In menu, or press Ctrl + H, and a small sketch of your controller appears along the foot of the canvas. It has the eight encoders and four faders, with the same numbered purple badges as the knobs they turn, and a row of pads when the patch maps any. Beside each control is what it does right now: the knob's name, and under it the module's name in the module's colour. A control that does nothing stays faint and says what it sends (CC 74), so you can find the free ones. What it shows follows what the controller does. While Hands Follow Selection is on, the encoders and faders show the selected module's knobs, and the sketch says which module they follow. Otherwise they show the patch's own mappings on the encoders and faders you taught. The pads are a Pads module's, if the patch has one, each saying what its gate is patched into ( Kick over Drum ). After them come the patch's mappings to notes, the Looper 's footswitches and the Scenes pads, lowest note first ( Rec over Looper ). A pad lights while you hold it. It moves as the hardware does. An encoder's pointer and a fader's cap sit where the knob they turn is, a control brightens as its message arrives, and a fader that hasn't picked its knob up yet shows a purple tick where the fader is. Endless encoders are drawn with a knurled rim. If you haven't taught Soba your controller , the sketch lays the patch's mappings on eight encoders and four faders in the order you made them, and offers Teach Your Controller… . While you teach it, the control Soba waits for breathes purple. Mappings that don't fit, or are on controls Soba wasn't taught, are counted at the left, with a link to the Controller Map . The sketch keeps its size as you zoom, stays clear of the status bar, and only takes the clicks that land on it. Hover a control to see what it sends. Soba remembers whether it's shown.

544.body: The Library has a Slicer group that rebuilds this module from stock modules. Add it and open it to see how a slicer pedal works inside. At its defaults it plays the Trance row as this module does, each slice as loud. Part of the Slicer Built from Rate , locked to the transport An LFO , square and unipolar, Tempo at the rate. A Logic module's Above turns it into a clock for the sequencer. The LFO's phase is the transport's beat, so it can't drift The row: rest, ghost, hit, accent, tie A Step Sequencer . A step's Gate off is a rest, Velocity 57, 102 and 127 are a ghost, a hit and an accent, and a Tie holds a slice into the next step. Patterns A to D hold Trance, Gallop, Son Clave and Sidechain: pick one in its Chain Duty The sequencer's Gate Length , a share of the step How a slice opens and closes An ADSR with Sustain at 100%, its Velocity from the sequencer. Atk and Rel stand in for Shape Depth A VCA 's CV Amount . The VCA's gain, 1 − amount + amount × CV, is the Slicer's depth exactly The step filter An SVF Filter , lowpass. A second ADSR, struck by each step as hard as its velocity and closing over Close , opens it through an Attenuverter at ×4, eight octaves. Turn Filter down to hear it Reset A jack into the sequencer's Reset What doesn't carry over: Swing. No transport-locked source swings except the patch's Clock . Timing that follows the step. The module stretches Shape and the filter's close with the step. An ADSR's times are in seconds, so the group's match at one tempo. Chopping with the transport stopped. A synced LFO holds still on a stopped Clock, so the group won't chop live input until you press Play. (With no Clock in the patch at all, it runs at 120 BPM.) Starting over with the transport. Patch the Clock's Reset into the group's Reset so the row starts on the bar. Ping-Pong , Mix , the Depth jack and stereo in. Each needs more modules (a Clock Divider and Logic gates for Ping-Pong, a crossfade for Mix and the Depth jack). The group stays mono so it reads at a glance. The face's row and pattern menu. Edit the steps on the sequencer inside the group.

544.title: Build it yourself

545.body: Start from a held sound. The Slicer only cuts what it's given, so it suits a sustained chord, a pad, a drone or a Looper 's layers more than a plucked note. After the slicer, add space. A Reverb or a Stereo Delay after it fills the gaps with tails, and the chop sounds like part of the room. Breathe a filter with it. Patch Env to an SVF Filter 's Cutoff jack for a sweep on every slice, or Gate to an ADSR for a different shape per note. Bring it in and out. An Arranger lane into Depth turns the slicing on for the chorus and off for the verse. Soften the edges for a tremolo. Shape up and Duty near 100% turn any pattern into a rhythmic tremolo, not a chop.
545.title: Tips

546.body: Module ID fx.compressor · Category Effect Compressor Module A kick on every beat over a low saw: each hit climbs the curve, and the reduction it brings hangs over the sound coming in The Compressor turns down a signal when it gets loud and leaves it alone when it's quiet. That evens out the level of a bass line, adds snap to percussion, holds a pad steady, or, with a kick in the Sidechain input, makes a pad pump in time. It also puts its gain reduction out as a control signal on GR , so the amount of compression can move other parts of the patch.
546.title: Compressor

547.body: The detector measures the level of In , or of Sidechain when something is patched there. When the level rises above Thresh , the compressor works out how far to turn it down: Ratio sets how much of the overshoot gets through. Atk sets how quickly that reduction is applied, and Rel how quickly it lets go. Mkup adds gain back afterward, and Mix blends the result with the dry input. Attack and release shape the gain reduction , in dB, not the measured level. So a steady tone above the threshold comes out exactly where the ratio says it should, however fast or slow the timing knobs are set; attack and release only decide how it gets there.
547.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Compressor » How it works
547.title: How it works

548.body: The display has two halves: the curve the compressor works to, and the last two seconds of it working. The curve. On the left, the level the detector hears runs across and the output's level runs up, both from −60 dB to 0 dB. Below the threshold the curve follows the faint diagonal, where nothing changes. Past it the curve bends flatter by the ratio, through a soft band as wide as Knee . Mkup lifts the whole curve, and Mix pulls it back towards the diagonal. The dot. The dot sits at the level the detector hears now, at the height the gain reduction applied right now gives it. While Atk is still clamping down, or Rel is still letting go, the dot is off the curve, and a short trail shows the path it took. It glows orange while the compressor is turning the sound down. The strip. On the right, time runs from the left up to now at the right edge. The sound coming into In is a faint blue landscape, and what leaves through Out is the line over it. The gain reduction hangs from the top in orange: 24 dB of reduction reaches the floor. A faint line marks the threshold, so you can see which peaks cross it and how the output ducks after each one. Words. The top left gives the ratio and threshold, plus RMS when the detector measures RMS and SC when the Sidechain is patched. The top right gives the reduction now. Hover over the display for more.
548.title: The display

549.body: Port Signal Type Description In Audio (Blue) Signal to compress Sidechain Audio (Blue) Signal the detector listens to instead of In. When unpatched, the detector listens to In
549.title: Inputs

55.body: With a room of hardware plugged in, choose The Rig… at the foot of the MIDI In menu, or press Ctrl + Shift + H. It shows every MIDI device Soba can hear or play on one panel. MIDI In has a row for each input found, and for each one Soba remembers that isn't plugged in. Each row has: a lamp: green while the input is open, flashing as it's heard; amber while it's unplugged; a tick to open or close it, as in the menu. An unplugged one has a ✕ instead, to forget it; its slot ( In 1 to In 8 ); the last message heard, as the MIDI Monitor writes it. It's bright when it arrives and fades to grey over a few seconds; how many modules have their Device set to it alone. Hover to see their names. An input a route comes from also has a thru chip by its name. Click it to make the input Thru only : it stays open and its routes pass as before, but the patch doesn't hear it. Modules set to any device, MIDI Learn, mappings learned from any device, the MIDI Monitor and the pianos all pass it by. A module whose Device names it still hears it, since naming it is asking for it. While it's Thru only, the chip is lit, the name steps back, and the row reads routes only where the modules would be. It's for a keyboard that's only there to play your hardware. Click the chip again to let the patch hear it. MIDI Out has a row for each of the eight ports, A to H , that a MIDI Out plays. Each row has: the port's device, which you choose here or on a MIDI Out's face. Its menu can also 📤 Send a SysEx file… to it: see Sending SysEx ; its Clock : what it sends of the patch's Clock. Clock + Transport sends the tempo with Start and Stop, Clock only the tempo alone, and Off nothing. The port sends it whether or not a MIDI Out plays it. While its device leads the Clock (see Leading or following ), it reads leads in purple and sends nothing; its Offset : how many milliseconds later than the sound its notes, CCs and clock go out, to line a slow device up with the rest. Drag it, or click to type. It's amber when it asks for earlier than your audio device's delay allows; beside the offset, a ping (•)) to measure the device's delay and set the offset for you: see Measuring a device's delay ; its Budget : how many messages a second it may send. No limit suits a USB device. A 5-pin DIN cable carries only about a thousand, so set DIN · 1000/s for a port that plays through a MIDI interface, or Gentle · 500/s for gear that falls behind at full speed. Over its budget, a port sends only the newest value of each CC, bend and pressure, and notes, programs and clock go on time; how the port is doing: Sending , Full (in amber, while its budget is thinning CCs), Ready (it has a device but nothing plays it), Unplugged , No device , or In use (another app has the device); a dot that lights on each beat while clock goes out; the last message sent. After SysEx it reads SysEx · 163 B , and while a long dump is still going out, how much is left ( SysEx · 2.4 KB to go ); how many MIDI Outs play the port. Thru has a row for each route. A route passes what one MIDI In plays straight to one port, past the patch, so with everything plugged into the computer, the computer is your patch bay: the Fantom's keys play the MicroFreak, or the Tracker drives the Volcas, while the patch does something else. Click + Route to add one. Each row has: a lamp that flashes as the route passes something, and a tick to set the route aside without losing it; From , the MIDI In it hears, and To , the port it plays. The input must be open (ticked under MIDI In) for Soba to hear anything to pass; Channel , the channel it passes ( All , or one), and Becomes , the channel they go out on ( Same , or all moved to one). Pass channel 1 and make it channel 10 to play a drum machine from any keyboard; what it passes: Notes , CC , Bend (pitch bend and pressure), Clock (clock, Start, Stop and Song Position) and Prog (program changes). Click one to turn it on or off. A new route passes everything but clock, since a keyboard's clock and the port's own Clock together would run the device at double time; what it's doing: Thru , Open input (click to open it), No input , No device , Unplugged or Loop ; a ✕ to take it away. Notes it was holding are let go. A route goes out the moment it comes in, ahead of anything else on the thread that sends MIDI, without waiting for the audio or for the port's Offset : it's for playing, and adds well under a millisecond. A route that would play the device it comes from is refused and says Loop , since a device that echoes what it hears would feed back forever; the To menu won't offer that port. The patch still hears an open input: a Note In set to any device plays along. To keep them apart, make the input Thru only with the chip by its name under MIDI In. Up to sixteen routes. Ports, with their clocks, offsets and budgets, routes, and inputs are settings of this computer, not of the patch. 🔄 Refresh looks for devices again at once. Otherwise Soba looks every couple of seconds. Sending SysEx. Some things only SysEx can do: give a Volca FM a DX7 voice, load a bank of 32, or set a device's settings that have no CC. Open a port's device menu, choose 📤 Send a SysEx file… and pick a .syx file. Every message in it goes to that port's device whole and in order, and a line under the ports says how many went. A port with a Budget paces a long dump to it, since some devices drop SysEx that comes faster than their cable carries: a bank of 32 DX7 voices (4,104 bytes) takes about 1.4 seconds at DIN · 1000/s . The notes and clock keep their time meanwhile, and CCs wait for the dump. In the browser, the first file you send asks for one more permission, since SysEx can rewrite a device's sounds and settings: the browser asks to let Soba "control and reprogram your MIDI devices". Allow it, then send the file again. Notes and CCs never need it. After a reboot. Windows numbers devices that share a name in the order they were plugged in (2- Digitakt), and numbers a device's extra ports (MIDIIN3 (FANTOM-06)). Linux adds the device's client and port numbers to its name. Those numbers can change when you reboot or plug things in a different order. Soba finds a device by its exact name first, then by its name without those numbers, so every port and input finds its device again. A module whose Device is set to it, or a mapping learned from it, still hears it. If two devices are left that both fit, Soba uses neither, rather than guess. Hover a port's device to see whether it was found under a new number. Measuring a device's delay Every device takes its own time to turn a note into sound. With its audio plugged into your interface and open as the Input in the toolbar, Soba can time it for you: Click the ping (•)) beside a port's Offset . A line opens under the port. Choose the channel and note to ping, and which of the input's channels the device comes back on ( In 1+2 , In 3 , and so on: a pair is heard as one). A sound with a sharp attack measures best: a kick, a rim shot or a pluck, on the channel of the track or part that plays it. Click Measure . Soba plays the note eight times, a little over half a second apart, and listens for each one. With the transport stopped it first waits a couple of seconds for the input to settle; while it plays, it starts at once. Quieten anything else the port plays while it listens. Soba then says how long the device took, from the note leaving to its sound, and how close together the eight answers were. It takes away the part of the trip that's Soba's and your interface's: the output's delay and the port's offset before the note leaves, and the input's delay and buffer once the sound is back. A strip draws the pings one over another from the note, that part shaded grey and the device's own in purple, with a green line where its sound begins. It also says where the device lands now against Soba's sound, and offers Set Offset : the offset that lines it up. A device slower than your audio device's delay can't be caught up all the way, since a message can't leave before its sound is made; the offer goes as early as it can, and says so. A larger buffer gives more room. It gives up rather than guess when too few pings come back clear of the noise, when they come back too far apart to trust, or when the input stalls or settles while it listens. One ping that lands far off (a stray sound) is left out. Only one port is measured at a time, and closing the Rig stops a measurement. How exact it is depends on how well the interface reports its own delays: an ASIO driver reports them to the sample. Windows' shared audio doesn't report the input's, so Soba takes it as the least it can be and says so; the device may then be a little quicker than measured.

553.body: Above the threshold, the ratio sets how many decibels go in for each decibel that comes out. At 2:1, a signal 10 dB over the threshold comes out 5 dB over. At 4:1 it comes out 2.5 dB over. At 20:1, the top of the range, the compressor is close to a limiter: almost nothing gets past the threshold. For example, with Thresh at −20 dB and Ratio at 4:1: In Out −30 dB −30 dB (below the threshold, untouched) −20 dB −20 dB (at the threshold) −10 dB −17.5 dB (10 dB over becomes 2.5 dB over)
553.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Compressor » Threshold and ratio
553.title: Threshold and ratio

554.body: With a hard knee (0 dB), compression starts abruptly at the threshold. A soft knee eases it in over a band centered on the threshold: with the default 6 dB, compression starts 3 dB below the threshold and reaches the full ratio 3 dB above it. Soft knees sound more transparent; hard knees more obviously compressed.
554.title: Knee

555.body: Atk decides whether the start of each note gets through. Below about 1 ms the compressor catches every transient, which can flatten a sound. Around 10 to 30 ms, the first moment of each hit punches through before the compressor reacts, which is how compression adds snap to drums. Slower still, and only sustained parts of the sound are reduced. Rel decides how the level recovers. A fast release (under 50 ms) recovers between notes and can pump audibly; 50 to 150 ms is musical for most material; slow releases hold the reduction for a smooth, sustained squash.
555.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Compressor » Attack and release
555.title: Attack and release

556.body: Detector Measures Character Peak Every peak of the waveform Catches transients and keeps peaks in check. Good for drums and limiting RMS Average power over about 20 ms Follows loudness, as the ear does. Smoother, gentler leveling for pads, buses and sustained sounds A sine reads 3 dB lower on RMS than on Peak, so the same settings compress it a little less.
556.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Compressor » Detector: Peak or RMS
556.title: Detector: Peak or RMS

557.body: Click the power switch in the node header, press Ctrl+B with the module selected, or choose Bypass from its right-click menu. In passes straight to Out; the sidechain isn't passed, and GR stays at zero. The switch crossfades over 20 ms, which makes it easy to compare the compressed and original sound while it plays.
557.title: Bypass

558.body: Start with Ratio around 4:1 and lower Thresh until the loudest moments are being turned down. Adjust Atk and Rel until the sound breathes the way you want. Raise Mkup until the level matches the bypassed sound, then compare with Ctrl+B . Louder nearly always sounds better, so compare at the same level. A few decibels of reduction on the loudest moments is usually plenty.
558.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Compressor » Setting it up

56.body: When something good happens (a filter sweep you rode by hand, a lucky generative passage, an improvisation on a MIDI keyboard), press ● Rec or Ctrl + R to keep it. If the patch is stopped, Rec starts it. While recording, the button turns red, with a slowly pulsing light and the length of the take so far. Press it again, press Ctrl + R, or press ⏹ Stop to end the take. A note pops up in the corner with the take's name and length, and 📂 Show in folder opens it in your file manager. What's recorded: exactly what you hear, after the output limiter, sample for sample. It's a 32-bit float WAV at your audio device's sample rate and channel count. Where it goes: Music/Soba, named after the patch and the minute you pressed Rec, such as First Sound 2026-10-08 14-03.wav. To use another folder, right-click ● Rec and choose Change… ; Open Folder opens it. The patch comes too. Every take is saved with the patch beside it, as a .json with the same name, so you can always open the patch that made a recording. It's saved when the take ends, so knobs you rode during the take are saved where you left them. Edit freely. Turning knobs, patching cables, even opening another patch: the recording keeps going through all of it. Switching the Output device ends the take cleanly. Closing the window while recording asks first, and then saves the take. Recording runs alongside the audio, never in its way. If your disk ever falls more than two seconds behind, the missing audio is skipped rather than allowed to cause a glitch, and the note tells you how much was lost.
56.title: Recording

560.body:
Sidechain pumping. A kick ducks a pad, and the pad swells back between hits: [Kick VCA Out] ──> [Compressor Sidechain]
[Pad VCA Out] ──> [Compressor In]
[Compressor Out] ──> [Audio Output Mono] The sidechain only drives the detector; it isn't heard through the compressor. Patch the kick to the output separately to hear it. Parallel compression. Set Ratio high (6:1 or more) and the threshold low, then bring Mix down to about 50%. The heavily compressed signal thickens the quiet details while the dry signal keeps the transients. Moving other things with GR. GR rises as the compressor works. Because 1.0 stands for 60 dB of reduction, the signal is small: 6 dB of reduction reads 0.1. Patched into a filter's Cutoff (1 per octave at the default CV Amt ), that moves the cutoff a tenth of an octave: enough for the tone to brighten slightly as the compressor clamps down. Turn the filter's CV Amt up to make more of it.
560.title: Patch ideas

561.body: EQ : often placed just before the compressor VCA : level control under direct CV Distortion : saturation is a kind of compression too Audio Output : the final output stage
561.title: Related modules

562.body: Module ID fx.vocoder · Category Effect Vocoder Module Frozen mid-word: a bar for each band shows how loud the voice was there, held solid while the snowflake shows. Flatten is halfway The Vocoder makes one sound speak with another's mouth. It takes the spectral envelope of a modulator , usually a voice: which parts of the spectrum are loud and which are quiet, moment to moment. It then lays that envelope over a carrier , usually a synth chord. The chord takes on the voice's vowels and consonants and keeps its own pitch and harmony. It's the sound of Kraftwerk's robots, Herbie Hancock's I Thought It Was You , and Air's Sexy Boy .
562.title: Vocoder

563.body: The modulator is split into Bands , a bank of band-pass filters spaced evenly in pitch from 100 Hz to 6.4 kHz. A follower on each band tracks how loud the voice is there. It rises at the Attack rate and falls at the Release rate. The carrier is split by a second, matching bank. Each carrier band is turned up and down by its twin's follower, and the bands are summed. Where the voice has a formant, the carrier gets one too. Each band is two band-pass sections in a row, so it's steep enough to keep neighbours apart. Neighbouring bands cross at −3 dB, so a carrier with every follower open comes through with an even spectrum. Three more paths help speech come through: Formant slides the carrier's bank against the voice's, by up to an octave either way, so the vowels land higher or lower on the chord. Sibilance lets the voice's own highs, above the bank, straight through. Unvoiced swaps the carrier for noise while the voice hisses. Two more change how the bank itself plays: Freeze holds every band where it is, so a vowel lasts as long as the chord does. Flatten evens out the carrier's own spectrum before the voice's is put on it, so a dull carrier speaks as clearly as a bright one.
563.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Vocoder » How it works
563.title: How it works

564.body: Port Signal Type Description Carrier Audio (Blue) The sound that's played: a synth, a chord, noise. A polyphonic cable is summed, so a whole chord can come in on one cable Modulator Audio (Blue) The sound whose spectrum the carrier wears: a voice from a Sampler or an Audio Input , or drums Formant Control (Orange) Adds to the Formant knob: +1 moves the carrier's bands an octave up Freeze Gate (Green) While high, the bands hold where they are. Patched, it takes over from the Freeze switch
564.title: Inputs

565.body: Port Signal Type Description Out L Audio (Blue) The odd bands (the 1st, 3rd, 5th...), leaning left as Width opens Out R Audio (Blue) The even bands, leaning right The sibilance and the dry carrier (below 100% Mix ) sit in the middle of both.
565.title: Outputs

566.body: Control Range Default Description Bands 8 / 16 / 24 16 How finely the spectrum is split (dropdown on the node) Freeze Off / On Off Holds every band where it is (a switch on the node) Attack 0.5 – 200 ms 4 ms How fast a band opens when the voice gets louder there Release 5 ms – 2 s 40 ms How fast a band closes again Formant −1 – +1 oct 0 The carrier's bands against the voice's: up for a smaller throat, down for a larger one Flatten 0 – 100% 0% How far the carrier's own spectrum is evened out before the voice is put on it Sibil (Sibilance) 0 – 100% 25% How much of the voice's highs pass straight through Unvoic (Unvoiced) 0 – 100% 25% How far noise replaces the carrier while the voice hisses Width 0 – 100% 50% How far apart the odd and even bands sit Mix 0 – 100% 100% From the carrier alone (0%) to the vocoded sound (100%) Level −24 – +12 dB 0 dB The output's gain, after everything else The Formant input adds to the knob, and the sum stops at an octave either way. While it's patched, the knob stays live and sets the centre the CV works around. Attack and Release are the time a band takes to cover most of a change (63%), like the RC follower on an analog vocoder's band.
566.title: Parameters

567.body: Bars stand on a frequency axis, one per band, each as tall as the voice is in that band right now. Watch them while the voice speaks and you can see the vowels change. An "ee" lifts the bars at both ends, and an "oo" piles them up at the left. Colours. Odd bands are cyan and even bands violet. The colours part as Width opens, to show which side each band plays on. Formant. When Formant moves the carrier's bands, each bar leaves a white cap where the carrier plays it, joined to its own foot by a slanting line. The shift shows top right. Sibilance. The strip on the right is the range Sibilance passes. Its column is the voice's level up there, lit as brightly as the knob lets it through. Unvoiced. While the voice hisses and Unvoiced lets noise in, the bank glitters. Freeze. Frozen, the bars stop and turn solid, with icy caps, and a snowflake sits beside the band count. The sibilance column goes dark, because the voice's own highs are muted while the bands hold. The feet. The dots under the bars lie along the carrier's slope as the bank plays it. A dull carrier's feet fall away to the right. Turn up Flatten and they level out, and a faint line stays behind on the slope the carrier came in with. Hover over the display to read both slopes in dB an octave.
567.title: The display

568.body: Bands. Eight bands sound like a machine talking: rough, buzzy and only just readable, the classic robot. Sixteen is the all-rounder. Twenty-four is the clearest and most like the voice itself. Loudness stays within a few dB whichever you choose. Changing Bands fades the bank out and in over a few milliseconds, so it never clicks. Attack and Release. Speech wants a fast attack (2 to 5 ms) and a short release (20 to 50 ms), so each syllable starts and stops cleanly. Lengthen the release past a few hundred milliseconds and the words smear into a choir that lingers on each vowel. Very short times on the low bands start to buzz, because the follower begins to trace the waveform itself. Formant. Moving the carrier's bank up makes a smaller throat: the voice turns childlike, then cartoonish. Moving it down makes a giant. The pitch you hear doesn't move, because that comes from the carrier. Small amounts (a quarter octave or so) change the character without hurting the words. An LFO on the Formant input makes the voice wobble between the two. Sibilance and Unvoiced. Consonants like "s", "t" and "f" are mostly noise above 4 kHz, where many carriers have little to give. Sibilance passes the voice's own highs straight through, so they stay crisp. Unvoiced handles the hiss inside the bank. When the voice's level above 4 kHz grows past 30% of its whole level, noise starts replacing the carrier, and by 60% it has replaced it as far as the knob allows. The "s" is then spoken by noise, through the voice's own bands. With no carrier at all, Unvoiced still lets the consonants through on their own. Vowels don't trigger it. Width. At 0% the vocoder is mono. Wider, neighbouring bands split left and right, and the voice seems to fill the space between the speakers. At 100% each side carries only its own bands. Mix. At 0% you hear only the carrier, centred. In between, a little of the raw chord fills the gaps between the words. Level. Turns both outputs up or down, the dry carrier, the bank and the sibilance alike, and changes nothing else: the bands, the display and Flatten's weighting hear the same thing at any Level. Set the part's loudness here and leave the faders after it free for the mix. Freeze. Sing an "ahh", switch on Freeze, and every band holds exactly where it was. Now play chords: each one says the same vowel for as long as you hold it, and you can stop singing. The voice's own highs (the Sibilance path) are muted while frozen, so whatever you say next doesn't leak through, and the Unvoiced noise holds where it was too. With Flatten up, the voice's weighting of the bands holds as well, so a held vowel keeps one level through the whole chord. Switch Freeze off and the bands carry on from where they were held, at the Attack and Release rates, so there's no jump. Patch a gate into the Freeze input and it takes over from the switch: high holds, low lets go. Flatten. The bank can only put the voice where the carrier has something to give. A dull carrier, like a pad through a low-pass filter or a triangle or sine chord, is loud low down and nearly silent at 2 kHz, where much of a vowel lives. Its words come out muffled. Flatten measures the carrier in each band and lifts the quiet bands and lowers the loud ones until they're even, before the voice's levels are applied. At 0% the carrier keeps its own tilt, exactly as before. At 100% every band of the carrier is the same level, the "spectral whitening" of modern vocoders. In between, it goes that share of the way, in dB. Flattened, a triangle chord speaks its vowels as plainly as a saw does unflattened. A few things keep Flatten clean: A band is lifted no more than about 40 dB above where the carrier has it, and nothing below −100 dBFS is lifted at all, so empty bands and a silent carrier don't turn into hiss. When a new note fills a band that was being lifted, the lift comes off at once, so the note doesn't burst through. The vocoder stays about as loud as you turn it, within a dB or so. The level every band is brought to is weighted by where the voice has been over the last second, so evening the carrier out doesn't turn down the bands the voice uses most. A chord and a voice are both loudest low down. Frozen, the weighting holds with the bands. Flatten can only even out what the carrier has. A pure sine chord has nothing above its top note, and there's nothing there to lift, so give it a little brightness first: a triangle or a soft saw is plenty. A bright saw is already close to even across the bank, so Flatten changes it little.
568.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Vocoder » Shaping the sound
568.title: Shaping the sound

569.body: The vocoder can only carry what the carrier has to give. A bright, sustained carrier works best: saws, pulses, a supersaw, a chord on a polyphonic cable, or noise for a whisper. A dark, filtered pad has nothing up high for the voice's upper bands to open, so the words come out muffled. Filter the carrier after the vocoder, not before, or turn up Flatten to bring out what highs it has. Keep the carrier low. A carrier's harmonics are where the vowels get drawn, and a high note spaces them too far apart to trace the formants. Measured with speech recognition on a spoken line, a saw at A2 or A3 kept about 60% of the words, and the same saw at A4 about 20%. A chord voiced low and wide, held while the words move, works best of all. Clair de Satellite sings on the string section's chord for this reason, not on its melody. The output follows both inputs: a loud chord and a loud voice make a loud vocoder. A five-note chord of detuned saws arrives several times louder than one voice, so turn Level down to sit it with the rest. Turning the carrier down is a poorer way to the same place. The bank does come down with it, dB for dB, with or without Flatten . But the Sibilance path and the Unvoiced noise take their level from the voice, not the carrier, so they stay where they were. The vocoder comes down by less than the carrier did, and the mix tips toward hiss. Level turns everything down together.

571.title: Starting points

572.body:
A phrase that speaks on every chord. A Sampler in One-Shot plays a recorded line, and a Clock Divider fires it every two bars. A Chord Sequencer plays the chords on a saw voice. The Soba Speaks example is built this way: [Sampler L] ──> [Vocoder Modulator]
[Oscillator Out] ──> [Vocoder Carrier] (a saw, on the Chord Sequencer's Pitch)
[Vocoder Out L] ──> [Mixer Ch 1]
[Vocoder Out R] ──> [Mixer Ch 2] Your own voice. Patch an Audio Input 's L into Modulator , and speak or sing into a microphone while the chords play. Wear headphones, or the mic will hear the speakers and the vocoder will start to howl. Drums that play chords. Patch a drum loop into Modulator and a held chord into Carrier . The chord pulses in the rhythm of the drums: the kick opens the low bands, and the hats open the high ones. A whisper. Patch Noise (white) into Carrier and the voice comes back whispered, with no pitch at all. A vowel to play chords on. Sing or play a sustained vowel into Modulator and switch on Freeze mid-vowel. Now the Chord Sequencer or a keyboard plays the chords, and each one comes out as "ahh" or "ooh", with no voice needed any more. A long Release before you freeze softens the held vowel. A stutter of held vowels. Patch a Clock Divider 's Gate into Freeze while a voice speaks. Each gate holds the syllable it lands on for as long as the gate is high, then lets the voice run on until the next one. Short gates on the beat give a rhythmic, chopped vocal, and longer ones give a held word at the start of each bar. Held Vowels turns this round: its gate is high for three beats of every four and lets go only for the beat a singer sings on, so each new chord holds the vowel sung just before it. [Clock Divider Gate] ──> [Vocoder Freeze]
[Sampler L] ──> [Vocoder Modulator] A pad that speaks. A triangle chord, or a saw through a low-pass, makes a soft pad but a mumbling vocoder. Turn Flatten up to 100% and the vowels come through. Mix the pad back in beside the vocoder and it still sounds soft. Held Vowels sings on a triangle chord this way.

573.body: Audio Input : a live voice to vocode Sampler : a recorded voice that plays itself Chord Sequencer : chords for the carrier, on one cable Compressor : the other effect that listens to a second signal Chorus and Reverb : space for the voice afterwards

574.body: Module ID util.clock · Category Utility Clock Module Four lamps count the beats of the bar, and INT says the Clock keeps its own time. The dots under the lamps are its sixteenths, swung at 62%: each orange one lands late. Jacks light while their gates are high. The Clock is the patch's metronome. It sends a steady stream of gate pulses at a tempo you set, for stepping a Sequencer , firing envelopes on the beat, or triggering a Sample & Hold . It also sets the patch tempo and beat . Tempo-synced modules follow it without a cable: the Delay with its Sync set to a note length, and the LFO with its Tempo set to a division. See Tempo and Sync . The Clock can keep its own time, follow the MIDI clock of a DAW, drum machine or another synth, or join an Ableton Link session, so the patch plays in time with them. On Auto it does both: it leads until a drum machine plays, follows it while it does, and carries the groove on when it stops.
574.title: Clock

575.body: Four lamps show the beats of the bar. The lamp of the beat playing flashes as the beat lands and fades through it, and the downbeat flashes brightest. A thin line under the lamps sweeps across the bar, with a dot where each pulse falls. With Swing turned up, the late pulses are drawn in orange, pushed along towards the next one. When the Clock stops, the beat it stopped on keeps a faint outline. Beside the lamps, a badge shows where the time comes from: INT for the Clock's own BPM , MIDI when it follows a MIDI clock, AUTO when it leads or follows, or LINK when it plays in a Link session. The MIDI badge fills in while clock ticks are coming in, and the AUTO badge while a device leads. The LINK badge fills in while anyone else is in the session, with a bubble on its corner counting them. Hover over the display to see what the Clock is doing. On MIDI and Auto , a line under the lamps says who leads: Soba leads , or the device's name in MIDI purple, such as Digitakt leads . On MIDI it reads Waiting for clock until ticks arrive.
575.title: The display

576.body: Port Signal Type Description Sync Gate (Green) A rising edge restarts the beat, so the next pulse starts right away Tempo Control (Orange) The BPM knob's jack. Bends the tempo around the knob by octaves: +1 doubles it, −1 halves it. See Tempo CV

579.body: BPM counts quarter notes, and Div sets how many pulses that makes: Div One pulse every At 120 BPM 1 4 beats (a bar of 4/4) 2 s 1/2 2 beats 1 s 1/4 Beat 500 ms 1/8 Half beat 250 ms 1/16 Quarter beat 125 ms A Clock has one output. For a second rhythm, divide its pulses with a Clock Divider : a sixteenth Clock divided by 3 plays dotted eighths against it, and divided by 64 pulses once every four bars, slower than the Clock's slowest setting. The divider counts the Clock's own pulses, so the two can never drift apart, and changing the BPM moves both.
579.title: Divisions

58.body: The 📚 Examples menu holds ready-made patches on two shelves. Recipes has First Sound , which opens when the app starts, and a patch for each recipe in this manual, each built around one idea. Songs has whole pieces that play themselves from start to end, each with a page of its own. Hover an example to read what it is. Each one is laid out in frames, with notes on how it works and what to try. Saving an example always asks for a file name, so you save a copy and the original stays intact.
58.title: Examples

580.body: Gate sets how long each pulse stays high, as a share of the time between pulses. At 50% the gate is high for half of each pulse. Short gates (5 to 20%) suit drums and plucks: the envelope gets its attack and goes straight to release. Long gates (80 to 99%) hold an envelope in its sustain, so notes run nearly into one another.
580.title: Gate length

581.body: Straight pulses are metronomic. Swing makes them shuffle, the way drum machines do: the pulses come in pairs, and the second of each pair arrives late. The knob says where it lands, as a share of the pair. Swing The second pulse lands Feel 50% Halfway: straight A grid 54 – 60% A little late A pocket: the groove most hip-hop, house and funk sits in 66.7% Two thirds of the way A triplet shuffle, as in a blues or a swing band 75% Three quarters of the way A dotted shuffle, hard and bouncy At Div 1/16 the pairs are eighth notes, so the off-beat sixteenths swing; at 1/8 the pairs are beats, and the off-beat eighths swing. The first pulse of every pair stays on the grid, so the downbeats, the bar length, a sequencer's EOC and a synced Delay or LFO are exactly where they'd be without swing. Only the late pulses move. Each late pulse's gate is shortened with its slot: Gate is a share of the time left before the next pulse, so even at 99% and 75% swing every pulse has its own edge. A Sequencer on a swung clock does the same with its notes, long on the beat and short off it. Swing moves everything the Clock drives. To swing one part and not another, such as hats against a straight kick, give the swung part its own Clock at the same BPM , then press Stop and Play so both start from the top together. From then on they stay locked to the sample.
581.title: Swing

582.body: The BPM knob has a jack. A CV there bends the tempo around the knob, by octaves: +1 doubles it, −1 halves it. Because the steps are octaves, an even ramp in the CV is an even change to the ear, the way a player slows. CV Tempo 0 The knob's −0.07 5% slower −0.15 10% slower −0.23 15% slower −0.42 Three quarters −1 Half +1 Double For any other change, the CV is log₂ of the new tempo over the old: log₂ 0.9 = −0.15 for 10% slower. The knob still turns while a cable is in its jack, and it reads the tempo the Clock is actually playing. The tempo stays within the knob's 20 to 300 BPM. Everything that keeps time by the Clock follows it. A sequencer's steps lengthen, and its gates with them, since a gate is a share of its step. An Arranger 's sections stay in bars and only their seconds change. A Clock Divider counts the same pulses. The patch tempo bends too, so a synced Delay's echoes stretch and a synced LFO slows with the Clock. The jack can take a cable from a module the Clock itself drives, such as an Arranger's lane. That cable closes a loop, so the Clock hears it one block late, a few milliseconds that a tempo never notices. While the Clock follows MIDI, Tempo CV does nothing: the master sets the tempo.
582.title: Tempo CV

583.body: A rising edge at Sync restarts the beat from the top. Use it to line the Clock up with another Clock, a sequencer's EOC , or any trigger. The Clock keeps its own tempo; Sync only moves where the beat falls. While the Clock follows MIDI, Sync does nothing: the MIDI clock places the beat. Unticking Run holds the gate low and stops the clock where it is. Ticking it again starts from the top of the bar, the way a drum machine's Play button does, and fires Reset . Patch Run and Reset into a Sequencer and the sequence stops and starts with the Clock, always from step 1. The Clock counts its beats with enough precision that even the slowest clock lands every pulse on its exact sample, however long it runs. Two Clocks at related tempos stay locked together.
583.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Clock » Sync and Run
583.title: Sync and Run

584.body: The Clock's BPM is the tempo for the whole patch, and its beat is the patch's beat. A Delay set to sync to 1/8 echoes on the eighth note of whatever the Clock is playing, and if you change the BPM the echoes move with it. An LFO synced to 1 bar sweeps once per bar, starting on the Clock's downbeat. Without a Clock in the patch, synced modules assume 120 BPM. If a patch has more than one Clock, synced modules follow the first one in the patch's processing order (usually the one nothing else feeds), so give them all the same BPM.
584.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Clock » The patch tempo
584.title: The patch tempo

585.body: Set Source to MIDI to slave the Clock to a MIDI clock master, such as a DAW, a drum machine or a hardware sequencer. Tick the master's port in the MIDI In menu, and set the master to send MIDI clock to it. In most DAWs this is a Send MIDI Clock or Sync setting on the MIDI output. With several devices open, choose the master under Device in the Clock's right-click menu, so a second device sending clock doesn't pull it off time (see Listening to one device ). Tempo. The Clock measures the master's tempo from the spacing of its clock ticks (24 per beat), fitted over the last two beats so that MIDI timing jitter averages out. The BPM knob dims and reads the received tempo, and every synced module follows it. When the master changes tempo, the Clock catches up within two beats. Until ticks arrive, the knob reads No clock . Position. The Clock counts the ticks, so its beat is always exactly where the master's is, whatever the tempo. It can't drift. Start restarts from the top: the next tick is the downbeat. The Clock fires Reset , and Run goes high with the downbeat. Stop holds the Clock where it is, and drops Run and the gate. Continue plays on from where it stopped. If the master located first (a Song Position message, which DAWs send when you move the playhead), it plays on from there. Run still works as an on/off switch: the Clock runs only when it's ticked and the master is playing. Some clock sources send only ticks, never Start or Stop. The Clock runs on their ticks alone. The Gate follows the master's beat too, so Div 1/16 pulses on every sixteenth of the DAW's grid. Patch Run and Reset into a sequencer to have it start, stop and restart with the DAW's transport. Soba never sends its clock back to the device it follows. A port in the Rig that plays the same device as the master (a Digitakt in and a Digitakt out, say) is sent none of the clock while the master leads, and its Clock reads leads in purple. So a drum machine set to both send and receive clock can't hear its own clock come back late and chase itself. The rest of the rig still gets Soba's clock, so the master leads the whole room. Soba's own Play button still has to be on: while Soba is stopped, it doesn't listen.
585.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Clock » Following MIDI clock
585.title: Following MIDI clock

586.body: Sometimes Soba leads the room, and sometimes a drum machine or a tracker does. Set Source to Auto and the Clock takes whichever role is free, with no knob to turn when the leader changes: Soba leads to begin with. The Clock keeps its own time at BPM , as on Internal, and sends it to every port whose Clock is on. A device starts playing (it sends Start , or its clock ticks start arriving) and the Clock follows it, exactly as on MIDI: its tempo, its beat, its Start and Continue. Start restarts the Clock from the top and fires Reset . The BPM knob dims and reads the device's tempo. The device stops (it sends Stop , or its ticks stop for a quarter of a second) and Soba leads again. The Clock carries on from the beat it had reached, at the device's tempo, with no gap and no jump, and the BPM knob turns to that tempo. Turn the knob and the tempo is yours again. Many drum machines keep sending clock ticks while they're stopped. Those don't make them lead: only playing does. A device that sends only ticks, never Start or Stop, leads while they come, and picks up from the beat Soba had reached rather than restarting it. Choose the device under Device in the Clock's right-click menu, so only that one can lead. On Any , whichever device sends clock leads. When Soba takes the lead back, the ports of the device that led get Soba's clock again, so it can follow along, but not a Continue : you stopped it, so it stays stopped until Soba's transport next starts (press Stop and Play). Ports set to Clock only follow the tempo straight away.
586.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Clock » Leading or following: Auto
586.title: Leading or following: Auto

587.body: Ableton Link keeps apps on the same network in time with each other, with no cables and no master to set up: Live, Bitwig, Reason, Traktor, dozens of phone apps, and other copies of Soba. Set Source to Link and the Clock joins the session. Every app in it plays at one tempo, with its bars lined up. Tempo. The Clock plays at the session's tempo, and the BPM knob follows it: when another app changes the tempo, the knob turns to match. Turn the knob yourself and the whole session changes tempo with you. The Tempo jack does nothing while the Clock follows Link. Bars. The Clock's downbeats land on the session's: beat 1 of Soba's bar is beat 1 of Live's. Bars are four beats long. Start and stop. Link shares the transport too ( Start Stop Sync , which other apps may have to switch on). Tick Run and every app in the session starts. With others in the session, the start waits for the next bar so it lands in phase. When another app starts or stops, the Clock does too, and its Run box follows. Starting fires Reset , so patched sequencers start from step 1 on the downbeat. Joining. A Clock that joins a session already playing takes the session's tempo and plays along. One that has the session to itself sets it from its own BPM and Run . The badge reads LINK , and fills in with a count of the other apps while there are any. Soba joins the network only while a Clock follows Link, and leaves a second after the last one stops (or Soba is stopped). Link is in the desktop app when it's built with Link: see Build with Ableton Link . The browser version can't join a session and doesn't offer it. A patch saved with Source on Link and opened in a build without Link keeps its own time at BPM .
587.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Clock » Playing in a Link session
587.title: Playing in a Link session

588.body: In the plugin , Source offers Host where the app offers Link. Set it and the Clock plays in the DAW's time: Tempo. The Clock plays at the DAW's tempo, tempo changes and all. The BPM knob shows it and can't be turned. The Tempo jack does nothing while the Clock follows the host. Beat. The Clock's beat is the DAW's: beat 1 of a Soba bar is beat 1 of the song's, wherever playback starts. Start and stop. The Clock runs while the DAW plays, if Run is on. Starting fires Reset , so patched sequencers start from step 1 as the song does. The badge reads HOST , filled in while the DAW plays. A patch saved with Source on Host follows Link when it's opened in the app (or keeps its own time in a build without Link), and a Link patch opened in the plugin follows the DAW.
588.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Clock » Playing in a DAW
588.title: Playing in a DAW

59.body: A Sampler keeps the path to its sound file in the patch. A file beside or below the patch is saved by a path relative to it, so the patch's folder can be moved or shared whole. Save As copies samples from anywhere else into a <patch name> samples folder beside the patch, asking first if they come to more than 50 MB. A patch whose sample has gone missing still opens, with the missing file among the load warnings. A Looper 's loop is kept the same way. Saving the patch writes each loop that changed as a WAV into a <patch name> loops folder beside it, asking first if they come to more than 50 MB, and opening the patch brings each loop back, stopped and ready to play. A loop whose file has gone missing is a load warning, and its Looper opens empty. See Keeping the loop .

594.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [Sequencer Clock]
[Clock Gate] ──> [Arranger Clock]
[Arranger Lane 1] ──> [Attenuverter In] (Amount −0.23)
[Attenuverter Out] ──> [Clock Tempo] Every pianist broadens into the last chord of a piece, and a sequenced patch can too. In the Arranger, set lane 1 to Jump to 0 at the start of the song, then to Ramp to 100% on Exp over the last two bars. The Attenuverter turns the lane into a slowing: at −0.23, the last bar ends 15% slower than it began, a gentle ritardando . At −0.42 it slows to three quarters, broad enough to hear as a gesture. Exp holds the tempo nearly steady and then gives way into the end, as players do. Linear slows evenly, and Log slows at once and settles, more like a new, slower section ( meno mosso ) than an ending. Other moves on the same cable: A positive Amount turns the same ramp into an accelerando . A Jump changes tempo on a section's downbeat. Glide on the lane eases a Jump, so the change takes a beat or two. Put the Arranger's last section after the ramp, with the final chord in it, and the chord lands at the slower tempo. From One Sine ends this way, broadening over its last four bars.
