Glides into a slide step Gate Gate (Green) High for each step that's switched on, for Gate of the step. Stays high across a tie and into a slide Velocity Control (Orange) The current step's velocity, 0 to 1 Step Control (Orange) The current position as a ramp: 0 on the first step, 1 on the last EOC Gate (Green) End of cycle: a 1 ms pulse each time the whole Chain comes round. With a cable in Pattern , each time a pattern does
751.title: Outputs

752.body: Control Range Default Description Steps 1 – 16 8 How many steps play before the pattern loops Gate (Gate Length) 1 – 100% 50% How long each gate stays high, as a share of the step. 100% holds it until the next clock Glide 0 – 1 s 60 ms How long a slide takes to reach its note Dir (Direction) Fwd / Bwd / P-P / Rnd Fwd Playback order Gate of (Gate Mode) Step / 100 ms Step What Gate is a share of: the time between clock pulses, or a fixed 100 ms Wander 0 – 4 0 How many degrees of the scale a note may stray from what's written. At 0 every note plays as written Scale Chromatic … Whole Tone Pentatonic Major The scale Wander steps along, as the Quantizer names them Root C – B C The scale's first note Keep Off / Step 1 / Accents Step 1 Notes Wander leaves as written: step 1, or accents (a velocity of 110 or more) Each of the 16 steps of each pattern also stores a note (default C4), a gate on/off (default on), a tie (default off), a slide (default off), a velocity (default 100 of 127) and a chance (default 100%). The Chain has up to eight slots. Patches save all of them. Steps , Dir , the gate settings, Glide and the Wander settings are shared by all four patterns.
752.title: Parameters

753.body: The grid shows one button per active step, in rows of eight. Steps beyond Steps are hidden, not lost: turn Steps back up and they return as you left them. Click a step to switch its gate on (green) or off (dark). An off step is a rest: Pitch still moves to its note, but no gate fires. Shift + click a step to tie it into the next step. A bar joins the two. Shift + click again to untie. Ctrl + click a step to slide into it from the step before. An orange slur arches over the two. Ctrl + click again to strike it instead. Drag a step up or down to change its note, a semitone for every few pixels. The note it will land on shows above the step as you drag, and you hear it: the step's note sounds at its Velocity as the drag begins and follows it up or down, each semitone gliding in under the held note the way a key held under the hand does. Let go and it stops; with the clock running, the sequence takes over again at its next note. Hold Shift while dragging to move by whole octaves. A drag is one undo step, however far it goes. Right-click a step to open its piano (below). While the patch plays, the current step is drawn brighter, with a white outline. A step with a chance under 100% is filled only part way up, like a glass: half full plays half the time.
753.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Programming a pattern
753.title: Programming a pattern

754.body: The step piano E2, G2 and A2 have just gone into steps 4 to 6. Step 6 was a rest, and playing a note on it switched it on. The orange outline on step 7 shows where the next key will land. The slur broken over the row's end is the patch's slide into step 9, which Slide into this step sets from the piano. Right-click a step and a two-octave piano opens under it, with the step's note lit. Click a key and three things happen: the step takes that note, the step switches on if it was a rest, and the outline moves along to the next step. Play a line of keys and you write the melody into the pattern one step after another, the way step-record works on a hardware sequencer. The piano stays where it opened, so the keys don't move while you play. After the last step it carries on at step 1. ◂ ▸ (or the ← → keys) move to the previous or next step without writing anything. Use them to skip a step you want to keep, or to leave a rest as it is. ‹ › move the piano down or up an octave. It stays on that octave as you move from step to step. Tie into next step ties the step being written, the same as Shift + click. Slide into this step slides into the step being written, the same as Ctrl + click. Chance sets how often the step being written plays, from 0 to 100%. Esc , or a click anywhere outside the piano, closes it. Each note you write is its own undo step, so Ctrl+Z takes back the last key you played.
754.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Writing a melody on the piano
754.title: Writing a melody on the piano

755.body: While the piano is open, you can also play the melody in from a MIDI keyboard or the computer's letter keys. Each note you strike writes the step and moves on, just like a click. Touch. A MIDI keyboard writes how hard you played each note into the step's Velocity , so a line played with accents keeps them. The letter keys have no touch, so they leave the velocity alone. Legato. Hold a note until the next one goes down and the first step ties into the second. Let go first and it doesn't. The phrasing you play is the phrasing written, as on a hardware step-record. A click on the piano has no length, so it never writes a tie. The letter keys play the piano with Z on its lowest C, so ‹ › move them an octave as well. While the piano is open the letter keys belong to it, so the patch's Note In modules don't hear them. A MIDI keyboard still plays the patch as usual.
755.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Playing it in from a keyboard
755.title: Playing it in from a keyboard

756.body: Each note you write sounds as it goes in, through whatever the sequencer is patched into, so you can hear the melody you're writing. The clock doesn't need to be running. The note plays on the sequencer's own Pitch , Gate and Velocity , in place of the sequence: A key you hold on the letter keys sounds for as long as you hold it. One struck while another is still down slides the pitch over without a new attack, which is how it's written: tied. A click on the piano is a short note, one Gate Length long. A MIDI keyboard is played by the sequencer only when no Note In in the patch hears MIDI (one with Source on Keys doesn't). If one does, it already plays your notes, so the sequencer leaves them to it and you hear each note once. Each note sounds as loud as its step will play it. Once you let go, the sequence takes over again at the next note it plays. If the clock was running, the note it played while your hand was down isn't heard. A note already held when the piano opens isn't written. Strike it again to write it. Velocities have no knob on the node. Each step plays at 100 until a MIDI keyboard writes its touch, or the patch file says otherwise. Patch Velocity into an envelope's Velocity input to hear the accents.
756.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Hearing it as you write
756.title: Hearing it as you write

757.body: The tabs under the grid pick which pattern you're editing: clicking, dragging and the piano all write to the pattern on show. The one playing wears a green dot, and the one coming next a green ring. Follow , beside the tabs, keeps the grid on whichever pattern is playing, so it turns over as the Chain (or the Pattern CV) moves on; clicking a tab to edit one turns it off. The playhead's outline only shows on the pattern playing. Which tab is open is the editor's choice: it isn't saved with the patch, and it isn't an edit. Right-click a tab to copy its pattern to another (to start a variation from it), or to clear it. Clearing turns every step into a rest but keeps the notes, ready for the piano to write a new line over. The Chain is the order the patterns play in, a pass each, round and round. The pass playing is underlined. It works as on the Trigger Sequencer : Click a slot to change its pattern: A, B, C, D, then A again. Right-click it to pick a pattern, or to remove the slot. The slots after it move up. + adds a pass of the pattern you're editing to the end. The Chain holds up to eight. A new Step Sequencer plays A, and so do patches saved before it had patterns, exactly as they always did. For a 64-step line, write four bars of it into A, B, C and D, and make the Chain A B C D. For a 16-bar verse whose first half repeats, A A B C will do. A pass ends where the pattern comes round: after the last step going Fwd , after step 1 going Bwd , and at each turn in P-P , so a ping-pong bounces from one pattern into the next. In Rnd a pass is Steps clocks long. A tie on the last step carries into the first step of the next pattern, so a phrase can hold a note over the join, and a slide on the next pattern's first step slurs in from this one's last note.
757.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Patterns and the Chain
757.title: Patterns and the Chain

758.body: With a cable in Pattern , the CV picks the patterns instead, and the Chain dims. The CV is read once a pass, on the clock that starts it, in the same four zones as the Trigger Sequencer's, so one CV means the same pattern on both. An Arranger lane is made for this: a verse section that holds the lane at A and a chorus that holds it at B make one sequencer play the song's two melodies. The Arranger moves its lanes on the same clock edge the sequencer steps on, so a section's first note comes from its own pattern, with no lag. Leave that lane's Glide at 0. Because the CV is only read as a pass starts, a lane that ramps can play a chain inside one long section. A Linear ramp from 12.5% to 87.5% over three passes stands in the middle of A, B, C and D at the start of each one. From One Sine grows its motif into a sixteen-bar line that way, and holds the lane at A wherever the motif plays alone.
758.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Pattern CV
758.title: Pattern CV

759.body: A sequencer plays exactly what's written, which is what makes a riff a riff. Sometimes a line wants to breathe instead: to leave a note out now and then, or to remember the tune slightly differently each time round. Two things on the Step Sequencer do that, and both leave the written pattern alone.
759.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Chance and Wander
759.title: Chance and Wander

76.body: A tone that never changes isn't much of an instrument. Add a Source › Note In to the left of the Oscillator. Patch Note In's Pitch output into the Oscillator's V/Oct input. Play the bottom row of your computer keyboard: Z is C, X is D, and so on up to M for B, with the sharps on S, D, G, H and J. Note In's piano lights up the notes you hold, and the Oscillator follows. Pitch is an orange control cable carrying volts per octave : each step of 1.0 is one octave, so the Oscillator stays in tune at every note. But the tone still never stops. For that, you need to shape each note.
76.breadcrumbs: Your First Patch » Step 2: Play it from the keyboard
76.title: Step 2: Play it from the keyboard

760.body: Each step has a Chance , set on its piano. When the clock reaches a step, its dice are thrown: at 100% it always plays, at 50% about every other time, at 0% never. A step that loses is a rest for that pass, and ends a note tied into it. On the grid, a step with a chance under 100% is filled only as far up as its chance. The Trigger Sequencer's steps have the same kind of probability. On a melody it works best on the passing notes, the ones between the notes that carry the tune.
760.title: Chance

761.body: Wander moves each note struck a few degrees along Scale and Root , up or down, then lets it go back to what's written on the next pass. At Wander 0.2 a note moves now and then, by one degree. At 1 about half the notes move, and at 2 or more the line can stray two degrees either way and starts to sound like an improvisation on itself. A degree is the next note of the scale: in C major pentatonic, one degree up from C is D and two up is E. Keep holds some notes where they are. Step 1 , the default, keeps each pattern's first step as written, so the line keeps its downbeat however far the rest wanders. Accents keeps the steps with a velocity of 110 or more, so the notes you've leaned on stay put. A tied note carries on where it wandered to, so a held note doesn't jump halfway through. A written note that's off the scale plays as written. When it wanders, its first degree is the nearest scale note in that direction. At Wander 0 with every chance at 100%, nothing is left to chance, and the sequencer plays exactly as it did before it had either. The playing step shows where it went. A note that wandered names the note it's playing, in orange, under its step, with a small arrow on the side it moved toward. A step that lost its dice keeps a grey outline instead of a white one. Wander has a jack. Patch a slow LFO into it and the melody drifts away and returns over a minute or two, or give it an Arranger lane, so a verse plays the tune as written and the outro remembers it loosely. The dice are seeded for each module in the patch, so a patch wanders the same way every time it plays, in the editor, in a render or in a DAW.
761.title: Wander

763.body: The sequencer has no tempo of its own. It moves on each rising edge at Clock , so the clock you patch in sets the speed, and its swing or irregularity carries through. Gate sets the length of each note as a share of the step. The sequencer measures the step from the clock itself, as the time between the last two pulses, so the notes follow the tempo. At 60 BPM in quarter notes, 50% is a 500 ms gate; at 120 BPM in sixteenths, it's 62.5 ms. Lower settings give staccato plucks, higher ones legato. If the tempo changes, the next step uses the new length. On a swung clock, whose steps go long, short, long, short, each note is a share of its own step: long on the beat and short off it, so the shuffle keeps its shape. At 100% the gate stays high right up to the next clock. If the next step plays, the gate drops for a single sample there, so an envelope still starts a new note. If the next step is a rest, the gate falls on that clock. Until it has seen two clock pulses, the sequencer has no step to measure. The first note after the patch starts uses the 100 ms rule below. A Reset doesn't count the time since the last pulse as a step. That gap might be a pause while the clock was stopped, so the sequencer keeps the step it measured before.
763.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Clock and gate length
763.title: Clock and gate length

764.body: A tied step holds its gate across the next clock. If the next step plays, it continues the same note: Pitch moves to the new step's note, but the gate never drops, so an envelope stays in its sustain instead of starting again. Tie several steps in a row for one long note over all of them. Tie two steps with different notes and the second is played legato: one envelope, two pitches, the way a monosynth player slurs a phrase. A tie into a rest just holds the note to the end of the tied step. A tie on a step that's switched off does nothing. The next step is whichever plays next, so in Bwd , P-P or Rnd a tie carries into that one, though the bar on the grid always points right. At the end of a row the bar reaches out of the step's right side and into the left side of the next row's first step. Tie the last step to carry the note into the first step of the next pattern in the Chain. With a Chain of one pattern that's its own first step, and the bar comes round into it. When the next pattern is another, the bar leaves toward its letter ( →B ), and that pattern's step 1 shows the tie arriving at its left side. With Pattern patched the next pattern isn't known ahead, so the bar only leaves. A held gate (a tie, or Gate at 100%) lets go after two steps' time if no clock comes, so stopping the clock doesn't leave a note hanging.
764.title: Ties

765.body: Slides on the grid D#2 slides down to C2, and G2 slides to C2. The slur into step 9 breaks at the end of the row: C2 slides up an octave to C3. Steps 4 to 5 and 15 to 16 are ties. A slide step is slurred into from the note before it. Two things happen at its clock: Pitch glides from the last note to this one over the Glide time, instead of jumping. The glide is Note In's Glide : even in pitch, and as quick across an octave as across a semitone, so a sequenced slide and a hand-played one sound alike. Glide is the time to get 99% of the way there. The gate stays high. The note before holds its gate until the slide begins, whatever Gate is set to, and the slide carries on from it without a new rising edge. An envelope isn't struck again, so a filter envelope with no sustain keeps falling through the slide instead of snapping open. That's the 303's sound: most notes are plucked, and the slid ones melt into the note before. A slide needs a note to come from. After a rest, or as the first note after a Reset , a slide step is struck like any other and starts on its own pitch. Its slur on the grid is drawn faint after a rest. A slide on a step that's switched off does nothing. Slides and ties combine. Tie a slide step into the next one on the same note to hold the slid note longer: a slow glide keeps gliding across the tie. A plain step after a slide jumps to its note and is struck as usual. With Glide at 0, a slide step jumps to its note but still keeps the gate high: one envelope, two pitches, the same as a tie into a different note. The note before is whichever plays before, so in Bwd , P-P or Rnd a slide comes from that step, though the slur on the grid always comes from the left. A slide on step 1 slurs in from the note before it, in this pattern or the last one: round the loop, or over the join from the Chain's previous pattern. Each pattern keeps its own slides. To hold the gate across the join, the note before a slide looks ahead to the step the next clock plays, in the pattern it will be in. With Pattern patched, it reads the CV as it is then, so a CV that changes pattern on the very clock of a slide can turn it back into a struck note.
765.title: Slides

766.body: With Gate of at 100 ms , Gate is a share of a fixed 100 ms instead of the step: 50% is always 50 ms, whatever the tempo. Short, even triggers like this suit drums. Ties still work in this mode. If a gate is still high when the next note starts, as 99% is at fast tempos, the two notes run together without a new attack. Patches saved before the sequencer measured its steps open in this mode, so they sound as they always did. Switch them to Step for gates that follow the tempo.
766.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » 100 ms gates
766.title: 100 ms gates

767.body: Each clock moves to the next step and sounds it, except the first clock after a Reset , which sounds the step the pattern starts from without moving past it. So a reset on the downbeat puts step 1 on the downbeat. The same goes for the first clock after the patch starts playing. The start step is step 1 in every direction but Bwd , which starts from the last step. Rnd starts on step 1 too, then picks at random from the next clock on.
767.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Reset and the first step
767.title: Reset and the first step

768.body: Dir Order (with 4 steps) EOC Fwd 1 2 3 4 1 2 3 4 … After step 4 Bwd 4 3 2 1 4 3 2 1 … After step 1 P-P (ping-pong) 1 2 3 4 3 2 1 2 … At each end Rnd A random step on each clock Never Ping-pong doesn't repeat the end steps, so a four-step pattern bounces over six clocks.
768.title: Directions

77.body: A VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) sets the level of whatever passes through it, under the control of another signal. Add a Utility › VCA between the Oscillator and the Audio Output. Patch the Oscillator's Out into the VCA's In . Patch the VCA's Out into the Audio Output's Mono . This replaces the cable that was there, because each input takes one cable. Nothing changes yet: with nothing patched into its CV input, the VCA lets the sound through at full level. The next step gives it something to listen to.
77.breadcrumbs: Your First Patch » Step 3: A VCA to control the level
77.title: Step 3: A VCA to control the level

770.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [Step Sequencer Clock]
[Step Sequencer Pitch] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct]
[Step Sequencer Gate] ──> [ADSR Gate]
[Oscillator Out] ──> [SVF Filter In]
[SVF Filter LowPass] ──> [VCA In]
[ADSR Out] ──> [VCA CV]
[VCA Out] ──> [Audio Output Mono] Set the Clock's Div to 1/8 or 1/16, switch a few steps off to make rests, and use the Oscillator's Oct knob to move the whole pattern up or down.
770.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » A sequenced voice
770.title: A sequenced voice

771.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [Step Sequencer Clock] (Div 1/16)
[Step Sequencer Pitch] ──> [Acid Bass Pitch]
[Step Sequencer Gate] ──> [Acid Bass Gate]
[Step Sequencer Velocity] ──> [Acid Bass Velocity]
[Acid Bass Out] ──> [Audio Output Mono] The Library 's Acid Bass snaps its filter open on every new gate. Write a 16-step line in the octave around C2, then Ctrl + click two or three of its notes to slide into them: an octave leap, or a step back down to the root. Those notes glide in under a filter that's still closing, and the rest stay plucked. Keep Glide short, 40 to 80 ms, for the 303's quick slur, or raise it to 200 ms or more for a lazier Minimoog lead.
771.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » An acid line
771.title: An acid line

772.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [Step Sequencer Clock] (Div 1/8)
[LFO Out] ──> [Step Sequencer Wander] (Rate 0.01 Hz, Bipolar off)
[Step Sequencer Pitch] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct]
[Step Sequencer Gate] ──> [ADSR Gate] Write a line in C major pentatonic and leave Scale on Pentatonic Major . The LFO takes the melody away over about fifty seconds and brings it home again over the next fifty, with step 1 kept as written so you can always hear where the bar starts. Set the passing notes' chances to 60 to 80% and some of them fall out too, more so as the line wanders.
772.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » A melody that drifts
772.title: A melody that drifts

773.body: Pitch is a control signal like any other. Patch it into a filter's Cutoff and each step sets a brightness instead of a note: one octave of cutoff for each octave of pitch. Combine with a second sequencer for melody, both clocked together.
773.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Modulation sequences
773.title: Modulation sequences

774.body:
Two sequencers on the same clock with different Steps settings drift against each other and line up again only every few bars. Eight steps against five repeats every 40 clocks. [Clock Gate] ──> [Step Sequencer A Clock] (Steps 8)
[Clock Gate] ──> [Step Sequencer B Clock] (Steps 5)
774.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Patterns of different lengths
774.title: Patterns of different lengths

775.body: Patch a gate into Run to pause the pattern in place. While Run is low, clocks are ignored and the sequencer stays on its current step. The Clock 's Run and Reset outputs are made for this. Patch them into Run and Reset and the pattern stops with the Clock and starts again from step 1 when it does, including when the Clock follows a DAW's MIDI clock and you press Play there.
775.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Stop and start
775.title: Stop and start

776.body: Clock : drives the sequencer Arranger : picks the pattern for each section of a song, through Pattern Chord Sequencer : a chord per step instead of a note, on polyphonic cables Trigger Sequencer : eight lanes of drum hits from one module, with chained patterns for fills Clock Divider : divides the clock, so a sequencer can play once every few bars from its Run and Reset ADSR Envelope : shapes each step's note from the Gate output Slope : slews any signal, every change alike, where a slide picks its notes Oscillator : plays the Pitch output Sample & Hold : stepped values that aren't programmed by hand
776.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Step Sequencer » Related modules
776.title: Related modules

777.body: Module ID seq.chord · Category Utility · Poly Chord Sequencer Module A line cliché, Am9 to E7. The keyboard strip shows Dm9 sounding: the bass voice in amber on D2, and the chord in orange above it, a dot for each voice. Esus4 is tied into E7, so the suspension resolves without a new attack. The Chord Sequencer plays a progression. Each of its 16 steps holds a chord: a root, a chord type and, if you like, a slash bass. Each clock pulse moves it on one chord. It sends that chord out as polyphonic Pitch , Gate and Velocity , one channel per note, the way Note In sends the notes you hold. So any polyphonic voice, every Library voice included, plays it with nothing else in between. It voices the chords itself. The notes go close together, opened out, or spread wide, in the octave you choose. With Voice Leading on, each chord takes the inversion nearest the one before. The voices then move a step or stay put from chord to chord, the way a pianist's hands do, rather than jumping in parallel. Changing one chord means changing one step. It holds four patterns, A to D, and plays them in the order its Chain gives, so one Chord Sequencer can play a 64-chord progression, or a song's verse, chorus and coda through the same voices (see Patterns and the Chain ). The Root and Bass outputs carry single notes as well: a bass line to play on a second voice, or a pitch to move an arpeggio around (see Afterglow ).
777.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Chord Sequencer
777.title: Chord Sequencer

778.body: Port Signal Type Description Clock Gate (Green) Each rising edge moves to the next chord Reset Gate (Green) A rising edge jumps back to step 1 Run Gate (Green) Steps advance only while this is high. With nothing patched, the sequencer runs Pattern Control (Orange) Picks the pattern for each pass in place of the Chain: 0 to 0.25 is A, 0.25 to 0.5 is B, then C, and D from 0.75 up
778.title: Inputs

779.body: Port Signal Type Description Pitch Control (Orange), poly One channel per note of the chord, as V/Oct, lowest first Gate Gate (Green), poly The chord's gate, one channel per note. The channels rise together, or one after another with Strum . Stays high across a tie Velocity Control (Orange), poly The step's velocity, 0 to 1, on every channel, or shaded along the strum by Taper Root Control (Orange) The chord's root as V/Oct, in the octave the step was written in Bass Control (Orange) The slash chord's bass note, at or below the root; the root when there's no slash EOC Gate (Green) End of cycle: a 1 ms pulse each time the whole Chain comes round. With a cable in Pattern , each time a pattern does
779.title: Outputs

78.body: An envelope draws a shape every time a note is played: it rises when the key goes down and falls when the key comes up. Add a Modulation › ADSR Envelope below the VCA. Patch Note In's Gate output into the envelope's Gate input. Gate is green: it's on while a key is held and off when it's released. Patch the envelope's Out into the VCA's CV input. Now each key plays a note that starts and stops. The envelope runs through four stages, each with a knob: Atk (attack): how long the note takes to reach full level. The default is 10 ms. Dec (decay): how long it then takes to fall to the sustain level. Sus (sustain): the level held for as long as the key is down. Rel (release): how long the note takes to fade after you let go. Try a pluck: turn Sus all the way down and Dec to about 300 ms, so each note dies away even while you hold the key. Then try a swell: Atk around 1 s, Sus up, Rel around 2 s. The display on the envelope draws each shape as you turn the knobs.
78.breadcrumbs: Your First Patch » Step 4: An envelope to shape each note
78.title: Step 4: An envelope to shape each note

780.body: Control Range Default Description Steps 1 – 16 4 How many chords each pattern plays before the next pass Gate (Gate Length) 1 – 100% 100% How long each chord is held, as a share of the step. 100% holds it up to the next clock Voices 1 – 8 4 How many channels the cables carry: the notes in each chord Range 1 – 6 3 The octave the chord's lowest note sits in. 4 is middle C's octave Strum 0 – 100 ms 0 ms Time between one note's gate and the next, as a guitar or harp sounds a chord (see Strum ). At 0 every note is struck at once Dir (Direction) Fwd / Bwd / P-P / Rnd Fwd Playback order Voicing Close / Open / Spread Close How the notes are spread out (below) Voice lead (Voice Leading) on / off on Each chord takes the inversion nearest the last Bass voice on / off off Puts the bass note under the chord as the first channel (below) Rootless on / off off The chord leaves out its root first, for a bass that plays it elsewhere (below). Always so with Bass voice on Strum dir Up / Down / Alt Up Where a strum starts: on the lowest note, on the highest, or on each in turn, clock by clock. A step can name its own Taper (Strum Taper) −100 – 100% 0% Softens the notes struck later in a strum, down to nothing at 100%. Below 0 they grow louder instead (see Taper ) Each of the 16 steps of each pattern also stores a root (a note, with its octave), a type, a bass (the root, or one of the twelve notes), a gate, a velocity, a tie, a top (Auto, or the chord tone to put on top), and a strum (Auto, Up or Down). The Chain has up to eight slots. Every knob and switch above is shared by all four patterns. A new Chord Sequencer starts every pattern on Cmaj7, Am7, Fmaj7, G7, with the roots walking down from C2. Patch a Clock into it and it plays a progression straight away.
780.title: Parameters

781.body: Each step shows its chord's name, with a slash bass written under it. A line along the foot of the step shows its velocity, a notch in its head shows that it names its top note, and a small arrow in its corner that it names its own strum, up or down. Steps beyond Steps are hidden, not lost. Click a step to switch it on (green) or make it a rest (dark). Shift + click a step to tie it into the next step. A bar joins the two. Drag a step up or down to move its root by semitones, or by octaves with Shift . The chord it will become shows as you drag. Right-click a step to open its chord (below). While the patch plays, the chord sounding is drawn brighter, with a white outline. The keyboard strip above the steps shows its notes, with the bass voice in amber. The strip covers four octaves, starting two below the Range octave, so a bass two octaves down still shows. Each voice has a dot that glides to its next note when the chord changes, which makes the voice leading easy to watch. Most dots creep by a step or stay where they are.
781.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Writing chords
781.title: Writing chords

782.body: The chord popover Step 1 of From One Sine : Dmadd9, with E on top. The bass row is spelled from the root, so the note a half step under D reads C#, as a lead sheet writes it. The top row offers only the tones the chord keeps: with Rootless on and three voices, Dmadd9 keeps F, A and E. Right-click a step and its chord opens under it: Root. A two-octave piano with the root lit. Click a key to set the root. ‹ › move the piano an octave. Bass. The root, or a note to put under the chord. The notes are spelled from the root (D/F#, Am/G#), the same way the step writes the name. Top. Auto , or one of the chord's tones to put on top of the voicing (see The top note ). Only the tones the voicing keeps are offered. Type. All 19 chord types, each named on this root. Clicking a type writes the step, switches it on if it was a rest, and moves to the next step. Velocity and Tie , for this step. Strum. Auto follows Strum dir . Up ▴ or Down ▾ strums this step that way, whatever Strum dir says (see A step's own stroke ). So a progression goes in the way a lead sheet reads: a root, then a type, then the next root and type. The popover stays where it opened, and an outline marks the step it's writing. ◂ ▸ (or ← → ) move between steps without writing. Esc , or a click outside, closes it. Each change is one undo step. Each choice sounds as you make it. Click a type, a bass or a top, and the step's chord sounds for a moment as it now stands, the same way a chord you play on the keys does (see Playing a chord into a step ): through the sequencer's own cables, voiced as the loop will reach it, and strummed as its step will be struck. A key on the piano sounds just its note, on the first channel, the way a piano would. Click Up ▴ or Down ▾ and the chord rolls that way (with Strum above 0), or let go of the Velocity slider and it's struck that hard. Tie stays quiet, because a tie changes the next step's attack, not this one's. To compare chords before you choose, rest the pointer on a chip without clicking. Its chord sounds, but nothing is written, so you can try Gm7 against Gm9 and then click the one you want. A pointer passing over the popover stays quiet, because it has to rest on a chip for about a third of a second. Once one chip has sounded, the chips next to it sound sooner, so you can play along a row by moving across it. Clicking the chip you're resting on writes it without striking the chord again.
782.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » The chord popover
782.title: The chord popover

783.body: A chord being played into the popover G#, A, C and E held on the letter keys over step 2. The held keys light on the piano, and the popover names the chord as it's played: Am over G#, with the E on top, which voice leading wouldn't have put there. When the keys come up, step 2 becomes Am/G# with E on top, and the popover moves on to step 3. With the popover open, you can also play the chord. Hold it on a MIDI keyboard, or on the computer's letter keys, and let go. The popover names what you played and writes it into the step: the root, the type, the slash bass and, where it's needed, the top note. It switches the step on if it was a rest, then moves to the next step. To write a progression, open the popover on its first step and play the chords one after another. The name shows as you play. The keys you hold light on the piano, and the line under it names the chord ("Hearing G# A C E → Am/G#"). Every note held since the first key went down counts, so the keys don't have to land or lift together. The lowest note is the bass. If it's a chord tone other than the root, you get an inversion, written as a slash chord (C/E). If it isn't in the chord at all, it goes under the chord as a slash bass (Am/G#). The root's octave is the first one above the bass, so the step's Bass output plays the note you held at the bottom. Where the same notes make two chords, the bass decides. A C E G is C6 over C and Am7 over A. The highest note is the top. The step keeps the voicing you played, as long as the voicing keeps that tone (see The top note ). Usually voice leading would put the same note on top anyway, so Top stays on Auto and goes on following the chords around it. It's written only where voice leading would choose another note. Either way, the line under the piano names your top note ("Heard F A E → Dmadd9 E on top"): bright when it's written into the step, dim when voice leading puts it there by itself. The popover works this out from the pattern looping in its Direction . Ping-pong and random reach a step from more than one chord, so with those a chord you play always writes its top. A top note the voicing leaves out, such as the root with Rootless on, sets Top back to Auto. A single note is only a root, and leaves Top as it was. Leaving out the 5th is fine. C E B♭ D is C9, and C E B♭ A is C13: players often leave out the 5th, and a 13's 9th. A single note sets the root. The step keeps its type and loses any slash bass. Notes that fit no chord get the nearest one. The popover shows what it heard and what didn't fit, such as "nearest: no G · Db left out". Fix it with the chips, or play it again. You hear the chord as it will play. While your hand is down, the sequencer plays the chord on its own cables, so the patch's voices sound it whether or not the Clock is running. You hear it already named and voiced: in the Range octave, as many notes as Voices , with your top note on top and the bass on the first channel if Bass Voice is on. Am/G# and G#dim7 sound different, even though you played the same keys. With Voice lead on, it's led from the chord before it, as the pattern will reach it once it loops, so a progression you type in sounds as it will play, whatever order you write its steps in. (Ping-pong and random reach a step from more than one chord, so with those you hear it in root position.) With Strum up, it's rolled the way its step will be struck: the step's own stroke, or Strum Dir 's, with Alt taking the step's place in the bar (up on the step a Reset starts on, then down and up in turn), and shaded by Strum Taper . Only the first key strikes. Fingers that land after it change the notes under the hand, and strings the strum hasn't reached yet take the new notes on their turn, so a chord you land a little unevenly still sounds as one stroke. When you let go, the chord fades out on its release, and the sequence comes back with its next chord. If a Note In in the patch hears MIDI, it already plays the MIDI keyboard, so only chords with letter keys in them are heard this way. The patch must be playing for any of this to sound. While the popover is open, the letter keys belong to it, the way a text field takes them. The Note In modules don't hear them, so writing chords plays the chord, not the patch's lead. The letter keys play the popover's piano, with Z on its lowest C, and ‹ › move them an octave as well. A MIDI keyboard still plays the patch as usual. Each chord you play is one undo step.
783.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Playing a chord into a step
783.title: Playing a chord into a step

784.body: The tabs under the steps pick which pattern you're editing: clicking, dragging, the popover and chords played in all write to the pattern on show. The one playing wears a green dot, and the one coming next a green ring. Follow , beside the tabs, keeps the grid on whichever pattern is playing, so it turns over as the Chain (or the Pattern CV) moves on; clicking a tab to edit one turns it off. The playing step's outline only shows on the pattern playing. Which tab is open isn't saved with the patch. Right-click a tab to copy its pattern to another, to start a chorus from the verse, or to clear it. Clearing turns every step into a rest but keeps the chords. The Chain is the order the patterns play in, a pass each, round and round, as on the Step Sequencer : click a slot to change its pattern, right-click it to pick one or remove it, and + adds a pass of the pattern you're editing. A new Chord Sequencer plays A, and so do patches saved before it had patterns, exactly as they always did. A pass ends where the pattern comes round: after the last step going Fwd , after step 1 going Bwd , at each turn in P-P , and after Steps clocks in Rnd . Voice leading carries straight over the join, so the next pattern's first chord is led from this one's last, and a tie on the last step holds the chord into it without a new attack. The popover's preview of how a step will be voiced (and so whether a top note needs writing) assumes its own pattern looping, so a pattern's first chord can come out a little differently after another pattern than the preview suggests.
784.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Patterns and the Chain
784.title: Patterns and the Chain

785.body: With a cable in Pattern , the CV picks the patterns instead, and the Chain dims. It's read once a pass, on the clock that starts it, in the same four zones as the Step and Trigger Sequencers', so one Arranger lane can pick the verse, chorus or coda for all three: hold it at A for the verse and at B for the chorus. Leave that lane's Glide at 0.
785.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Pattern CV
785.title: Pattern CV

786.body: The tones are listed in the order the sequencer keeps them. With fewer Voices than tones, it plays the first ones, so the 5th, which adds the least colour, is the first to go. With more voices than tones, it doubles the chord's notes an octave up, in the same order. Type On C Tones, kept in this order Notes maj C 1 3 5 min Cm 1 ♭3 5 7 C7 1 3 ♭7 5 Dominant seventh maj7 Cmaj7 1 3 7 5 m7 Cm7 1 ♭3 ♭7 5 m7b5 Cm7b5 1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7 Half-diminished; the ♭5 is what makes it, so it's kept dim Cdim 1 ♭3 ♭5 aug Caug 1 3 ♯5 sus2 Csus2 1 2 5 sus4 Csus4 1 4 5 6 C6 1 3 6 5 m6 Cm6 1 ♭3 6 5 add9 Cadd9 1 3 9 5 A triad with the 9th, no 7th maj9 Cmaj9 1 3 7 9 5 In four voices: C E B D m9 Cm9 1 ♭3 ♭7 9 5 9 C9 1 3 ♭7 9 5 11 C11 1 ♭7 9 11 5 No 3rd: it would clash with the 11th. A B♭ triad over C, the soft suspended 11 of soul and jazz 13 C13 1 3 ♭7 13 9 5 No 11th, for the same reason. In four voices: C E B♭ A madd9 Cmadd9 1 ♭3 9 5 Minor add 9, Cm(add9) on a lead sheet: a minor triad with the 9th, no 7th The app writes flats and sharps as b and #, as in Bbmaj7 and F#m7b5.
786.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Chord types
786.title: Chord types

787.body: Voicing decides how the notes are spread out. Cmaj7 with Range 3: Voicing Cmaj7 Sound Close C3 E3 G3 B3 Packed inside an octave, the way a hand plays a chord. Compact, for keys and comping Open G3 C4 E4 B4 Drop-2: the second note from the top goes down an octave. The jazz guitar and horn-section sound, more open than Close and still in one hand Spread C3 G3 E4 B4 Every other note goes up an octave, spanning two. Wide and airy, for pads and strings Range puts the chord's lowest note in its octave. With voice leading on, the lowest note can wander up to a fifth either side of that octave to stay close to the last chord, and no further. A long progression can't climb off the top of the keyboard.
787.title: Voicing

788.body: With Voice lead off, every chord is in root position. With it on, the sequencer tries each inversion of the new chord and keeps the one whose notes are nearest the last chord's, note for note. Common tones stay where they are and the rest move by step. The textbook ii–V–I in C, with Range 3 and four voices: Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 Voice lead off D3 F3 A3 C4 G3 B3 D4 F4 C3 E3 G3 B3 Voice lead on D3 F3 A3 C4 D3 F3 G3 B3 C3 E3 G3 B3 With voice leading on, D and F hold through G7 while A falls to G and C to B. Then B holds and the rest fall a step into Cmaj7. No voice moves more than two semitones. That's the movement a pad or string section needs: the chords change while the sound stays smooth. The first chord after Reset or a stop is in root position, and the rest lead on from it.
788.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Voice leading
788.title: Voice leading

789.body: A step's Top picks the chord tone that goes on top of the voicing, the way an arranger writes a pad's top line. The sequencer then chooses only among the inversions with that tone on top. With voice leading on, it takes the nearest of those; otherwise, the one whose lowest note is in the Range octave. Auto leaves the choice to the voicing. Most steps can leave it on Auto. Set it where voice leading picks a different voicing from the one you hear. A progression that loops back to its first chord is the usual case. Voice leading moves the first chord as close to the last one as it can, so each pass round can start lower than the one before. A Top on the first step starts every pass from the same place. From One Sine sets two tops in sixteen chords, and voice leading finds the rest. You don't have to set them by hand: play the voicing you want into the step (see Playing a chord into a step ) and the popover writes the top if the step needs one. A top that the voicing can't put on top is ignored, as if it were Auto. That happens if the tone isn't in the chord, or if Voices leaves it out, or if a voicing can't reach it: Spread can't put every tone on top. Change the chord and its top stays, so it comes back if the new chord has that tone.
789.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » The top note
789.title: The top note

79.body: A filter removes part of a sound's spectrum. A lowpass filter lets the low frequencies through and cuts the high ones, darkening the tone. This is the heart of subtractive synthesis: start with a bright waveform, then carve it. Add a Filter › SVF Filter between the Oscillator and the VCA. Patch the filter's LowPass output into the VCA's In , replacing the cable from the Oscillator. Patch the Oscillator's Out into the filter's In . Play a few notes and turn the filter's knobs: Cutoff sets where the filter starts cutting. Turn it down and the saw goes dark and muffled; turn it up and the brightness returns. The display draws the filter's response as you turn it. Res (resonance) adds a peak at the cutoff, giving the sound a vocal, nasal edge. The default is 0.5. Near the top of its range the filter starts to ring on its own.
79.breadcrumbs: Your First Patch » Step 5: A filter to color the tone
79.title: Step 5: A filter to color the tone

790.body: A step's Bass puts a different note under the chord: C/E is C major over E, and D/F# is D over F#. That's how a line cliché writes a moving bass under a held chord: Am, Am/G#, Am/G, D/F#. The sequencer places the bass note at or below the root you wrote, so write roots where you want the bass line to sit, usually octave 2. The bass is always on the Bass output. Patch it into a second voice for a bass part. Root carries the root itself, ignoring the slash. When another voice plays the bass from Root or Bass , switch on Rootless . The chord then leaves out its own root first, as it does with Bass voice , so its voices are free for the 3rd, 7th and 9th. With Voices 3, Dmadd9 is F, A and E over a bass playing D. To hear the bass in the chord itself, switch on Bass voice . The cables' first channel then carries the bass note, under the chord, and the chord takes the remaining channels. A single pad then plays the whole slash chord. Because the bass already has the root, the chord drops its own root first when there are more tones than voices. With Voices 4, Cmaj9 is C under E, B and D (its 3rd, 7th and 9th), and with 5 it's C under E G B D. These are the rootless voicings a jazz pianist's left hand plays.
790.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Slash chords and the bass
790.title: Slash chords and the bass

791.body: Timing works as on the Step Sequencer . The sequencer moves on each rising edge at Clock , and Gate is a share of the time between the last two pulses, so chords follow the tempo and a swung clock. At 100%, a chord holds right up to the next clock. The gate then drops for one sample, so each envelope starts again on the new chord. A tie carries the gate into the next step without that drop. The notes change, but nothing is struck again: the envelope carries on rising or sustaining across the change. A sus4 tied into its major chord resolves this way, as do pads that glide from chord to chord. A rest lets the gate fall but leaves the notes where they were, so a long release fades out on the chord it began on. Before two clocks the sequencer has no step to measure. A held first chord then lasts until the next clock, so the first chord after ▶ Play is as long as the rest. A shorter gate is a share of half a second until the clock is measured. Before the first clock , the cables already carry the first chord, with the gate low. A voice whose VCA is always a little open plays that chord quietly from the start. Edits are heard at once. Change the chord that's playing, or Voices , Voicing or Range , and the notes move to match without waiting for the next clock.
791.title: Timing

792.body: Normally every note of a chord starts on the same sample. That suits pads and string machines, but a chord sounds stiff on a guitar, a harp or an electric piano, whose players never strike all the notes at once. Strum delays each channel's gate by its place in the chord: at 20 ms, the second note starts 20 ms after the first, the third 40 ms after, and so on. Strum dir decides which end starts: Up starts on the lowest note, like a guitar's downstroke from the bass string, or a harp rolling a chord upward. Down starts on the highest note. Alt strums up on one clock and down on the next, like a rhythm guitarist's hand going down and up in time. The hand keeps moving through rests and ties, so the strokes stay on the beat they belong to: the first clock after Reset strums up, the next down, and so on. Until the strum reaches a note, that channel keeps playing the chord before, as a string rings until it's struck again. When the strum reaches it, its pitch changes and its gate drops for one sample and rises, all on the same channel. The pitch never arrives after the gate, so no note is struck on the last chord's pitch. Ties are never struck again. A tied chord still changes its notes in strum order, one channel after another, under gates that stay high: the chord rolls from one to the next without an attack. A strum fits inside its step. Once the clock has been measured, the notes are spaced no further apart than the step divided by the number of voices. The last note then sounds before the next chord's first, however fast the clock. Until the clock has been measured, the first chord after ▶ Play takes the full Strum spacing. If the next clock comes before its upper notes, they're skipped. Gate applies to each note from its own strike, so every note of a strummed chord is held equally long. Bass voice is the first channel, so Up strums the bass first and Down strums it last. For a guitar, 10 to 30 ms is a quick strum, and around 50 ms a slow one. A harp's rolled chord is 60 to 100 ms. Sixteenth notes at a fast tempo leave little room, so there the strum shortens to fit the step.
792.title: Strum

793.body: A real strum isn't even. A downstroke digs into the low strings and only brushes the top ones, and an upstroke catches the top few and fades out before the bass. Taper gives each note a velocity by its place in the strum. At 50%, the first note plays at the step's velocity and the last at half of it, with the notes between stepping down evenly. At 100% the last note has no velocity at all: an upstroke that misses the bass strings. Below 0 the shading runs the other way, so the notes struck last are the loudest. With Strum dir on Down , a negative Taper leans on the bass notes at the end of the strum. Taper follows the strum's order , not the pitch. Up shades from the bottom note, Down from the top, and Alt changes direction with each stroke, as a guitarist's hand does. It works with Strum at 0. The notes all start together, but they're still shaded lowest first (Up) or highest first (Down). With Down and a little Taper , the top of a pad's chord carries over the rest. Each note keeps its velocity until the strum reaches it , along with its pitch. A string still ringing from the chord before stays as loud as it was struck. How much you hear depends on the voice. The Electric Piano gets quieter as its velocity drops, so Taper is plain on it. A voice whose velocity only shapes its attack shows it less.
793.title: Taper

794.body: Alt strums up and down by the clock, which suits a steady eighth-note rhythm. A written rhythm needs more control than that: an upstroke on the "and" of 2, a downstroke on the next beat after a rest. Each step has a Strum of its own in the popover: Auto follows Strum dir , Alt included. Up or Down strums this step that way, whatever Strum dir says. A small arrow marks the step. The hand keeps time through a step that names its own stroke, as it does through rests. Under Alt , a step written Up where a down was due is strummed up, and the step after it takes the stroke the clock gives it.
794.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » A step's own stroke
794.title: A step's own stroke

795.title: Example patches

[Clock Gate] ──> [Chord Sequencer Clock]
[Chord Sequencer Pitch] ──> [Supersaw Pad Pitch]
[Chord Sequencer Gate] ──> [Supersaw Pad Gate]
[Chord Sequencer Velocity] ──> [Supersaw Pad Velocity]
[Supersaw Pad Out] ──> [Reverb] ──> [Audio Output] Add the Supersaw Pad from the Library, set the Clock to a slow division (1/1, a chord a bar), and leave Voice lead on. Try Voicing Spread with Voices 5 or 6 for strings.
