796.title: A pad that plays a progression

797.body:
[Chord Sequencer Pitch / Gate / Velocity] ──> [a mallet or FM voice]
[Chord Sequencer Bass] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct] (a second, mono voice)
[Chord Sequencer Gate] ──> [ADSR Gate] (the bass's envelope) Voicing Close, Range 4, Gate around 60%, and velocities that vary from step to step. Write the roots in octave 2 so Bass plays a real bass line, slash notes included. A Strum of 10 to 15 ms loosens the chords the way a player's hand does.
797.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Electric piano comping with a bass
797.title: Electric piano comping with a bass

798.body: Patch Root into an oscillator's Exp FM (at 1.0 octave per volt) while a Step Sequencer plays an arpeggio into its V/Oct . The oscillator adds the two pitches, so the arpeggio follows the chord roots. Afterglow is built this way, with the chords themselves on a pad underneath.
798.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Moving an arpeggio through the chords
798.title: Moving an arpeggio through the chords

799.body: Voices sets the colour. Three voices give shells (root, 3rd, 7th), and four give full seventh chords. Five or more add the 9ths and doublings that make pads lush. Bass voice and four Voices give the classic rootless voicings for jazz and neo-soul. Rootless gives the same when the bass is a voice of its own. Ties on a pad turn a progression into one long breath. Dir Rnd over a set of related chords (Fmaj7, Am7, Cmaj7, Em7) makes ambient harmony that never quite repeats. EOC can clock a second sequencer once per progression, or a Clock Divider for a turnaround every few passes. Strummed rhythm guitar: clock at eighth notes, write each chord on two steps, set Strum dir to Alt, Strum to about 25 ms and Taper to about 40%, and give the upstrokes a lower velocity. Where the rhythm needs a stroke the clock doesn't give, set that step's Strum to Up or Down . Voicing Spread with five or six voices and Bass voice on spreads the notes out like a guitar's six strings. Front Porch is built this way, with ties for the strokes the hand misses. A song in one sequencer: a chord a bar and 16 steps make each pattern a 16-bar section. Write the verse in A and copy it to B for a chorus that starts the same way. A Chain of A B A C gives verse, chorus, verse, coda.
799.title: Tips

8.body: Each release on GitHub has a download for Windows, macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Linux.
8.title: Download a release

80.body: Real instruments are brightest at the start of a note. You can do the same by letting the envelope move the filter's cutoff. Patch the envelope's Out into the filter's Cutoff input. One output can feed any number of inputs, so the envelope keeps driving the VCA too. Turn the Cutoff knob down to about 400 Hz. Each note now opens the filter and closes it again as the envelope decays. The Cutoff knob stays live and sets where the sweep starts. CV Amt sets how far the envelope carries it: one octave at first. Turn CV Amt up to 3 and each note opens with a squelch. An orange arc on the Cutoff knob's rim shows each sweep, and the number under the knob turns orange to read where the envelope has taken the cutoff. For a plucky, percussive bass, set Atk to its minimum, Dec to about 200 ms and Sus low. For a slow, brightening pad, lengthen Atk .
80.breadcrumbs: Your First Patch » Step 6: Let the envelope open the filter
80.title: Step 6: Let the envelope open the filter

800.body: Step Sequencer : one note per step, and the same clocking and ties Note In : chords played live, on the same kind of cable Polyphony : how one cable carries several voices Arranger : a song's sections, which can clock or reset the progression, or pick its pattern through Pattern Vocoder : a whole chord on one cable makes a carrier that speaks in harmony, as in Soba Speaks
800.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Chord Sequencer » Related Modules
800.title: Related Modules

801.body: Module ID seq.trigger · Category Utility Trigger Sequencer Module Pattern B of the Roll Call example, playing: a fill whose snare roll splits into ratchets, two, then three, then four hits a step. Each lane sits beside its own Gate and Vel jacks. The rim loops every 3 steps and the cowbell every 5, and the orange lines mark where they turn round. The Chain plays C A A B, and C, ringed, comes next. The Trigger Sequencer is a drum machine's sequencer. It has eight lanes of sixteen steps, and each lane has its own Gate and Vel output, so one module plays a whole kit: patch each lane into a Drum . It holds four patterns, A to D, and plays them in the order its Chain gives, so A A A B is a groove with a fill every fourth bar. Each step can play only some of the time, or roll two to four hits across its length. Where the Step Sequencer plays a melody, one note at a time, the Trigger Sequencer plays rhythm, many hits at once. It has no pitch.
801.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Trigger Sequencer » Trigger Sequencer
801.title: Trigger Sequencer

802.body: Port Signal Type Description Clock Gate (Green) Each rising edge plays the next step Reset Gate (Green) A rising edge starts over: the next clock plays step 1 of the Chain's first pattern Run Gate (Green) Steps advance only while this is high. With nothing patched, the sequencer runs Pattern Control (Orange) Picks the pattern for each new bar in place of the Chain: 0 to 0.25 is A, 0.25 to 0.5 is B, then C, and D from 0.75 up
802.title: Inputs

803.body: Port Signal Type Description Accent Gate (Green) A gate on every accented step, whichever lanes play on it Gate 1 – Gate 8 Gate (Green) Each lane's hits. Patch into a Drum's Trig , or an envelope's Gate Vel 1 – Vel 8 Control (Orange) The velocity of the lane's last hit, 0 to 1, raised on accented steps. It holds until the lane's next hit. Patch into a Drum's Accent
803.title: Outputs

804.body: Control Range Default Description Steps 1 – 16 16 How many steps make a bar. The pattern changes, and the Chain moves on, only where a bar starts Gate (Gate Length) 1 – 100% 50% How long each gate stays high, as a share of its step, or of its share of the step in a ratchet Accent (Accent Amount) 0 – 100% 50% How far an accented step raises every lane's velocity toward full Each pattern also stores, for every lane and step, whether the step plays, its velocity, its probability and its ratchet. It also stores an accent row. Each lane has a length, and the Chain has up to eight bars. The grid, the tabs and the Chain under it edit all of these, and patches save them.
804.title: Parameters

805.body: Each lane is drawn on the two rows its jacks hang from. Pads sit on the Gate row, and each hit's velocity is an orange bar on the Vel row below. A lane is named after what its Gate cable plays: a Drum's type (Kick, Snare, C Hat, …), or the name of the module it feeds. A lane with nothing patched shows its number. Click a pad to add a hit, or take it away. A new hit plays at 80%, so an accent has room above it. Drag a pad up or down to set its velocity. Dragging an empty pad adds a hit at the velocity you drag to. Shift + click steps the ratchet through ×1, ×2, ×3 and ×4. A ratcheted pad splits into slivers, one per hit. Ctrl + click steps the probability through 100, 75, 50, 25 and 10%. A pad that only sometimes plays is outlined and filled only as far as its chance. Alt + click ends the lane at that step, so it loops on its own length (see Polymeter ). Alt + click the last step again and the lane follows the bar. Right-click a pad for all of these in a menu. Right-click a lane's name to set its length from a grid of 1 to 16, or to clear the lane in this pattern. Click a step on the top row to accent it. Notation's accent mark, > , shows on accented steps. Steps past the end of a lane fade. Each one keeps its settings for when the lane grows again. Every click, and every drag, is one step of undo , with a name that says what it did ("Ratchet ×3 on Snare step 14 of B"). Fast clicks on the grid don't run together. While the patch plays, each lane's current step has a white outline, and a pad lights as it fires. The outline is faint while the grid shows a pattern other than the one playing.
805.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Trigger Sequencer » Programming a beat
805.title: Programming a beat

806.body: The tabs under the grid pick which pattern you're editing. The one playing wears a green dot, and the one coming next a green ring. Follow , beside the tabs, keeps the grid on whichever pattern is playing, so it turns over as the Chain (or the Pattern CV) moves on; clicking a tab to edit one turns it off. Which tab is open is the editor's choice: it isn't saved with the patch, and it isn't an edit. Right-click a tab to copy its pattern to another, which is the quick way to start a fill from the groove, or to clear it. The Chain is the order the patterns play in, a bar each, round and round. The bar playing is underlined. Click a bar to change its pattern: A, B, C, D, then A again. Right-click it to pick a pattern, or to remove the bar. The bars after it move up. + adds a bar of the pattern you're editing to the end. The Chain holds up to eight. A new Trigger Sequencer plays A. For a fill every fourth bar, write the groove in A, copy it to B, change B's last few steps, and make the Chain A A A B. Every pattern change lands on a bar line, counted from the same clock as the steps, so the fill never drifts, however long the patch runs.
806.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Trigger Sequencer » Patterns and the Chain
806.title: Patterns and the Chain

807.body: With a cable in Pattern , the CV picks the patterns instead, and the Chain dims. The CV is read once a bar, as the bar starts, so a pattern change always waits for the next bar line. A Clock Divider 's Gate through an Attenuverter can switch to a fill on a phrase of its own, and an LFO or Sample & Hold can wander between patterns.
807.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Trigger Sequencer » Pattern CV
807.title: Pattern CV

809.body: The sequencer has no tempo of its own. Each rising edge at Clock plays the next step, so a Clock at 1/16 plays sixteenths, and its swing carries through. Gate is a share of the step, which the sequencer measures from the clock, as the Step Sequencer does. On a swung clock, each step's gates are a share of that step, long or short. A Drum only listens for the rise of its trigger, so for drums Gate hardly matters. Envelopes care. When a hit lands while its lane's gate is still high, the gate drops for one sample first, so every hit starts with a rising edge.
809.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Trigger Sequencer » The clock
809.title: The clock

81.body:
[Note In Pitch] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct]
[Note In Gate] ──> [ADSR Envelope Gate]
[Oscillator Out] ──> [SVF Filter In]
[SVF Filter LowPass] ──> [VCA In]
[ADSR Envelope Out] ──> [VCA CV]
[ADSR Envelope Out] ──> [SVF Filter Cutoff]
[VCA Out] ──> [Audio Output Mono] Save it with 💾 Save (Ctrl + S). The signal path runs left to right: the oscillator makes the tone, the filter colors it, and the VCA shapes its level. The keyboard and envelope sit off to the side, controlling the others. Nearly every subtractive synthesizer, hardware or software, is built this way.
81.breadcrumbs: Your First Patch » The finished patch
81.title: The finished patch

810.body: A ratchet plays 2, 3 or 4 hits, evenly spaced across the step: ×3 on a sixteenth at 120 BPM is three hits 41.7 ms apart. The spacing comes from the measured step, so ratchets follow the tempo. On a swung clock, a step that runs long spreads its hits wider than a short one. Each hit has the step's velocity, and a gate that's Gate of its share of the step. The next clock ends any hits still to come. Before the sequencer has seen two clock pulses it can't measure a step, so for the very first step it assumes a sixteenth at the patch's tempo (120 BPM if nothing sets one).
810.title: Ratchets

811.body: A step with a probability below 100% rolls the dice each time its turn comes. If it plays, all of its ratchet's hits play. The dice fall the same way every time you press Play, so a take you liked can be played again.
811.title: Probability

812.body: An accented step raises the velocity of every lane that plays on it, part of the way to full: at 50% Accent , a 60% hit plays at 80%, and a 100% hit stays at 100%. At 0% the accent row does nothing to the velocities. Accent also fires its own gate on every accented step, for anything else that should hear it: a filter's envelope, say, or a VCA.
812.title: Accents

813.body: A lane left at its default follows the bar. Give a lane its own length and it loops that many steps however long the bar is. A lane 3 steps long against a 16-step bar plays a figure of three over a bar of four, and the two only line up again after 3 bars. Two lanes of 3 and 5 against 16 meet the bar again after 15 bars. The bar and every lane count the same clock, so they drift against each other only on purpose. Reset starts them all together again.
813.title: Polymeter

814.body: Patch a gate into Run to pause the pattern in place. While Run is low, clocks are ignored and the sequencer stays on its current step. A step that played just before Run fell still plays out its ratchet. When Run comes back high, the next clock plays the step after the one it stopped on. Hold Run low for whole bars and the Chain picks up as though those bars never came. The Clock 's Run and Reset outputs are made for this. Patch them into Run and Reset and the pattern stops with the Clock and starts again from step 1 when it does, including when the Clock follows a DAW's MIDI clock and you press Play there. To let a song's last chord ring with no more hits, patch an Arranger lane's Gate into Run and bring the lane to zero for the closing bars.
814.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Trigger Sequencer » Stop and start
814.title: Stop and start

815.body: Every step is one parameter, named for its pattern, lane and step: Step A1 01 is pattern A, lane 1, step 1. Its value reads as digits, ratchet , probability , velocity , and it's negative while the step is off: Value Step 1100080 One hit, always, at 80% 3050100 Three hits, half the time, at 100% -1100080 Off. Click it and it plays one hit, always, at 80% An off step keeps its settings, so turning it off and on again changes nothing else. The accent row is Accent A 01 to Accent D 16, the lanes' lengths Length 1 to Length 8 (0 follows the bar), and the Chain Chain 1 to Chain 8.
815.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Trigger Sequencer » How patches store it
815.title: How patches store it

816.body: One lane per drum. Patch Gate 1 into the kick's Trig and Vel 1 into its Accent , and so on down the kit. The lane names follow. A choke group. Patch the closed hat's Gate into the open hat's Choke as well as the closed hat's Trig , and a closed hat cuts an open one short. Ghost notes. Drop a snare hit to 25–35% velocity. Through a Drum's Accent it plays darker as well as quieter. Rolls. A ×2 on the last hat of a bar is a flam into the downbeat. ×3 and ×4 on the last snare hits of a fill are a press roll. Humanize. A few hats at 75% or 50% chance keep a loop from sounding like one. Two kits. A second Trigger Sequencer on the same Clock and Reset plays in lockstep with the first.
816.title: Tips

817.body: Roll Call – a full kit on one Trigger Sequencer, with a fill and crash every four bars Arranger – a song's sections, with a lane that can pick this sequencer's pattern for each one Drum – the voice each lane plays Step Sequencer – notes rather than hits Clock – tempo and swing Clock Divider – phrases, for Pattern or Reset
817.title: Related

818.body: Module ID seq.arranger · Category Utility Arranger Module A five-section song, playing its Build. Each section is a block as wide as its bars, and each lane's level runs under them as an orange line, with a green strip wherever its gate is high. The ticks on the Crash lane are Hits. The white line is the playhead. The Arranger is a song's timeline. It holds up to 32 named sections , each some bars long and played ×1 to ×16 times, in order, and eight lanes of automation that the sections move. A lane can ride a part's fader, pick a drum pattern, open a filter over a build or press a Looper's button, and each section says what it does when the section starts: hold, jump, ramp or hit. It counts bars from a Clock , like the sequencers, so the song stays in step with everything else the Clock drives. Press ▶ Play and it starts from the first section.
818.title: Arranger

819.body: Port Signal Type Description Clock Gate (Green) Each rising edge is a step, and Steps of them make a bar. Patch the Clock that drives the sequencers Reset Gate (Green) A rising edge starts over: the next clock starts section 1 Jump Gate (Green) A rising edge goes to the section Jump To picks, at the next bar line Jump To Control (Orange) The section a Jump goes to, as its number ÷ 32 (section 1 is 0, section 5 is 4/32). It reads the same as the Section output Follow Control (Orange) Patch another Arranger's Section here to follow it: its sections become this one's, and it goes wherever the leader goes
819.title: Inputs

82.body: Modules are added from the right-click menu or with Space, and connected by dragging from an output to an input. Audio (blue) is the sound itself; control (orange) moves things, like pitch and cutoff; gates (green) say when a note is on. An envelope through a VCA turns a constant tone into notes. One output can drive several inputs, and a cable into a knob's jack moves that knob.
82.breadcrumbs: Your First Patch » What you've learned
82.title: What you've learned

820.body: Port Signal Type Description Section Control (Orange) The section playing, its index ÷ 32. A repeated section reads the same on every pass Section Trig Gate (Green) A trigger on each section's downbeat, and on every pass of a repeated one Bar Gate (Green) A trigger on every bar's downbeat Last Bar Gate (Green) High through each section's final bar, for a fill. A repeated section has one on every pass End Gate (Green) A trigger when the last section finishes, whether the song loops or stops Next Control (Orange) The section the next bar line goes to, as its index ÷ 32. It reads the same as Section until the section's last bar throws its Next , or a Jump is asked for. Before the first clock, it names the section the song starts on. Patch it into a Setlist , which tells the hardware ahead of the bar Lane 1 – Lane 8 Control (Orange) Each lane's level, 0 to 1. A ramp is smooth enough to drive a Mixer 's Level directly Gate 1 – Gate 8 Gate (Green) High while the lane is above zero, and for a moment on each Hit Triggers last half a step.
820.title: Outputs

821.body: Control Range Default Description Steps 1 – 96 16 How many clocks make a bar: 16 for a Clock at 1/16 in 4/4, 12 for 3/4 Loop to Off, 1 – 32 1 The section to go back to after the last one, or Off to stop there Width Compact, Wide, Extra wide Compact How wide the timeline is drawn: 440, 760 or 1080 points. Wide or Extra wide suits a long song read whole on a big screen. The module plays the same at any width The sections, their names, lengths and repeats, the lanes' names and glides, and every section's cue for every lane are edited on the timeline, and patches save them. So is Width . The jacks keep their rows at every width, and so do the lanes beside them.
821.title: Parameters

822.body: The song runs left to right across the node. Each section is a block as wide as its share of the bars, though a short one keeps enough room to click. The blocks sit beside the song's own jacks: Section, Trig, Bar, Last, End and Next. Each lane is drawn on the two rows its CV and Gate jacks hang from, so a lane reads straight across into its cables. A lane is named for what its cable drives (a Mixer's Level 2 , say) until you give it a name. The bar count at the top left shows where the song is, and the section playing is lit green, with its name in the header too. Click a section to pick it. The bar under the timeline shows it. Double-click a section to rename it. Press Enter to keep the name, or Escape to leave it. Drag a lane up or down inside a section to set the level that section takes it to. A section that held the lane now jumps it. Shift-drag a lane inside a section to set where its ramp starts. Any other cue becomes a ramp from there to its level, or for a Hold, to where the lane was. Right-click a lane inside a section for how it gets there (see Cues ), its level, and a ramp's length, curve and start. Double-click a lane's name to rename it. Right-click it to set its Glide , or to clear it. Right-click a section for its length and repeats, to add, copy, move or delete it, and to split or merge its copies. The bar under the timeline does the same for the section you picked. ◀ and ▶ step through the sections. The bars field sets its length, and the × field how many times it plays. + adds a blank section after it, and Copy adds a copy. ◀ Move and Move ▶ swap it with its neighbours, and Delete takes it out. Loop to follows the section it named when sections move. A section's final bar is shaded, since that's where a fill goes. A repeated section has one shaded on each pass. Every edit is one step of undo , named for what it did ("Groove · Pad jumps to 48%"). Name… , at the left of the bar under the lanes' names, names the Arranger itself. The name shows in its header beside the section playing, and an Arranger that follows this one calls it by its name. A name too long for its block is cut short with "…". Hover the block and the whole name shows on a tag just above it. Pick the section and the bar under the timeline shows it in full too.
822.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Arranger » Writing a song
822.title: Writing a song

823.body: A long song packs its short sections tight: in a 128-bar song a one-bar fill is a sliver. Zoom the timeline rather than the whole canvas: Ctrl+scroll over the timeline (or pinch, on a trackpad) zooms it about the pointer, in as far as two bars across. Scroll over the timeline, once it's zoomed in, moves along the song. While it shows the whole song, the scroll wheel zooms the canvas as usual. The thin strip over the ruler is the whole song in little, with the part in view framed. Drag along it to move the view, or click somewhere to go there. Double-click it to see the whole song again. Zoomed in, the ruler numbers the bars inside each section, and each section's name stays in view as you move past its start. While the song plays, the view turns the page whenever the playhead nears its right edge, so the playhead stays in view. It waits a few seconds after you move the view yourself. The zoom belongs to the editor, like the section you picked. It isn't saved with the patch and isn't a step of undo. For a song you want to read whole, set Width instead.
823.title: Zooming in

824.body: Songs repeat themselves: a groove four times round, a verse that comes back. Give a section a × count, ×1 to ×16, and it plays that many times before the next. ×N plays exactly as N copies of it would , sample for sample: Every pass gives the section's cues again. A Jump jumps again, a Ramp runs again (from its own start if it has one, or from wherever the lane is), and a Hit fires again, so a crash on every pass of a 4-bar groove is one cue. Section Trig , Bar and Last Bar fire on every pass, so a fill on the last bar lands at the end of each one. A Ramp "over the section" takes one pass. Jump to a repeated section starts its first pass, and so does Loop to . The section is one block on the timeline, as wide as all its passes, with ×N in its corner and faint dashes between the passes. While it plays, the pass playing is lit, the corner counts the passes off ("3/4"), and so do the bar count and the header: "Groove 3/4". Since ×N means N copies, either can become the other. Right-click a section: Split into copies turns a section ×N into N sections, each ×1, named "Groove", "Groove 2" and so on. Do it when one pass needs to differ. Merge with copies after it folds the sections straight after this one that play the same (the same length and cues, whatever their names) into it, up to ×16. It stops at a section Loop to goes back to, which has to stay a section of its own. Each is one step of undo, and neither changes what you hear. The one thing that does change is the sections' numbers after it, so a Jump To CV that picked a later section by number needs moving too. Loop to follows by itself.
824.title: Repeats

825.body: A song can need more than eight lanes. Patch one Arranger's Section output into another's Follow input, and the second one follows the first. It has the first one's sections, the same number of them, as long, played as many times, with the same names and the same places to wander to , and the same Steps and Loop to . Its lanes are its own, and you edit them on its own face as before. Edit the sections on the leader. On the follower they can be picked but not changed, and its bar says Follows Desk (or whatever the leader is called). Its Steps knob and Loop to are the leader's too. The follower's cues move with their sections. Add, copy, move, delete, split or merge a section on the leader, and the follower does the same with its own cues. A merge folds only copies that play the same on every Arranger down the chain. Lengthening or renaming a section does too. The leader's edit and the follower's are one step of undo, so undo takes both back. The follower zooms with its leader. Zoom or scroll either one and both move, page turns included, so the two scores stay lined up section for section. A whole chain shares one view. Unpatch Follow and the follower keeps the sections it had, and you can edit them on it again. It keeps the view it had too, and zooms on its own from then on. Chains. A follower can lead another, so three Arrangers give 24 lanes. A chain can't come back round: an Arranger that would end up following itself refuses the cable and says why. Follow takes only an Arranger's Section . Two Arrangers that count the same Clock already change section on the same sample. But a leader can wander , or jump on a Jump of its own, so on every bar line a follower goes to the section its leader is in. It throws no dice of its own. A Jump patched into the leader alone moves the whole chain.
825.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Arranger » More than eight lanes: Follow
825.title: More than eight lanes: Follow

826.body: Each section gives each lane one of four cues as the section starts: Cue What the lane does Hold Carries on as it was. If it was ramping, the ramp carries on. A new section holds every lane Jump Goes straight to the level, on the downbeat Ramp Glides to the level over the whole section or over a number of bars, on one of four curves . It starts from wherever the lane is, or from a level of its own. A ramp longer than its section carries on through the sections after it that hold Hit Goes to the level for half a step, then back: a trigger, with the level riding on the CV, for a Drum's Trig and Accent or a Looper's Rec
826.title: Cues

827.body: The four ramp curves: S-curve, Linear, Exp and Log A ramp takes one of four shapes, chosen in its right-click menu and drawn to shape on the lane: Curve Shape Suits S-curve Leaves gently and arrives gently, like a hand on a fader. The default, and how every ramp moved before there was a choice Fades. A Mixer's Level moves without a click, however slow or quick the ramp Linear The same pace all the way A steady build, or a tempo-like push Exp Slow to start, fast to finish: a fifth of the way there at half time A filter sweep or a riser that rushes into the downbeat Log Fast to start, slow to finish: four fifths of the way there at half time A swell that settles, or a fade that tails away Exp and Log are mirror images, so an Exp fade-out holds on and then drops away, and a Log one falls quickly and then lingers. From sets where a ramp starts. Where it is carries on from the lane's level as the section starts. A level jumps the lane there on the downbeat, as a Jump would, gate dip and Glide included, and ramps from there. A part can then come in at one level and grow through the same section: a pad that enters at 28% and swells to 42% over twelve bars is one cue.
827.title: Ramps

828.body: A lane's Gate is high while the lane is above zero. One lane can therefore be a part's level and its envelope's gate at once. A riser that jumps to 30% for a section and back to 0 is heard for that section and gated for exactly as long. When a Jump or Hit lands while the gate is already high, the gate drops for one sample first, so an envelope starts again. So does a ramp that starts from a level of its own. A ramp up from zero opens the gate as it leaves zero.
828.title: The gate

829.body: A Jump moves on one sample, and a Mixer's Level adds its CV without smoothing, so a jump under a ringing note clicks. Glide smooths the lane's CV: it's how long the CV takes to move all the way from 0 to 1, so 1 s brings a half-way fader up in half a second, the same as a Sample & Hold 's Slew . A second or so suits a pad, and 40 ms keeps a rhythmic part on the beat while still saving its tails. The gate follows the cue, not the glide. Leave Glide at 0 on a lane that picks something: a Trigger Sequencer 's, Step Sequencer 's or Chord Sequencer 's Pattern , say. The sequencer reads the CV on the downbeat, the same sample the lane jumps on, and a glide would still be on its way there.
829.title: Glide

83.body: Use separate envelopes. Add a second ADSR Envelope for the filter, also gated by Note In, so brightness and loudness can have different shapes. Add velocity. Patch Note In's Velocity into the envelope's Velocity input, then lower its Key Vel knob for quieter notes. Add movement. Patch a Modulation › LFO into the filter's Cutoff for a slow sweep. Its Out swings the cutoff CV Amt octaves either way. Add space. Put an Effect › Reverb between the VCA and the Audio Output: VCA Out into Reverb In L , then the Reverb's Out L and Out R into the output's Left and Right . Watch it. Patch the VCA's Out into a Utility › Oscilloscope as well as the output to see the envelope shape the wave.
83.breadcrumbs: Your First Patch » Things to try
83.title: Things to try

830.body: The Arranger has no tempo of its own. It counts clock edges: a bar is Steps of them, and a section is its length in bars. It changes section on the clock edge that starts the section's first bar, the same edge the sequencers step on, so it can't drift from them, swing or not. A ramp moves between clock edges too, smoothly. It measures each step from the clock, as the sequencers do, so on a swung clock it moves a little faster through the short steps. It still lands on the clock edge that ends it. Before the Arranger has seen two clock pulses it can't measure a step. For the first triggers it assumes a sixteenth at the patch's tempo, or at 120 BPM if nothing sets one.
830.title: Timing

831.body: After the last section, the song goes back to Loop to , and End fires. With Loop to off, End fires and the song stops where it is. The lanes keep their last levels, and the bars stop counting, until a Reset, a Jump or the next Play. Jump waits for the next bar line, so a live change of section always lands on the beat. Patch a button, a Note In gate or a Logic decision into Jump , and a constant or a Sample & Hold into Jump To . While a Jump waits, the section it's going to is outlined green.
831.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Arranger » Looping, ending and jumping
831.title: Looping, ending and jumping

832.body: A song doesn't have to play in the order it's written. Right-click a section, and When it ends says where it may go: On as written – the section after it, or Loop to after the last one, or stopping there with Loop to off. Or… – up to two other places: any section (itself included, to maybe play it again), or Anywhere , which is any section but this one. Each place has a weight from 0 to 9, and its chance is its weight against the others'. Window with on to Rain 1 , Home 1 , Late 1 goes each way a third of the time. On 0 never goes on as written. Always on as written puts the section back in order. The dice are thrown on the downbeat of the section's last bar, on its last pass if it repeats. They don't wait for the bar line. Over the timeline, a faint arc leads from the end of each section that may wander to each place it may go, fainter the less likely it is, and a small ? marks Anywhere . Once the dice are thrown, the arc to where they went lights green, a bar before the song gets there. A Jump that lands in that bar still wins. Repeatable. The dice are seeded, so an offline render plays the same wandering every time, and so does the app each time the patch is opened. Stopping and starting again carries on with new throws. End fires only when the last section goes on as written. A last section that wanders back into the song hasn't ended it. Followers wander with their leader. A follower has its leader's places to go, and goes where its leader went. Its timeline lights the same arc. Moving sections. Add, copy, move, delete, split or merge sections and each place keeps pointing at the section it named, wherever that has moved. One that names a deleted section is dropped. Splitting a section ×3 gives only the last copy its wandering, and a merge stops at a copy that may wander off.
832.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Arranger » Wandering: where a section goes next
832.title: Wandering: where a section goes next

833.body: Every section's cue for every lane is one parameter, named for both: Section 03 Lane 2 is section 3's cue for lane 2. Its value reads as digits, move , ramp bars and level in tenths of a percent. The move is 0 Hold, 1 Jump, 2 Ramp and 3 Hit, and a ramp on another curve takes 4 Linear, 5 Exp or 6 Log: Value Cue 0 Hold 1000700 Jump to 70% 2000500 Ramp to 50% over the section, on the S-curve 2080250 Ramp to 25% over 8 bars, on the S-curve 4000500 Ramp to 50% over the section, in a line 5160900 Ramp to 90% over 16 bars, on Exp 6040000 Ramp to 0% over 4 bars, on Log 3000850 Hit at 85% A ramp's start is a second parameter, Section 03 Lane 2 From: the level in tenths of a percent (280 starts at 28%), or -1 to start from where the lane is. Patches saved before ramps had curves and starts have no From parameters and only 2 for ramps, so they play as they always did. Where a section may go is Next 01 to Next 32, read as digits too: the weight of going on as written, then each other place's section (01 to 32, or 00 for anywhere) and weight. 1062051 goes on with weight 1, to section 6 with weight 2 and to section 5 with weight 1. 0 (the default, and every patch from before) always goes on as written. The sections' lengths are Length 01 to Length 32, their repeats Repeat 01 to Repeat 32 (a patch from before repeats plays every section ×1), the lanes' glides Glide 1 to Glide 8, and Sections is how many sections the song has. The names you give sections and lanes, and the Arranger's own name, are saved with the module as labels. A follower saves its own copy of its leader's sections, so it plays them even where Follow isn't known.
833.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Arranger » How patches store it
833.title: How patches store it

834.body: Faders at zero. On a Mixer , set a channel's Level knob to 0 and patch a lane into its Level input. The lane then is the fader. Fills. Either give each phrase a one-bar Fill section that jumps the drum lane to the fill pattern, or patch Last Bar into something that plays a fill. With Last Bar , a 4-bar groove ×4 has a fill at the end of every pass. Two Arrangers, one song. When eight lanes aren't enough, clock a second Arranger from the same Clock and patch the first one's Section into its Follow (see Follow ). From One Sine splits its score into faders and cues this way, with a third Arranger for its tape and its tempo. Pedals. Hit a Looper's Rec at the start of a section to record it, and its Clear at the top of the song so each pass starts fresh. A brightness lane. Ramp a lane over a build and patch it through an Attenuverter into filter cutoffs or drive amounts: the whole build opens up together. A shorter song. Set Loop to a later section, and the intro plays only once. An endless song. Give each section a chance of going somewhere else, and set Loop to back near the start: the song never quite repeats. Weight its way home a little higher, so it keeps coming back to its centre. Ride the room. Patch a lane into a Mixer 's Return with its knob at 0, and the lane is the reverb's fader: dry and close for the opening, the hall for the second verse. A lane into one channel's Send steps just that part into the room. Canopy does the first. Tell the hardware. Patch Section , Next and Bar into a Setlist , and each section moves the Digitakt to its pattern and the FANTOM to its scene, ahead of the bar.
834.title: Tips

835.body: From One Sine – a whole song on three Arrangers: eight faders; the drums, crash, riser, brightness, Looper pedals and the melody's patterns; a lane that warps the master tape, and one that slows the Clock into the end Trigger Sequencer – patterns for an Arranger lane to pick Mixer – the faders, sends and return a lane rides Clock – tempo and swing Clock Divider – phrases without a timeline
835.title: Related

836.body: Module ID util.scenes · Category Utility Scenes keeps the knobs of a patch as scenes , A to H, and glides between two of them with one knob. A verse and its breakdown, a dry sound and a drenched one, the calm before a drop: store each as a scene, and Morph carries every knob from one to the other at once. A change that would take eight hands becomes one gesture, and the space halfway between two scenes, where nobody set the knobs on purpose, is often where the good sounds are. The scenes live on the module, so you can see them in the patch, and they're saved with it.
836.title: Scenes

837.body: A Scenes module at the top of the patch holds every knob and switch in the patch. Put one inside a group , and it holds only that group's knobs (and those of the groups inside it), so a voice can have scenes of its own without touching the drums. A scene leaves out the Audio Output, other Scenes modules, and switches that start, stop or record rather than shape the sound (a Clock's Run , a Sampler's Rec , an Audio Input's Channel ), or say which device a module plays (a Port ). An Instrument 's knobs are kept like any others, so a scene can hold a sound on the hardware. A knob of named values (an arpeggio type) flips at halfway, as a dropdown does. A knob that nudges the device rather than setting it (the FANTOM-06's Cutoff) isn't kept, because it has no place to come back to.
837.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Scenes » What a scene holds
837.title: What a scene holds

838.body: Port Signal Type Description Morph Control (Orange) Replaces the Morph knob: 0 is the From scene, 1 the To scene. Patch an LFO (with Bipolar off), an envelope or an Arranger lane

84.body: Signal Types explains what each cable color carries and what can connect to what. Basic Subtractive Synth takes this patch further, with separate envelopes for brightness and volume. It's in 📚 Examples too. The module reference has a page for every module.
84.title: Next

840.body: Each pad is a scene. A pad with a scene in it draws the scene's knobs as a row of ticks, each as high as the knob is turned. The pad the knobs stand at right now is ringed in blue. Click an empty pad to keep the knobs as they stand. Click a full pad to recall it: every knob it holds jumps there. Shift+click a full pad to keep the knobs there instead. Alt+click a full pad to clear it. Right-click a pad and choose Learn MIDI , then hit a pad on your controller, to recall the scene from it. A mapped pad wears a small purple dot. The From and To pads glow, each in proportion to how near Morph has carried the knobs to it, so the light crossfades from one to the other as Morph turns. Along the bottom, a dot rides a line from From to To. The header says what the module reaches ( PATCH , or its group's name) and where Morph is. Keeping, recalling and clearing a scene are each one undo step.
840.title: The pads

841.body: As Morph moves, each knob the two scenes share moves from its place in one to its place in the other: Knobs glide round their own travel , as a hand would turn them. A frequency knob moves by octaves, so halfway between 200 Hz and 3200 Hz is 800 Hz, not 1700. Whole-number knobs, switches and dropdowns hold the From scene's setting until Morph passes halfway, then flip to the To scene's. A knob a cable drives is left to the cable. A knob only one scene holds (on a module added after the other was kept) stays where it is. The knobs turn on screen as Morph moves, and reach the sound through the same smoothing as a hand on the knob, so a glide has no zipper noise, even when an LFO drives it. Morph only moves the knobs when it moves. Turn a knob by hand after a glide and it stays where you put it until Morph moves again. Undo works the same way: undoing a turn of Morph (or a change of From or To) puts the knobs back with it.
841.title: Morphing

842.body: By hand: turn Morph, or map it to a MIDI controller (right-click it, Learn MIDI ) and ride it. An LFO: a very slow sine with Bipolar off breathes between two scenes. At 0.03 Hz it takes 32 seconds to go there and back. The Arranger: patch a lane into Morph, and give each section a level. Jump switches scenes on the downbeat; Ramp glides over the section, for a build. An envelope: a long ADSR swells into a scene and back as a key is held.
842.title: Driving Morph

843.body: Mutate wanders the knobs at random. When it lands somewhere you like, press Ctrl + Shift + M to keep the knobs in the next free scene of the Scenes module that reaches the selection (the one in its group, else the patch's). Then set From to the scene you started at and To to the new one, and Morph finds everything between them.
843.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Scenes » Keeping a mutation
843.title: Keeping a mutation

844.body: The Breakdown recipe glides an acid line between a verse and a breakdown.
844.title: Patches

845.body: Keep a home scene. Store A before you start exploring, so you can always click your way back. Morph between near neighbours. Two scenes far apart sweep everything at once; two close ones make a subtle, living change. Several Scenes modules can share a patch: one inside each group, each with its own Morph, and one at the top for the whole song. Morph plays anywhere the patch does. The engine turns the knobs, so the render tool, the plugin with its window closed and a patch embedded in a web page all hear the glide. A patch opens and starts with its knobs where they were saved, and they follow once Morph moves.
845.title: Tips

846.body: Module ID util.midi_monitor · Category Utility MIDI Monitor module The newest event is at the top, colored by kind. The MIDI Monitor shows the MIDI arriving from your device as it happens. Use it when you connect new gear, when a note won't play, or to find out which CC number a knob on your controller sends before you map it. It has no ports and makes no sound. It listens to every device ticked in MIDI In on the toolbar (see Choosing a MIDI device ), so you can drop it anywhere in a patch without patching anything. To watch one device only, right-click it and choose it under Device .
846.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » MIDI Monitor » MIDI Monitor
846.title: MIDI Monitor

847.body: Control Options Default Description Ch (Channel) All / 1 – 16 All Shows only events on this MIDI channel Notes On / Off On Shows Note On and Note Off CC On / Off On Shows control changes: knobs, faders, pedals PB (Pitch Bend) On / Off On Shows pitch bend wheel movements
847.title: Controls

848.body: The log shows the most recent events, newest at the top. Each line starts with the time it arrived, in seconds since the first event the app received, then the event itself: Event Example Color Note On NoteOn Ch1 C4 vel=100 Green Note Off NoteOff Ch1 C4 Green Control change CC Ch1 #1 val=64 Orange Pitch bend PitchBend Ch1 2048 Purple Channel pressure Pressure Ch1 45 Gray Polyphonic pressure PolyPres Ch1 C4 45 Gray Program change Program Ch1 #5 Gray Note names put middle C (MIDI note 60) at C4. Pitch bend runs from −8192 to 8191, with 0 at the center. Pressure and program change can't be filtered out. The log holds the last few events and applies the filters to those, so turning a filter on hides lines rather than reaching further back. Notes played on the computer keys into a Note In module show up here too, marked Keys where a channel would be. While two or more devices are open and the Monitor hears any of them, each line ends with the name of the device it came from, shortened to ten letters.
848.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » MIDI Monitor » Reading the log
848.title: Reading the log

849.body: Is anything arriving? Play a note. If the log still says No MIDI events , the problem is upstream: check that the device is selected and connected in MIDI In , and that the controller is sending. Which channel? Play each device in turn and read the channel off the log. Then set Ch on your Note In modules to match, or leave them on Omni. Which CC? Move a knob on your controller and read its number after the #. You don't need the number for MIDI Learn , which listens for you, but it helps when a controller sends more than you expect. A stuck note? Look for a Note On without a matching Note Off. If the Note Off never arrives, the controller or its connection dropped it. Is velocity working? Play softly, then hard, and watch vel=. A controller that always sends the same number has fixed velocity switched on in its own settings.
849.title: Uses

85.body: Lessons are short tutorials that run inside Soba, and you learn by doing each step yourself. A caption sits beside the part of the patch it's about, and that part glows. A ghost pointer shows the move once, then the lesson waits until you've made it. When the patch shows you've done the step, it ticks and moves on to the next one. Shaping with a Filter, its third step: the ghost pointer shows a cable from the Oscillator's Out to the filter's In A lesson's caption and its ghost pointer, showing the cable to make. Open them from ❓ Help › 🎓 Lessons . Each lesson starts from its own patch, or from an empty canvas, so if the patch you have open has unsaved changes, Soba first asks whether to save them. The same menu's 🎬 Present… is for the other side of the desk: it plays a script over a patch one beat at a time, while you talk an audience through it. See Presenting .
85.title: Lessons

850.body: Note In – turns the notes into CV, one voice or chords, and covers MIDI Learn

851.body: Module ID output.audio · Category Output Audio Output Module The meter shows what reaches your speakers, and in orange, what the limiter caught. Audio Output is where a patch meets your speakers. Whatever arrives at its inputs goes through a short mastering chain (DC blocking, volume, optional saturation and a peak limiter) and on to your audio device. Every patch that makes sound needs one. If a patch has more than one Audio Output, only one of them is heard, so route everything to a single output.
851.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Audio Output » Audio Output
851.title: Audio Output

852.body: Port Signal Type Description Left Audio (Blue) Left speaker Right Audio (Blue) Right speaker Mono Audio (Blue) Sent equally to both speakers. The easiest way to hear a patch The module has no outputs.
852.title: Inputs

853.body: Control Range Default Description Vol (Volume) 0 – 100% 80% Master volume Limiter On / Off On Catches peaks before they can clip Character On / Off Off Rounds off peaks above -3 dBFS, for a little warmth. See Character or Tape?
853.title: Parameters

854.body: Mono is added to both channels, on top of anything patched into Left and Right . Left and Right stay separate: a cable into Left alone plays only in the left speaker. For a mono source, use Mono . For stereo, patch a module's left and right outputs (an Oscillator's Out L and Out R , or any effect's Out L and Out R ) into Left and Right . The inputs are audio inputs, so a polyphonic cable is summed to one channel on the way in. A whole polyphonic voice can go straight to the output.
854.title: Routing

855.body: The signal passes through these stages, in order: Mix. Left and Right, with Mono added to both. Any sample that isn't a valid number (NaN or infinity) is replaced by silence, so a misbehaving module can never send a burst of noise to your speakers. DC blocker. A 5 Hz high-pass removes any constant offset, such as a stray control signal or the lopsided output of an asymmetric distortion. It is far below anything you can hear. Volume. Character (when on). A soft clipper that leaves everything below about -3 dBFS untouched and rounds off peaks above it, never going past full scale. It adds a little warmth and density to loud material and none at all to quiet passages. Limiter (when on). A stereo-linked, look-ahead peak limiter with a ceiling of -0.3 dBFS. It sees each peak 1 ms before it arrives and turns the gain down just in time, so peaks are caught rather than clipped. It lets go quickly after a single transient and more slowly when it's working continuously, so it neither ducks audibly nor pumps. Linking the channels keeps the stereo image from shifting. The output never goes over the ceiling. The limiter's look-ahead delays the output by 1 ms. The delay stays in place when the limiter is off, so switching it doesn't shift the timing.
855.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Audio Output » The output stage
855.title: The output stage

856.body: Character and the Tape module both add warmth, but they do different jobs. Character works only on the peaks. It has no memory and no tone of its own: below -3 dBFS it does nothing, and above that it rounds every sample off on the same curve, whatever its pitch. Quiet passages pass through unchanged, and loud ones gain a little density and reach the limiter a little softer. It needs no setting up, and on a patch that never gets loud it changes nothing. Tape colours everything that passes through it, quiet or loud. You patch it in front of the output, and it has its own level calibration (0 VU is a sine at -18 dBFS RMS). The record head squashes the treble first, the head bump lifts the lows, the top end rolls off with speed and age, and wow, flutter and hiss make the sound move. Putting a patch on tape is a decision about how the whole patch sounds. The two work together. Tape colours the mix, Character rounds whatever peaks still reach the output, and the limiter holds the ceiling. Clair de Satellite and From One Sine use the whole chain.
856.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Audio Output » Character or Tape?
856.title: Character or Tape?

857.body: The node shows a stereo peak meter, one bar per channel, scaled from -48 to +6 dBFS. The bar is the level you hear, after the limiter. It runs blue through the body of the signal and warms to amber near full scale. A faint orange extension beyond the bar appears while the limiter is working. It reaches as far as the patch drove into it: the longer the extension, the harder the limiter is working. A thin tick marks the ceiling: -0.3 dBFS with the limiter on, 0 dBFS with it off. A peak-hold mark stays at the highest recent level for a moment and then falls. The readout to the right shows the limiter's gain reduction, such as -2.4 dB . It reads off when the limiter is switched off. With the limiter off, anything over 0 dBFS shows in red . Those peaks will clip your audio device. Hover the meter for exact levels: what's going out, what's going into the limiter, and how much it's reducing.
857.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Audio Output » The meter
857.title: The meter

858.body: The limiter is a safety net, not a volume knob. A few decibels of reduction on the loudest peaks is inaudible. Constant reduction of 6 dB or more squashes the patch and dulls its transients. If the orange extension is always showing, turn something down earlier in the chain (the VCA's Level , the Mixer's levels, or an effect's output) rather than leaning on the limiter. Remember that voices add up. A four-note polyphonic chord is about four times as loud as one note. Turn Limiter off when you want to hear exactly what the patch produces, for example while checking how an effect behaves at full scale. Keep Vol low while you do.
858.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Audio Output » Setting levels
858.title: Setting levels

86.body: Take them in order. Each one builds on the one before, and the five together cover what Your First Patch explains on paper. Lesson What you do In the browser 1. First Sound Add an oscillator and an output, patch them together, and change the wave. Start 2. Shaping with a Filter Carve a bright saw with a lowpass filter, then hold Alt over a cable to hear what it carries. Start 3. Envelopes Give a tone that never stops a shape in time, from a pluck to a swell. Start 4. Your First Sequence A Clock and a Step Sequencer play a bass line, and you write the tune. Start 5. Groups Fold four modules into one, go inside the group, and come back out. Start

If the meter moves but you hear nothing, check your audio device and system volume. Sound in one speaker only. A cable into Left or Right plays on that side alone. 865.body: Module ID output.link · Category Output Link Out plays Seoul , a music visualizer, from your patch. Seoul already hears Soba through your speakers, but from the sound alone it can only guess what the patch means. Link Out tells it: whatever you patch into its eight CV lanes and four Gates goes to Seoul with the patch's Clock, and Seoul's presets read them as cv1 to cv8 and gate1 to gate4. The cables decide what the picture follows. The LFO that sweeps your filter can sweep Seoul's zoom too, the kick's trigger can flash it, and a preset that turns on the beat turns on your Clock's beat exactly, not one Seoul has guessed at. Link Out makes no sound and changes none. It works in the desktop app. In the browser it shows what it would send but sends nothing.
865.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Link Out » Link Out
865.title: Link Out

866.body: Port Signal Type Description CV 1 … CV 8 Control (Orange) Sent to Seoul as /soba/cv/1 … /soba/cv/8, as they are: 0 to 1, or -1 to 1. An empty lane sends 0 Gate 1 … Gate 4 Gate (Green) Sent to Seoul as /soba/gate/1 … /soba/gate/4. Every rising edge gets there, however short the trigger Every input is optional. The module has no outputs.
866.title: Inputs

867.body: Control Range Default Description Port 9137 – 9140 9137 The port Seoul listens on. 9137 unless Seoul's seoul.toml names another
867.title: Parameters

868.body: The lamp and port , top left. Green and breathing while Link Out is sending and Seoul is listening. Amber, with no Seoul , while nothing listens on that port: start Seoul, or pick the port its seoul.toml names. The tempo , top right: the Clock's BPM, or no Clock . Eight columns , one per CV lane, filling up from the middle line for a positive value and down for a negative one. A lane with no cable is an empty slot. Four lamps for the gates, lit while a gate is high and flashing on each rising edge, so even a 1 ms trigger shows. The beat in the bar , bottom right, as the Clock draws it.
868.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Link Out » The display
868.title: The display

869.body: The Clock. Link Out sends the patch's tempo and its place in the bar, from the first Clock , with no cable needed. While the patch plays, Seoul locks to it: every preset that moves on the beat moves on this one, and Seoul's tempo reads exact. Stop the Clock and Seoul goes back to finding the beat by ear. A patch without a Clock still sends its lanes and gates. Gates as edges. Seoul counts a gate's rising edges, so a trigger is never lost between two of its frames. Link Out sends every edge it sees, even a trigger that rises and falls between two sends, and a gate that falls and rises again between sends is sent low and then high, so both count. Seoul's side. The values travel as OSC to 127.0.0.1 on the chosen port, about 200 times a second. Nothing leaves your computer. Seoul's docs/LINK.md has the whole protocol, so anything that speaks OSC can listen in, and its [link] delay_ms setting lines the picture up with the sound you hear. More than one. Two Link Outs on the same port share it: each sends the lanes it has cables in. On different ports they play two copies of Seoul. Latency. Seoul gets the lanes within a few milliseconds, sooner than it hears the sound, which goes the long way round through your audio device. Set Seoul's delay_ms by ear until a gate's flash lands with the kick.
869.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Link Out » How it works
869.title: How it works

87.body: Do it your way. A step checks the patch, not how you got there. A cable dragged from either end counts. So does a module added from the right-click menu or from the Space palette, and a knob turned by dragging or by a cable. If you do a step before the lesson asks for it, the lesson ticks it off as soon as it gets there. 👁 Show me plays the ghost pointer's move again. Lost the part? At the start of a step, the view pans to bring the part it's about into sight. After that, the view is yours to move. Leave at any time. Click × on the caption. The lesson goes, and the patch stays exactly as you left it: an ordinary, unsaved patch to keep playing or to save. Opening another patch or example also ends the lesson. When you're done, the caption offers the next lesson.
87.title: Taking a lesson

870.body: Seoul's link-aware presets agree on what each lane does, so a patch wired this way plays all of them: Lane Plays Gate 1 the kick Gate 2 the snare Gate 3 the hats Gate 4 a downbeat, or any accent CV 1 energy: a brighter, busier picture CV 2 color CV 3 motion A gate takes over from the drum Seoul hears only once it has played, and the CV lanes only add to what a preset does, so leave any lane empty and the preset follows the music there instead. Han River, Jongno Rain, Hongsalmun, Window Within and Cheonggyecheon Lanterns follow the convention, and Gayageum and Obangsaek give each lane a part of their own.
870.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » Link Out » One patch, many presets
870.title: One patch, many presets

871.body: A preset should look good without Soba. Seoul's link presets blend between what they hear and what Link Out sends, so a lane with no cable falls back to the music. Unipolar for brightness, bipolar for motion. An LFO with Bipolar off gives 0 to 1, which suits a colour's weight or a glow. Bipolar suits a swing either way, such as a pan or a tilt. Envelopes make good lanes. A Slope or ADSR on the kick's gate sends a swell that rises and falls with each hit. Mark the bar. A Clock Divider at 16 on a 1/16 Clock gives a gate on every downbeat, and its Count is a ramp through the bar. See Pinwheel for a patch built for the link.
871.title: Tips

872.body: Module ID output.midi · Category Output MIDI Out plays other instruments from your patch: a hardware synth, a drum machine, or a soft synth in a DAW. A Gate and a Pitch cable become notes, a poly cable becomes chords, a Bend and a Pressure cable become pitch bend and aftertouch, and four control cables become CCs, each a plain CC, a fine 14-bit one or an NRPN. A Program , with its bank, picks the sound the device plays. Turn on a port's Clock in the Rig and the patch's Clock goes out on it too, so the gear on that port follows Soba's tempo, starts when it starts and stops when it stops. Patch a Step Sequencer into it and the sequencer plays your synth. Patch a Chord Sequencer and it plays chords. MIDI Out makes no sound of its own. It works in the desktop app, and in the browser in Chrome, Edge and Firefox once you've clicked 🎹 Connect MIDI (in the device menu on its face, or the toolbar's MIDI In). Safari has no MIDI.
872.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » MIDI Out » MIDI Out
872.title: MIDI Out

873.body: Port Signal Type Description Pitch Control (Orange), poly V/Oct, 0 = C4 (note 60), rounded to the nearest note. Read as each gate rises Gate Gate (Green), poly A note starts as a channel's gate rises and ends as it falls Velocity Control (Orange), poly How hard each note is struck, 0 to 1 (1 to 127). 0.8 with no cable Bend Control (Orange) -1 to 1, full throw down to full throw up, sent as Pitch Bend wherever it moves. Unplug it and the bend springs back to the middle Pressure Control (Orange), poly 0 to 1, sent as aftertouch wherever it moves. A one-channel cable sends Channel Pressure; a poly cable sends each note its own (Poly Pressure), from its voice's channel CC 1 … CC 4 Control (Orange) 0 to 1, sent on the lane's CC number (0 to 127), or finer in 14-bit or NRPN mode, wherever the value moves Send Program Gate (Green) Sends the Bank and Program again as it rises: at the top of a song, say, so the device is on the right sound however it was left Every input is optional. The module has no outputs.

874.body: Control Range Default Description Port A – H A Which device plays. Each port's device is a setting of this computer, not of the patch (see below) Ch 1 – 16 1 The MIDI channel the notes and CCs go out on CC 1 … CC 4 0 – 127 1, 74, 71, 10 The controller number each lane sends. The defaults are the mod wheel, cutoff, resonance and pan, which most synths answer to Bend (Bend Range) Off, 1 – 24 st Off How far a full bend goes. Off leaves the device's own range alone, for gear that sets it on its panel Prog (Program) Off, 0 – 127 Off The Program Change to send, as the number goes out. Many manuals count programs from 1: their program 1 is 0 here Bank (Bank MSB) Off, 0 – 127 Off The Bank Select MSB (CC 0) sent before the program LSB (Bank LSB) Off, 0 – 127 Off The Bank Select LSB (CC 32) sent before the program Each lane's mode , and its NRPN, are in the right-click menu of its bar on the face (see CC lanes ).

875.body: The lamp and device , top left. Green while notes are going out, and it flashes with each one. Amber while the port has no device, or its device is unplugged. Red when the device won't open, usually because another app has it. Click the device's name to choose another. The channel , top right, and before it the program ( P4 ), if one is chosen. It glows as the program goes out. Two wheels , at the left, as on a keyboard: the bend, from the middle, and the pressure, from the bottom. Hover them for the values. A keyboard of five octaves, C2 to C7, with every note the module is holding lit, so a chord shows its shape. A note beyond either end lights the arrow at that end. Four bars , one per CC lane, showing the value last sent, with what the lane sends beneath: CC 74 , CC 1+33 for a 14-bit pair, NRPN 1:20 . A lane with no cable is an empty slot. Right-click a bar to change its mode. The clock , bottom right: four beat lamps that take turns while the port sends clock. The word clock under them is dim while the port's clock is off. An amber ring round the lamp while the port's budget is full and its CCs are thinning.
875.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » MIDI Out » The display
875.title: The display

876.body: A patch doesn't name a device. It names a port , A to H, and this computer remembers which device each port plays. Choose port A's device once and every MIDI Out on port A plays it, in this patch and the next. Share the patch and it plays whatever synth is on port A on the other computer. So it travels without either of you editing it. Click the device's name on the face to choose. The list shows every MIDI output this computer has, and it updates as you plug devices in. In the browser the menu offers 🎹 Connect MIDI first, until you've allowed it. A port's device stays chosen while it's unplugged and plays again once it's back, even if the system has renumbered it (2- Digitakt is now 3- Digitakt). To see all eight ports at once, open the Rig (Ctrl + Shift + H, or The Rig… in the MIDI In menu). It shows each port's device, its clock and offset, how the port is doing, and the last message it sent. It lists the MIDI inputs too, and its Thru routes pass an input straight to a port with no MIDI Out at all: a keyboard playing a synth through Soba, with no cables in the patch. On Windows only one app can open a MIDI port at a time. If the lamp is red, close whatever else has the device (a DAW, or the maker's editor app), and MIDI Out tries again within a couple of seconds. To play a DAW on the same computer, use a virtual MIDI port such as loopMIDI : MIDI Out plays the port, and the DAW listens to it.
876.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » MIDI Out » Ports, not devices
876.title: Ports, not devices

877.body: In time with the sound. Notes don't go out when the patch works them out. They go out when the audio beside them reaches your speakers, which is your audio device's delay later. So a hardware synth and Soba's own sounds play together, and each note is on time to within a millisecond or two. The browser can't promise to send at a given millisecond, so there Soba hands each message over up to a tenth of a second early, with the moment it's due, and the browser sends it then. Chords. Each channel of a poly cable is a voice. A Chord Sequencer's four-voice cable plays four-note chords, every note starting and ending with its own channel's gate. A one-channel Gate with a poly Pitch strikes the whole chord together. Two voices on the same note keep it sounding until the last of them lets go. No stuck notes. Notes end cleanly: when the Clock stops, even mid-chord. A gate still held stays quiet until it rises again; when you delete the module or open another patch, and when the audio stops. Soba lets go of every note the module was holding, springs its bend back to the middle, and sends All Notes Off on its channel, unless another MIDI Out plays the same port and channel. Then that one's notes keep sounding; when you change the channel, the port or the port's device, on the one the notes started on. Clock belongs to the port. Each port's Clock , in the Rig, says what it sends of the patch's Clock, with no cable and no module needed: Clock + Transport : Start when the Clock starts from the top (after a count-in, on the first downbeat), 24 ticks a beat placed on the beat to the sample, Stop when the Clock stops, and Continue when it plays on, after a Song Position telling the other gear where. Most gear picks up from the next sixteenth; Clock only : the ticks alone. The gear follows the tempo but starts and stops on its own, as a looper whose loops you start by foot wants; Off : none of it. The port sends it once, however many MIDI Outs play it, and a port no MIDI Out plays sends it too: a drum machine needs only its port's clock to follow Soba. Turn a port to Clock + Transport while the song plays and its gear comes in on the next sixteenth. A patch with no Clock sends no clock. See Tempo and Sync . CC lanes. Each lane sends its cable wherever it moves within a block, up to a thousand times a second, so an LFO sweeps a synth's filter as smoothly as the synth can follow. Right-click a lane's bar for its mode: 7-bit : one CC, 0 to 127. What most gear listens for. 14-bit : two CCs, the lane's number and the one 32 above it (CC 1 and 33, say), coarse half first, for 16,384 steps. MIDI pairs the controllers 0 to 31 this way, so a lane set above 31 sends 31 and 63, and its menu says so. NRPN : a Non-Registered Parameter, for settings a device has no CC for. Set its number in the menu as the device's manual lists it, MSB and LSB ( NRPN 1:20 is number 148). Each value goes as CC 99 and 98, which choose the parameter, then Data Entry, CC 6 and 38, with 14 bits of value. Gear that reads only 7 bits of an NRPN takes the coarse half. Busy ports. A USB device takes everything Soba sends. A 5-pin DIN cable carries only about a thousand messages a second, and four fast LFOs into CCs ask for four thousand. Give a port a Budget in the Rig ( DIN · 1000/s ) and it keeps to it: notes, programs and clock always go the moment they're due, and the CC lanes, bend and pressure share what's left. While the port is full, each sends only its newest value and skips one the device already has. Each lane ends where its cable did, and the notes stay in time. SysEx sent to the port keeps to the budget too, whole message by whole message (see Sending SysEx ). Sounds and programs. Set Prog and the module sends the Program Change as it starts and whenever you change it. With Bank or LSB set, the Bank Select goes first, MSB then LSB, as most gear wants. Some gear only takes a bank with a program, so the bank alone sends nothing. Bank and program numbers are in each device's manual. A program sends the Bend Range again after it, in case the new sound brought its own. Like a port's device, its clock is a setting of this computer. A patch saved when MIDI Out had its own Send Clock switch turns that port's clock on as it opens, if it was off, and the load notes say so. Offset. Every device takes its own time to turn MIDI into sound. A port's Offset , in the Rig, sends its notes, CCs and clock that many milliseconds later than the sound beside them, up to 50, to line a quick device up with a slow one. A negative offset sends them earlier, but only by as much as your audio device's delay, since a message can't leave before its sound is made. The Rig shows an offset it can't reach in amber. With the device's audio coming back into an input, the Rig can measure its delay and set the offset for you.
877.breadcrumbs: Module Overview » MIDI Out » How it works
877.title: How it works

878.body: One synth per channel. Two MIDI Outs on the same port, on channels 1 and 2, play two parts on a multitimbral synth or two tracks in a DAW. Line the room up. Measure each device from the Rig (the ping beside its port's Offset ), or play a Soba hi-hat beside its arpeggio and nudge the Offset until they land together. Every MIDI Out on the port moves with it. Wheels from your keyboard. A Controls slot hearing your controller's bend, patched into Bend , plays the hardware's bend from your keys. Another on its pressure, into Pressure , plays aftertouch. The right sound at the top. Patch a gate that rises at the top of the song into Send Program , so a device that was left on another sound starts the song on the right one. Velocity from anywhere. A Step Sequencer's second row, an LFO or a Sample & Hold on Velocity gives a part its accents. CCs for movement. An LFO with Bipolar off on CC 2 sweeps the synth's own filter. An ADSR on the same gate opens it with each note. Bipolar sources go below 0, which sends 0. Use an Attenuverter to lift them into 0 to 1.
878.title: Tips

879.body: Soba can be the brain of a room of hardware. It keeps the time, plays the synths and drum machines, turns their knobs from cables, and changes their patterns and scenes as the song moves on. It also remembers each device's sound in the patch, so a volca that forgets everything when you switch it off gets its sound back when the patch opens. This page goes through it in the order you'd set a room up. Each step links to the page with the details. The The Rig example does all of it in one song.
879.title: Playing Hardware

88.body: soba --lesson first-sound starts a lesson as Soba opens, and in the browser, so does ?lesson=first-sound on the end of the address. The name is the lesson's file in the lessons folder of the source, without its .txt.
88.title: From the command line

880.body: Plug each device into the computer, over USB or through a MIDI interface. Then open the Rig (Ctrl+Shift+H, or MIDI In ▸ The Rig… ), which lists every MIDI device Soba can hear or play. Out ports A to H. Choose a device for each port. Modules play ports, not devices: a node set to port B plays whatever device is on B. Lend the patch to a friend and they choose their own devices for its ports. Which device is on each port belongs to this computer, not the patch. Names that survive a reboot. Windows renumbers devices that share a name (2- Digitakt). Soba finds each port's device again by its name without the number. A budget for 5-pin DIN. A DIN cable carries about a thousand messages a second. Set a port that plays through a MIDI interface to DIN · 1000/s , and Soba paces what it sends so a sweep of CCs never chokes the notes. MIDI In. Open every input you want to hear. They can all be open at once, and each event knows which device it came from. See The Rig for every column of the panel.
880.breadcrumbs: Hardware Overview » 1. Plug in and name the ports
880.title: 1. Plug in and name the ports

881.body: One clock leads, and everything else follows it. Soba leads. Set a port's Clock to Clock + Transport , and its device follows the patch's Clock : 24 ticks a beat, with Start, Stop and Song Position. Clock only sends the tempo, for gear that starts and stops by itself. A device leads. Set the Clock's Source to MIDI , and choose the device under Device in the Clock's right-click menu. Either. Set Source to Auto . Soba leads until a device starts playing, then follows it, and when the device stops Soba carries on from the beat it had reached. See Leading or following . Offsets. Each device takes its own time to make a sound. A port's Offset sends its notes and clock that much later, or earlier, so a slow synth lands with the rest. With the device's audio coming back into your interface, Soba can measure the delay for you. Tempo and Sync explains how Soba keeps every tick on its sample.
881.title: 2. Keep time

882.body: To play Use Any device, with notes, CCs by number, bend, pressure and program changes MIDI Out A synth, with its own knobs by name, to turn and patch Instrument A drum machine's tracks or a sampler's pads, from a Trigger Sequencer Kit A volca fm's whole DX7 voice, bred by ear FM Voice An Instrument or a Kit reads its device's profile , which names its knobs and says which CCs they send. Soba comes with profiles for the Digitakt, the SP-404MKII, both RC-505s, the MicroFreak, the Polyend Tracker, the volca fm and volca drum, the FANTOM-06 and the ZOIA. You can add your own by turning a device's knobs while Soba listens. See Instrument Profiles . Three things make a device feel like part of the patch: The patch remembers its sound. Opening the patch sends every knob of every Instrument, and an FM Voice's voice, to its device. The knobs listen back. Turn the MicroFreak's real Cutoff and the node's Cutoff turns with it. Save the patch, and it keeps what you did by hand. See The hardware turns it too . Cables reach the hardware. Patch an LFO into an Instrument's Cutoff and the real filter sweeps, up to a thousand times a second.
882.title: 3. Play it

883.body: An Arranger knows when the verse ends. A Setlist passes that on to the room. Each section can move the Digitakt to another pattern, the FANTOM to another scene, the RC-505 to another memory. A row can go a little ahead of the bar line, for gear that queues its next pattern, so every device changes on the downbeat. The Arranger's lanes can press buttons too. A lane's gate into a MIDI Out's CC jack presses whatever that CC is assigned to on the device, such as the RC-505's Rec/Play.
883.breadcrumbs: Hardware Overview » 4. Change it with the song
883.title: 4. Change it with the song

884.body: With every device plugged into the computer, the computer is your patch bay. In the Rig's Thru , a route passes what one MIDI In plays straight to one port, past the patch. Play the MicroFreak from the FANTOM's keys, or drive the volcas from the Tracker, while the patch does something else. A route can pass only some kinds of message, and move them to another channel. See The Rig .
884.title: 5. Wire the room

885.body: Mutate on hardware. Select an Instrument and press Ctrl + M: its knobs move a small random step, and the device follows. Each press is one undo step. See Exploring its sounds . Scenes on hardware. A Scenes module morphs an Instrument's knobs as it does any others, so one fader can carry a synth from one sound to another. Breeding voices. An FM Voice mutates and crosses DX7 voices, and keeps the ones you like in a garden the size of the volca's memory.
885.title: 6. Explore

886.body: Most rooms mix the hardware somewhere else, on a desk or a mixer. If you do bring it back into Soba, an Audio Input can take any channel of a multichannel interface ( Every input of a mixer ), so each device can have its own.
886.breadcrumbs: Hardware Overview » 7. Hear it come back
886.title: 7. Hear it come back

888.body: To MIDI, every synth is just numbers: "CC 74 on channel 3". A profile puts a device's numbers into its own words. It names the device, says which CC is its Cutoff, says what each value of its oscillator type means, which note plays its kick, and how its programs are numbered ("A05", "Scene 12"). It also says whether the device keeps time with MIDI clock. Profiles are what the Instrument , Kit and Setlist modules read. A profile on its own sends nothing: it describes the device for the modules that do.
888.title: Instrument Profiles
