89.body:
A lesson is a text file in lessons/. Each line says something, points at something, shows a move or waits for one, and each wait closes a step: title First Sound
about An oscillator, an output and one cable: a sound from nothing say Drag from the Oscillator's **Out** jack to the Audio Output's **Mono** jack.
point osc.sine out:Out
point output.audio in:Mono
show drag osc.sine out:Out to output.audio in:Mono
wait connect osc.sine Out -> output.audio Mono Parts are named the way capture scripts name them. Steps can wait for a module, a cable, a knob's value, the transport, notes played or a cable probed. The whole format is described at the top of src/app/lesson.rs, and the tests check every shipped lesson against the modules it names.
89.title: Writing a lesson

890.body: Your own profiles go in Documents/Soba/Instruments , one JSON file each. Soba reads the folder when it starts, and again each time you open an Instrument's list of profiles. If one of yours has the same name as a shipped profile (in any case), yours replaces it. That's how you'd add the parameters the shipped one leaves out, or swap its first twelve knobs for the twelve you play most. A file that isn't a profile is skipped, and Soba tells you why. That covers a CC past 127, two parameters with the same name, and a kit with no parts.
890.title: Your own profiles

891.body: A device that sends its knobs as CCs can teach Soba its own profile. The Digitakt, the MicroFreak and many others do this. Open the device in MIDI In . Choose MIDI In ▸ Listen to an Instrument… . Give the profile a name. Turn each knob on the device, one at a time. Each knob shows up as a row the moment it moves, with its lamp glowing and a bar showing where it stands. Type its name into the row; the newest row takes your typing. Click Save Profile . Turn the knobs in the order you want them on the node, because the first twelve become an Instrument's knobs. A knob you don't name keeps its number ("CC 83"). A knob you moved by mistake can be dropped with its ✕. A knob that sends on a different channel from the rest keeps its own, as the Digitakt's delay and reverb do on its FX channel.
891.breadcrumbs: Instrument Profiles » Listening to an instrument
891.title: Listening to an instrument

892.body:
A profile is a small JSON file, like a patch: { "name": "MicroFreak", "maker": "Arturia", "port": "MicroFreak", "kind": "synth", "channels": [1], "voices": { "paraphonic": 4 }, "parameters": [ { "name": "Cutoff", "cc": 23, "group": "Filter" }, { "name": "Mode", "cc": 80, "values": ["Mono", "Poly"] }, { "name": "Fine", "cc": 1, "lsb": 33, "mutate": false }, { "name": "Deep", "nrpn": 1234, "range": [0, 100] }, { "name": "Delay", "cc": 85, "channel": 9 }, { "name": "Nudge", "cc": 74, "relative": true } ], "parts": [{ "name": "Kick", "note": 36, "channel": 10 }], "buttons": [{ "name": "Rec", "cc": 80, "mode": "momentary" }], "programs": { "what": "Pattern", "style": "lettered", "letters": "ABCDEFGH", "per_bank": 16 }, "clock": { "sends": true, "receives": true, "transport": true }, "notes": "Turn on Receive CC in the device's MIDI settings."
} port : part of the name the device's MIDI port shows up as. Soba uses it to suggest the profile for that port. kind : synth is one instrument played with notes. kit is a drum machine, sampler or groovebox whose parts each have a note, a channel, or both. parameters : one per CC, in the order an Instrument's knobs take them. Each is one of three kinds: a CC ("cc"), a 14-bit pair ("cc" plus "lsb"), an NRPN ("nrpn"). A parameter can also have: range : the values it takes, when they aren't all of them. values : for a stepped parameter, its steps. Plain labels share the range evenly, and each is sent from the middle of its share, so the device lands on the right step however it divides the range. A step written as { "label": "Poly", "value": 64 } sends exactly that value. curve : "log", for times and frequencies. default : where it starts. mutate : false keeps Mutate away from a volume or a tuning. channel : its own channel, 1-16, when it isn't the device's or a part's. The Digitakt's delay and reverb are on its FX channel, and the SP-404MKII's effects choose their bus by channel. relative : true when the CC nudges the device's value instead of setting it, as the FANTOM-06's Cutoff does. The middle of the range (64) is no change, and the knob shows an offset: +12, −5. group (Oscillator, Sample, Voice, Filter, Envelope, LFO, Arp, FX, Amp, Mix, Global) colours the knob after the matching module category: oscillators blue, filters teal, envelopes and LFOs orange, effects cyan, and the rest grey. cc_per_part : each part takes the same CCs on its own channel, a track a channel. buttons : CCs a gate presses (momentary) or flips (toggle), with their on and off values (127 and 0 unless given). programs : what program changes choose and how the device numbers them. The style is either numbered (from first, with count) or lettered, like the Digitakt's A01 to H16. It can also give a channel, and banks reached by Bank Select (msb, lsb). A lettered device whose banks are chosen by channel instead, as the SP-404MKII's are, says "bank_by_channel": true: bank A is on the programs' channel, B on the next, and so on. clock : whether the device sends MIDI clock, follows it, and starts and stops with it.
892.title: The format

894.body: In Settings > MIDI Config > Port Config turn Receive CC/NRPN and Receive Notes on. Tracks 1-8 are on their default channels 1-8 (notes 0-7 trigger tracks 1-8 only then). The Delay and Reverb parameters go to the FX Control channel, not a track's: set FX Control Ch to 9 in Settings > MIDI Config > Channels (the manual gives no factory setting). The compressor and the external-in mixer (also in B.7) are left out, because the manual doesn't say which channel they listen on.

9.body: Download soba-windows-setup.exe and run it. It installs Soba for you alone, in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Soba, without asking for an administrator. It adds Soba to the Start Menu, and you can remove it from Settings → Apps → Installed apps , like any other app. For playing live, download soba-windows-asio-setup.exe , the low-latency build, instead. It runs exactly like the standard one, and can also use an audio interface's ASIO driver: see Build with ASIO for what that gives you, and skip the building. Installing either one replaces the other. The first time, Windows may show "Windows protected your PC" : the downloads aren't signed yet. Click More info , then Run anyway . If you'd rather not install anything, the zips (soba-windows.zip and soba-windows-asio.zip) hold the same app as one file. Unzip it anywhere and run soba.exe.
9.title: Windows

90.body: Presentation mode is for talking over Soba while it plays: a video, a class, or a talk in front of a room. You write the script ahead of time and split it into beats . Each beat is a few moments of the patch moving: the camera turns to a module, a knob sweeps, a note plays. On stage you press one key, a clicker or a footswitch, and the next beat plays while you talk. What to say is in a notes window of its own, so a screen recorder filming Soba's window doesn't pick it up. Each run is also kept as a take , a capture script that films the run again frame by frame, in time with what you said. So you can rehearse it live as many times as you like and film the run you liked exactly.
90.title: Presenting

900.body: Pad notes and channel are MIDI mode A, bank A on channel 1: pads 1-4 are notes 48-51 (the bottom row is 13-16, notes 36-39), and bank B..J are channels 2..10 with the same notes (the chart's note-map layout); set the MIDI mode in UTILITY > SYSTEM > MIDI. In MIDI mode B the notes run across banks instead (12-91). The chart's default channel entry is ambiguous. The FX CCs choose their bus by channel (1-4 are buses 1-4, 5 is Input FX); FX Number picks the effect by number (see the manual's effect list, p. 251). The DJ CCs work in DJ mode, the buttons in Looper mode. Program changes 0-15 pick a pattern, and the channel picks its bank (PC 15 on channel 4 is D16). Chart does not list a Bank Select.
900.breadcrumbs: Instrument Profiles » SP-404MKII » Before you play

92.body: Key What it does Page Down or → Plays the next beat. If one is still playing, it finishes first. Shift + Page Down or → Finishes the beat on show now: knobs and the camera get to where they were going. Page Up or ← Plays the beat on show again from its start. Pressed within a second of a beat starting, it goes back to the beat before. Escape Stops presenting. The patch stays as the beats left it. A presentation clicker sends Page Down and Page Up, so it works without any set-up. The keys work from the notes window too. They don't reach the beats while a knob's value field or a menu has the keyboard: the notes say so, and a click on the canvas gives the keys back. You can still turn knobs and move the view by hand between beats. A beat played again puts back the knobs, the view and the transport as they were when it first began.

926.body: The volca fm has a MIDI In only (no MIDI Out), and takes no Program Change. The manual does not state the factory MIDI channel (channel 1 is assumed): set it by holding MEMORY while powering on and pressing keyboard button 1-16. Hold FUNC while powering on and set global parameter 7 'MIDI RX ShortMessage' to On (the factory default), or notes, CCs and pitch bend are ignored; clock, Start and Stop are followed only while parameter 6 'MIDI Clock Src' is Auto (the default). Transpose steps shown apply when 'TRANSPOSE NOTE' is On; with it Off, CC 40 gives octave-range transposition of -36 to +36 semitones instead. Modulator/Carrier Attack and Decay run -63 to +63 around the voice's own setting (64 is no change). Korg's hex and decimal columns disagree in a few of the step tables, so Soba sends each step from the middle of its band, inside it whichever column is right.

930.body: Factory default is split-channel mode: Part 1-6 on MIDI channels 1-6, any note triggers the part (sounds do not map to note numbers) and the CCs are per part on its channel. Set the global parameter MIDI RX ShortMessage to On (the factory default) or the CCs are ignored. Clock, Start, Stop and Continue are received only when MIDI Clock Src is Auto (the factory default); nothing is transmitted. Single-channel mode (chosen by setting a MIDI channel with REC held while powering on; all six parts on that one channel) uses other CC numbers per part: Part 1 Select 14, Level 15, Mod Amt 16, Mod Rate 17, Pitch 18, EG Attack 19, EG Release 20, Send 103, Pan 109, each acting on both layers; the later parts continue in blocks (Part 2 from 23, Send 104, Pan 110, up to Part 6 at 89-100, Send 108, Pan 114), and the waveguide stays on 116-119. No Program Change is documented. The chart marks Program Change as received, and the Owner's Manual keeps 16 programs on the step buttons; which program change picks which isn't stated, so program change 0 is taken as program 1.

94.body:
A script is a text file. It starts with a title and any footswitches, then the beats. Each beat has the lines to say and the cues to play, timed in seconds from the moment the beat starts: title The Filter That Sings
advance cc 64 # a footswitch on CC 64 plays the next beat beat Cutoff
say A lowpass filter keeps the lows and takes the highs away.
say **Cutoff** is where it starts cutting. Bring it down, and the buzz goes dark.
0 look frame:Tone 0.8
0 cursor on
0 move filter.svf knob:Cutoff 0.6
0.6 note 36 80 5.0
1.0 param filter.svf Cutoff 260 3.6 beat Resonance
say Now **resonance**. It pushes back right at the cutoff, so that one spot rings.
1.0 param filter.svf Resonance 0.85 3.4
auto 6 title names the presentation in the notes and the status bar. window <width>x<height> sizes Soba's window as presenting starts, in points, so what you see live is what the film shows. A film at --size 1920x1080 --ppp 1.5 is window 1280x720. If the window can't be that size, the status bar says so at the first press, and the take notes the size it was and how to film it. beat <name> starts a beat. A beat with no name is called by its number. say is a paragraph for the notes. Use one say line per paragraph. A beat with nothing to say is fine: the notes then tell you to let it play. auto <seconds> moves on to the next beat by itself that long after this one starts, without a press. Use it for a cold open that runs straight into the first explanation. # starts a comment. The cues are the ones a capture script uses, so anything Soba can be filmed doing, a beat can do live. These are the ones a presentation uses most: Cue What it does look filter.svf 0.8 Glides the camera to frame a module, as F frames a selection, over 0.8 s. look osc.sine 1.4 2.0 Centres a module at zoom 1.4, over 2 s. The canvas zooms in as far as 5×. look close util.vca 0.8 Frames a module as close as it fits, so its knobs and displays fill the screen. Use it to show one control up close. A frame works too: look close frame:Tone. look frame:Tone 0.8 Frames a frame, by its title. param filter.svf Cutoff 260 3.6 Turns a knob to a value over 3.6 s. Frequencies and times glide evenly in octaves. note 36 80 5.0 Plays a MIDI note into Note In: note number, velocity, length in seconds. chord 48,55,60 70 3.0 Plays several notes at once. play / stop Starts or stops the transport. Soba opens with it stopped, so the first beat usually starts with 0 play. cursor on Draws a pointer over the picture. Real mouse moves don't show up in a take, so this is how a viewer sees where to look. move filter.svf knob:Resonance 0.6 Glides that pointer to part of a module (a knob, a jack, a button), wherever the module is drawn. move off takes it away. enter Bells / leave Dives into a group, or back out. A module is named by its kind, like filter.svf, and filter.svf#2 is the second one. The full list of cues and of the parts a move can aim at is at the top of src/app/capture.rs in the source. A beat can't use the cues that only make sense while recording: still, layout, input and end. If the script has a mistake, Soba won't start it, and the message names the line.

947.body: A saw wave through a lowpass filter, with one envelope shaping its brightness and another its volume. Every note opens bright and settles darker as you hold it. This is the architecture behind most classic monosynths, and the patch to learn first: once you understand it, most other patches are variations on it. Load it: choose 📚 Examples → Basic Subtractive in the toolbar. Press ▶ Play , then play the Z to M keys. The patch file is patches/basic-subtractive.json . Or play it here: press ▶ Play in the corner. The full app is a click away under Open in Soba . Two envelopes from one gate: one for the filter, one for the VCA.

948.body: Subtractive synthesis. Start with a waveform rich in harmonics and take some away with a filter. Separate envelopes for tone and volume. Brightness and loudness can move on different schedules. Filter CV in octaves. The envelope opens the filter by a musical interval, not a number of hertz.

95.body:
A USB footswitch or any MIDI controller can step the beats. Name its CC before the first beat: advance cc 64 # the next beat
back cc 65 2 # the beat again, or the one before: CC 65 on channel 2 only
finish cc 66 # finish the beat on show A footswitch counts as pressed when its value goes from below 64 to 64 or above. CC 64 is what a sustain pedal sends, so a sustain pedal plugged into a MIDI keyboard makes a good one. While you present, Soba keeps these CCs away from everything else, so the patch doesn't hear the pedal as sustain, and no mapping or MIDI thru route does either.

950.title: How it's built

951.body:
[Note In Pitch] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct]
[Oscillator Out] ──> [SVF Filter In]
[SVF Filter LowPass] ──> [VCA In]
[VCA Out] ──> [Audio Output Mono] The saw wave contains every harmonic, so it's the richest raw material for a filter. The SVF's lowpass output keeps what's below the cutoff. At 700 Hz with a little resonance, the tone is warm, with a slight edge at the cutoff.
951.breadcrumbs: Basic Subtractive Synth » The audio path
951.title: The audio path

952.body:
[Note In Gate] ──> [ADSR (filter) Gate] ──> [ADSR (amp) Gate]
[ADSR (filter) Out] ──> [SVF Filter Cutoff]
[ADSR (amp) Out] ──> [VCA CV] One output can feed any number of inputs, so Note In's gate starts both envelopes at once. The amp envelope shapes the volume through the VCA. It rises in 5 ms, which is quick but not a click, falls to 70% over 200 ms, and fades out over 300 ms after you let go. The filter envelope shapes the brightness. The SVF's Cutoff input works in octaves, and its CV Amt is at 1, so +1 doubles the cutoff. As the envelope jumps to its peak of 1.0, the filter opens one octave above the knob, to 1.4 kHz. Over the next 300 ms it settles to its 30% sustain, about 860 Hz. That fall in brightness, faster than the fall in volume, is what makes each note sound plucked rather than switched on.
952.breadcrumbs: Basic Subtractive Synth » Two envelopes from one gate
952.title: Two envelopes from one gate

953.body: Fatter bass. Replace the SVF with a Ladder Filter and use its LP24 output. Turn Oct on Note In down to −1, set the Ladder's Drive to about 2x, and lower its Cutoff to 300 Hz. Acid squelch. Raise Res to 70% and lower Cutoff to 400 Hz. The filter envelope now sweeps a sharp resonant peak across each note. Pluck. Set the amp envelope's Sus to 0% and Dec to 400 ms, so every note dies away even while held. Supersaw. On the Oscillator, set Voices to 7 and Detune to about 40%. Seven detuned saws through the same filter make a wide, shimmering lead. More sweep. Turn the filter's CV Amt up to open it by more than an octave: 2 takes the peak to 2.8 kHz, 3 to 5.6 kHz. Lower Cutoff as you go, so the notes still settle dark. Space. Add a Stereo Delay and a Reverb between the VCA and the Audio Output.
953.title: Variations

954.body: Your First Patch – build a similar voice step by step FM Synthesis – a different way to make harmonics
954.title: Related

955.body: One sine wave bends the pitch of another, hundreds of times a second, and a bell comes out: bright and clangorous when struck, fading to a pure tone as it rings. There's no filter in this patch. All the harmonics come from frequency modulation, and an envelope on the modulator's level decides how many there are. Load it: choose 📚 Examples → FM Synthesis in the toolbar. Press ▶ Play , then play the Z to M keys. The patch file is patches/fm-synthesis.json . Or play it here: press ▶ Play in the corner. The full app is a click away under Open in Soba . A modulator and a carrier, each with its own VCA and envelope.
955.title: FM Synthesis

956.body: Carrier and modulator. The carrier is the oscillator you hear. The modulator is an oscillator you don't hear directly: it wobbles the carrier's pitch so fast that the wobble becomes tone color. Ratio sets the character. Whole-number pitch ratios between the two sound harmonic. Other ratios sound like bells and metal. Index sets the brightness. The more the modulator moves the carrier, the more harmonics appear. An envelope on the index makes the tone evolve.
956.title: What it teaches

957.body: Module Settings Note In Source Keys, Voices 1, Key Vel 100% Oscillator (modulator) Wave Sine, Semi +6 VCA (modulator) Defaults ADSR Envelope (modulator) Atk 1 ms, Dec 500 ms, Sus 10%, Rel 500 ms Oscillator (carrier) Wave Sine, FM 2.5 VCA (carrier) Level 42% ADSR Envelope (carrier) Atk 1 ms, Dec 2 s, Sus 0%, Rel 1 s Audio Output Vol 80%
957.title: Modules

959.body: [Note In Pitch] ──> [Oscillator (modulator) V/Oct] ──> [Oscillator (carrier) V/Oct] Both oscillators follow the keyboard, so the ratio between them stays the same on every note and the timbre stays the same up and down the keyboard. The modulator's Semi is +6, a tritone above the carrier. That's a frequency ratio of √2 : 1, about 1.41. No whole-number ratio is that close, so the harmonics it creates don't line up with the carrier's harmonic series. The result sounds like a bell, not a string.
959.breadcrumbs: FM Synthesis » Two oscillators, one keyboard
959.title: Two oscillators, one keyboard

96.body: Every run is kept as a take. A take is a capture script: each cue the beats played, timed from your first press, with the lines you said written in as comments. It begins two seconds before the first press, setting the view, the transport and any knob you'd turned by hand, so it starts from where you did. To keep a take, either start with --take, which writes it when you stop presenting: soba patches/basic-subtractive.json --present presentations/ep4-filters.txt --take ep4-take.txt or click Save take… in the notes at any point. A take keeps the script's cues, not your hands. A knob you turn or a view you move by hand during a beat isn't in it, so anything the film needs to show belongs in the script. A beat you played again replaces the first try: the take holds still where you went back, which is where the editor cuts your retake of the narration. The take says so in a comment under that beat (# Played again: the film holds still from 1:10.2…). A take is text: it records no sound or picture. The picture and the patch's sound come from filming it, and your voice from your own recorder.
96.title: Takes

960.body:
[Oscillator (modulator) Out] ──> [VCA (modulator) In]
[ADSR (modulator) Out] ──> [VCA (modulator) CV]
[VCA (modulator) Out] ──> [Oscillator (carrier) FM]
[Note In Gate] ──> [ADSR (modulator) Gate] The carrier's FM input is through-zero linear FM: it multiplies the carrier's pitch by 1 + FM × input. With FM at 2.5 and the modulator at full level, the carrier's frequency swings well past zero and back on every cycle. That's what produces the glassy, crowded spectrum of a struck bell. The FM knob has no CV input, so the patch controls the depth from the other side, by turning the modulator down. The modulator's VCA, driven by its envelope, does that: the modulation is at full depth for the strike, then decays over 500 ms to 10%. As it falls, the harmonics fall away, and the bell's clang mellows into a near-pure tone.
960.breadcrumbs: FM Synthesis » The modulator, through a VCA
960.title: The modulator, through a VCA

961.body:
[Oscillator (carrier) Out] ──> [VCA (carrier) In]
[ADSR (carrier) Out] ──> [VCA (carrier) CV]
[VCA (carrier) Out] ──> [Audio Output Mono]
[Note In Gate] ──> [ADSR (carrier) Gate] The carrier's envelope is a bell's: an instant strike and a 2-second decay to silence, with a 1-second release if you let go early. Because the modulator's envelope is shorter, the tone gets purer as it gets quieter, the way real bells and struck metal behave.
961.breadcrumbs: FM Synthesis » The carrier, through a VCA
961.title: The carrier, through a VCA

962.body: Harmonic tones. Set the modulator's Semi to +12 (a 2:1 ratio) or +19 (3:1). The harmonics now line up with the note, giving organ-like and reedy tones in place of bells. Electric piano. Set the modulator's Semi to 0 (1:1), lower the carrier's FM to about 1.5, and shorten the modulator envelope's Dec to 150 ms. The bright attack becomes a short "tine" over a mellow body. Gong. Lengthen the carrier envelope's Dec to 8 s and the modulator's to 3 s. Try Oct −1 on Note In. Shimmer. Add a few cents of Fine to the modulator. The ratio drifts off true, and the spectrum slowly beats and turns. Brighter or darker. Turn the carrier's FM up toward 5 for a harsher, more metallic strike, or down toward 1 for a gentler one. Space. Bells want a room. Put a Reverb between the carrier VCA and the Audio Output.
962.title: Variations

964.body: A wide, slow-blooming pad for holding chords. Each note fades in over most of a second, a filter breathes open and closed over ten seconds, the notes of a chord fan out across the stereo field, and chorus and reverb fill the space between them. This is the polyphonic example: every note you hold gets its own oscillator, filter, envelope and VCA. Load it: choose 📚 Examples → Lush Pad in the toolbar. Press ▶ Play , then hold chords on a MIDI keyboard or on the Z to M keys. The patch file is patches/lush-pad.json . Or play it here: press ▶ Play in the corner. The full app is a click away under Open in Soba . The bundled cables carry one strand per voice.
964.title: Lush Pad

965.body: Polyphony. One chain of modules plays every note of a chord, each as its own voice. See Polyphony . Unison. Several detuned copies of one oscillator make a single note sound wide and alive. Mono and poly together. A mono LFO moves every voice at once, and the effects at the end hear all the voices as one stereo pair. Spreading voices. The Mixer gives each voice of the chord its own place between the speakers.
965.title: What it teaches

966.body: Module Settings Note In Defaults: 8 voices, Rotate Oscillator Wave Saw, Voices 5, Detune 30%, Spread 60% SVF Filter Cutoff 2.5 kHz, Res 15% LFO Rate 0.1 Hz, Wave Sine, Bipolar on ADSR Envelope Atk 800 ms, Dec 500 ms, Sus 80%, Rel 2 s VCA Level 50% Mixer Width 1 80%, Master +3 dB Chorus Rate 0.5 Hz, Depth 40%, Delay 10 ms, Voices 2, Mix 50% Reverb Size 70%, Decay 4 s, Damp 40%, PreD 50 ms, Mix 50% Audio Output Vol 80%
966.title: Modules

968.body:
[Note In Pitch] ──> [Oscillator V/Oct]
[Note In Gate] ──> [ADSR Gate]
[Note In Velocity] ──> [ADSR Velocity] Note In gives each held note a channel of its own, and these three cables carry all eight channels. The Oscillator and the ADSR are polyphonic, so they run one copy per channel: a four-note chord is four oscillators and four envelopes, each starting and releasing with its own key. Velocity reaches each note's envelope, so softer notes bloom quieter.
968.breadcrumbs: Lush Pad » Voices from Note In
968.title: Voices from Note In

969.body: The Oscillator stacks five saw waves per note with Voices 5, detuned 30% apart. They drift in and out of phase with each other, which gives each note its slow, chorused movement before any effect is added. Only the mono Out is used here. The stereo width comes later, from the Mixer, the chorus and the reverb. Five unison voices on each of eight notes is forty saws. If the patch strains your CPU, turn Note In's Voices down, or the Oscillator's.
969.breadcrumbs: Lush Pad » One note, five saws
969.title: One note, five saws

97.body: This is how a video gets made with it: Write the script against the patch, one beat per idea, each ending on something to listen to. Rehearse live. Give the script a window line the shape of the film (tall for a Short, wide for a video), because the camera frames modules to fit the window and the take keeps that view. Play the beats, rewrite them and go again until the pacing feels right. Fix the script between runs and present it again: there's no need to restart Soba. Record the take. Present with --take, and record two tracks as you go: your mic, and Soba's own sound (desktop or loopback audio). OBS in audio-only mode does it, as do Reaper and Audacity. Wear headphones, so the mic doesn't hear the patch. Play a beat again if you fluff a line. Film the take. A capture films it with the patch's sound, frame by frame, so nothing stutters however busy the patch is: soba patches/basic-subtractive.json --capture ep4-take.txt --out target/showcase/ep4 --size 1080x1920 --fps 30 Line up the voice. The film's zero is your first press. take_sync.py finds it in your recording by matching the film's sound against the Soba track, and writes your voice from that moment on, ready to put at 0:00 under the film: python tools/showcase/take_sync.py target/showcase/ep4 narration.mkv --track 1 --voice-track 0 --out voice.wav It also says whether the recorder's clock drifted from Soba's, and stretches the voice to match if it did. Cut it. take_markers.py lists each beat where it starts in the film and every retake to cut. With --edl it writes them as markers DaVinci Resolve imports, and with --script it prints the presentation's sections as YouTube chapters: python tools/showcase/take_markers.py ep4-take.txt --script presentations/ep4-filters.txt --edl markers.edl Cut picture and patch sound together, where the patch holds still, and never inside a moment of listening. Encode it. python tools/showcase/encode.py ep4 ep4.mp4 --lufs -14 makes a clip of the film alone, at the loudness video sites play at. With narration, mix and export from your editor at −14 LUFS instead, with the patch about 10–12 dB under your voice while you talk. A take plays its cues against the patch as it stands, so if you change the patch or the script, present it again for a new take.
97.title: From rehearsal to film

970.body:
[Oscillator Out] ──> [SVF Filter In]
[LFO Out] ──> [SVF Filter Cutoff] The LFO takes ten seconds per cycle. The filter's Cutoff input works in octaves, so the bipolar LFO swings the cutoff an octave either side of 2.5 kHz, from 1.25 kHz to 5 kHz and back. The LFO is a mono cable into a polyphonic filter, so every voice's filter moves together, and the whole chord brightens and darkens as one.
970.breadcrumbs: Lush Pad » A filter that breathes
970.title: A filter that breathes

971.body:
[SVF Filter LowPass] ──> [VCA In]
[ADSR Out] ──> [VCA CV] The 800 ms attack makes each note swell in rather than start, and the 2-second release lets chords overlap as you change them. Rotate allocation helps here: a released note keeps ringing on its own voice while the next chord takes fresh ones. The VCA's Level sits at 50%. Voices add up, so a full chord is several times louder than one note, and the headroom keeps chords out of the limiter.
971.breadcrumbs: Lush Pad » The envelope and the VCA
971.title: The envelope and the VCA

972.body:
[VCA Out] ──> [Mixer Ch 1]
[Mixer Out L] ──> [Chorus In L]
[Mixer Out R] ──> [Chorus In R] The Mixer hears each voice of the polyphonic cable on its own. With Width 1 at 80% it fans them out across the stereo field. Note In hands each new note the next voice, and neighbouring voices sit on opposite sides, so the notes of a chord alternate left and right. Hold a chord and watch the lights on the Mixer's panorama open out. Panning costs a centred sound 3 dB on each side, so the Mixer's Master sits at +3 dB to win it back. The pad is as loud as it would be summed to mono, only wider.
972.title: Spreading the chord

973.body:
[Chorus Out L] ──> [Reverb In L]
[Chorus Out R] ──> [Reverb In R]
[Reverb Out L] ──> [Audio Output Left]
[Reverb Out R] ──> [Audio Output Right] The Chorus and the Reverb aren't polyphonic: they hear the chord as one stereo pair. The Chorus modulates its two sides differently, which blurs the edges between the voices, and the Reverb's long, modulated tail does the rest.
973.title: Effects

974.body: Brighter or darker. Turn the filter's Cutoff up for a glassier pad or down to 800 Hz for a warm, distant one. The LFO keeps sweeping an octave either side of wherever you set it. Supersaw. Set the Oscillator to Voices 7 and Detune 40%. Strings. Shorten Atk to 300 ms and Rel to 1 s, and set the reverb's Decay to 2 s. Swell. Lengthen Atk to 3 s. Hold a chord and let it rise. Each voice its own. Replace the LFO's cable into the filter's Cutoff with Note In's Velocity . The filter is polyphonic, so each note's filter opens by up to an octave according to its own velocity, and harder notes come out brighter. Cheaper. Set the Oscillator's Voices to 1 and add more chorus Depth . It's thinner, but costs a fifth of the CPU. Narrow or wide. Turn the Mixer's Width 1 down to 0% and the chord gathers in the middle, the way it sounded before it was spread. At 100% the outer voices sit hard left and right.
974.title: Variations

975.body: Polyphony – how polyphonic cables work Note In – voice allocation and the sustain pedal Oscillator – unison in detail

976.body: A bell you can play across the keyboard, made from one recorded note. The recording is a single strike of the FM Synthesis bell at middle C, rendered by Soba itself. A Sampler plays it back faster for higher keys and slower for lower ones, a voice for every key you hold, through a filter and a room. Load it: choose 📚 Examples → Sampled Keys in the toolbar. Press ▶ Play , then hold chords on a MIDI keyboard or on the Z to M keys. The patch file is patches/sampled-keys.json , and its sample is patches/samples/fm-bell-c4.wav . Or play it here: press ▶ Play in the corner. The full app is a click away under Open in Soba . Hold a chord and a white line runs along the waveform for each key, playing the recording at its own speed.
976.title: Sampled Keys

977.body: Sampling. A recording becomes an instrument. One note, played faster or slower, covers the whole keyboard. Pitch is speed. As on tape, an octave up plays twice as fast and lasts half as long. The bell rings shorter at the top of the keyboard and longer at the bottom, as real ones do. Polyphony from one module. The Sampler runs a voice for every channel of Note In's cables. Resampling with Soba itself. The bell was rendered from another example with the render tool, so the sample has no licence to worry about.
977.title: What it teaches

98.body: presentations/ep4-filters.txt in the source is the pilot for Synthesizer 101 with Soba , a video series that teaches how synthesizers make sound. It's a Short about the filter, presented over the Basic Subtractive example in six beats: The sound first. With nothing said, the camera frames the filter and its envelope, and a resonant filter sweeps through one low note. It moves on by itself. Every harmonic. The filter opens wide on the oscillator's saw wave, which has every harmonic in it. Cutoff. The pointer takes the Cutoff knob down, and the buzz goes dark. Resonance. Resonance comes up, and the cutoff starts to ring. It sings. The cutoff sweeps up through the note, and the ring picks out its harmonics one at a time. Play it. A short phrase, each note's envelope opening the filter. Open Basic Subtractive, choose Present… and pick the script. Then press Page Down for each beat: the first runs on into the second by itself.
98.title: A worked example

980.body:
[Note In Pitch] ──> [Sampler V/Oct]
[Note In Gate] ──> [Sampler Gate]
[Note In Velocity] ──> [Sampler Velocity] Note In gives each held key a channel of its own. The Sampler plays each channel as a separate voice, starting the recording from the top when that key goes down. Root is C4, the note the bell was struck at, so C4 plays the recording exactly as it is. D4 plays it 12% faster, and C5 twice as fast. Mode is Gated: letting go of a key lets its bell go over Rel , 700 ms. In One-Shot mode every strike would ring its full three seconds, however briefly you touched the key. Velocity sets each note's level as it starts, so a soft touch rings quietly.
980.breadcrumbs: Sampled Keys » Keys into the Sampler
980.title: Keys into the Sampler

981.body: The bell comes from the FM Synthesis example. Its Note In was swapped for a Clock to strike it once, held two seconds, and the render tool recorded it at 44.1 kHz. The result was trimmed to three seconds, peaked at -1 dBFS and saved as 16-bit mono. The Sampler resamples it to your device's rate when it loads. The patch names its sample by a path relative to itself, samples/fm-bell-c4.wav. Save the example somewhere and Save As copies the bell into a samples folder beside your copy.
981.title: The sample

982.body:
[Sampler L] ──> [SVF Filter In]
[SVF Filter LowPass] ──> [Reverb In L]
[Reverb Out L] ──> [Audio Output Left]
[Reverb Out R] ──> [Audio Output Right] Played above its root, the bell's top harmonics climb high, and past an octave or so they begin to alias. The filter at 5.2 kHz takes the edge off. It's polyphonic, a filter per voice. The Reverb hears the voices summed, and spreads its tail across both speakers.
982.title: Filter and room

983.body: A different instrument. Click Open… on the Sampler and load a recording of your own: a piano note, a sung "ah", a guitar chord. Set Root to the note it was recorded at. Music box. Set Tune to +12 and Rel to 2 s. Short, high, and ringing on. Endless bell. Set Loop to Ping-Pong, drag the loop markers over the steady part of the ring (about 30% to 60%), and set Rel to 3 s. Held keys now sustain like an organ. Tape warble. Patch a slow LFO (about 0.3 Hz) through an Attenuverter at 2% into the Sampler's Speed . The whole chord wavers in pitch, like a stretched tape. Reverse. Set Speed to −1. Each key plays the bell backwards, swelling up to the strike.

985.body: Your own instrument, layered by yourself. Plug in a guitar, a microphone or a keyboard's audio out, and a Looper records four bars of it on the downbeat, plays them back, and lets you play over them, layer on layer. A soft click keeps you in time, and the whole thing goes through tempo-synced echoes and a room. Load it: choose 📚 Examples → Live Looper in the toolbar. Pick your interface under Input in the toolbar, press ▶ Play , tap Rec on the Looper and play. The patch file is patches/live-looper.json . The Live Looper patch The patch as it opens. The Looper's ring is grey dashes: empty, waiting for Rec.

986.body: Building a piece in layers. Record a part, then play the next over it, as a solo looping player does. Takes on the beat. The Looper's Clock is once a bar, so takes start on the downbeat and close on a bar line. Latency, and taking it back. Live sound reaches the patch late. The Looper writes each layer back by the measured round trip, so layers sit where you played them. A click you can switch off. The metronome runs into the Mixer, where two mute buttons silence it once the loop is going.

987.body: Module Settings Audio Input Channel Stereo (choose 1 or 2 for a single instrument in one input) Clock BPM 90, Div 1/4, Gate 10% Clock Divider Div 4: once a bar Looper Bars 4, Auto latency on, FB 100% Stereo Delay Sync 1/8D, P-P and Tape on, FB 30%, Mix 20%, HiCut 6 kHz, LoCut 150 Hz Reverb Size 55%, Decay 2.2 s, PreD 15 ms, Mod 30%, Mix 22% Drum ×2 A Rim on every beat ( Decay 25%, Level 50%), a Cowbell on each bar ( Decay 15%, Level 35%) Mixer The click on channels 1 and 2 at 60%, the effects on Return L/R Audio Output Vol 80%

989.body:
[Audio Input L] ──> [Looper In L]
[Audio Input R] ──> [Looper In R] The Looper's Out carries what you play now and the loop together. Everything after it, echo and room, treats them as one performance.
989.breadcrumbs: Live Looper » You, into the Looper
989.title: You, into the Looper

99.body: Every jack in Soba has a signal type, and every type has a color. The color of a jack tells you what it sends or expects, and a cable takes the color of the output it comes from, so you can read a patch's signal flow at a glance. Type Color Range Carries Audio Blue −1.0 to 1.0 Sound Control Orange 0.0 to 1.0, or −1.0 to 1.0 Modulation and pitch (CV) Gate Green 0.0 or 1.0 Notes, clock pulses, triggers MIDI Purple Note and controller events Reserved; see MIDI Bus Pale steel A whole stereo mix and its sends A Mixer's Chain Out into the next Mixer's Chain In ; see Bus Underneath, audio, control and gate signals are all the same thing: a stream of numbers at the audio sample rate. The type describes what the numbers mean, and it decides which jacks a cable may connect (see Which types connect ).
99.title: Signal Types

990.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [Clock Divider Clock]
[Clock Divider Trig] ──> [Looper Clock] The Clock ticks quarter notes at 90 BPM. The Divider passes every fourth tick, the downbeat of each bar, to the Looper's Clock . A tap on Rec waits for the next downbeat, then records four Bars and closes the loop by itself: one tap to start, none to stop. A tap that lands up to 50 ms after a downbeat counts as on it. A bar is 2.67 s at 90 BPM, so four bars are 10.7 s. Change the Clock's BPM before you record, and the loop is four bars at the new tempo.
990.title: The bar clock

991.body: Once the loop is playing, tap Rec to overdub (the ring turns amber), play your next part, and tap Rec again when it's done. Each overdub pass lays a thin band inside the ring. Undo takes back the layer you just made, if it didn't work, and a second Undo brings it back. Stop silences the loop and Clear empties it to start over. Turn FB down before an overdub to let the older layers fade as the new one goes on, so a loop can change gradually rather than only pile up.
991.title: Layers

992.body: Your layers are part of the patch. Save it (an example has no file of its own, so Save asks where), and the loop goes into a <patch name> loops folder beside it. Open the patch tomorrow and the loop is there, stopped at the top: tap Rec to hear it and go on overdubbing from where you left off. What's kept is the loop as you hear it, so a layer you've undone stays out. See Keeping the loop .
992.title: Keeping your layers

993.body: The status bar's In figure is the round trip from the input jack to your speakers, typically 20 to 50 ms. You play along with the loop you hear, and what you play arrives that long after the moment you were playing to. Auto latency writes each overdub that much earlier, so a strum on beat one lands on beat one. If layers still feel a hair late (your converters add delay no timestamp reports), trim with Offset .
993.title: Latency

994.body:
[Clock Gate] ──> [Drum (Rim) Trig] ──> [Mixer Ch 1]
[Clock Divider Trig] ──> [Drum (Cowbell) Trig] ──> [Mixer Ch 2]
[Looper Out L/R] ──> [Stereo Delay In L/R] ──> [Reverb In L/R] ──> [Mixer Return L/R]
[Mixer Out L/R] ──> [Audio Output Left/Right] The click goes straight to the Mixer, never through the Looper, so it isn't recorded. Mute channels 1 and 2 when you no longer need it. The echo is a dotted eighth, ping-ponging, with tape wobble: it fills the space between a picked guitar's notes.
994.breadcrumbs: Live Looper » Click, echo and room
994.title: Click, echo and room

995.body: Learn a footswitch. Right-click Rec on the Looper, choose Learn MIDI , and press a MIDI pedal or hit a pad. Now your hands stay on the instrument. Octave down. Set Speed to ½× after recording a guitar part: it becomes a bass line, twice as long. Free time. Set Bars to Free and unpatch the Looper's Clock : the loop is exactly as long as you held it, for playing out of time. Effects on the loop only. Patch Loop L/R through a filter or the Distortion while Out carries you dry.
995.title: Things to try

996.body:
The render tool can play a recording into the Audio Input and press the footswitches from a cue script: # cues.txt: press Rec before the first downbeat; four bars record by themselves
0.5 param util.looper Pedal Rec 1
0.8 param util.looper Pedal Rec 0
14.0 param util.looper Pedal Rec 1 # overdub
14.3 param util.looper Pedal Rec 0 cargo run --release --bin render -- patches/live-looper.json out.wav --seconds 30 --input take.wav --cue cues.txt A copy saved with its loop renders that loop too: it opens stopped, so press Rec (or Stop ) in the cues to start it.
996.title: Rendering it offline

997.body: A patch that plays itself. A slow pentatonic melody repeats every twelve seconds, but its brightness shifts in threes against it, and a second voice wanders around it, never taking the same path twice. The tuning drifts, and long echoes and an eight-second reverb blur one phrase into the next. Press Play and leave it running. Load it: choose 📚 Examples → Generative Ambient in the toolbar and press ▶ Play . It needs no keyboard. The patch file is patches/generative-ambient.json . Or play it here: press ▶ Play in the corner. The full app is a click away under Open in Soba . Clock and sequencer play the melody, top left, with the Clock Divider under the Clock. Below, the LFO and Sample & Hold set the brightness, and Noise and the Quantizer sing the second voice.
997.title: Generative Ambient

998.body: Clock and sequencer. A clock sets the pace and a step sequencer turns each pulse into a note. Sample & hold. Freezing a moving signal at a pulse gives each group of notes its own setting, a step at a time. Cycles that don't line up. When loops of different lengths run against each other, the combination takes a very long time to repeat. That's where the brightness gets its variety. Chance, in key. A quantizer snaps a random voltage to the notes of a scale, so chance can write a melody without a wrong note.
998.title: What it teaches
